en: Preface to the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* with Collected Annotations,
composed by Shen Ying of Zhuzhai, Chamberlain for Court Deliberations and Acting Assistant Commissioner of the New Huaidong Pacification Commission.
Our Buddha appeared in this world for the sake of the one great cause and condition, preaching the Dharma in over three hundred assemblies to deliver sentient beings;

fundamentally, there was no duality in his intent. However, because the natures of sentient beings are distinguished as superior, middling, and inferior, the Buddha’s words exhibit differences in depth and shallowness.
Among the various sutras, works such as the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* and the *Awakening of Faith* were taught for those of the highest faculties; therefore, its...
The language is profound and far-reaching; only those of the highest faculties can comprehend it, while beginners find it difficult to fathom.

As for the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which takes Laṅkā as its name, true reality (*dharmatā*) as its essence, the Buddha’s mind-essence as its core principle, and self-realized noble wisdom as its function—its language is even more profound and far-reaching than that of the *Śūraṅgama* and *Awakening of Faith* sutras.
Therefore, among those of superior capacity spoken of today, none can compare with the Inner Secretary, Master Su Shang.

He remarked that the meaning and intent of the *Laṅkāvatāra* are profound and subtle, and its phrasing is concise and archaic; even readers cannot yet parse every sentence, let alone understand the meaning through its lost passages, or realize the mind by forgetting the meaning.
Thus, it has been desolate in the world, nearly extinct and barely surviving; how much more so for others?

In the poems by the Junior Tutor Bai Juyi (Bai Gong Lètiān) and Chan Master Cháng regarding this illness, he requested that the Master treat it by recommending only the reading of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
He further stated: "For this ailment in the human world, there is no medicine; there is only the four-fascicle *Laṅkā* scripture.
Lord Wang Jiefu of Jingzhou likewise said: "I have also seen a semblance of the *Laṅkā*. Thus, one knows that this scripture is for those of the highest capacity alone.

Those of superior faculties deeply cherish and investigate this [teaching], while others do not recognize it. Bodhidharma said to the Second Patriarch, "I have observed all the scriptures and teachings in China;
only the four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* can serve as the seal for the mind (*citta-mudrā*).

From patriarch to patriarch they have transmitted one another, taking the mind as the dharma of the mind. Thus we know that the seal for transmitting the mind does not exceed this sūtra, and it has its origins in antiquity."
Nowadays, those who discuss Chan are as numerous as the vast waters, yet they are utterly ignorant of this sutra;
it is not that they do not know of its existence, but rather because their insight is not lofty, they cannot deeply comprehend its meaning and intent, and thus they dare not open their mouths.
Furthermore, the Imperial Scribe Su remarked that scholars of recent times each follow their own master, striving for simplicity and convenience so as to obtain a single phrase or a single verse.
Believing themselves to have attained full realization, they cause even women and children to clap their hands in mirthful laughter as they vie to discuss the joy of Chan;

those of superior standing seek fame, while those of inferior standing seek profit, and thus the Buddha-Dharma has declined. Yet it is said that every sentence of this sutra contains principle and every character contains the Dharma, like the *Nan-king* (Difficult Classic) of medicine.
Now, when vulgar practitioners of medicine do not rely on the canonical treatises but teach directly [from hearsay], [they fall into error].
Using prescriptions and formulas to treat illnesses is not necessarily without occasional success;

however, when one encounters a disease and immediately responds with a diagnosis that accurately predicts life or death, this cannot be compared to those who merely know the classics or study antiquity.
When people see such singular achievements or instances of skill surpassing the ancients, they claim that the *Nan jing* can be mastered without study—how mistaken this is! This...
It is precisely for this reason that the ceremony is being held today. I respectfully reflect that the late Master Leian Shou was one who had both deeply studied and profoundly investigated;
possessing such authentic learning, he attained the realization of the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), which is not comparable to the superficial practitioners of Chan found these days.

While others cannot even manage to read the sentences of this scripture correctly, you, Master, have dared to set your will upon it and provide a commentary—this would not be possible without diligent and strenuous study.
Furthermore, this commentary is not like that of those who lecture today; it corrects the errors of previous scholars word by word and explains the full intent of the sutra sentence by sentence.
Its phrasing is neither obscure nor pedantic, and its meaning is clear and straightforward.
Even if Su Shi, the Imperial Scribe, were to be reborn and see it, he would surely rejoice and offer praise beyond measure—how much more so for others? Indeed, all...
For those who have found their way upon this path and observe it, they should grasp it with their hands and never let go.

Having seen this book, Shen Ying of Zhuzhai joined his palms in homage and universally exhorted the fourfold assembly to recite it with a sincere heart, examining its annotations and meanings so that the Buddha’s words might be as clearly resolved as ice melting away.
Within a single phrase, one may suddenly clarify the ground of realization; this is precisely the transmission of Bodhidharma.
The intent of this entrustment is right before our eyes; thus, that mass of eight loads of entangling vines may be set high upon a shelf.
Formerly, during the Qingli era, the Grand Guardian Lequan Zhang Gong Dao served as the Prefect of Chuzhou. Upon arriving at a monastery, he happened to see this scripture fall into his hands;
he was struck with a sudden realization, as if recovering an old possession. Before he had even finished opening the scroll, his long-standing karmic obstructions were cleared away like melting ice.
Examining the fine brushstrokes, the handwriting was vividly present; moved by both sorrow and joy, he sighed deeply and attained realization through this.
He constantly used the four verses at the beginning of the sutra to elucidate the essential point of the mind.

When Su Shi (Sū Neihan) visited Nandu, he personally witnessed the Master speak of this and entrusted him with three hundred thousand coins to have the sutra printed and distributed throughout the Jianghuai region, while Sū himself personally transcribed it.
The spiritual realization of the people of Yin has been clearly verified in this way.
Layman Jing’an, Huang Gong, the son of Layman Jingzhao Zhongwei and the grandson of Layman Miaode Jiefu, has transmitted this from heart to heart.
Having deeply understood the meaning and purport of this sutra, he has donated gold to carve it upon wooden blocks for wide circulation; this is also the intention of Layman Lequan.
As for the details of his commentaries, they are fully documented in the *Leian Ge Biji* (Notes from the Leian Pavilion), which need not be recounted here.

I shall merely place at the beginning of this work two matters commonly known to the world—those concerning Su Shi, the Imperial Secretary, and Zhang Shangying, the Grand Protector—to inspire the reader’s faith.
Furthermore, Leian also authored the thirty-volume *Pudeng* (Universal Lamp) and the *Lengyan Helun* (Combined Treatise on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra).

Luo Ji continues this work in the world—how magnificent! How magnificent! Preface to the Collected Annotations on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, written on the Dragon Boat Festival (Duanwu) of the second year of the Qingyuan era.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* taught by the Great Hero has undergone three translations in total. The four-fascicle version was translated during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty by Guṇabhadra from Central India.
The ten-fascicle version was translated during the Yanchang era of the Later Wei dynasty by Bodhiruci from Northern India.
As for the [twenty-fascicle version], it reached China during the Tang dynasty through the arrival of Śikṣānanda.
Xuanzang further considered that Guṇabhadra’s translation had not been widely disseminated and that Bodhiruci’s version contained many errors;

thus, together with Saṃghavarman and Fuli, he retranslated it in seven fascicles during the early years of the Jiushi era. Subsequently, various masters who categorized the teachings summarized its essential principles:
Li Tongxuan spoke of the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of non-self, while Yanzhou (Yanshou) [discussed] Yanji (Zhijue).

Thus, taking the *dharmatā* (real mark), the Buddha’s word, the mind-essence, and the noble self-realized wisdom as the primary discourse—on one hand, manifesting phenomena through principle, and on the other, inferring principle from phenomena—the profound meanings of the sutras will be fully exhausted once both principle and phenomenon are investigated together.
However, since the arrival of Bodhidharma in China, it has been held that these four fascicles of this sutra can serve as a seal for the mind; consequently, [the focus shifted].

He transmitted it to his disciple Huikě; those who have inherited this tradition have long practiced its teachings on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), yet its phrasing is so concise and rigorous that it has ultimately remained difficult to comprehend.

Consequently, the transmission of it became increasingly obscure until Zhang Wending Gong Fangping, while in Nanqiao, recognized it as a text written by his own previous incarnation. He then entrusted thirty thousand coins to Su Wenzhong.
Duke Su Shi personally transcribed this and recorded its origins for distribution throughout the Jianghuai region;

from then on, its circulation gradually spread. Master Chanshi Zhengshou of Leian found the phrasing difficult to comprehend and, together with his fellow practitioner Zhideng, consulted the version by Buddhabhadra while cross-referencing the translations of Wei and Tang dynasties, meticulously annotating their differences and similarities.

Below the scriptural text, I have again consulted the Tang dynasty commentary on the ancient edition, as well as the exegeses of the Song monk Baochen and the Fujian scholar Yang Yanguo, synthesizing their views to reach a definitive conclusion.
Furthermore, wherever the commentaries on the sutras and treatises, or the catalogs, touch upon this scripture, I have also extracted their essential insights and appended them here.
This work is titled *The Collected Commentaries on the Precious Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. It was completed in the third month of the year of Yimao (1205) of the Qingyuan era.
In the fourth month of the Bingchen year, it was finally completed; his dedication to this task can truly be called diligent.

Furthermore, when the Tathāgata preached the sūtras, he did not rely on words, yet he was not separate from words. How much more so for this *Laṅkāvatāra*, which truly expounds the perfect and sudden [teaching]:

the eight consciousnesses are transparently clear and are called the Tathāgatagarbha. Encompassing all, it is without exterior; entering minutely, it is without interior. Its original nature is entirely true, and thus it is perfected.
When the function of wisdom contemplates the true mark of the body, it is identical to that of Vimalakīrti.

If those of the Two Vehicles extinguish consciousness and seek quiescence, they are like a person who has lost their way and, forgetting their own head, runs about in a frenzy crying out while seeking another head elsewhere.

This is the Dharma-gate of the Buddhas' mind-ground, wherein one attains Buddhahood manifestly without relying on cultivation or realization; indeed, nothing is more essential than this for the essentials of the Chan school.

Alternatively, some may say that the school from the West does not establish a single word; yet if one claims that the First Patriarch held this as the seal of his mind, is this not either foolishness or delusion?
Do you not hear the words of Master Daguanying? He said: "It is not so. The Buddha-dharma adapts to the world to form its teachings.
At the time of Dharmatrāta, sentient beings were mired in appearances and alienated from the mind; therefore, those who studied the meaning [of the teachings]..."
To completely reject these [views] is the spirit of "Ultimate Observation" (Daguan), which is identical to the intent of Bodhidharma.

If one fails to examine the subtle expedients he employed to remedy defects and instead relies upon them as literal truth, then would not the practice of *dhyāna*—one of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and that which the World-Honored One pointed to as the foundation of ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)—be rendered obsolete? Leian’s commentary has indeed merited great credit.
Regarding the Chan school, this is a most profound matter that those without superior faculties or prior wisdom cannot understand; thus, I know my words will be deemed appropriate.

This sutra was previously carved into woodblocks but was recently destroyed by fire. Master Bai’an Jin of Tianjie Temple, desiring to circulate it widely, purchased materials for carving and re-engraved it at Zhantanlin.
He has now requested me to write a preface. When I was young, I [studied] quite extensively...

Seeing that Zhengping Zhang Jie’s collection combined the strengths of three translations and adopted the commentaries of various masters to form an eight-fascicle work for transmission—its general meaning being largely consistent with others—I regretted that Leian did not live to see it.
Baian Miaowu, having attained true insight into the Mahayana vehicle and possessing a broad mastery of Confucian classics, was revered as a patriarch by the monastic community;
had one sought out his explanations and incorporated them [into this work], then his merit would have been truly great.

Furthermore, how could this not be greater than Leian? In the fifth month of the summer of the fourth year of Hongwu, Song Lian of Jinhua, Director of the National Academy, composed this preface for the *Collected Annotations on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, reprinted under the Great Ming in the Xinsi year. This concludes the general principles of the work.
The Song Qinyuan edition of the *Lengqie jing* by Leian is the "old edition"; this reprinted version is the "new edition.
There have been three translations of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, and their exegeses are fully contained in the "Old Edition Notes" (*Gebi*) and the "Preface to the New Edition" (in four fascicles).
Among these, the Song translation is particularly prevalent; it is upon this that Leian’s annotated commentary is based.
Wherever the phrasing is concise yet the meaning is profound, I have appended the translations from the Wei and Tang dynasties beneath them;
if readers consult these for comparative study and integration, their obstructions will naturally be resolved.

However, there are passages that are not particularly difficult to understand yet are corroborated by a single translation; such cases have now been removed, though where it was appropriate to cite all versions, they remain.
I have now fully cited those that provide such critical analysis.

As for the various commentaries collected in the old edition, they include the version obtained by the eminent Tang-era master Zhou Yuánwēng from the ancient sutra repository at Mount Lúshān, as well as the new exegesis by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Bǎochén and the commentary by the man from Fúmiàn, Yáng... [text truncated].
Regarding the characters annotated in the works compiled by Yanguo, as well as in the *Zongjing lu* and other sutras and śāstras, those instances where the sutra, the śāstra,
or the person are not explicitly named are the descriptions of Leian. However, since the new commentary was composed based on the seven-fascicle Tang translation,
and because the Tang translation differs from the textual readings of the Song translation, [the following concerns] the sutra...
Does this not contradict what was previously stated? However, Minister Gong is of extensive learning and lofty insight;

his prose and reasoning are refined and lucid, and he has deeply grasped the essential purport of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*. His mastery of its structural脉络 (pulses/lineages) is such that there is nothing he cannot handle.

In this present edition, where the new interpretation is fully adopted, it is designated as "New Interpretation. As for those points where his explanation differs from the text of this sūtra, [they shall be noted].
To avoid the labor of composing rhetoric and following the literal meaning to conform to the scriptural text, new interpretations are not explicitly set forth.

Furthermore, in places where the commentary states "Yang says" or where new interpretations are integrated into the explanation, because these are not the assertions of a single school, [the author] does not explicitly label them as "Commentary says," "Yang says," or "New Interpretation says," but instead directly appends the phrase "it is said that... (*yún yún*) to the text.

Beneath the scriptural text, I humbly reflect that the intent behind the ancient commentaries was fundamentally to enable people to understand easily and enter [the path] well, thereby forgetting the literal meaning and realizing the mind.
When it is said "so-and-so says" or "so-and-so says," one should not initially compare them against one another.

In previous editions, whenever one or two characters in the scriptural text differed from other versions, it was noted that "the annotated edition reads such-and-such a character," or "the Yang edition and the Su edition read such-and-such a character. Now, I have selected only those readings that are superior in meaning and appropriate in principle;
all others have been omitted, so as to ensure that students are not led astray by manifold divergences.

In general, commentaries and sub-commentaries—whether divided by chapter or explained word-by-word—possess their own internal logic; however, to further fragment a single sentence is not entirely optimal.
Now, having carefully examined the old versions, I have in some cases merged them into one and in others differentiated them into sections.
For the most part, my main ideas are based on new interpretations rather than being mere products of my own imagination; although the precedents for these principles have not yet...
This [new] edition is entirely convenient for reading and recitation; it is hoped that the essential meaning of the scripture may thereby be attained.
Since the punctuation and phrasing of most scriptural teachings are generally not easily altered, how much more so in the case of this sutra?
Thus, Jiang Yingshu remarked that he had long suffered from the difficulty of reading the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, and Su Dongpo said that some readers were unable even to parse its sentences.
That I now immediately provide the punctuation and word-division is truly intended for the convenience of beginners; as for the errors that may occur in the interim, how could they be avoided?
Those of superior capacity who have attained full realization will certainly not be fettered by this.
As for the method of marking sections (*kezi*), which is found in Confucian texts, the current edition follows it entirely in its sectioning, whether preceding—

Regarding those cases where a character has already been marked with a phonetic transcription but is subsequently lost, one should later follow the precedent of the preceding instance and pronounce it accordingly.

As for instances where a certain Sanskrit character ought to be pronounced with a specific sound, if one who has frequently read Buddhist scriptures is already habituated to it through long practice of the oral and aural tradition, no further transcription mark need be added; such as *abhadra*, *āra*, *āṭa*, *parinirvāṇa*, and *prajñā*.
The two characters "jiětuō" (解脫), meaning *vimukti*, are not of Indic origin; they exist only within the Buddhist scriptures.

Therefore, this treatise does not discuss the phonology or semantics of "jiětuō" (with the first character pronounced as *huò* [upper tone] and the second as *huó* [lower tone]; both characters retain their original sounds).

There are two pronunciations and two meanings for these two characters, which are not recorded here in detail. How could one possibly list every instance of such terms? May the reader understand this.
This principle should be applied by analogy.
The Preface concludes here. *The Lankavatara Sutra*, Volume One.
Translated by the Indian Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Song Dynasty;
compiled with annotations by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhengshou of the Great Song Xu Tai.

*Lakṣaṇa* (Lengqie) here means "unapproachable" (*agantavya*); *anuttara* (A) means "unsurpassed"; *ratna* (Bavaduoluo) means "precious and honorable. Because this sutra encompasses and integrates these meanings, it is titled the *Unapproachable Unsurpassed Jewel Sutra*, referring to the ultimate state of self-realized noble wisdom.

Because the realm cannot be fabricated by erroneous wisdom, it is called "unapproachable" (*agocara*). Because it is like a *maṇi* jewel that manifests various colors, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*). This means that within this unapproachable place, there exists this unsurpassed treasure.

"Unapproachable" is a metaphor for the unsurpassed treasure, and it is also a metaphor [for the teaching itself]. This sutra establishes its title based on a single analogy. The *Avataṃsaka-śāstra* states: "The World-Honored One preached the Dharma at Laṅkāpurī on the summit of Mount Malaya in the Southern Sea.

That mountain is five hundred *yojanas* high; looking down upon the great ocean, there is no path by which to ascend. The city is composed of various jewels, its radiance outshining the sun and moon, and there is no gate through which to enter. Only those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are able to ascend and go there; this symbolizes the Dharma of the Mind-Ground."

Only those who have neither cultivation nor realization can ascend through this gate. Looking down upon the great ocean represents that the ocean of the mind is inherently clear and pure; yet, driven by the winds of external objects, the waves of consciousness arise accordingly. When the mind is empty and objects are stilled, these waves of consciousness will no longer stir.

Once the waves of consciousness have subsided, there is nothing that is not reflected, just as when the great ocean is windless, the sun, moon, stars, and other celestial forms appear with brilliant clarity. This sutra is taught for those whose faculties are mature, providing an immediate exposition of the seed-consciousness and karmic consciousness as the *tathāgatagarbha*.

It differs from the followers of the Two Vehicles who extinguish consciousness to pursue quiescence, and it also differs from those Bodhisattvas practicing Prajñā who emphasize the cultivation of emptiness. It directly clarifies that the fundamental nature of the substance of consciousness is entirely true, and thus constitutes [the realization].

The function of wisdom is not that [of the *Saṃdhinirmocana*], which establishes nine consciousnesses separately as a profound mystery to guide those of initial faculties, gradually causing them to retain afflictions (*kleśa*) so as to grow toward great bodhi; nor does it allow the mind to plant seeds in emptiness, nor does it allow the mind to be like a rotten seed.

The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* is the initial gateway for entering into afflictions; the *Laṅkāvatāra* and the *Vimalakīrti* directly reveal the fundamental reality of afflictions. The *Laṅkāvatāra* clarifies that the eight consciousnesses are the Tathāgata-garbha, while the *Vimalakīrti* contemplates the true mark of the body, and the contemplation of the Buddha is likewise so.

The *Vimalakīrti* and the *Laṅkāvatāra* are identical in depth, whereas the text of the *Saṃdhinirmocana* differs slightly from these two sections. One should know that regarding entry into the womb, exit from the womb, youth, old age, and even the means of subsistence and dwelling places—whether form or emptiness, whether nature or... [the text continues].
All marks are but one’s own consciousness; only a Buddha can know this—the general purport of this single sūtra is seen herein).
Chapter One: The Heart of the Speech of All Buddhas (*Sarvabuddhavākcittavarga*).

"The Heart of the Speech of All Buddhas" refers to the *svabhāva-paramārtha-citta* (the ultimate reality-nature) taught by all Buddhas of the three periods of time. "Chapter" (*varga*) means a category or a classification; because items of similar meaning are grouped together, it is called a chapter. "First" indicates that this is the first [chapter] of this sūtra.

The great compendium consists of one hundred thousand verses, one million phrases, and thirty-six thousand words, totaling one hundred and fifty-one chapters. What is currently transmitted contains only the "Chapter on the Heart of the Buddha’s Words," which is divided into four sections; hence it is called the "First."
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was dwelling on the peak of Mount Laṅkā by the shore of the southern ocean (according to Śikṣānanda’s translation:

the Bhagavān was dwelling on the peak of Mount Malaya within the city of Laṅkā by the great ocean; that city was occupied by the yakṣa king Rāvaṇa). It was after the Buddha had taught the Dharma for seven days in the palace of the Naga King of the Ocean and emerged from the great sea that immeasurable billions of assemblies—Brahmās, Śakras, world-protecting deities, nāgas, and others—came to welcome him.

At that time, the World-Honored One raised his eyes, beheld the city upon the mountain peak, and spoke these words: "In the past, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, likewise taught their own [realizations] within this very city."

"The realization of the Dharma through noble wisdom is not within the realm of the speculative false views of the non-Buddhists, nor is it the sphere of practice for the followers of the Two Vehicles. I shall now reveal this Dharma to King Rāvaṇa. At that time, by the Buddha's spiritual power, the Yakṣa King Rāvaṇa heard the sound of the Buddha’s voice;

he immediately set out with his retinue in a flower-palace toward the World-Honored One’s abode. He circumambulated the Buddha three times to the right, performed various musical offerings, and requested the Buddha to return to his city with verses, saying... [and so forth].

The general outline of the translation by Bodhiruci is similar, except that this sutra merely states that the Buddha dwelt on the peak of Mount Laṅkā on the shore of the southern sea, without mentioning a "city. This is likely because Buddhabhadra’s text was still concise and archaic; therefore, in the following passage:

Regarding the passage "The Heart of the Speech of All Buddhas" spoken for the great Bodhisattvas on Mount Malaya in the kingdom of Laṅkā, concerning the realm of the *ālayavijñāna*—the ocean-waves praised by the Tathāgata—it should be understood that the name of the mountain has been omitted in brief and the names of the city and mountain are conflated.

Nevertheless, as for the seven characters "Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha," all masters of past and present have categorized them according to the six perfections (*ṣaḍ-ākāra-sampad*) of faith, hearing, time, teacher, place, and assembly; they read the first four characters and the last three characters as two separate phrases.

According to the treatise of Nāgārjuna, when the World-Honored One was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, Aniruddha instructed Ānanda to ask the Buddha about four essential matters for the future. Following these instructions, Ānanda asked: "While the Tathāgata is in the world, he personally teaches the Dharma to people."

"All shall believe and accept [this]. After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, what words should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras? The World-Honored One replied: "One should place these six characters as a phrase: 'Thus have I heard at one time' (*evam mayā śrutam ekasmin samaye*). This is the first of the four questions.
Therefore, the two characters 'at one time' (*ekasmin samaye*) are joined with the preceding word 'thus' (*evam*), and the word 'Buddha' is appended to the following text.

Adorned with various precious flowers, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a multitude of great bodhisattvas—who came from various and diverse buddha-fields (the śrāvakas are mentioned first and the bodhisattvas later for the sake of conforming to worldly conventions)—[they all arrived].

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—headed by the Mahāmati Bodhisattva-mahāsattva—possess the power of mastery over immeasurable samādhis and sport with supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). All Buddhas personally bestow the consecration upon their crowns;
they are well-versed in the meaning of the objective realms manifested within their own minds, and they understand the various mentalities and forms of the diverse classes of sentient beings.

Through immeasurable gates of liberation, he universally manifests according to the capacities of beings, ultimately attaining thorough penetration of the five dharmas, the three natures, consciousness, and the two kinds of selflessness.

(The five dharmas are: name, appearance, conceptualization, correct wisdom, and suchness; the three natures are: conceptualization, dependent origination, and perfected nature; consciousness refers to the eight consciousnesses; and the two kinds of selflessness refer to the selflessness of persons and phenomena. Mazu said:

"The *Laṅkāvatāra* takes the Buddha’s words on the mind as its essence and 'no-gate' as its dharma-gate; that by which it is accomplished lies herein. Regarding the ultimate meaning, from the passage "and the great assembly of bhikṣus" onwards, the re-translation states: "All those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas..."

These Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have all thoroughly mastered the five dharmas, the three natures, the various consciousnesses, and selflessness; they well understand the meaning of objects as manifestations of one's own mind, sport in immeasurable sovereign samādhis, supernatural powers, and strengths, manifest various forms according to the minds of sentient beings to skillfully subdue them, and have all had their crowns consecrated by the hands of all Buddhas.
Having come from various Buddha-lands, these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, with the Bodhisattva Mahāmati as their leader, have gathered for this assembly.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati and the Bodhisattva Mati (Mati means "Wisdom") together traveled through all the Buddha-fields.
Empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, they rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground,
joined their palms in reverence, and praised the Buddha in verse.
The world is free from arising and ceasing, like flowers in the sky; though wisdom perceives neither existence nor non-existence, one gives rise to great compassion.
All phenomena are like illusions, far removed from mind and consciousness; though wisdom perceives neither existence nor non-existence, one gives rise to great compassion.
Far removed from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, the world is ever like a dream (*Iśvara says: "The world is ever like a dream, far removed from annihilationism and eternalism"*).
Wisdom does not apprehend existence or non-existence, yet it gives rise to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Knowing that persons and phenomena lack selfhood (*pudgala-nairātmya* and *dharma-nairātmya*), and understanding that afflictions (*kleśa*) and cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—[here, *jñeyāvaraṇa* is translated as "cognitive obstruction" following Paramārtha, while Xuanzang takes it as "obstruction to what is known," which is the wisdom-obstruction; *kleśa* is likewise an obstruction; *jñeya* is the Sanskrit for "what is known" and *āvaraṇa* is the Chinese "obstruction";

the two editions [of the text] read *yan* for *yáng*, henceforth similar cases follow]—are eternally pure and signless (*animitta*), it gives rise to the mind of great compassion. All things are *nirvāṇa*.

The "Gate of the Suchness of Mind" provides a comprehensive answer to the one hundred and eight propositions by stating that they are all "not so. As Maitreya (Aśvaghoṣa) said: "One should know that the self-nature of Suchness is not characterized by existence, not characterized by non-existence, not characterized by the negation of existence, not characterized by the negation of non-existence, not characterized by both existence and non-existence, not characterized by unity, not characterized by difference, not characterized by the negation of unity, not characterized by the negation of difference, and not characterized by both unity and difference. From the very beginning, because all defiled phenomena and all sentient beings possess a deluded mind that discriminates moment by moment, [Suchness] is in non-correspondence with them;

it is thus the true mind, eternally constant and unchanging, fully endowed with pure dharmas. Furthermore, it has no characteristics to be grasped, for its realm is free from thought and can only be realized through direct correspondence. Mahāmati, these one hundred...
"These eight phrases were spoken by the Buddhas of the past; you and all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice and study them. (The new commentary states:

This is an exhortation to all bodhisattvas and others that they should thus learn the bodhisattva path and cultivate the bodhisattva practices. The mention of the Buddhas of the past is intended to clarify and inspire sincere faith.)

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing are there for the various consciousnesses? The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"There are two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing for the various consciousnesses, which cannot be known through discursive thought (*cintā*). There are two kinds of arising for the various consciousnesses:

namely, arising as a continuous flow (*pravāha-utpāda*) and arising as manifestation (*nimitta-utpāda*). [Yang says: This refers to the arising of mental objects through conditions, like the flowing of water, and the perception of a single object...]"
[The arising] from all phenomenal characteristics has two kinds of abiding: the abiding of the continuous flow (*pravāha*) and the abiding of the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

There are also two kinds of cessation: the cessation of the continuous flow and the cessation of the characteristic. (The Ancient Commentary states: "The 'continuous flow' refers exclusively to the eighth consciousness; because its three phases—latent seeds, manifest activity, and uninterrupted continuity—are called the 'continuous flow,' and because it arises due to ignorance as the condition for the initial production of the active consciousness (*karmavijñāna*), it is termed 'arising.

Because it continues through long kalpas, it is termed 'abiding. Upon reaching the Vajra-like Samādhi, when the fundamental ignorance is severed in a single thought-moment, this is termed the 'cessation of the continuous flow. As for the arising, abiding, and cessation of the characteristics, these refer to the coarse and manifest mental objects of the remaining seven consciousnesses.")

Therefore, they are called "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*). Although seven [aspects] are distinguished based on conditions and eight based on objects, they are considered subtle when compared to the six; yet because they possess the four afflictions, they are also called coarse. Thus, based on that manifest consciousness, the various objects produced from their own seeds arise through the convergence of conditions—these seven are taught as the "arising of characteristics.

The habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) accumulated throughout kalpas is called the "abiding of characteristics. From the derivative toward the fundamental, through gradual subduing and severance until the fulfillment of the seventh stage, it is called the "extinction of characteristics. The three characteristics that are subtle and hidden are the characteristic of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of transformation (*pariṇāmalakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of manifestation (*pratibhāsalakṣaṇa*), as explained in the *Awakening of Faith*.

Mahāmati, the various consciousnesses have three kinds of characteristics: namely, the characteristic of transformation, the characteristic of karma, and the characteristic of reality (*tattvalakṣaṇa*). "Transformation" refers to the five consciousnesses encompassing the characteristics of the six consciousnesses; "karma" refers to the six consciousnesses encompassing... [the characteristics of the five].

Regarding the characteristics of the seven consciousnesses: if they are viewed from the perspective of the True [Nature], then the seven consciousnesses encompass the characteristics of the eighth consciousness. These three aspects constitute the pivot for the phenomena of arising, abiding, and ceasing, and serve as the medium for all consciousnesses;

they can only be clarified through wisdom and are therefore said to be "not known by discursive thought. Mahāmati, briefly stated there are three kinds of consciousness; extensively stated, there are eight aspects. What are the three?

They are the True Consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*), the Manifesting Consciousness (*khyāti-vijñāna*), and the Discriminating Consciousness of Objects (*vastu-vikalpa-vijñāna*). (According to the *Zongjing*, the "True" refers to Original Enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), the "Manifesting" refers to the eight consciousnesses, and the remaining seven are all considered the Discriminating Consciousness of Objects. Furthermore, it says: "The 'True' refers to Original Enlightenment, which is the eighth [consciousness].")

The nature of consciousness is clarified in the sūtras; by establishing the name of the "ninth consciousness" outside of the eight, it refers to the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*). If categorized according to its essential nature (*dharmatā*), it does not depart from the eight consciousnesses, because that nature pervades all places.

Master Yang also takes the true consciousness as the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (real aspect) and the manifesting consciousness as the eight consciousnesses, while the discriminative phenomenal consciousness is the six consciousnesses. Regarding the names and meanings, Vasubandhu’s *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya* presents two divergent interpretations between the Northern and Southern schools:

the Southern school regards the *ālayavijñāna* as the pure consciousness, whereas the Northern school regards the *ālayavijñāna* as ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus, the *Miaoxuan* states: "Now we clarify that the mind of ignorance is neither self-caused, nor other-caused, nor common, nor causeless; all four propositions are inconceivable. This concerns the refutation of conceptual attachments through one's own practice (*svayam-pratipatti*); here, [the Southern view] is not maintained.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* by Asaṅga also has two translations. That translated by Master Tandi of the Liang dynasty establishes nine consciousnesses, asserting that the eight consciousnesses give rise to all phenomena through the twelve links of dependent origination. The translation by Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty establishes only eight consciousnesses, maintaining that the ninth is merely another name for the eighth consciousness.

Thus, there are differences between the Liang and Tang versions, as well as distinctions between the Northern and Southern schools. The *Zongjing* further states: "This ālayavijñāna is the true mind (*tathatā-citta*). It does not maintain its own nature but follows along with defiled or pure conditions;

though it does not conjoin [with them], it conjoins [with them], and it is able to contain and store all mundane and supramundane objects. Therefore, it is called the 'store-consciousness' (*ālayavijñāna*). It is like a clear mirror which, though not conjoining with reflections, contains reflections. This is explained from the perspective of the meaning of 'conjunction. If, however, one considers the meaning of 'non-conjunction,' it is the essence itself."

Because it is eternally unchanging, it is termed *tathatā* (Suchness). Depending on whether it is conjoined with or separated from [defilements], two meanings are distinguished; yet fundamentally, it is the one true mind, serene and unmoving.

If there are those who do not believe in the *ālayavijñāna* as being identical to the *tathāgatagarbha*, and instead seek *tathatā* as a separate principle, they are like those who seek the mirror apart from its reflection—they possess false wisdom. This arises because they have not understood the meaning of "the unchanging following conditions" and "following conditions while remaining unchanging," thereby giving rise to dualistic attachments. What is discussed in the *Zongjing Lu* is profound, penetrating, and clear, and can certainly resolve the doubts of later generations.

However, the truly eternal and pure consciousness (*viśuddhavijñāna*) is in no way different from the "true consciousness" (*tathatāvijñāna*) of this sutra. It is simply that the proponents [of other schools] are unable to discern in detail that this consciousness is the very essence of the *ālaya*. Although it is divided [into various aspects], it possesses no separate essence. One must know that this sutra merely [stops at this point].

Within the eight characteristics, three types of consciousness are briefly explained; unlike other sutras which establish nine consciousnesses, these eight characteristics are also merely consciousness.
Mahāmati, just as a bright mirror holds all forms and images, so too does the manifesting consciousness (darśana-vijñāna) appear in its locus. (The *Zongjing lu* states:

"In this way, the seven consciousnesses arise in complete correspondence within the ālayavijñāna, just as various reflections appear simultaneously in a mirror. Mahāmati, there is the manifesting consciousness and the discriminating consciousness of phenomena (nirūpaṇa-vastu-vijñāna).

These two—the perishable and the imperishable characteristics—are mutually dependent causes. (Realśā states: "The manifest consciousness and the discriminating consciousness of objects—these two consciousnesses have no difference in their mutual causality.

[Commentary: This clarifies that the seventh and sixth consciousnesses, along with the fifth, possess the characteristics of arising and ceasing. Regarding the perishable and imperishable characteristics of the five consciousnesses: when the eye-consciousness and the others encounter an object for a single moment, they cease; this is called "perishable. The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of form then transfer into the sixth consciousness; this is called "imperishable. Regarding the perishable and imperishable characteristics of the seventh consciousness:

the seventh consciousness conditions the sixth consciousness to create good and evil karma, arising and ceasing from moment to moment; this is called "perishable. The karmic habitual tendencies rely upon the *tathāgatagarbha* to obtain future birth and death; this is called "imperishable. O Mahāmati, do not conceptualize this.

The perfuming of consciousness (*vijñāna-vāsanā*) and inconceivable transformation (*acintya-pariṇāma*) are the causes of the manifesting consciousness (*ādarśa-vijñāna*). (Xianshou says: This means that ignorance can perfume True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is a locus incapable of being perfumed;

because it can nevertheless perfume it, it is called "inconceivable perfuming. It means that the mind of True Suchness receives the perfuming of ignorance; because it undergoes transformation despite being immutable, it is called "inconceivable transformation.

Mahāmati, the grasping of various objects (*viṣaya*) and the perfuming of beginningless false conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa-vāsanā*) are the causes of the consciousness of discriminating phenomena (*nirvikalpa-vastu-vijñāna*). (Paramārtha says: The manifesting consciousness takes inconceivable perfuming and transformation as its cause; the consciousness of discriminating phenomena...)

"Mahāmati, when the various unrealities that obscure the true consciousness—caused by the discrimination of objective spheres and the habitual tendencies of beginningless conceptual proliferation—are extinguished, then all sense-faculties and their cognitions are extinguished;

this is called the extinction of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-nirodha*). (Yang says: 'To obscure' carries the sense of reversal; it means to turn the light back upon itself and reflect toward the true consciousness, whereby all faculties and objects vanish into the Dharma-realm.

As for all natures and characteristics, what more could one behold? Mahāmati, as for the extinction of the continuity [of existence] (*saṃtati-nirodha*): this means that once the false habitual tendencies of beginninglessness have been extinguished, then..."

All faculties, objects, consciousnesses, and characteristics are naturally extinguished while not being extinguished. When the cause of continuity is extinguished, continuity is extinguished; because continuity exists by depending on false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), when that cause is extinguished, continuity finds no further support.

When that from which [consciousness] proceeds and that which is its object are extinguished, continuity is extinguished; since both the consciousness from which it proceeds and the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) which are its conditions are extinguished, where then could continuity find support?
Why is this so, Mahāmati? Because these are its supports. By "supports" is meant that which has been without beginning.

The "conditioning cause of deluded conceptualization" refers to the objects of the deluded conceptualizations of the consciousnesses, such as the "seeing" aspect of one's own mind (the commentary notes: "this is the external object"; *Paramārtha* says:
"the causal basis" refers to the beginningless habit-energies of false and frivolous discourse; "the object-condition" refers to the discriminated realms perceived by one's own mind).
Mahāmati, it is like this: for example, a lump of clay and its atoms are neither different nor non-different; the ornaments made of gold are likewise so. (That is to say:

if the lump of clay were different from its atoms, then since the lump of clay is produced by means of those atoms, one could not say they are different. If the lump of clay were not different from its atoms, then because the name "lump of clay" is distinct from "atoms," one could not say they are non-different.

Furthermore, it is like a skilled craftsman who fashions vases, basins, hairpins, and bracelets from gold; the distinction between them and the gold is similar. Therefore, as stated in the subsequent passage... Mahāmati, if the lump of clay and its atoms...

If they were different, then that which is not produced by them would in fact be produced by them; therefore, they are not different. If they were not different, then there would be no distinction between the lump of clay and its subtle particles.

In this same way, Mahāmati, if the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) were different in their true nature, then the storehouse consciousness would not be their cause.

(Note: The evolving consciousnesses are the fifth, sixth, and seventh consciousnesses; the storehouse consciousness is the eighth consciousness. The evolving consciousnesses exist because of the storehouse consciousness; if they were different, they would not exist because of the storehouse consciousness. Since they do depend on it...)

If consciousness exists, it is not different [from its nature]. If it were not different, then when the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) ceases, the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) would also have to cease;

yet its own true nature (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) does not actually cease. Since the true nature of the storehouse consciousness is real and does not cease, it is therefore different from the evolving consciousness. This clarifies that they are neither different nor non-different.

For this reason, Mahāmati, it is not the cessation of consciousness in its own true nature, but rather the cessation of its karmic aspect (*karma-lakṣaṇa*). If consciousness in its own true nature were to cease, then the storehouse consciousness itself would cease. (Suyang)

[The two aspects of the true nature are as follows: Below [the aspect of] "no-cognition" (anupalabdhi), there is no written character [to indicate it]. [This means that while] the karmic aspect of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) is extinguished, the true nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) is truly not extinguished.

Mahāmati, if the storehouse consciousness were to be extinguished, it would not differ from the nihilistic theories of the externalists (*tīrthika*). Mahāmati, those externalists maintain such a doctrine:

they claim that when the grasping of objects ceases, the stream of consciousness (*vijñāna-srotas*) also ceases; yet if the stream of consciousness were to cease, the beginningless stream [of existence] would have to be severed. If the consciousness...

Regarding the "extinction of the flowing stream" (*pravṛtti-nirodha*): this means that when the various consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) cease, the beginningless storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) would also have to cease. If it were to cease, it would be identical to the nihilistic view (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). This statement serves as a restatement of the fact that the storehouse consciousness does not, in reality, undergo extinction. The term "flowing stream" has the meaning of "continuity.

As for the previous statement that the sense organs and consciousnesses both cease, this refers to their transformation into wisdom (*jñāna*) as the cessation, not a cessation through annihilation. Mahāmati, the non-Buddhists speak of a cause for the arising of the flowing stream; they claim that visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is not produced by the assembly of form (*rūpa*), light (*āloka*), and attention (*manasikāra*), but rather by some other cause.
Mahāmati, regarding that cause, they say it is either the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) or... [the text continues].

"Exquisite [is this]—whether it be a person (*puruṣa*), or Īśvara, or time (*kāla*), or atoms (*paramāṇu*). (Śikṣānanda says: Those non-Buddhists claim that the continuous consciousness arises from a creator;

they do not say that visual consciousness arises from the conjunction of form, light, and so forth, but rather maintain that the creator alone is the cause of its arising. What, then, is this creator? They reckon *pradhāna*, the *puruṣa*, Īśvara, time, and atoms to be the capable creators.

The New Translation says: *Pradhāna* is also called *praṇīta*; he is the Lord who gives birth to the Brahmā-heaven. The *puruṣa* is another name for the *ātman*. *Īśvara* refers to Maheśvara. They also reckon time, seasons, and atoms to be the capable creators.)"

A "shifu" (士夫) is also called a "zhongfu" (丈夫). Yang says: "The unextinguished true nature is precisely the 'one mind' transmitted by Bodhidharma. It is luminous, spiritual, and voidly penetrating, spanning from antiquity to the present. When its source is investigated, there is no admixture of delusive thoughts;

it is through their conjunction that the various consciousnesses arise. What the various consciousnesses manifest are the various phenomena. Since these phenomena are not permanent, they possess arising, abiding, and ceasing. To awaken to this is the bliss of *nirvāṇa*; to be deluded regarding this is the river of birth and death.

One who has realized the Way awakens to the fact that the illusory objects manifested before them are unreal, all being permeated by beginningless delusive thoughts. By turning the light back to reflect within, one returns to the true consciousness. It is like water returning to its basin where the turbulent flow naturally ceases, or fire returning to the void where its radiance is instantly extinguished. Thus, the mind can attain carefree and sovereign ease."

When both object and subject are forgotten, one forever transcends all sensory dust; this is the state of the true reality (*dharmatā*). Yet, because habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) still persist, one cannot yet avoid clinging to conditions. Throughout the day, one relies on others and lacks self-awareness; occasionally, one forcibly generates intellectual views, establishing them as one's own fundamental mind.

Thus, one vainly seeks the Buddha within the Buddha—on one hand relying on external objects, and on the other using the mind to condition the mind. These two ailments being unremoved, delusive appearances continue in succession. Therefore, the Tathāgata intends that one must cause both conditions and causes to cease together, and abandon both karma and its basis, so that the true nature may be eternally pure.

This Way is not obtained from another; it is simply one’s own treasure, vividly manifest before one’s eyes. If you recognize it as such, you will sink back into oblivion as before. There is no need for acceptance or rejection; it is originally perfect and complete. One need only leave behind delusion.
The conditions are precisely the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); this is what is clarified in the "Chapter on the Buddha-Speech Mind.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*): namely, the self-nature of accumulation, the self-nature of manifestation, the self-nature of characteristics, the self-nature of the great elements, the self-nature of cause, the self-nature of condition, and the self-nature of accomplishment.

(This means: Because that which is accumulated through perfuming constitutes the *saṃgraha-svabhāva* (the nature of accumulation); once the *saṃgraha-svabhāva* is established, because phenomena are each such in themselves, it constitutes the *svabhāva-svabhāva* (the nature of self-nature). Once the *svabhāva-svabhāva* is established, because the nature manifests according to its substance, it constitutes the *lakṣaṇa-svabhāva* (the nature of characteristics).

Once the *lakṣaṇa-svabhāva* is established, because characteristics depend upon formal divisions, it constitutes the *mahābhūta-svabhāva* (the nature of the great elements). Once the *mahābhūta-svabhāva* is established, because the great elements are established based on delusion, it constitutes the *hetu-svabhāva* (the nature of cause). Once the *hetu-svabhāva* is established, because the cause arises in dependence upon conditions, it constitutes the *pratyaya-svabhāva* (the nature of condition).

Once the *pratyaya-svabhāva* is established, because cause and condition are mutually identical, it constitutes the *siddhi-svabhāva* (the nature of accomplishment). Indeed, "nature" (*svabhāva*) takes non-transmigration as its meaning; therefore, all are appended with the term "self-nature" (*svabhāva*). [In the seven kinds of nature translated by Śikṣānanda, the category of "nature" is excluded.]
The nature of self-existence is the supreme nature (the character *svabhāva*). [Note: The seven aforementioned [factors] constitute the arising and ceasing body of deluded consciousness.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), namely:

the realm of mind, the realm of wisdom (*jñāna*), the realm of cognition (*vijñāna*), the realm of vision, the realm that transcends the two views, the realm that transcends the stages of the sons [of the Buddha], and the realm of the Tathāgata’s own attainment.

"The realm of the mind means that the mind fundamentally has no realm because it is quiescent and immovable; thus, various delusions cannot enter it. Since the mind is quiescent, it can give rise to wisdom (*prajñā*). When the power of wisdom is supreme, the function of gnosis (*jñāna*) is perfected. Once the function of gnosis is perfected, right view manifests before one.

When right view manifests, one transcends the two views of existence and non-existence, and further transcends the stages of the Sons (*putrabhūmi*) and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi-bhūmi*), reaching the Tathāgata’s own self-attained realm.

The 'stage of the Sons' refers to the nine stages [of the Bodhisattvas]. "Mahāmati, this is the teaching of all the Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present. (Note: The seven preceding types constitute the True Consciousness, the non-arising Dharma-body.)

The nature of the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of intrinsic nature; by means of this ultimate reality of intrinsic nature, one accomplishes the Tathāgata’s supramundane, mundane, and superior-to-the-supramundane dharmas.
Through the noble eye of wisdom (*āryaprajñācakṣus*), one enters into the establishment of specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
As thus established, it does not coincide with the evil views of the heterodox treatises. (Real-śa says: "By means of the noble eye of wisdom, one enters...")

The various establishments of self-characteristics and common characteristics do not coincide with the evil views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Mahāmati, what are the evil views shared with the treatises of the non-Buddhists? They are as follows:
they perceive their own realm through the vision of false imagination (*parikalpita*), failing to realize that it is a manifestation of their own minds.

Lacking the discernment of limits, Mahāmati, foolish ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*) formulate dualistic theories regarding existence, non-existence, and the self-nature of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). [Yang says: The evil views of the non-Buddhists arise only within their own realm...]

Regarding the views of false conceptualization, Paramārtha and Ratnamati both maintain that consciousness is what knows. This means that ordinary beings do not penetrate the limits of what is manifested by their own minds; they fail to know that it is neither a nature nor a lack of nature, yet they formulate theories of existence and non-existence regarding the ultimate reality of self-nature.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the cessation of the suffering of the three realms of existence through false imagination, the cessation of the conditions of ignorance, craving, and karma, and the manifestation of the illusory world as one's own mind, according to how it is perceived.
(The claim that Nirvana is attained by the extinction of all dharmas—caused by ignorance, afflictions, and the conditions of good and evil—is the illusory realm manifested by one's own mind;

following the false views of the non-Buddhists, I shall now explain this. Mahāmati, if there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas... (Yang says: from here onwards, up to the point where they falsely claim to be "All-Knowing Ones," [the text] explains...)

The views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*)—desiring to establish the manifestation of cause and effect whether they are seedless or seeded, and asserting that things abide during their time of occurrence within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*)—or claiming that once produced they perish, O Mahāmati, [regarding] whether it be continuity, entities, birth, existence, nirvāṇa, the path, karma, its fruit, or the truths—all these constitute the nihilistic doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*).
(Yang states: "The nihilistic view of the non-Buddhists concerns the phrases 'whether it be continuity' and so forth.")
All things are destroyed and brought to annihilation. Why is this? Because they cannot be apprehended in the present, and because seeing a beginning is not within one's scope (Yáng says:

"Because one does not see a fundamental root, it is said that seeing a beginning is not within one's scope"). Mahāmati, it is like a broken jar that no longer performs the function of a jar, or like a scorched seed that no longer performs the function of a sprout (Yáng says:
"The nihilistic views of the non-Buddhists regarding all phenomena are exactly like a broken jar or a scorched seed"). In the same way, Mahāmati, if the aggregates...

Because the elements (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), and natures (*svabhāva*) have been extinguished, are being extinguished, and will be extinguished, and because one’s own mental constructions (*svacittavikalpa*) are seen to be without cause, they do not arise in succession.

(Realśa says: "Mahāmati, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who falsely imagine non-existence and existence regarding causes and effects, asserting that external objects manifest and abide according to time; or they imagine that the aggregates (*skandha*), elements, and bases arise and abide dependent on conditions, and once having existed, they perish.

Mahāmati, whether it be regarding continuity, activity, arising, cessation, existence, nirvāṇa, the path, karma, its fruit, or the truths—these are proponents of a nihilistic doctrine of destruction and annihilation. Why is this so? )

Because they cannot be manifested in the present life and because their root is not perceived, Mahāmati, it is like a broken jar that no longer performs the function of a jar, or like a scorched seed that cannot produce a sprout; this is also the case here.

If the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases have already perished or will perish in the future, then there would be no continuous arising, as there would be no cause; it is merely what is falsely seen by one's own mind.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, if you say that consciousness arises from the combination of three conditions—whether from non-seeds or seeds—then a tortoise should grow hair and sand should yield oil; your own tenet would be destroyed, contradicting certainty.
If one asserts that there are both seeds and non-seeds, such faults as these arise: all purposeful activities would be entirely empty and meaningless. (The New Commentary states:

This is repeated here to refute the further counter-argument in the preceding text. That is to say, regarding their counter-argument that what is produced arises from the conjunction of the three conditions—namely, seeds, non-seeds, and existence—if so, a tortoise should produce hair and sand should yield oil.

Yet, since a tortoise originally has no hair and sand originally has no oil, even when combined they do not produce them. How can a result be produced if the substance of the three conditions is empty? Your own thesis is thus destroyed, contradicting the definitive meaning. This uses a metaphor to reject the lack of proof; it says the thesis is destroyed because it contradicts your definitive meaning of "that which is capable of producing"). Furthermore...

Within a single characteristic, they falsely conceptualize three conditions, which contradicts the definitive meaning of my Mahāyāna; thus, the activities they perform are entirely empty and useless. "Activity" refers to the result, and "action" refers to the cause; to speak of causal activity as such is merely false discourse and possesses no real meaning.

(In this context, *arthika* is taken by Paramārtha to mean "useless. Mahāmati, those non-Buddhists who claim that things arise from the conjunction of three conditions, and whose various skillful means regarding cause and effect and their own specific characteristics involve the presence or absence of seeds in the past, future, and present—[all these are likewise false].

From the very beginning, based on the transmission of established phenomena, those at the stage of conceptual awakening (*jiaoxiang-di*) have turned their own views and transformed their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), making such statements.

(The note says: "This cites the views of the non-Buddhists; through the skillful means produced by three conditions, the self-characteristics of the causes and effects of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are established as the dharmas of the three periods of time. [Yang says: "That which is not self-awakened but possesses awakening according to objects is called 'conceptual awakening'.

This refers to how non-Buddhists, from the beginning, have used the characteristics of existence and non-existence of seeds to produce the existence and non-existence of the activities of cause and effect throughout the three periods of time. When these activities depend upon conceptual awakening, they turn their own evil views and fail to realize that these are merely habitual perfumings (*vāsanā*).

Because they speak thus out of error, Śikṣānanda says: "Those who dwell on the stage of conceptualization (*vikalpa-bhūmi*) speak thus due to the remaining habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-śeṣa*) of their own evil views and the scriptural principles upon which they rely.
In this way, Mahāmati, foolish ordinary people (*bāla-pṛthagjana*), harmed by evil views, crooked and deluded, lacking wisdom, falsely claim to speak as one of all-knowledge (*sarvajña*).

Mahāmati, furthermore, as for other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—[from here below, the text discusses right view and how it differs from that of the non-Buddhists]—they see [phenomena] as being devoid of self-nature (*svabhāva*).

"Nature is like floating clouds, a fire-wheel, a *gandharva*-city, non-arising, an illusion, a mirage, the moon in water, and a dream (the note says: seeing that there is no self-nature is like the floating clouds, etc.;

knowing non-arising is like the illusion, etc.). These are manifestations of the internal and external mind, false imaginings from beginningless time, deceptive and not separate from one's own mind (Yang says:

the reason one can detach from that self-nature is by realizing that all manifested falsehoods do not depart from one's own mind). When the causes and conditions of false imagination are extinguished, one is liberated from false imagination."

The *ālayavijñāna*—which establishes the body and its enjoyment through the discourse of the speaker and the spoken, and the contemplation of the object contemplated—is such that when the causes and conditions of deluded thought (*vikalpa*) are extinguished, this deluded thought is suddenly detached from the objects of discourse, the objects of contemplation, the requisites for life, and the realm of the *ālayavijñāna*. Within the realm of consciousness, there is no correspondence between the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).

(The commentary states: "Because one contemplates the emptiness of 'self,' the deluded mind does not correspond with the preceding objects. [Yang says: "To call them non-corresponding means that their emotional attachments are extinguished. This is the realm of non-existence.)

The realms are free from arising, abiding, and ceasing; they are the entry into the discrimination that arises from one’s own mind. (Yang says: When consciousness and its objects do not correspond, there is nothing at all;
when there is nothing at all, one is free from all arising and ceasing—this is what is called the true mind, which functions through universal cognition.

Mahāmati, before long those bodhisattvas shall attain the great compassion of the equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, as well as skillful means that are unmanifested. Mahāmati, regarding all sentient beings...
All realms are entirely like illusions; without exerting effort toward causes and conditions, one remains far removed from internal and external objects.

Seeing nothing outside the mind, one enters successively into the signless state. Entering successively from stage to stage, one attains the realm of samādhi and discerns that the three realms are like illusions.
Through such analytical observation, one shall attain the illusion-like samādhi and transcend the manifestations of one's own mind.
[Paramārtha says: "Because one enters the tranquil realm of one's own mind. One abides in the *prajñāpāramitā* and relinquishes those skillful means (*upāya*) produced by birth;
one enters the *vajropama-samādhi*, enters the body of the Tathāgata, and enters the transformations of suchness (*tathatā*).
Being endowed with the adornments of sovereign spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*), compassion, and skillful means, one enters all Buddha-fields and the dwelling places of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

[Paramārtha] says: "Because they enter all Buddha-lands and because they enter the places where all sentient beings find joy. To be free from mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is for the Bodhisattva to gradually transform their body and obtain the body of a Tathāgata.

[Xuanzang] says: "This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva will before long attain the two kinds of equality regarding saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, the skillful means of great compassion, and effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*).

Observing sentient beings as being like illusions and shadows, arising without origin from conditions, knowing that all objective realms are devoid of mind and cannot be attained, he practices the path of signlessness (*animitta-mārga*), gradually ascending through the stages (*bhūmi*), dwelling in the state of samādhi, and thoroughly penetrating that the triple world is solely one's own mind."

Through the samādhi of illusion, one cuts off all mental images and achieves wisdom that realizes the non-arising of phenomena. Entering the Vajra-like Samādhi, one shall attain the Buddha-body, which eternally abides in suchness (*tathatā*).

Arising various transformations, with powers, superknowledges, mastery, and great compassion as its adornments, one wanders through the lands of all Buddhas, remaining free from all heterodox paths and the revolutions of mind, intellect, and consciousness. Following this sequence, one accomplishes the body of a Tathāgata. The "New Explanation" states: This Bodhisattva is precisely the aforementioned śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa of right view who practices the path of signlessness (*animitta*).

"Practicing the path of signlessness" means cultivating all myriad practices while the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are essentially quiescent. "Gradually ascending the stages" refers to first attaining the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage, the Stage of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*). "Realizing the non-arising of phenomena" means attaining the state of effortlessness (*anābhoga*).

"Ascending the Path" refers to entering the eighth stage, the Immovable Bhūmi (*acalā-bhūmi*). "Entering the Vajra-like Samādhi" means that a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) has newly attained non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and severed the obstacle of the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-dharmatā-āvaraṇa*).

From the second through the tenth stages, the Bodhisattvas practice according to reality, gradually severing various obstacles and increasing their superior merits. In the eleventh stage, the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) suddenly severs the seeds of the two innate obstacles (*sahaja-āvaraṇa*) via the Vajra-like Samādhi.

"Transforming in succession to accomplish the body of a Tathāgata" means that immediately after the moment of equal enlightenment, through the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one severs the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the two obstacles and thereby attains the two fruits of transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*): the unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) and Great Nirvāṇa (*mahā-parinirvāṇa*) of a Tathāgata. The first refers to transforming the defiled into the pure; the second refers to transforming delusion into awakening. — *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Póshā Lùn)

It is said that "mind" (*citta*) is synonymous with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), just as fire is called a "flame," a "blaze," and also "that which burns fuel"; it is but a single mind that has three distinctions. The *Commentary on the Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas* states: "The eighth is called 'mind,' the seventh is called 'intellect' (*manas*), and the first six are called 'consciousnesses' (*vijñāna*)."
Mahāmati, therefore, those who wish to attain the Tathāgata’s body of conformity should remain far removed from the false imaginings of the aggregates,
elements, sense-bases, mind, causes, conditions, and the skillful means of arising, abiding, and ceasing; they should directly advance by observing that all is but mind-only,
and reach the Buddha-ground of non-arising through the contemplation of the non-existence of the habitual tendencies of beginningless false imaginings which cause the three realms of existence.

The Noble Path of Self-Awakening (meaning that those who wish to attain the Buddha-body should distance themselves from the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; knowing that all phenomena are mind-only, they advance directly without doubt; by observing the beginningless falsity and contemplating samādhi, they find not a single dharma to which the mind can cling;

thus they realize the stage of Buddhahood, the non-arising, and reach the Noble Path of Self-Awakening). Attaining mastery over one’s own mind, they reach the stage of effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*);
like a mani jewel reflecting various colors, they enter the subtle minds of sentient beings and manifest transformation bodies.

Teaching the gates of liberation according to the measure of the mind (the note says: teaching the gates of liberation according to the magnitude of the minds of sentient beings through the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*), the various stages (*bhūmi*) are established in gradual succession (the note says:

clarifying that those who receive transformation attain the succession of the various stages). Therefore, Mahāmati, you should diligently practice and study the excellence of your own *siddhānta* (the note says:

exhorting him to learn by taking the noble path of his own school as excellent). [The New Commentary says: This Dharma-gate of the one mind is the root of both the ordinary and the sage; if one is deluded by it, one falls into the birth-and-death of the world; if one awakens to it, one realizes the supramundane Bodhi. Thus the former sages said: *Note: The original text contains a lacuna following the quote from the New Commentary.*

The mundane world does not transcend the three categories, and the supramundane does not exceed the two fruits. The two fruits are as explained above: the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s body, which is the fruit of the two-fold transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). The three categories are these very aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)—the various dharmas of the deluded mind.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding what has been taught—the mind, the intellect, the mental consciousness, the five dharmas, the self-natures, and the characteristics;
the sphere of objects consisting of the manifestations of one's own mind as practiced by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; the demonstration of the non-conjunction [of subject and object];
and the manifestation of the true nature of all teachings—this 'Heart of All Buddha-Speech' is for the sake of Laṅkā."
