Although the elements of eye, form, light, and attention arise one after another, once arisen they are real only to return to destruction; this is called the characteristic of establishing what lacks a cause.

(This means that while consciousness initially arises without cause and is subsequently unreal like a phantom, it is said to be "fundamentally unarisen. Although the eye, form, light, and attention arise in succession, even though they are real upon arising, they return to destruction; this also carries the sense of being fundamentally unarisen. Mahāmati, this is not [the case].
The characteristic of establishing existence (*bhāva-vyavasthāna-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the conceptual attachment to the nature of space, cessation, and *parinirvāṇa* as being produced.
This [nature] is established as being free from both existence and non-existence; all phenomena are like the horns of a rabbit or a horse, or like the appearance of falling hairs.

To be free from both existence and non-existence is called the characteristic of establishing non-existence (*abhāva-vyavasthāna-lakṣaṇa*). (The New Commentary states: "It is said that non-Buddhists establish existence within the three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and unproduced phenomena. The Buddha says: 'This is free from...'"")

The nature and non-nature of all phenomena are clearly understood as being free from existence and non-existence, like the appearance of hair-tufts or floating hairs produced by an obscured eye, or like the horns of a rabbit or a horse which are fundamentally non-existent.
To establish [existence] or to deny [non-existence] is the deluded imagination of fools who do not skillfully examine the manifestation of their own minds; it is not the way of the noble ones.
Therefore, one should train oneself to remain free from the evil views of establishment and denial.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva thoroughly understands the mind, the thought, the mental consciousness, the five dharmas, the self-natures, and the characteristics of the two kinds of non-self;

having reached the ultimate goal, for the sake of bringing peace to sentient beings, he manifests various kinds of forms according to their dispositions, based upon the dependent origination of the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva).

(The Bodhisattva, having already thoroughly understood the mind, the thought, and the mental consciousness, as well as the self-nature and the non-self, reaches the ultimate state; for the sake of bringing peace to all sentient beings, he accords with their types of roots of goodness.)

The emanation-body (nirmāṇakāya) entices them, just as deluded thoughts arise based on dependent origination; this provides an analogy to correctly clarify the lands of those to be converted and the Dharma taught therein.

For example, it is like a mani-jewel of manifold colors that universally manifests all Buddha-lands and the great assemblies of all Tathāgatas, wherein they all hear and receive the Buddha-Dharma—namely, that all phenomena are like illusions, like dreams, like reflections, and like the moon in water—within a single [moment].
All phenomena are free from arising and ceasing, and free from the extremes of annihilation and permanence; they transcend the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
One attains hundreds of thousands of samādhis, even up to hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of samādhis.

Having attained these samādhis, one travels through the buddha-fields, makes offerings to the Buddhas, is born in the celestial palaces, proclaims the Triple Gem, and manifests the body of a Buddha before the great assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.

Surrounded by those who have been liberated through the direct realization of the manifestation of one’s own mind, he analytically expounds that external natures lack intrinsic existence (Realśa says:
"He explains that external objects are all merely mind"), causing them all to distance themselves from views such as existence and non-existence (the New Translation says:

"Like a mani jewel that does not form a thought yet changes according to color, so too the Tathāgata, without deliberate effort, can manifest according to the size of the water of sentient beings' roots of goodness; and like a mani jewel that changes according to the object, so the Tathāgata manifests the taking up of Buddha-lands and great assemblies according to the roots of goodness of sentient beings").

Gathering therein, he taught the Dharma; the various dharmas he taught were unreal, like illusions, dreams, and so forth. Having realized that all dharmas are like illusions, the Bodhisattva became free from views of arising and ceasing, or of annihilation and permanence; he was also free from the views of the two vehicles regarding self-characteristics and common characteristics.

He attained immeasurable billions of samādhis across the various stages, manifested perfect enlightenment, and further taught the dharma of the manifestation of one's own mind, causing the assembly to be free from views of non-existence and inequality.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The sons of the Buddha observe that the world is mind-only; having abandoned the activities of conditioned effort,

they attain mastery over the powers and superknowledges and achieve accomplishment (by skillfully observing that the world is mind-only, through the power of the *māyopama-samādhi*, they manifest the Tathāgata’s body of various kinds and attain all accomplishments such as effortless action).
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again requested of the Buddha, saying:

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will, for our sake, expound the emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and the absence of self-nature in all dharmas. (The new commentary states: Because it was previously taught that all dharmas are like illusions and dreams, which is to say they are the teaching of the emptiness of dharmas, Mahāmati cites this dharma of emptiness to request [an explanation from] the Tathāgata.

What is called 'emptiness' clarifies that the aforementioned five dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent; it reveals the non-arising of the eight consciousnesses, their non-duality—which means the dualities of the two selves are both extinguished—and the departure from self-nature.)

That is, the three natures are empty and quiescent. Having awakened to this emptiness—unborn, non-dual, and free from the characteristics of intrinsic nature—we, as well as the other assemblies of Bodhisattvas, have abandoned the conceptualizations of existence and non-existence and shall swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well."
"I shall now explain this in detail for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction.

The Buddha told Mahāmati, "As for 'emptiness of emptiness' (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), it refers to the locus of the nature of false conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). [Bodhiruci says: 'It is the phrase regarding the essence of false conceptualization';

Paramārtha says: 'It is the phrase regarding the meaning of the nature of false discrimination']. Mahāmati, those who are attached to the nature of false conceptualization speak of emptiness, non-arising, and non-existence."
Second, the characteristic of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-vivikta*). Mahāmati, that is briefly explained as seven kinds of emptiness:

namely, the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the self-nature of things (*bhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of activity (*kriyā-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-activity (*akriyā-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of all dharmas being beyond verbal expression (*sarva-dharma-nirabhilāpya-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the ultimate noble wisdom (*paramārtha-āryajñāna-mahā-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of this and that (*itaretara-śūnyatā*).

(Although various teachings differ in their enumeration of these emptinesses—some increasing or decreasing them—the meaning remains no different even though this sutra provides only a brief summary. What is the emptiness of characteristics? It refers to the fact that all natures lack both specific (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general (*sāmānya*) characteristics.

Because the contemplation of the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) involves their successive accumulation, conceptualization lacks intrinsic nature; thus, self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and the nature of both self and other do not arise.

Since there is no nature in either self or other, characteristics have no abiding place. Therefore, it is said that all natures and characteristics are empty; this is called the emptiness of characteristics.

(When one contemplates the emptiness of the characteristics of all phenomena, because they are accumulated through successive causes and conditions, conceptualization lacks intrinsic nature, and thus self-characteristics and common characteristics do not arise. Since there is no essence in either self or other, upon what could characteristics depend? How is there the intrinsic nature of things? What is the intrinsic nature of things?

"Emptiness of intrinsic nature" means that the intrinsic nature of self does not arise; this is called the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena. Therefore, it is said to be the "emptiness of intrinsic nature.
(If the intrinsic nature of self does not arise, then the intrinsic nature of all phenomena does not arise; since they do not arise, they are empty. What is the "emptiness of conditioned formations"?
It means that the aggregates are devoid of "I" and "mine," being produced through causes, conditions, karma, and skillful means. This is called the emptiness of conditioned formations.

(The emptiness of practice [caryā-śūnyatā] arises from conditions and is devoid of "self" and "what belongs to self. Mahāmati, it is precisely this kind of emptiness of practice—wherein the self-nature of dependent origination is itself without self-nature—that is called the emptiness of non-practice (*acaryā-śūnyatā*).

(Previously, emptiness of practice was defined by the absence of "self" and "what belongs to self"; here, emptiness of non-practice is defined by the fact that the nature of practice is itself without self-nature.

What is the emptiness of all phenomena being beyond verbal expression (*sarva-dharmābhilāpa-vivikta-śūnyatā*)? It is because the self-nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is inexpressible; thus, all phenomena are empty.

To be free from verbal expression is called the emptiness of all phenomena being free from verbal expression (because all phenomena arise from conceptual construction and lack intrinsic nature, they are free from verbal expression).
What is the great emptiness of the ultimate noble wisdom regarding all phenomena? It refers to attaining the noble wisdom of self-realization, wherein all views and habitual tendencies are empty;
this is called the great emptiness of the ultimate noble wisdom regarding all phenomena. What is that?

That emptiness refers to the absence of something in a particular place; this is called "emptiness of this in that" (itaretara-śūnyatā). (This is because when "this" is absent from "that," and "that" is absent from "this," they are both mutually empty.
Mahāmati, it is like the house of Mṛgāramātṛ: it is empty of elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and so forth, yet it is not that there is no community of bhikṣus.

When one speaks of its being empty, it is not that the nature of the house itself is empty, nor is it that the nature of the bhikṣus themselves is empty; it is simply that these things are absent from that specific location. It does not mean that they do not exist elsewhere.

Elephants and horses (Śikṣānanda says this does not mean the hall lacks the self-nature of a hall, nor that the bhikṣus lack the self-nature of bhikṣus, nor that other places lack elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep).

[The New Commentary says: "Mṛgāra" is a personal name; his mother was the upāsikā Viśākhā. She deeply revered the Triple Gem, constructed a vihāra, and settled bhikṣus within it. Because she did not keep elephants, horses, and so forth, and because these were absent, it is called an "empty house. However, if bhikṣus were present, it would not be called empty. If there were elephants and horses in other places, one would likewise not say those elephants and horses were empty.

This is called the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). That which is not present in a certain place is said to be "empty" of that thing. This is called [emptiness].

"Mutual emptiness" (the true meaning being that when one seeks the individual and common characteristics of all phenomena within one another, they are not found; therefore it is called mutual emptiness)—this is known as the seven kinds of emptiness.

Mutual emptiness is the coarsest form of emptiness; you should distance yourself from it. (The new commentary states: "To say this is the coarsest emptiness means it is not the true emptiness, and thus one is exhorted to distance oneself.

This is the doctrine followed by non-Buddhist outsiders in their pursuit of mutual emptiness, where they either reckon it as a self (*ātman*) or cling to it as annihilationism or eternalism. The ultimate, noble wisdom of the Great Emptiness is not what they have heard. Mahāmati, do not [cling to it]."

That which arises of itself is not non-removed; abiding in *samādhi* is called "non-arising" (the note states: removing the abiding in the eighth stage, the illusion-like *samādhi*, is called true non-arising).
Being free from self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is precisely non-arising (Paramārtha says: that which lacks self-nature does so because it is non-arising).
Free from self-nature, the momentary continuity of the stream and the manifestation of diverse natures—all these natures are free from self-nature; therefore, all natures are free from self-nature.

Regarding "nature" (*svabhāva*): [Vimalamitra] says that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature because they do not abide for even a moment and because one perceives their subsequent transformation; thus, there is no intrinsic nature therein. [Yogācāra] says that in the span of a single moment, they flow into another nature, and by this, it is shown that all natures are devoid of intrinsic nature.
What is meant by "non-duality"? It means that all phenomena are like "shade and heat," like "long and short," or like "black and white.

[Bodhiruci] takes "shade and heat" to mean the shadows and light of the sun; [Vimalamitra] takes them to mean "like light and shadow. This implies that while clouds and mist constitute "shade" and brilliant radiance constitutes "heat," although shade, heat, long, short, black, and white differ from one another, [they are non-dual].
The sun’s orb is without distinction; this serves as an analogy for the non-duality of *nirvāṇa* and *saṃsāra*. Mahāmati, all dharmas are non-dual.
It is not that *nirvāṇa* exists apart from *saṃsāra*, nor that *saṃsāra* exists apart from *nirvāṇa*. Because they arise from the nature of causal characteristics, they are called "non-dual.

Just as it is with *nirvāṇa* and *saṃsāra*, so it is with all dharmas. (Realśā says: It is not that there is *nirvāṇa* outside of *saṃsāra*, nor that there is *saṃsāra* outside of *nirvāṇa*. *Saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa*...)

The aspect of non-contradiction is such that all phenomena, including both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, are likewise; this is called the aspect of non-duality. [The New Commentary] says: "It means that when one realizes that the nature of false discrimination is empty, then saṃsāra becomes nirvāṇa;

if one is deluded regarding the existence of true reality, then nirvāṇa becomes saṃsāra. Just as saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are not of two distinct categories, so it is with all phenomena. Because their aspects arise from causes and possess a nature, they are not non-existent.

Since nirvāṇa and saṃsāra differ from these aspects arising from causes and possessing a nature, they are naturally equal and non-dual. Therefore, one should practice and study emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and the absence of self-nature.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"I have always taught the Dharma of emptiness, which is far removed from the extremes of annihilation and permanence; birth and death are like illusions and dreams, yet karma is not destroyed.

(The *Zongjing Lu* says: 'Because its nature is empty, the path of karma is not destroyed, and the causes and effects of fruition remain distinct. This is also true for space and nirvana—the two types of cessation are likewise so."

Fools give rise to false imaginings, while the noble ones are free from existence and non-existence. (The New Commentary states: One cannot posit nirvana by means of the three aforementioned unconditioned emptinesses, nor can one posit samsara by means of nirvana;
this is because fools give rise to false imaginings and speak of them as two, whereas the bodies of the noble ones penetrate and realize [reality], thus being free from existence and non-existence.)
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying:
"Mahāmati, emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and the departure from the marks of self-nature universally enter into all the sūtras of the Buddhas;

in every scripture, this meaning is fully explained. (The new commentary states: 'The meanings of emptiness and so forth universally enter all sūtras; there is not a single dharma that does not accord with this principle. All sūtras follow the capacities of sentient beings."
It is out of a desire to benefit beings that I have provisionally analyzed and explained this to reveal its meaning;
it does not exist as a reality within words, just as the mirage of a thirsty deer deceives a herd of deer, who cling to the appearance of water while no water exists there.

(The "New Explanation" states: this refers to returning the provisional to the real. There are some sutras that do not speak of emptiness or non-arising because the aspirations of sentient beings are not uniform; thus, the Tathāgata provides various different teachings according to the minds of sentient beings, yet the reality remains as it is.)

Awakening resides in the mind and does not lie in words and phrases. It is like a herd of deer, driven by thirst, who see a springtime mirage and perceive it as water; they run toward it in confusion, yet that solar illusion is not actually water.
In this same way, all the dharmas taught in the sūtras are for the purpose of inspiring joy in the foolish;
true noble wisdom does not reside in verbal expression. Therefore, one should rely on the meaning and not cling to words and phrases.

Kambu (qú yān), Vaṃśa (wú fàn). Vīṇā (pinyin: kōng hóu). Hasta (zhí jiǔ). Yūkā (jǔ qǐ). [Gǔ měng]. [Nú hóu]. Niṭṭha (zhù jià). Śaṅkha (qiū hé).

*Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, Scroll II, Chapter II:
The Essence of the Words of All Buddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, the Sūtras state that the Tathāgatagarbha is pure by nature and, manifesting the thirty-two marks, enters into the bodies of all sentient beings.

(In all versions, the two characters "World-Honored One" (*shizun*) are repeated; however, in the Xuanzang version alone they are absent. Examining the meaning of the scripture, the former two characters represent Mahāmati’s address, while the latter two characters introduce the Dharma spoken by the World-Honored One as the subject of his inquiry, as in the fourth [chapter]).

In this fascicle, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has stated in the sūtras... [The translations by Paramārtha and Śikṣānanda both render *parivarta* as "complete" and *praveśa* as "abiding. The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) states:

"The sūtra says that within the bodies of sentient beings there is a Buddha, possessing the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, sitting upon a precious lotus flower, no different from the Buddhas themselves. It is only because they are shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*) that they have not yet attained its function. Furthermore, it says: 'The Buddhas are like a great round mirror; my body is like a mani-jewel.
The Dharma-body of all Buddhas enters my essence, and my body constantly enters the bodies of all Buddhas. It is like a treasure of great value wrapped in a soiled garment."—Thus, the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgatagarbha is likewise eternally abiding and unchanging; yet it is enveloped by the soiled garments of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, and defiled by the dust and toil of unreal conceptualizations such as greed, hatred, and delusion—this is what all Buddhas have proclaimed.
Why then, World-Honored One, do you speak of a "Tathāgatagarbha" in a manner identical to the non-Buddhists' doctrine of a self? World-Honored One, the non-Buddhists also say that there is [a self].
"World-Honored One, that which is eternal, acts as an agent, is free from *guṇas*, is omnipresent, and is indestructible—this is what they call the 'Self' (*ātman*).

(The New Translation states: This objection is that if the Tathāgata speaks of the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha*, it contradicts all the preceding *sūtras* which teach emptiness; thus it would be identical to the non-Buddhists who speak of a 'divine spirit. However, their conception of the Self has three aspects: first, its essence is eternal and it is called the 'agent';

second, although it exists within the five aggregates, it is free from *guṇas*; third, it pervades all realms of existence and is truly not subject to birth or extinction. Now, when you speak of the meaning of the 'garbha,' is this not identical to the 'Self' of the non-Buddhists? [Bodhiruci] says: Because it is free from *guṇas*..."

(Regarding the meaning of "not relying on conditions," see the previous fascicle. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The Tathāgatagarbha that I teach is not the same as the 'self' (ātman) spoken of by the non-Buddhists.

Mahāmati, it is described by such terms as emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), the dharma-nature (dharmatā), the dharma-body (dharmakāya), nirvāṇa, being devoid of self-nature, non-arising, non-ceasing, originally quiescent, and parinirvāṇa by its very nature."

Having thus explained the *tathāgatagarbha*, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of severing the fear of the foolish regarding the phrase "selflessness," has taught the gateway of the *tathāgatagarbha* as a realm free from conceptual construction and devoid of anything existing.

Mahāmati, future and present Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should not form attachments based on the view of a self. (The Buddha taught that the *tathāgatagarbha* is also called emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and so forth, up to selflessness...)

Nirvāṇa by nature is thus a single essence; it is only named differently according to its manifestations. This is not the same as the "self" (ātman) spoken of by non-Buddhists. Furthermore, because foolish people fear selflessness, the Tathāgata employs skillful means to teach that the realm of nothingness is the gate of the Tathāgata-garbha, encouraging all bodhisattvas not to share with non-Buddhists the attachment to the conceptualization of a self.

It is like a potter who, from a single lump of clay, uses human effort, water, wood, a wheel, and rope as skillful means to fashion various vessels (the meaning of which is seen below in the commentary on the "clay jar"). The Tathāgata is also like this regarding the Dharma.

Being selfless and free from all marks of conceptual construction, through various forms of wisdom and skillful means, [the Buddha] sometimes speaks of the *tathāgatagarbha* and sometimes speaks of selflessness.
For these reasons, he speaks of the *tathāgatagarbha*. This is not the "self" spoken of by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*);
it is called the teaching of the *tathāgatagarbha* because it is taught in order to attract and lead those non-Buddhists who cling to a self. Thus, he speaks of the *tathāgata*.
The Treasury [of Teachings] commands that one depart from the false conceptualization of the view of a self and enter the sphere of the three gates of liberation (yāna-trimukha). [Yang says:

The *Avataṃsaka* states that when a bodhisattva contemplates dependent origination and realizes the emptiness of intrinsic nature, they attain the gate of liberation through emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*). By contemplating the extinction of the intrinsic nature of the twelve links of existence (*bhavāṅga*), they attain the gate of liberation through signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣa*). Entering into emptiness and wishlessness, yet acting solely for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, they attain the gate of liberation through wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa*);

hence, these are called the three gates of liberation. One should aspire to swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, for by departing from the false conceptualization of the view of a self, one immediately enters [into realization].

The three gates of liberation lead to the swift attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Regarding the term "aspiration," as stated in the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "Originally I had no mind to seek anything; now this treasure-trove has appeared spontaneously.
These are all states of sudden realization (*tun-cheng*). Therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, speaks thus:

"If the Tathāgatagarbha were not such [as it is], it would be identical to the views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). For this reason, Mahāmati, in order to depart from the views of the non-Buddhists, one should...

Relying on the *tathāgatagarbha* of selflessness (this clarifies that those who wish to leave behind delusion and realize unsurpassed *bodhi* should understand the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha* of selflessness).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The continuity of the person, the aggregates (skandhas)—[Paramārtha says: the person, the self, and the aggregates]—are conditioned by atoms, the Primal Lord (Iśvara), or the creative mind;

these are but delusive imaginings of the mind-only (cittamātra). [The new commentary states: Non-Buddhists reckon that it is because of a divine self (puruṣa) that the aggregates continue; they further reckon that atoms and so forth serve as conditions for the arising of phenomena, or they reckon that everything is created by the supreme and wondrous Lord (Iśvara);
all of this is merely the delusive imagination of the mind.]
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, observing future sentient beings, again entreated the World-Honored One, saying:
"I only pray that you will explain for them the practice of uninterrupted continuity, such as the great skillful means of those who practice like the Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas.

(Observing that among future sentient beings there are those of sudden capacity whose faculties have matured, he requested the World-Honored One to explain the Dharma-gate of practicing and immediately realizing uninterruptedness; this is unlike the gradual entry of the Lesser Vehicle, whereby Bodhisattvas practice to attain great skillful means.)
The Buddha told Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: "There are four dharmas by which a practitioner attains great skillful means. What are the four? They are:

(1) skillfully discerning that what appears as external objects is but the manifestation of one's own mind; (2) realizing the non-existence of external natures; (3) being free from views concerning arising, abiding, and ceasing;
and (4) attaining the noble wisdom of self-realization and taking great delight therein. These are called the four dharmas accomplished by a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva."
What is the great skillful means of the practitioner? It is when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva skillfully discriminates that which is manifested from his own mind;

that is, he contemplates in this way that the triple world is merely the limit of mind (the note says: "one contemplates that the triple world arises solely from the limits of the deluded mind"), being free from self and what belongs to self, unmoving, free from coming and going, and devoid of the various forms of the triple world as perfumed by beginningless false habitual tendencies.

The manifestation that enters into the false discrimination established by the body and wealth through the activities of the fetters is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s skillful discernment of what is manifested as one's own mind.
(Yang says: this means that by establishing body and wealth through the activity of form, one enters into one's own mind and manifests false discrimination.

What is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s skillful contemplation of the non-existence of external natures? It is the contemplation of all natures—such as mirages and dreams—as being without external reality. (This means skillfully contemplating the external nature of all dharmas as being like mirages and dreams.)
Because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are said to be "non-nature. [Bodhiruci] says: "Because there are no external dharmas, the various consciousnesses do not arise.

Due to the causal conditions of beginningless, false, and delusive habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates that the self-nature of all phenomena is non-existent, and thus skillfully observes that external natures are non-natures—this is called a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva skillfully observing that external natures are non-natures. (This is because, by realizing that it is "mind-only," one skillfully observes that external natures are non-natures. What is meant by this?
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully distance themselves from views of arising, abiding, and ceasing;

they perceive all natures—whether self-nature, other-nature, or both—as being like illusions and dreams, unarisen, and conforming to the limits of their own mind (as Śikṣānanda says: "because they appear according to the measure of one's own mind").

They see that external natures lack inherent existence, and they see that consciousness does not arise and that conditions do not accumulate (Yang says: "It is not only that they see external natures as lacking inherent existence, but the consciousness that perceives them is likewise...")

Since there is no arising, conditions do not assemble either. Seeing that the false discrimination of dependent origination gives rise to all phenomena within and without the triple world, one realizes they are unobtainable;

seeing that they are devoid of intrinsic nature, all views of arising are extinguished. (Bodhiruci says: "Because they lack substantial reality, they are far removed from arising; because they are improper views regarding all phenomena. Śikṣānanda says: "Knowing they have no real substance, one is far removed from the view of arising.

Knowing that the self-nature of all phenomena is like an illusion and so forth, one attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Having attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas...

Having already abandoned the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing, this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s skillful discernment of the abandonment of the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing (the note states:
because one knows there is no arising, there is no arising, abiding, or ceasing). What is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s skillful delight in the noble self-realized wisdom?

It refers to attaining the stage of non-arising dharma (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), dwelling in the eighth Bodhisattva stage, and attaining freedom from mind, thought, mentation, and the five dharmas.

Attaining the mark of the two kinds of selflessness in their intrinsic nature, one obtains the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*). (The note states: "One attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas in the eighth stage and is able to leave behind the remedial dharma-gates of the two kinds of selflessness, such as mind, thought, and consciousness.

[Yang says: "In the aforementioned eighth stage, everything is entirely left behind; as for the other stages, it is not yet sufficient to speak of this. The World-Honored One, regarding the mind-made body, by what causes and conditions does it arise? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"The mind-made body is so called because it goes as swiftly as the mind, unhindered and unimpeded; therefore, it is named 'mind-made.'"
Just as the mind travels without obstruction through stone walls to immeasurable *yojanas* in other directions, remembering without forgetting what was previously seen,
with the flow of its own mind uninterrupted, so too does great wisdom arise without obstruction within the body. Thus,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) attains simultaneity through the power of the illusion-like samādhi.
The body of the noble lineage, adorned with the wondrous marks of sovereign supernormal powers, is born simultaneously and without obstruction, as if produced by thought.
In accordance with whatever realm of past vows is recalled, it attains the sublime bliss of self-realized noble wisdom for the sake of maturing sentient beings.

(Realśikṣa says: "It is like the mind and its faculties, which, even beyond immeasurable hundreds of thousands of yojanas, recall various objects previously seen; through the continuous succession of moments of thought, it swiftly reaches them.")

Just as it is impossible for a physical body, mountains, rivers, rocks, or walls to create obstacles for a mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*), so it is with this [body]: through the power of the illusion-like samādhi, mastery over supernormal faculties, and the adornment of various marks, and because it remembers its original vows to bring sentient beings to maturity, it proceeds at will to be born among all the assemblies of noble ones, and so forth.

Thus, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the stage of non-arising dharma (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and enters the eighth bodhisattva ground, they completely relinquish the body characterized by the mind, thought, mental consciousness, the five dharmas, the three natures, and the two kinds of selflessness.

Furthermore, attaining the body born of mental mastery (*manomayakāya*) and obtaining the sublime joy of the noble self-realized knowledge—this is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the four dharmas that constitute the great skillful means of a practitioner;
one should train in this manner. (In the translations by Ratnākaraśānti and Śikṣānanda, the texts regarding these four dharmas are incomplete.)
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again requested of the World-Honored One:

"I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of the causal conditions (*pratyaya-hetu*) of all dharmas, so that by awakening to the characteristics of causal conditions, I and the other Bodhisattvas may be free from the false views of existence and non-existence regarding all natures, and free from the views of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), whether arising successively or simultaneously.
(In the translation by Paramārtha, *jue* [awakening] is rendered as "skillfully knowing," while *reśaka* is rendered as "thoroughly penetrating. (Paramārtha says: "Free from...")

Regarding the incorrect views of existence and non-existence, Mañjuśrī said: "One who is free from the views of existence and non-existence does not falsely cling to the idea that phenomena arise either gradually or suddenly. The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"All phenomena have two kinds of causal conditions: external and internal. External conditions refer to such means as a lump of clay, a staff, a wheel, a string, water, wood, human effort, and various other skillful means, through which a jar arises—just as a jar arises from clay, or cloth from threads, or a mat from grass, or a sprout from a seed, or curd and butter from milk. Thus it is with all things.

One must first have the cause and subsequently the effect, arising in a continuous succession; that which directly produces is called the "cause" (*hetu*), while that which indirectly assists is called the "condition" (*pratyaya*). Regarding the cause of what-is-to-be: once the cause of action has functioned, internal and external phenomena arise. The five-membered syllogism consists of: first, the thesis (*pakṣa*); second, the reason (*hetu*); third, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*); fourth, the application (*upanaya*); and fifth, the conclusion (*nigamana*). The three—thesis, reason, and example—are also called the "three members" (*trirūpa*) of inference. Application and conclusion merely serve to complete the argument.

For instance, when non-Buddhists falsely speculate and cling to the notion that sound is permanent, they formulate a syllogism within the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*) as follows: - **Thesis:** Sound is a permanent entity. - **Reason:** Because it is produced (*kṛtakatva*). - **Example:** Like space (*ākāśa*).

Form is not non-tree-form; thus, the views of the externalists, perfumed by habitual tendencies and clung to through false imagination, rely on notions of identity, difference, both, or neither, existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, permanence, or impermanence, and are unable to know that these are merely the manifestations of their own minds.
For example, just as a clear mirror reflects all forms and images according to conditions without any false imagination, so too is that [reality] not [as they conceive it].
It is not an image, yet it is not non-image; though it is an image, it is seen as a non-image. Fools with deluded thoughts conceive of it as an image.

Thus, the evil views of the outsiders are the manifestations of images within their own minds, which they falsely conceptualize and cling to based on notions of identity, difference, both, or neither, existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, permanence, or impermanence.
It is like the sound produced by the conjunction of wind and water; that sound has no inherent nature and is not real.

The nature of non-existence (*abhāva*) is thus: the false imaginings (*vikalpa*) of the evil views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) rely upon [the concepts of] identity and difference, bothness and not-bothness, existence and non-existence, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence and impermanence.
It is like a great earth where there is no grass or trees, yet where mirages (*marīci*) flow like rivers, and vast waves surge like clouds.
(Realśa says: when sunlight strikes them, the waters of the mirage ripple. That is neither nature nor non-nature, because of the presence of both greed and non-greed. (Zongjing)

It is said: "If one gives rise to false conceptions regarding desire and, through delusion, develops attachment to it, then one is bound by that desire. If one directs right reflection toward desire and realizes that desire has no self-nature, then one attains liberation from desire.

In this same way, ordinary people—perfumed by beginningless, false habitual tendencies—rely on their conceptual constructions and attachments to the gates of phenomena that abide in themselves, such as arising, abiding, and ceasing;

identity and difference; conjunction and non-conjunction; existence and non-existence; neither existence nor non-existence; permanence and impermanence; and so forth, just as in those previous examples.

The waves of the blazing flames (Śikṣānanda says: within the gateway of the dharma-nature realized by noble wisdom, one perceives the nature of arising, abiding, and ceasing; unity and difference; existence and non-existence; both and neither.
This means that when non-Buddhists take the self-abiding realm of noble wisdom as their object, it conversely becomes unreal waves like a blazing flame).

For example, suppose there were a person who, through incantations and mechanical devices, combined the efforts of *piśāca* spirits—entities not classified among sentient beings (Liuzhi says: wooden automatons have no substance of a sentient being)—to create something that moves and shakes. (*Piśāca* means "eater.")

(Regarding the statement that the vital essence is the beam of the deluded ghost: All such foolish, ignorant, and deluded conceptualizations regarding coming and going belong to the evil views and aspirations of externalists.

Relying on the discursive proliferations (*prapañca*) of oneness, otherness, both, neither, existence, non-existence, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence, and impermanence, they cling to what is unreal and establish false constructions.
Mahāmati, therefore, if you wish to attain the reality of self-realized noble wisdom (*svapratyātma-āryajñāna*), you must abandon [the notions of] arising, abiding, and ceasing.

[The Tathāgata’s] evil views and delusive imaginings—such as identity and difference, both and neither, existence and non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, permanence and impermanence, and so forth. (The New Commentary states:

"The Tathāgata exhorts those who have realized the truth that they should abandon the aforementioned evil views and discriminations of birth-and-death, identity, difference, and so on, held by ordinary people and non-Buddhists. However, roughly speaking, there are three types of heterodox views in India: first, non-Buddhist paths outside of the Buddha-dharma; second, non-Buddhist paths attached to the Buddha-dharma;

and third, those who study the Buddha-dharma and become non-Buddhists—meaning those who cling to Buddhist teachings yet give rise to afflictions, fail to attain awakening, lose the gate of skillful means, and fall into heterodox attachments, which are called 'internal heterodoxy. Thus, one knows that dharmas are non-existent.)

If the characteristics of meditative concentration revolve and follow the mind’s attachments, they become non-penetrating; this is not a fault. As with the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), their penetration or obstruction depends on the person. In terms of the Dharma, they are called the "four propositions"; awakening to them is called the "four gates"; false conceptualization is called the "four attachments"; and disparaging them is called the "four slanders.

When the four propositions are unmoving, gain and loss give rise to emptiness, and while there is no difference in the single Dharma, the ascent and descent differ of themselves. If even a hair’s breadth of a viewpoint is not forgotten, one becomes an outsider (*tīrthika*).
Thus we know that when views exist, one is an ordinary person; when they are extinguished, one is a Buddha. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
One should contemplate the three realms of existence as being like a magical illusion, a dream, the reflection of trees in water, a mass of hair seen by one with cataracts, or a mirage;

thus one ultimately attains liberation. Just as a deer, its mind deluded by a shifting mirage, perceives it as water though no actual water exists, so too do the seeds of consciousness shift and perceive objects, giving rise to the false imaginings of the ignorant. Thus it is.

Obscured by the obscuration of beginningless birth and death, one clings to and grasps at the nature of things, like a person who uses a wedge to remove another wedge yet fails to let go of the grasping of desire.
(Sentient beings cling to and grasp at things as if using one wedge to pry out another; they are unable to achieve liberation.

Out of compassion, the Tathāgata uses various metaphors for unreality as wedges to wedge away their delusions, causing them to emerge from liberation, so that they are no longer obstructed by the nature of evil views, conceptualization, and grasping. Like illusions, spells, mechanical devices, floating clouds, dreams, lightning, and flashes of light.

By contemplating this, one attains liberation and forever severs the three continuities (*tri-saṃtati*)—as explained in the third fascicle under the passage on the three continuities (the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* also mentions three kinds of continuity).
Within that state, there is no agent, like a mirage in the sky (Paramārtha says: "like a solar mirage in the air").

Knowing all phenomena in this way is to have nothing known (the New Translation says: "to say that all phenomena lack substance is to have nothing that can be known"). Verbal teachings are merely provisional names; they too...

There are no marks; yet therein arise false imaginings regarding the aggregates (skandhas) and formations (saṃskāras), like falling hair, like a painting, like falling hair [in the eyes], like a phantom, a dream, a city of the Gandharvas, a fire-wheel, or a mirage—appearing though non-existent.
So it is with the notions of existence and non-existence, permanence and impermanence, unity and difference, bothness and not-bothness.
These are the continuous succession of faults from beginningless time, the deluded imaginings of foolish people. They are like a clear mirror or pure water.
Within the eye-maṇi jewel, various colors appear, yet in reality they do not exist at all. (The clear mirror, water, and the pure eye-jewel constitute four of the twelve metaphors;

the Tathāgata cites them in verse to represent the nature of perfected completion (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), which remains unchanging despite following conditions. This is the same intent as that expressed in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:

"For example, the substance of empty space is not composed of manifold characteristics, yet it does not obstruct the manifestation of those various characteristics. "Pure eye" refers to being free from cataracts. All natures manifest like a painting or the shimmering heat-haze.
Various flames manifest in manifold colors, like a dream, having no substantial reality (this clarifies that although all phenomena appear, they lack any real substance).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is free from these four positions: namely, identity and difference, both and neither, existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence;
it is free from permanence and impermanence, and transcends the conceptual proliferation of establishing, denying, and discriminating between existence and non-existence.
The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma takes as its primary focus the truth of dependent origination, the path, cessation, and liberation;

it does not teach that things arise from primordial nature (*prakṛti*), from a creator god (*īśvara*), from no cause, from atoms (*paramāṇu*), from time, or from the continuity of self-nature (the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma takes the truth of reality and liberation as its primary focus, unlike the non-Buddhists who teach through the continuity of such characteristics as *pradhāna*, *īśvara*, and lack of cause). Furthermore, Mahāmati, for the sake of purifying the afflictions...

Because they afflict you with the obstacles of passion and ignorance, the Tathāgata establishes one hundred and eight propositions and discriminates the characteristics of the various vehicles and stages,
just as a caravan leader sequentially establishes one hundred and eight propositions and skillfully distinguishes the characteristics of the various vehicles and stages.

Just as a caravan leader guides his merchants toward the place of jewels, employing various skillful means at dangerous and obstructed places to ensure they all pass through them, so too does the Tathāgata guide sentient beings, leading them to purify and eliminate the two obstacles and sever all delusions.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of dhyāna. What are the four? They are: the dhyāna practiced by fools, the dhyāna that contemplates meaning, the dhyāna that takes suchness as its object, and the Tathāgata-dhyāna. What is the dhyāna practiced by fools?

It refers to the practice of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and followers of external paths who contemplate the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), as well as specific and general characteristics, the skeleton, impermanence, and suffering.

To be fixated on the mark of impurity as primary, such that these marks are not seen as distinct from one another, and yet one proceeds through successive stages without eliminating them—this is called the "dhyāna practiced by fools.

(The note states: The followers of the two vehicles contemplate the emptiness of persons, and further contemplate the specific and general characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, performing meditations on impermanence, suffering, and impurity.

Such marks are not distinct from such contemplations; although there is progressive advancement in contemplating general and specific characteristics, impermanence, and so forth, because they do not transcend these marks, it is called the dhyāna practiced by fools. What is the "contemplation of meaning"?
Dhyāna refers to [the realization that] persons lack selfhood in terms of both specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Having realized that external paths (non-Buddhists) lack intrinsic nature in themselves and in relation to others, one subsequently observes the meaning of the signs of the stages (*bhūmi*) regarding the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). As it is said [in the *Ṭīkā*]:

"Regarding the selflessness of phenomena, one observes in accordance with the meanings of the signs of the various stages. This is called the dhyāna of observing the meaning. What is the dhyāna of taking suchness as its object? It refers to the false...

To conceive of the two kinds of selflessness as being conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), yet not to give rise to conceptual construction regarding their true state—this is called "meditation that takes suchness as its object" (*tathatālambana-dhyāna*).

(The note says: What is meant by "conceptual construction"? It means these two kinds of selflessness are conceptual constructions. Why are the two kinds of selflessness conceptual constructions? Because they are taught as the two kinds of selflessness in order to eliminate the two kinds of conceptual construction regarding the view of self;

since that which is to be remedied is unreal, the remedy is likewise false. Thus it is said that the two kinds of selflessness are conceptual constructions. If one knows them as they truly are, according to the equality of reality (*yathāvad-yathābhūta*), and does not give rise to the conceptual construction of the two kinds of selflessness, this is called "meditation that takes suchness as its object. What is suchness?

"Coming Tathāgata-meditation" refers to entering the stage of the Tathāgata, attaining the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization, and abiding in the three kinds of bliss (Paramārtha says:

"Because one enters the characteristics of the noble wisdom within the body and the three kinds of blissful practice in the three emptinesses"; Śikṣānanda says: "Abiding in the three kinds of bliss of self-realized noble wisdom"; the commentary states: "These are meditative concentration, bodhi, and nirvāṇa").
It accomplishes inconceivable deeds for the sake of sentient beings; this is called Tathāgata-meditation. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke [this verse]:
The verse says:

The dhyāna practiced by fools, the dhyāna of observing the characteristics and meanings, the dhyāna of relying on suchness as it truly is, and the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata (the above verses summarize the four types of dhyāna;
those that follow are all non-Buddhist dhyānas). They are like the shapes of the sun and moon, the *padma* lotus, and deep precipices.

When the fire in space is extinguished, the practitioner observes it. (The new commentary states: this clarifies the characteristics of the dhyāna practice of non-Buddhists and those of the Two Vehicles.

It says that non-Buddhists, clinging to a self-soul (*ātman*), during their meditative observation see forms like the sun and moon—bright, pure, and radiant—or they see red lotuses beneath deep precipices. The followers of the Two Vehicles take the self-characteristics and common-characteristics to be truly existent;

by "extinguishing the body and annihilating wisdom," they become like space, regarding the extinction of the fire when the fuel is spent as ultimate *nirvāṇa*. [Padma, here translated as "red lotus flower. Such various signs are the commonality of the paths of non-Buddhists.)

Meditation also falls into the realm of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas (the aforementioned various signs are the meditations traversed by the paths of the non-Buddhists and the meditative realms of the two vehicles).
To abandon all of those is "nothingness" (Vasubandhu says: "to abide in the absence of objects"; the New Translation says:

"the former phrase refers to the meditation of contemplative observation, while the latter phrase refers to the meditation of conforming to reality through objective conditions"). At that moment, the Buddhas of all lands simultaneously stroke [the practitioner] with their inconceivable hands.
Its summit enters into accordance with the suchness (tathatā) [this refers to entering the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata].
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding what you speak of as 'Parinirvāṇa,' what dharma do you designate as Nirvāṇa?

[The new commentary states: Non-Buddhists take the perception of a self-soul (ātman) to be Nirvāṇa; the two vehicles take the extinction of body and consciousness—like the extinguishing of fire when fuel is spent—to be Nirvāṇa.]”

Therefore, he asked: "In what way does the Tathāgata teach the Dharma that constitutes *nirvāṇa*? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The transformation of all self-nature (*svabhāva*), habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the mentation (*manas*), and the evolving consciousnesses (*vijñāna*)—along with the views and habits—is called *nirvāṇa*.
For all Buddhas and myself, *nirvāṇa* is the sphere of reality (*dharmadhātu*) characterized by the emptiness of self-nature.

Because it is empty of self-nature, it is the suchness of principle and the suchness of phenomena; this is the sphere of the *nirvāṇa*-reality of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. As for 'the sphere of phenomena,' it is like the 'non-obstruction of phenomena within phenomena' in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*."

This obstructs the Dharma-realm; the text of this sutra is for the most part largely abbreviated. Furthermore, Mahāmati, as for nirvāṇa, it is the realm of the self-realization of noble wisdom, free from the false imaginings of annihilation and permanence, and beyond the nature of existence and non-existence.
Why is it not permanent? Because the false imaginings of specific and general characteristics have been severed, it is not permanent.
Why is it not annihilated? Because all noble ones—of the past, future, and present—attain self-realization, it is not annihilated.
Mahāmati, nirvāṇa is neither destroyed nor does it die. If nirvāṇa were subject to death, it would follow that one must undergo rebirth and continuity once again;
if it were subject to destruction, it would fall into the category of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

Therefore, nirvāṇa is free from destruction and free from death; thus, it is the refuge for those who practice. (The New Commentary states: Nirvāṇa is not subject to death because one no longer undergoes the continuity of rebirth; it is not subject to destruction because it is not a conditioned phenomenon characterized by arising, abiding, and ceasing. Because there is no destruction... [text ends]

Because death has been transcended, it is that upon which practitioners rely. Furthermore, Mahāmati, nirvāṇa is neither abandonment nor attainment, neither annihilation nor permanence, neither a single meaning nor manifold meanings;

this is called nirvāṇa. (Realśa says: Because there is nothing to abandon and nothing to attain, because it is neither annihilated nor permanent, and because it is neither one nor different, it is called nirvāṇa.

The New Commentary says: In nirvāṇa, there are no afflictions to be abandoned and no bodhi to be attained; therefore, it is neither annihilation, permanence, oneness, nor difference. Only that which is realized through correspondence is called the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa. Furthermore, Mahāmati...

Regarding the nirvāṇa of the wise śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas: they realize the specific and general characteristics [of phenomena] and do not associate with external objects (*iśvarakṣa* says this means "abandoning clamor and bustle").
With non-perverted views, their false conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) do not arise; thus, they conceive of that state as nirvāṇa. (The *Xin* commentary states:

The two vehicles realize that within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), there is no primordial principle (*tattva*) or self (*ātman*). They abandon clamor and bustle, extinguish the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and do not give rise to perverted views or future birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Because they give rise to the notion of nirvāṇa regarding that state, it is called the Dharma [of the two vehicles].)
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "To merely exhaust birth and death is called liberation; in reality, one has not yet attained all-encompassing liberation.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, what are the two characteristics of self-nature? They are:

the characteristic of attachment to the self-nature of verbal expression, and the characteristic of attachment to the self-nature of objective entities. Attachment to the self-nature of verbal expression arises from beginningless verbal discourse.
The attachment to the signs of the self-nature of phenomena arising from the habitual tendencies of falsehood is produced from not awakening to the limits of what is manifested by one’s own mind.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata establishes Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas through two kinds of spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Saddharma-puṇḍarīka [or the relevant interlocutor] prostrates to all Buddhas and requests to hear the meaning of their teaching: "What are the two kinds of supernatural power (rddhi-bala) by which [the Tathāgata] establishes [his teachings]?
They are: the supernatural power of manifesting all bodies, faces, and speech through the attainment of samādhi, and the supernatural power of empowerment by hand.

(Because ordinary beings give rise to two kinds of marks of self-nature based on their attachments, the Tathāgata establishes [the path] by means of these two kinds of supernatural power. This was at the initial stage of Bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mahāmati.
Abiding by the Buddha’s spiritual power— namely, having entered the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna Illumination Samādhi—
and having entered this samādhi, all Buddhas of the worlds in the ten directions, through their supernormal powers, manifest for him all bodies, faces,
and speech (according to Śikṣānanda: "All Buddhas of the ten directions appear before him universally"), just as with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha and others of such appearance.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Accomplished in Merit (just as the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, when dwelling in the first stage at the assembly of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
was empowered by the Tathāgata’s spiritual power, and so it was for the other bodhisattvas as well)— O Mahāmati, this is called the first bodhisattva stage.

It is that which has been accomplished through the roots of goodness accumulated over hundreds of thousands of kalpas by the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who has attained the samādhi and supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, proceeding through the successive stages.
Having attained ultimate mastery over the antidotes and their opposites, they reach the Dharma Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*),
where they dwell in a subtle and wondrous palace of great lotuses and sit upon a precious lion throne of great lotuses, surrounded by a retinue of similar Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas;
their bodies are adorned with various precious necklaces, like the radiance of gold, *campaka* flowers, the sun, and the moon— most supreme among all lights.
Hands come from the ten directions and bestow the consecration upon the crown of his head while he sits upon the throne of the Great Lotus Palace;
it is like the consecration of the sovereign Wheel-Turning King or the Crown Prince of Śakra, Lord of the Devas. This is called the Bodhisattva’s power of hand-consecration.
Mahāmati, these are the two kinds of supernatural powers of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva...
The Bodhisattva dwells by means of two kinds of spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) to behold the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas; were it not for these, he could not see them.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, all the various practices of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas—whether they be analytical discernments, meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), or the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*)—all of these abide within the two kinds of spiritual power of the Tathāgata. (Iśvara says: "All Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas enter into samādhi and manifest...")
It is taught that all such things are due to the two kinds of sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddhas.

Mahāmati, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva were able to expound [the Dharma] apart from the Buddha’s sustaining power, then all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) should also be able to speak it. Why is this?
It is because they do not abide in the sustaining power. Mahāmati, when the Tathāgata enters [a place], mountains, stones, trees, musical instruments, cities, and palaces [all produce sound].
By the majestic spiritual power of the city, the sounds of music spontaneously emerge; how much more so for those with minds!
Countless beings suffering from deafness, blindness, and muteness all attain liberation. The Tathāgata possesses such immeasurable spiritual powers to benefit and bring peace to sentient beings.

(The preceding section clarified the ten stages (*bhūmi*); because of the selflessness of wholesome dharmas, one soon attains the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of non-existence in the first stage. One proceeds through the stages in succession, transcending the nine stages until reaching the Cloud of Dharma.)

The Ground is established by these two kinds of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata; that is to say, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abides in these two kinds of supernatural power, he beholds the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, face-to-face, but if it were not so, he would be unable to see them.

Furthermore, it is said: "If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva were able to expound [the Dharma] apart from the Buddha's supernatural power, then all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) should also be able to speak. The former refers to the merit of sudden realization, while the latter refers to the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*); therefore, it is accomplished through the accumulation of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) over hundreds of thousands of eons.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, for what cause and condition does the Tathāgata, the Arhat..."

When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who are Samyaksaṃbuddhas dwell in the meditative absorption of samādhi, as well as at the time of the empowerment of the stage of supreme advancement, the Buddha bestows his supernatural power upon them.
Mahāmati, the Buddha told him: "This is for the sake of abandoning the karmas of Māra and afflictions;

for the sake of not falling into the dhyāna of the Śrāvaka stage; for the sake of attaining the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization; and for the sake of further increasing the dharmas already attained."
Therefore, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas all establish the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas through their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).

If they were not established by these supernormal powers, they would fall into the false views, delusions, and hopes of the various śrāvakas and māras, and would fail to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason, the Buddhas...

The Tathāgata, through his supernormal powers, universally sustains all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—[meaning that if one does not apply effort at the first stage, one will inevitably fall into the evil views of externalists or the realm of the śrāvaka-māras, whereas if one does not apply effort up to the tenth stage, one cannot swiftly attain bodhi]. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The Sovereign of Men with supernormal powers whose great vows are entirely pure; the samādhis and consecrations of the first and tenth stages (*bhūmi*).
(According to Śikṣānanda: "O World-Honored One, the pure vows possess the power of great empowerment; [they pertain to] the samādhis and consecrations within the first and tenth stages.")
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, when the Buddha speaks of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), he is speaking of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and does not speak of a self-established path (Paramārtha says: 'The Tathāgata also speaks of all dharmas arising in dependence upon causes and conditions, but does not say there is a dharma established by itself').
World-Honored One, non-Buddhists also speak of causes and conditions, claiming that such natures as the Supreme Lord (*īśvara*), Time (*kāla*), or atoms (*aṇu*) give rise to these various phenomena."

[Regarding] "arising" (the meaning is found in the first fascicle; see the note below "if it were a minute particle"): Now, as for the Blessed One’s statement that all natures arise from causes and conditions, there is the *siddhānta* with intervals and the *siddhānta* without intervals.

(The real meaning is: "Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, merely speaks of dependent origination using different names; there is no difference in the underlying meaning. Regarding the *siddhānta* with intervals and the *siddhānta* without intervals:

if one asks whether the verbal expression of the Blessed One’s teaching on all natures arising from causes and conditions differs in meaning from what is taught by the non-Buddhists, or does not differ—*siddhānta* is a term combining both the Chinese and Sanskrit, translated as "universal bestowal" (*biànshī*). This refers to the Dharma of the Buddha.

[Regarding] giving: The World-Honored One, non-Buddhists also say that existence arises from existence and non-existence arises from non-existence (the note says: "existence" means arising from an existent cause; "non-existence" means arising from a non-existent cause).

The World-Honored One also says that there is no arising, and once arisen, it ceases. As the World-Honored One has said—that ignorance conditions volitional formations, and so on up to old age and death—this is the World-Honored One’s teaching of causelessness, not a teaching of causality. The World-Honored One establishes [the doctrine] in this manner.

To say that "because this exists, that exists" does not establish a gradual arising (meaning that because ignorance exists, formations exist; because formations exist, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and even old age and death exist—all of these lack priority and posteriority;

it is not established as a gradual production, for otherwise one would suspect them of being causeless). One should observe that the doctrines of the non-Buddhists are superior, yet they are not like those of the Tathāgata.

(Bodhiruci says: "If that were so, the teachings of the non-Buddhists would be superior while the Tathāgata’s would not be. Why is this? Because the World-Honored One [is distinct from] the non-Buddhists...

To say that causes do not arise from conditions yet produce something else—wherein the Blessed One has taught that by observing the cause one finds the effect, and by observing the effect one finds the cause—is a confusion of causes and conditions.

Such a process would result in an infinite regress. (The "New Explanation" states: This refers to the non-Buddhist claim that causes such as the "supreme, subtle atoms" do not arise from other conditions yet can produce others;

these causes are eternal, acting only as causes and never as effects. This is the superior teaching of the non-Buddhists. In contrast, according to the Buddha’s teaching, when one observes formations, they are the effect of ignorance; when one observes consciousness, it is the cause. Thus, a single dharma is both...)

"Because the cause is itself the fruit, causes and conditions would become confused: ignorance would produce formations, and formations would produce old age and death; old age and death would produce ignorance, and so on, revolving endlessly. This would result in the fallacy of contradiction, as it would destroy the [Buddhist] reason that things arise from causes. Therefore, Mahāmati, I teach that all natures are unarisen.
Mahāmati, the foolish masses of externalists desire for existence and non-existence to arise; they do not understand that these are merely various attachments to their own false imaginings.

Mahāmati, I do not hold that there is arising from existence or non-existence; therefore, I speak by means of the teaching of non-arising. (Paramārtha translates this as: "The externalist multitudes together give rise to evil...")

It is said that all phenomena arise from existence and non-existence; they do not have self-attachment and conceptualization as their condition. Mahāmati, I teach that all phenomena do not arise from existence or non-existence, and for this reason they are called "unborn.

Mahāmati, the teaching on "nature" (svabhāva) is for the purpose of encompassing birth and death (*saṃsāra*), for the purpose of destroying the view of non-existence and the view of annihilationism, and for the purpose of enabling my disciples to encompass various karmas and the places of rebirth.
By means of the nature of sounds, I speak of encompassing birth and death. (Paramārtha translates this as: "The teaching of all phenomena is for the sake of causing disciples to know...")

By means of the various karmas, one embraces birth and death (*saṃsāra*) in order to prevent the view that there is annihilation. "Sound" refers to the Dharma. When it was previously stated that the nature of all dharmas is such as to embrace birth and death, it was for the purpose of refuting the nihilistic views of emptiness held by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Furthermore, it is intended to cause disciples to abandon these two views by embracing birth and death through the teaching of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). Mahāmati speaks of the characteristics of the self-nature of illusion in order to depart from the characteristics of self-nature;
[otherwise,] one would fall into the false views and expectations of fools, failing to understand that [the world] is a manifestation of one's own mind. It is ruined [by such views].
Because of attachment to the characteristics of self-nature arising from causes and conditions, one speaks of the illusory and dream-like nature of all phenomena.

This is done to prevent foolish people from falling into evil views and desires, and to prevent them from being attached to themselves and all other phenomena by failing to see them as they truly are.

[Realśa says: "To speak of the characteristics of all phenomena as being like illusions is to cause them to abandon the characteristics of the self-nature of phenomena; it is for the sake of those fools who have fallen into evil views and desires, and who do not know that all phenomena are but mind-only."

In order to cause them to abandon the signs of arising from causes and conditions that give rise to attachment, I teach that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams. Yet those fools, clinging to evil views, deceive themselves and others, unable to clearly perceive the true abiding state of all phenomena.

The "New Commentary" states: "The 'true abiding state' means there is no place of abiding; therefore it is called the true abiding state. This is the realm realized by the noble wisdom of self-awakening, the teacherless wisdom, and the spontaneous wisdom.

It is not realized through another. If there were a place of abiding, it would not be the true abiding. Because they cling to the phenomena of self and other, they produce perverse arguments contrary to the vision of reality. Therefore, the Tathāgata does not allow fools to give rise to such evil views. O Mahāmati!

"Seeing all dharmas in their true state" means transcending the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*). [Paramārtha says: "Seeing all dharmas as they truly are" means being able to thoroughly comprehend that which is seen is only the mind.

[The New Translation says: "All dharmas are established from the root of non-abiding"; how could one clearly see this without comprehending that it is only one's own mind? Therefore, there is no contradiction between what the Tathāgata has taught—that all dharmas are unarisen and like illusions—and this.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

The non-arising of that which is produced is the inclusion of both non-existence and existence within saṃsāra; it is the observation that [all things] are like illusions and so forth, and thus not conceptualizing regarding their marks.

(That is to say, because all dharmas are non-arising and produced as non-existent, this is taught to refute the view of nihilism; by teaching that karma and its nature include saṃsāra and observing all dharmas as being like illusions, one does not give rise to discrimination regarding their marks.)
Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the characteristics of the body of names (*nāma-kāya*), the body of phrases (*pada-kāya*), and the body of syllables (*vyañjana-kāya*).

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who skillfully contemplate the characteristics of the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables will accordingly penetrate the meanings of those names, phrases, and syllables (Iṣvarakṣa says: "I shall explain the characteristics of the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who skillfully contemplate these characteristics will thoroughly understand their meaning").
They will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Having awakened in this way, they awaken all sentient beings.

[Sheng] (The New Commentary states: Because the Tathāgata, for the sake of sentient beings, employs compassionate skillful means to provide various different explanations, desiring to cause sentient beings to understand the true meaning within names and phrases rather than clinging to the verbal expressions, he speaks of the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables.

*Jue* means awakening; it refers to the previously awakened awakening those who awaken later. Mahāmati, as for the "body of names" (*nāmakāya*), it refers to when a name is established based on a thing; this is called the body of names. As for the "body of phrases" (*padakāya*), it refers to a phrase that possesses meaning;
when its self-nature is determined and its ultimate limit is reached, this is the body of phrases. As for the "body of syllables" (*vyañjanakāya*), [it consists of the phonemes].

"Body" (*kāya*) refers to the manifestation of names and phrases; this is called the "body of forms. (Paramārtha says: "The 'body of names' (*nāmakāya*) means that names are established based on things; the name itself is the body; thus it is called the 'body of names.

Regarding the "body of phrases" (*padakāya*), it refers to those names and phrases that are able to manifest the definitive and ultimate meaning. Regarding the "body of phonemes" (*vyañjanakāya*), it refers to that by which names and phrases are formed; this is called the "body of phonemes. (The New [translation] says:

"Just as names such as 'jar' or 'bowl' are established based on the things 'jar' and 'bowl,' these names—whether singular, dual, or plural—that express their own intrinsic nature are called the 'body of names. As for the mention of the "body of phrases" and so forth, it is because phrases are formed based on names, and meaning is manifested based on phrases. For example, jars made of copper or iron have different meanings for the phrase 'jar,' namely: one [type], etc.)

A phrase (*pada*), a group of two phrases, or a group of many phrases that can express distinctions is called a "phrase-body" (*padakāya*). Because these [phrases] enable the establishment of names, they are called "names" (*nāman*); the basis for these two [types of phrases]—consisting of one, two, or many syllables—is called the "syllable-body" (*vyañjanakāya*).

"Body" (*kāya*) has the meaning of a collection of many dharmas. Regarding "name" (*nāman*): it refers to relying on categories to represent forms; when phonemes correspond to their shapes, they are called "syllables" (*vyañjana*). Syllables are identical to characters (*akṣara*).

Furthermore, the "form-body" (*rūpakāya*) refers to length and shortness, or height and depth (Bodhiruci says: it refers to the length of sounds and the high or low pitch of the cadence). Furthermore, the "phrase-body" (*padakāya*) refers to tracks or traces, such as those left by elephants, horses, humans, beasts, and so forth.

"Traces of conduct result in the acquisition of words and names" (all spoken words are merely traces; the commentary states that this is like seeking the tracks to find the elephant or horse, meaning one awakens through words).

"Great Wisdom consists of name and form": this means that because the four formless aggregates (*skandhas*) are explained by means of names, they are called "name"; because their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) manifest, they are called "form. (Śikṣānanda says:

"Name" refers to the four non-material aggregates (*skandhas*), as they are explained by means of names; "text" refers to the own-characteristics of names, as they are manifested by the text. This means that the four aggregates—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—possess only the characteristics manifested by names and phrases.)

When abiding within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), these are manifested; this is called the exposition of the bodies of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*). One should study the characteristics and boundaries of the bodies of names, phrases, and phonemes.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
