Ordinary, deluded worldlings cling to the distinctions between the collection of names (*nāmakāya*), the collection of phrases (*padakāya*), and the collection of syllables (*vyañjanakāya*), like an elephant sinking into deep mud.

(The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma through the expedient means of the conventional collections of names, phrases, and syllables; yet if ordinary, deluded people still cling to these verbal expressions and do not awaken to the true meaning, how can they escape, being like an elephant sunk in deep mud?)
Furthermore, Mahāmati, in the future there will be wise ones who, using the meaning established by me— which is free from the views of identity,

difference, both, or neither— will question those who lack wisdom. Those lacking wisdom will reply, "This is not a correct question," [meaning that when the wise ones ask about the meaning established by me as being free from such characteristics as identity and difference,
the unwise answer that this is an improper inquiry] because they claim that the impermanence of form and so forth is either different or not different [from the entity itself].

In this way, regarding nirvāṇa, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*), the qualities (*guṇa*) and the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*)— as Real-śikṣānanda says, the support (*āśraya*) and the supported (*āśrita*)—

the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derivative elements (*bhautika*), the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) and the seen (*dṛśya*), the objects (*viṣaya*), and atoms (*paramāṇu*)— as Liu-zhi says, "clods of earth and atoms"— as well as cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and the cultivator (*bhāvaka*), and so forth, such questions concerning these successive mutual relations:
the Buddha declared them *avyākṛta* (unexplained), halting further discussion, for they are not within the capacity of those deluded people.

"Knowledge" refers to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), which is incomplete; therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, causes them to be free from phrases that provoke fear by declaring these matters "unexplained" (*avyākṛta*) and not providing an explanation.
Furthermore, he does not speak of them in order to cease the speculative views and theories of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). [It is said:

"The ignorant, because they do not know the true meaning, take up characteristics (*nimitta*)—such as identity or difference—and pose them as correct questions. The wise should say to them: 'Questions such as these are called "unexplained" by the Buddha; they are the cessation of debate. This is for the sake of those foolish people."

Because they lack the wisdom of hearing, they do not know what exists or does not exist, nor what is erroneous or correct; therefore, [the Tathāgata] sets it aside and does not answer. Desiring to cause them to abandon the fears arising from the erroneous views of annihilationism and eternalism, the Tathāgata declares these matters "undeclared" (*avyākṛta*) and does not provide a definitive explanation.

Furthermore, in order to cease the non-Buddhists' theories of a self (*ātman*) and to cause them to reflect and thereby attain understanding, he does not speak of them. Mahāmati, the non-Buddhists make such assertions as "the life-principle is identical to the body," and so forth—these are undeclared propositions.

(This is because the non-Buddhists conceive of a self either as being identical to or distinct from the aggregates; therefore, their claims that the body and life-principle are one or different are all merely erroneous doctrines that remain undeclared.)
Mahāmati, those various non-Buddhists are deluded regarding causes and propound the doctrine of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);

this is not what I teach. (Bodhiruci says: "Because non-Buddhists are confused about the meaning of cause and effect, they therefore hold them to be indeterminate; in my Dharma, it is called 'indeterminate' for this reason. Mahāmati, that which I teach is free from the grasping of subject and object, and thus conceptual construction does not arise.
How could there be any cessation [of such construction]? (Bodhiruci says: "Therefore, in my Dharma, there is no setting aside of answers. Mahāmati, if there were grasping of subject and object...

Those who are attached do not understand that [the world] is a manifestation of one's own mind; therefore, they should be stopped. (*Vīryaśrī* says: "If there is attachment to the grasper and the grasped, and one does not realize it is merely what is seen by one's own mind, that should be stopped.

Mahāmati, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas teach the Dharma to sentient beings by means of the four kinds of categorical explanations (the four *vyākaraṇas*, as seen in the subsequent verse).
Mahāmati, I have taught from time to time that those who stop categorical explanations are for those whose faculties are not yet mature.
"Because it is not yet ripe for those who are not [yet ready]" (Paramārtha says: "Because the faculties are not yet mature, one temporarily ceases the teaching").
Furthermore, Mahāmati, all dharmas are free from the causes and conditions of action; they do not arise because there is no agent. Therefore, all dharmas are unarisen. (Bodhiruci says:

"All dharmas are free from an agent and causes; therefore they do not arise. Because there is no agent, I say that all dharmas are unarisen. Mahāmati, why is it that all natures are devoid of self-nature? Because of their own...

When one is in the state of vitarka and vicāra (Paramārtha says: "one observes by means of one's own wisdom"), because the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) cannot be apprehended, it is said that all phenomena are unarisen.

Why are all phenomena neither able to be brought nor able to be taken away? Because when one wishes to bring them by means of their specific and general characteristics, there is nowhere from which they come;
when one wishes to take them away, there is nowhere to which they go. Therefore, all phenomena are free from coming and going. (Śikṣānanda)
Why is it that all phenomena have no coming or going? Because their specific and general characteristics have nowhere from which they come and nowhere to which they go.

Mahāmati, why is it that all phenomena are not extinguished? Because the nature of intrinsic self-nature is non-existent; because all phenomena are unattainable; therefore, all phenomena are not extinguished.

(Because all phenomena lack the characteristic of an intrinsic nature and are unattainable, they are not extinguished. Mahāmati, why is it that all phenomena are impermanent? Because the arising of their characteristics is non-existent.

Because their nature is constant, it is said that all phenomena (*dharma*) are impermanent. (The note says: this means that the characteristics of all phenomena arise and immediately perish; therefore, it is said that all phenomena are impermanent. Mahāmati, why is it said that all phenomena are permanent?
Because the arising of characteristics is non-arising, and because their nature is non-existent and eternally constant, it is said that all phenomena are permanent.

(Paramārtha says: this means that the arising of all characteristics is precisely non-arising; because they are non-existent, impermanence itself is constant; therefore, I say that all phenomena are permanent. At that time, the World-Honored One...
Wishing to restate this meaning, he spoke in verse:
"There are four kinds of formal discourse: direct response, counter-interrogation, analytical response, and setting aside the question.

These are used to subdue the various non-Buddhists, such as the Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika teachers, regarding existence and non-existence. (Liu-zhi says: "Direct answer, counter-questioning answer, analytical answer, and setting aside the answer.")

*Sāṃkhya* and *Vaiśeṣika*: *Sāṃkhya* is correctly called *Sāṃkhyā*, which means "calculation" (*saṃkhyā*) or "theoretical system" (*sāṃkhyā*). *Vaiśeṣika* is also named *Vaiśeṣa*; this means "the theory of distinction" (*vaiśeṣa*).

These are the teachers of these two systems of philosophy. [The Buddha] declared that all of them are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); he manifested it in this way. *Vaiśeṣika* says: "All such dharmas as these are entirely indeterminate.

Regarding the Tathāgata’s four kinds of formal declarations (*vyākaraṇa*): first, answering according to the question is called "categorical" (*ekāṃśa-vyākaraṇa*); second, answering by counter-interrogating the questioner is called "counter-interrogative" (*paripṛcchā-vyākaraṇa*); third, [answering by] distinguishing...

To answer by means of analysis is called "discriminative" (vibhajya-vyākaraṇa). The fourth is to set aside without answering, which is called "stopping the discussion" (sthāpanīya-vyākaraṇa). For example, regarding the various views of existence and non-existence held by externalists such as the Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika masters, all their manifold doctrines are entirely unspeakable.
That which is discriminated by the Perfectly Awakened One—when observed with wisdom, as Viśākha says—is such that its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) cannot be apprehended;
because it is free from verbal expression, it is said to be devoid of intrinsic nature.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the specific distinctions and the general characteristics of the various types of *srotāpanna* and the paths leading to the state of a *srotāpanna*. (Note: Mahāmati, because the aforementioned foolish worldlings perceive the phenomena of delusion, they give rise to the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle;

since within the Śrāvaka teachings there are four distinct fruits, he raises these four distinct fruits as a question regarding the flow [of the stream-enterer]. Paramārtha and Śikṣānanda both take 'path' (*yāna*) to mean 'practice'; that is, the causal practice cultivated by a person who has entered the stream, which is precisely the causal practice they intend to cultivate.)"

Because the faculties of those proceeding toward the fruit of Arhatship vary—being either sharp or dull—there is a distinction between the general and the specific. If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva thoroughly understands the specific and general characteristics of the stages leading to the fruit of Srotāpanna, as well as the skillful means (*upāya*) for the fruits of Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat, and having distinguished and known them thus, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings accordingly, namely:
the characteristics of the two kinds of non-self (*anātman*) and the purification of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).
Having thoroughly and ultimately penetrated the characteristics of the various stages (*bhūmi*), one attains the inconceivable, ultimate realm of all Tathāgatas.
Like a mani-jewel that manifests in various colors, one is well able to benefit all sentient beings, sustaining them with the inexhaustible body and wealth of the realm of all dharmas.

Regarding the "characteristics of differentiation" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*): although the characteristics are common [to all], their realization possesses distinctions. Regarding the "characteristics of skillful means" (*upāya-lakṣaṇa*): these are the characteristics of the skillful means of practice for the four fruits. [The first fruit is] the Srotāpanna.

This is called *srotāpanna* (Stream-enterer), meaning that when the eighty-eight *anuśaya* (latent afflictions) of the view-delusions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the four truths of the three realms are completely severed, one realizes the first fruit. Because one has for the first time entered the stream of the noble ones (*ārya-srotas*), it is called "Stream-enterer. *Sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returner) means "one who goes and returns once.

This refers to the stage where, among the eighty-one grades of cultivation-delusions (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) across the nine stages of the three realms, one has severed the six grades of the desire realm; thus, one realizes the second fruit. After passing away from this life, one must go once more to the two higher realms and return once to the desire realm to sever the remaining three grades of delusion;

hence, it is called "One who Goes and Returns Once. *Anāgāmin* (Non-returner) means "one who does not return. This refers to the stage where the nine grades of cultivation-delusions of the desire realm are completely severed, and one realizes the third fruit. Consequently, when taking birth in the form realm, one will never again return to the desire realm; hence, it is so called.

The three fruits from the stage of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) upward are called those in training (*śaikṣa*). The Arhat (*arhat*)—here translated as "one for whom there is no further birth" (*anutpāda*), "slayer of thieves," or "worthy of offerings"—is so named because when the eighty-one categories of afflictions of the desire realm and the eighty-one categories of afflictions of the eight stages in the two upper realms have been completely severed, one realizes the fruit of the fourfold Arhatship and enters the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*);

hence, it is called "no further birth. Having skillfully distinguished and known these characteristics of the four fruits, the Bodhisattva preaches such Dharma of the Śrāvakas and such Dharma of the Bodhisattvas for the sake of sentient beings, enabling them to realize the non-self of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*), purify the obstacles of affliction and knowledge (*kleśajñeyāvaraṇa*), transcend the characteristics of the various stages (*bhūmi*), and ultimately attain thorough penetration into the realm realized by the Tathāgata.

By attaining the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* and the wealth of the Dharma, they benefit sentient beings inexhaustibly. Because these benefits exist, he requests the Tathāgata to explain the distinctions between the four fruits. [Signature: Yang.
The "cloud-body wealth" is precisely the ocean of practice of the *Avataṃsaka*. The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well;
I shall now speak for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One! Indeed, we shall listen and receive [your teaching].

The Buddha told Mahāmati, "There are three kinds of *srotāpanna* and distinctions regarding the fruit of *srotāpanna*. What are the three? They are the inferior, the middling, and the superior. [The superior one asks about all the *srotāpannas*...]

Regarding the question of the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and the path to stream-entry, the present answer states that there are three types of stream-enterers. These distinctions in the fruit of stream-entry are mentioned to mutually clarify the differences; because their faculties are either sharp or dull, there are indeed three. The "lowest" refers to one who has at most seven more births (*sapta-kṛtvah-parama*).

(Realśa says: "Among all states of existence, there are at most seven rebirths. "At most seven births" means: the first grade of defilement moistens two births; the next three grades each moisten one birth; the next two grades together moisten one birth; and the final three grades together moisten one birth.

Thus, the nine grades of co-arising afflictions within the single stage of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) collectively moisten seven births. This stream-enterer is of the lowest capacity and is extremely dull-witted, as they have not yet severed the afflictions of the desire realm.

[Those who] undergo seven more rebirths among humans and devas before realizing the fruit of Arhatship; those of middling capacity undergo three or five more births before attaining Parinirvāṇa (those of middling faculties attain Arhat-nirvāṇa after three or five births);

and those of superior capacity attain Parinirvāṇa in that very life (those of superior faculties attain the fruit of Arhatship in this very life and are called *Srotāpanna* who attain extinction in the present;

the intermediate stages between the two fruits are not mentioned). These three types possess three grades of fetters—lower, middling, and superior (the note states: within these three types of fetters there are all three grades—lower, middling, and superior—referring to the highest-of-the-high).

Because there are superior-superior, superior-middle, superior-inferior, middle-superior, middle-middle, middle-inferior, inferior-superior, inferior-middle, and inferior-inferior [grades], the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) collectively comprise nine grades. What are the three fetters?

They are the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—the meaning of which will be explained below. Regarding the distinctions among these three fetters, by progressing through the superior-superior stage, one attains Arhatship.

Mahāmati, the view of a self-body is of two kinds: that which is innate (*sahaja*) and that which is conceptual construction (*parikalpita*). This is like the nature of conceptual construction based on dependent origination; it is a metaphor for conceptual construction.

Just as various attachments to the nature of conceptual construction arise based on the nature of dependent origination (meaning that various attachments to the nature of conceptual construction arise depending upon the nature of dependent origination, serving as a metaphor for how the view of a self arises from the five aggregates), because those [conceptual constructions] are neither existent nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, and lack the characteristics of real conceptual construction, the foolish engage in conceptual construction and become attached to the characteristics of the various natures of conceptual construction. (Paramārtha says: "Those dharmas are merely conceptual...")

The conceptualized marks are neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent; yet foolish ordinary beings grasp at them erroneously. Just as a deer in a hot mirage perceives it as water, so too does the *srotāpanna* falsely imagine the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
By means of the realization of the non-self of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), they apprehend the absence of intrinsic nature and thereby sever their long-standing ignorance and attachments.

(Bodhiruci says: "This is called the *srotāpanna*'s conceptualized view of a self. Why? Because due to a lack of wisdom, they have falsely grasped at signs since beginningless time. O Mahāmati, this is the defilement of the view of a self.
By seeing the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), one is able to distance oneself from [the view of a self]. Mahāmati, as for the innate view of a self-body (*sahaja-satkāya-dṛṣṭi*):

because the four aggregates (*skandha*)—beginning with the body—of oneself and others lack the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*); because form arises from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*); because they are mutually dependent causes and characteristics;

and because the primary elements and form do not aggregate [into a self], [it is abandoned]. (Paramārtha says: "The innate view of a self-body is abandoned by universally observing that the body, feelings, and so forth—the four aggregates of oneself and others—lack the characteristic of form; for form is produced by the primary elements.")

Because the primary elements (mahābhūta) are mutually dependent causes and because form (rūpa) does not accumulate, [it is empty]. The New Commentary says: "One should universally contemplate that one's own body and the bodies of others are equal; the aggregates (skandha) of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, together with the aggregate of form, all have names but no substance and lack the characteristic of self-nature.

One contemplates that the aggregate of form is produced from the four primary elements and arises through their reciprocal causality. Since there is no sovereign within the four primary elements, who could assemble them to constitute form? If the aggregate of form, which possesses substance, is yet empty, how much more so the other four aggregates such as feeling, which lack physical characteristics—how could they not be empty?
Thus, when a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) contemplates existence and non-existence, the manifestation of the body and views is severed.

When the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) eliminates craving, it does not arise; this is called the characteristic of the view of a self-body. (That which "exists" is the aggregate of form; that which "does not exist" refers to the four [other] aggregates. By observing that these five aggregates have no substantial essence, the view of a self-body is severed.

Generally, those who possess craving do so because they hold to the view of a self-body; by abandoning the view of a self-body, from where could craving arise? Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The cause of all suffering is rooted in craving. Because craving does not arise, this is called the characteristic of severing the view of a self-body. Mahāmati, as for the characteristic of doubt:
it arises from having attained various dharmas and perceiving their characteristics well, as well as from the two previous types of false views regarding the self-body.

Because conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) is severed, doubt regarding the Dharma does not arise. (This means that by clearly perceiving the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths as they have been attained, one is able to sever the two kinds of co-emergent deluded thoughts previously held regarding views;
thus, doubt regarding the Dharma does not arise. One does not give rise to the view of a "Great Teacher" elsewhere [than in the Buddha] regarding what is pure or impure;

this is called the characteristic of doubt, which is severed by the *Srotāpanna*. (Previously, when honoring devas, Māras, or non-Buddhists, one would conversely doubt whether the Buddha was pure or impure. Now that one knows he is not so, one no longer has any further doubts. This is called the severing of the characteristic of doubt. Great Wisdom Precept.
Regarding "clinging" (*parāmarśa*): why does the *srotāpanna* not cling to the precepts? It is because he clearly perceives the characteristic of suffering inherent in the places where one is born;

therefore, he does not cling. (It is said that the *srotāpanna* does not cling to the precepts for future births; observing that wherever there is birth there is suffering, he does not seek the pleasure of being born.

Mahāmati, "clinging" refers to the way foolish people resolutely undertake the practice of asceticism (*duḥkha-caryā*) for the sake of the pleasure of various requisites, thereby seeking rebirth. (Bodhiruci says: "Clinging to the precepts... [is as follows].)

This refers to ordinary worldlings who, through observing precepts, exerting diligence, and performing various virtuous deeds, seek pleasant realms and are reborn among the devas. They do not grasp at these [precepts], except for those practiced as skillful means for the sake of dedicating merit toward the supreme self-awakening and the state free from false discrimination and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) dharmic characteristics.
To thus uphold the branches of the precepts is called the "grasping at the characteristics of precepts" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) of a *srotāpanna*.

(Śikṣānanda says: A *srotāpanna* does not grasp at such characteristics; he seeks only the most supreme, outflow-free, non-conceptual dharma that is to be realized, and thus practices the categories of the precepts. This is called the characteristic of grasping at precepts and prohibitions.)
The Srotāpanna has severed the three fetters, and craving and delusion do not arise. If the Srotāpanna were to think, "I am not possessed of these fetters," there would be two faults:

falling into the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and failing to sever the various fetters (that is, by maintaining the mind that seeks to sever them, one falls into the view of a self-identity and is consequently unable to sever the fetters;
these are the two faults). Therefore, Ratnamati said: "If he were thus, he would not be free from the three fetters. Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
The World-Honored One has spoken of many forms of craving; what is that craving which is to be severed? (That is to say, what kind of craving is it that must be abandoned? The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"It is the fondness for women, the entanglement and attachment through various means, and the evil karma of body and speech, which results in the experience of pleasure in the present while sowing the seeds of future suffering.
That [craving] does not arise. Why is this? Because one attains the bliss of samādhi and right reception (samyak-prativedha). For this reason..."
He has severed the craving that does not lead to nirvāṇa (though he has severed the craving for the five worldly desires, he has not yet severed the supramundane craving that leads to nirvāṇa).

Mahāmati, what are the characteristics of a *sakṛdāgāmin*? It means that because he suddenly illuminates the characteristics of form, the characteristics of the arising of false conceptualization, and the characteristics of the arising of views, and because he correctly perceives the characteristics of the stages of dhyāna, he returns once more to this world to reach the end of suffering and attain nirvāṇa; therefore, he is called a *sakṛdāgāmin*. (Śikṣānanda)
It is said that having gone once to and fro, one has well cultivated the practice of dhyāna, reached the limit of suffering, and entered parinirvāṇa. Mahāmati, why is one called an Anāgāmin?
It is because one perceives the faults of the arising of the characteristics and the nature—or the lack of nature—of form (*rūpa*) in the past, future, and present;

because one’s false conceptualizations no longer arise; and because one has severed the fetters (*saṃyojana*), one is called an Anāgāmin. An Anāgāmin has already departed from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and is born entirely within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Observing that the nature of form throughout the three periods of time is without reality, one sees that wherever there is birth, there is inevitably suffering.

When the wisdom that realizes emptiness regarding faults and outflows arises, one cuts off all fetters and latent tendencies; because the characteristics of future delusive thoughts do not arise, this is called *anāgāmin*.

Mahāmati, as for the *arhat*, it refers to one who, through the power of the various dhyānas, samādhis, and liberations, and by means of clear insight, realizes that afflictions, suffering, and delusive thoughts have no inherent nature; therefore, they are called *arhats*. (The new commentary states:

"It is said that the *arhat* practices the four dhyānas and the three samādhis, fully realizes the eight liberations, and has already accomplished the ten powers, the three clarities, and the six supernormal knowledges; thus, the suffering summoned by the arising of karma from afflictions and delusive thoughts are forever extinguished.")
"Therefore, they are called Arhats. Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the World-Honored One speaks of three kinds of Arhats. To which of these does this refer?
World-Honored One, is it the Arhat who has attained the path of the single vehicle of tranquility? Or is it an Arhat manifested through the skillful means of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva?
Or is it an Arhat created by a Buddha [as *ṛṣi* says, 'transformed by the Buddha']? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is the one who has attained tranquility..."

Regarding the path of the single vehicle of tranquility, it is for the śrāvakas and not others; "others" refers to those who practice the bodhisattva path, those emanated by the Buddha, and those produced through skillful means and original vows.
For the purpose of adorning the Buddha’s retinue, they manifest birth within the great assembly. (The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"Those Arhats of fixed destiny who have entered the state of tranquility—having severed the four abiding afflictions, emerged from the suffering of birth and death, and attained nirvāṇa—are not the others who, having fallen back, again give rise to the mind of great enlightenment, nor are they those emanated by the Buddha.")

As for those to be converted, because they have already previously generated skillful and vast vows and practices to mature sentient beings, the Bodhisattva manifests birth among them as a skillful means; as for those to be converted, it is for the purpose of adorning the Buddha-lands and their assemblies and retinues.

Mahāmati, regarding the locus of deluded discrimination, various teachings are spoken—such as attaining fruits and attaining dhyāna. "Dhyāna" refers to entering meditative absorption, which is entirely free from [delusion];
thus, the manifestation of attaining the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind is called "attaining fruits. (Paramārtha says: "Regarding the false...")

In this context, various dharmas are taught, namely the fruits of realization for those who practice dhyāna and the dhyānas themselves; for both are by nature detached, and the signs of attaining the fruit are merely what is seen by one's own mind.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, one who wishes to transcend the realms of dhyāna, the immeasurables, and the formless should abandon the marks of the "manifestation of what is perceived by one's own mind" (that is, one must eliminate the previously attained signs of the fruit of the manifestation of one's own mind).

Mahāmati, it is not the case that one transcends the manifestation of one's own mind through the meditative attainments of sensation and perception; why? Because there is still the measure of the mind (citta-mātra). (That is to say, it is not...)

The cessation of sensation and perception is the realization of right attainment (*samyaksamādhi*), as stated in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*. Without extinguishing sensation, one attains realization; here, both the ultimate and the conventional are simultaneously brushed aside, and both emptiness and existence are eliminated together. When one reaches the limit, the center is realized, yet there is no limit to be abandoned; when one realizes the center, the limit is reached, yet there is no center to remain.

Since the wisdom that realizes has vanished, the principle that is realized is likewise quiescent. Only then does one transcend the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*), which is why it is said that this is not like those who dwell in the various dhyānas that still possess the measure of the mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The various dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), and the cessation of sensation and perception—all these are merely the measure of the mind;

they do not exist [independently]. (The new commentary states: "The various dhyānas" refers to the four dhyānas. "Immeasurables" refers to the four immeasurable minds—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—which deliver sentient beings. "Formless attainments" refers to the four formless concentrations.

"Cessation of sensation and perception" means that in the four dhyānas and the four formless concentrations, sensation and perception are entirely stilled; all are merely the measure of the mind, and none of them exist [apart from it]. The fruit of *srotāpanna*, the *sakṛdāgāmin*, and the... [anāgāmin]...
Furthermore, [the state] equal to that of an Arhat is a delusion of the mind (see note to the first fascicle).

For a practitioner of dhyāna, when dhyāna and its objects are severed, one perceives the True Reality; this, however, is merely the measure of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). If one awakens to this, there is liberation. (According to Paramārtha, "that which is known" is itself a delusion.

The first four lines clarify the dharmas to be practiced; the subsequent four lines clarify the person who realizes them. These four lines explain both the subject and object together as being entirely the measure of the conceptualizing mind. If one awakens to the fact that this measure of the conceptualizing mind is unreal...

One immediately attains ultimate liberation). Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of awakening: namely, the awakening of discernment (*pravicaya-buddhi*) and the awakening that establishes through the grasping and attachment to the characteristics of false discrimination (*vikalpa-lakṣaṇa-parigraha-abhiniveśa-pratisthāpana-buddhi*).

(According to Paramārtha: "There are two kinds of awakening-wisdom, namely, the wisdom of discernment and the wisdom that takes up characteristics, discriminates, clings, and establishes. [The former] takes the awakening of discernment as true awakening; the latter takes the awakening of establishment as [false].")

"Deluded awakening. Mahāmati, as for "investigative awakening," it refers to when one investigates the self-nature and characteristics of the essence [of phenomena], and having discerned them, finds them to be unobtainable as they transcend the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*);

this is called investigative awakening. (If one realizes that the self-nature and characteristics of the essence are fundamentally empty and quiescent, and having selected and examined all dharmas, finds not a single dharma to be real—transcending the four propositions such as identity, difference, and so forth—then all dharmas are utterly unobtainable. Mahāmati, those four propositions refer to transcending identity, difference, both, and neither.
"Coexistence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, and neither permanence nor impermanence—these are called the four propositions, Mahāmati.

To be free from these four propositions is called 'all dharmas' (the *ṭīkā* says: 'Therefore it is said that all dharmas are free [from conceptual extremes]'). Mahāmati, one should study and practice the examination of all dharmas as being free from these four propositions.
Mahāmati, what is meant by the establishment of the perception of the characteristics of false discrimination through grasping and attachment?"

To grasp through false discrimination, to be attached to the characteristics of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion—which are unreal false discriminations—and to establish based upon attachment to the signs of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) through [fallacious] propositions, reasons, and examples; this is called the establishment based on grasping and attachment to the characteristics of false discrimination.

This is known as the two kinds of characteristics of awakening. (Paramārtha translates this as: "It means that regarding the natures of the various great elements—solidity, moisture, heat, and motion—one grasps their signs and becomes attached to them, which is empty...")

To falsely establish [doctrines] through propositions, reasons, and examples is called the conceptualization of grasping at signs (*nimittagraha-vikalpa*). To establish wisdom through attachment is called the characteristic of the two types of awakening-wisdom (*bodhi-jñāna-lakṣaṇa*).

If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes these two characteristics of awakening—the characteristic of the selflessness of persons and phenomena—and thoroughly understands skillful means, he attains the awakening that nothing exists;

he observes the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), attains the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), enters into one hundred samādhis, and attains various distinguished samādhis, seeing one hundred [Buddhas].
The Buddha and one hundred bodhisattvas know the events of the past and future for one hundred kalpas each; their light illuminates one hundred buddha-fields.

(If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva integrates the true and the false, accomplishes these two aspects of awakening, realizes the emptiness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*), and understands that a self cannot be apprehended, then through the awakening to non-existence, they skillfully investigate on the stage of practice and understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) and immediately attains the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).

They enter one hundred samādhi-doors, such as the Mahāyāna-āloka-samādhi. By the power of these differentiated samādhis, they see one hundred Buddhas and even have their light illuminate one hundred buddha-fields. Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "When a bodhisattva enters the first stage, they realize ten sets of one hundred gates of illumination. First, [regarding...]

1. In a single kṣaṇa, one realizes one hundred samādhis. 2. With the pure divine eye, one sees one hundred buddha-fields. 3. By the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), one can shake one hundred buddha-worlds. 4. One can travel to one hundred buddha-worlds to teach and transform sentient beings. 5.

One can, with a single body, manifest one hundred types of physical forms so that sentient beings may see them. 6. One can bring to maturity one hundred types of sentient beings who are to be transformed. 7. For the sake of benefiting others, one can maintain the body and remain in the world for one hundred kalpas. 8. One can know the events of one hundred kalpas of the past and the future. 9.

One can, through wisdom, enter the "Gate of Illumination of One Hundred Dharmas" (*śatadharmaprakāśamukha*), penetrating and thoroughly understanding them. 10. One can, with the body, observe one hundred types of retinues. (In the subsequent stages, these qualities increase tenfold. This is the knowledge of the characteristics of the progressively higher stages (*uttarottarabhūmilakṣaṇajñāna*).
Through the empowerment of the Dharma-cloud of sovereign power over great vows and sublime spiritual faculties, one shall attain the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening;

by firmly binding the mind to the ten inexhaustible phrases, one matures sentient beings through various transformations, adorns them with radiant light, and attains the samādhi of the noble bliss of self-awakening (the second stage, Vimalā-bhūmi, up to the stage of the Tathāgata, all constitute the accomplishment of the ten inexhaustible phrases within the first stage; this is seen in the *Avataṃsaka*).

(The remaining meanings of the *Śūraṅgama* and other sūtras are self-evident in their texts. Furthermore, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, you should skillfully understand the four great elements and the matter derived from them.

(Because non-Buddhists previously reckoned that there is a substantial nature of the four great elements which produces the characteristics of the four great elements, he next exhorts the Bodhisattva to skillfully realize that the great elements and the derived matter have no reality.

How does a Bodhisattva skillfully understand the four great elements and the derived matter? Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva forms this realization: those who perceive the ultimate truth... [four]... are as follows.

The Great Elements do not arise therein; one should observe that the Great Elements do not arise. Having observed thus, one realizes the limits of names, marks, and conceptual constructions, as well as the limits of what is manifested by one's own mind.
External natures are not real; this is called the limit of conceptual construction manifested by the mind.
Regarding the observation of the three realms, one sees that the nature of the Great Elements and derived matter is free from the four propositions, universally pure, and devoid of "I" and "mine."

Abiding in the self-characteristics of the divisions of the true mark (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*), they are established in the self-characteristic of non-arising. (Paramārtha says: "How does one understand? Mahāmati, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, you should observe those great elements (*mahābhūta*) as truly non-arising.

Since the three realms are merely conceptualization and what is seen by mind-only, there are no external objects. When observing in this way, that which is derived from the great elements is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature; it transcends the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*) and, being without self or what belongs to a self, it abides in the state of reality and establishes the characteristic of non-arising. [Paramārtha: Because the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is eternally quiescent, the four great elements do not arise. Having observed that in the ultimate truth the four great elements do not arise, one then knows the limits of names and characteristics. This is one's own..."]** **Note:** The bracketed section reflects the specific commentary provided by Paramārtha regarding the meaning of the preceding passage.

The core translation of the main text is as follows: Abiding in the self-characteristics of the divisions of the true mark, they are established in the self-characteristic of non-arising. (Paramārtha says: "How does one understand? Mahāmati, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, you should observe those great elements as truly non-arising. Since the three realms are merely conceptualization and what is seen by mind-only, there are no external objects. When observing in this way, that which is derived from the great elements is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature; it transcends the four propositions and, being without self or what belongs to a self, it abides in the state of reality and establishes the characteristic of non-arising. [Paramārtha: Because the ultimate truth is eternally quiescent, the four great elements do not arise. Having observed that in the ultimate truth the four great elements do not arise, one then knows the limits of names and characteristics. This is one's own...]")

Because external natures do not exist apart from the limits of what is manifested by the mind, one should skillfully contemplate that the nature of the four great elements and their derivative matter is fundamentally non-existent. Being free from the four extremes (*catuskoṭi*), there is neither impurity nor non-impurity; thus, one is free from "I" and "mine.

By thoroughly knowing the self-characteristics of phenomena as they abide in their suchness, one realizes that these self-characteristics are unarisen. Mahāmati, how do those four great elements give rise to derivative matter?

It is said that through the delusion of moisture, the great element of water arises within and without. (The water element has moisture as its nature; it is like the moisture produced by the *śubhavyūha* jewel, where the light of fire rises and steams, thereby producing moisture.)

The water-element wheel contains the worlds of the ten directions; this is it. From the great element of the delusion of capability arise the internal and external fire-elements (*tejodhātu*). (Real-śāstra: "Capability produces intense flames. The fire-element takes intense flaming as its nature;

this is the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*’s statement that when the solid jewel of awareness is formed and the radiant wind emerges, the wind and gold rub against each other, thereby producing the light of fire, which is the nature of transformation.

From the great element of the delusion of agitation arise the internal and external wind-elements (*vāyudhātu*). (The wind-element takes agitation as its nature; this is the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*’s statement that because the clarity of awareness and the dullness of emptiness depend upon one another, they form agitation, whereby the wind-wheel arises to support the world-system.)
This is so. The great elements (*mahābhūta*) arise from the conceptualization of form through cutting and severing, producing the internal and external earth elements.

(In the *Ṛkṣa-sūtra*, it says: "Cutting and severing form constitutes the divisions of form. The earth element takes these divisions of form as its nature; this is like the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* where fire ascends and water descends, alternating to establish solidity, and moisture forms the vast ocean while dryness forms the islands and sandbanks.

This describes the four great elements of the external realm. Furthermore, it says: "Solidity is earth; moisture is water; warm touch is fire; movement is wind. This describes the four great elements of the internal realm. There have been those who attempted to correlate the five elements with the four great elements of the external realm, yet they failed to realize that outside of metal, wood, water, fire, and earth, there remains only wind.

It is likewise with the wheel: gold originates from earth, and wood exists because of earth; thus, both substances belong to the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*). By inferring from this, they do not exceed four in number. For instance, there are those who correlate the four internal elements with the five phases (*pañca-bhūta*):

as medical practitioners take the heart to be fire, the liver to be wood, the kidneys to be water, the lungs to be metal, and the spleen to be earth. Although these five entities each have their own specific functions, one must realize that they all likewise belong to the earth element.

Is this not what the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (or *Awakening of Faith*) means when it says that hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, marrow, brain, and impurities—all material forms—return to earth? Inferring from this, they likewise do not exceed four in number. Therefore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke only of the four great elements regarding the internal and external realms.

This may be called an enlightened instruction; however, while the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* traces the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) back to "awakened clarity" (*jue-ming*), this scripture traces them to their arising from "delusory thought" (*wangxiang*). Thus, each places "delusory thought" above the great elements.

One thereby knows that crawling through the three realms and brewing the four modes of birth are all the fault of awakened clarity and delusory thought. Matter and empty space are both clung to as false truths; the five aggregates (*skandha*) gather, and the matter produced by the four great elements arises.

(This is because one cannot understand that the four great elements fundamentally lack the characteristic of arising, yet falsely calculates that matter and space together constitute a false truth, and further falsely recognizes the five aggregates as deriving from the four great elements.)

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) enclose empty space, it is called the body. Within this, the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*) combine through causes and conditions to produce the seeds of consciousness. Having obtained these seeds, they act in concert to perform various functions, and so forth.
"Mahāmati, as for 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*), it is because it delights in the traces and objects of various realms that it continues into other destinies (*gati*).

[This means that] 'consciousness' refers to the deluded consciousness within the aforementioned five aggregates (*skandha*). Due to being deluded regarding the True Mind, the five aggregates, six sense bases (*āyatana*), twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are all the traces and objects of consciousness. Because the deluded consciousness takes pleasure in and clings to these various traces and objects..."

(The continuity of karma and rebirth persists without interruption among other realms of existence. Mahāmati, the four great elements such as earth and so forth, as well as the derived forms, have the four great elements as their conditions;

they do not have those [other] four great elements as their conditions. (The Tathāgata takes up the opponent's statement regarding the false truth that the four great elements and derived forms serve as conditions, and refutes it accordingly, stating that the four great elements do not serve as conditions for derived forms. Why is this?
Because when the nature, form, characteristics, location, activity, and application are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) do not arise.
The nature of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) arises from the conjunction of causes, conditions, and the application of effort;

it is not formless. (Paramārtha says: "Why? Because if a dharma possesses form and characteristics, it is something produced, not something formless. Therefore, the characteristics of matter produced by the four great elements are the false imaginings of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and not mine.

(The New Translation says: "It is not that the four great elements act as the cause for the great elements; rather, all are manifested by the mind. Thus, it concludes: 'These characteristics of matter produced by the great elements are the false conceptualizations of the non-Buddhists.'"")

Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the characteristic of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the aggregates (*skandha*). (Note: This refutes the false calculations of the aforementioned non-Buddhists regarding the arising of the five aggregates from the intrinsic nature of matter produced by the four great elements.

What is the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates? It refers to the five aggregates. What are the five? They are form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Among them, the four aggregates other than form—namely sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—are not form. (Note: These four aggregates are not material forms. Mahāmati, as for "form," it consists of the four great elements.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived forms (*bhautika*) each have distinct characteristics.

It is not that there are four numbers [of categories] for formless things as there are for space. For example, Mahāmati, space transcends numerical characteristics; it is apart from number, yet through false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one speaks of "one space. (Iśvara says:

Mahāmati, "form" refers to the four great elements and their derived forms, the characteristics of which are each different. Sensation and the other aggregates are not form. Mahāmati, "non-form" refers to the aggregates, which are like space and do not possess four numbers. Mahāmati, for example, space exceeds all numerical characteristics, yet through discrimination one says, "This is space.")

"O Great Wisdom, emptiness is like space; space is fundamentally without measure or number, yet it is falsely described by a single word. Thus, the aggregates (*skandhas*) transcend the characteristics of number and are free from number;

they are free from existence and non-existence, and are free from the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*). These characteristics of number are the speech of the foolish, not that of the noble ones. (The various aggregates are like space; transcending the characteristics of number, they are free from number;

being free from existence and non-existence, they are free from the four propositions. [New Commentary states: From here on, he further refutes that the five aggregates are all empty and lack the characteristic of self-nature, not merely that the aggregate of form and the four great elements are unreal. O Great Wisdom."
The Noble Ones are like an illusion, possessing various forms and images that are free from the conceptualization of being either different or non-different;

they are also like dreams or reflections, for the body of a person is free from being either different or non-different. Therefore, Mahāmati, the movement of noble wisdom is identical to the manifestation of the false discrimination of the aggregates (*skandha*). [Paramārtha says:

"The Noble Ones merely speak of what is produced like an illusion as being a mere conventional designation, free from difference or non-difference, like a dream or a reflection, having nothing else apart from it; because they do not understand the sphere of activity of noble wisdom, they see the various aggregates appearing before them through discrimination. This means that noble wisdom is identical to the various aggregates.]

Because that which manifests through deluded conceptualization is no different from what is manifested by the deluded conceptualizations of ordinary fools, the *Zhongjing* (Mirror of the Source) says: "The aggregates (*skandhas*) of sentient beings across the ten dharma realms and the aggregates of the Buddhas differ not in the slightest degree; the Buddha-activities of the three periods of time and the four modes of conduct of sentient beings are all perfectly complete.
This is called the characteristic of the self-nature of the aggregates. You should eliminate them;

having eliminated them, you shall preach the Dharma of tranquility to sever all heterodox views within all Buddha-fields. (The *Xinshuo* [New Explanation] says: "This means that the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena has been devoid of any characteristic of transition since the very beginning. Mahāmati speaks of tranquility.
During periods of stillness, one purifies the vision of the selflessness of phenomena (Dharmānātman; translated by Liu Zhi as "realizing the mark of pure selflessness").
Upon entering the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), one attains mastery over immeasurable samādhis and the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*).

Having attained the Illusion-like Samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*), one penetrates ultimate power and luminous mastery, gathering, benefiting, and sustaining all sentient beings, just as the great earth supports and nurtures all things.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s universal salvation of sentient beings is also like this.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of nirvāṇa among the non-Buddhists (the new commentary states: the preceding section clarified awakened wisdom to distinguish the superiority or inferiority of manifested virtues;

this section clarifies nirvāṇa to discern the correctness or error of those manifested virtues—this refers to the two fruits of the transformation of the basis, namely *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*). What are the four? They are: the intrinsic nature of self-nature, and the absence of self-nature.
Nirvāṇa as various characteristics and the non-existence of nature; nirvāṇa as the non-existence of the self-characteristics and self-nature [of dharmas];
nirvāṇa as the cessation of the continuous flow of the individual and common characteristics of the aggregates (*skandhas*);

these are called the four kinds of nirvāṇa of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and are not the Dharma I teach. (The new commentary states: The non-Buddhists reckon that the essence and nature of all phenomena exist, which they call "nature and self-nature"; subsequently, when these are removed and deemed non-existent, they call it "non-nature. They take the *pradhāna* (the Primordial Essence) as nirvāṇa.)

There are those who reckon that the various phenomena (dharmas) possess characteristics and names, which constitute their manifold appearances and natures; yet they later contemplate these as being nameless and devoid of nature, taking the *puruṣa* (spiritual self) to be *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, there are those who reckon that appearances and natures exist as names and intrinsic characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*, *svabhāva*), yet they later contemplate these as being nameless and devoid of nature, taking false awakening to be *nirvāṇa*.

These three types above are specifically the reckonings of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Then there are those who sever the flow of the five aggregates (*skandha*) through the six paths of existence, taking the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) to be *nirvāṇa*; this is the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). If one sees that the five aggregates exist, this is likewise the same as the non-Buddhists. [Note:

The original meaning is the same as this [text], all of which point to the latter type as the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles. If one were to claim that these are the four kinds of *nirvāṇa* of the non-Buddhists and not the Dharma taught by me, upon examination, it seems these are not the [nirvāṇa] of the two vehicles.]

Regarding the various attachments described in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, non-Buddhists establish that within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the manifestation of five [aspects] constitutes *nirvāṇa*. Some even claim it is because the two states of suffering and pleasure in the four dhyānas have perished, and one no longer undergoes the nature of saṃsāric birth and death;
thus, this sutra defines the severance of the continuous flow of the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) within the five aggregates as *nirvāṇa*.

Mahāmati, what I teach is that the cessation of the deluded consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*) is called *nirvāṇa*. (Paramārtha translates this as: "The cessation of the *vijñapti-mati-vijñāna* is called *nirvāṇa*. The new translation states: "The former refers to realizing the realm of self-cognizing wisdom and transforming the *ālayavijñāna*, which is the basis of reliance, into Great *Nirvāṇa*; furthermore, it refers to the cessation of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the intrinsic nature of all consciousnesses.")

"When the *ālayavijñāna* and the *manovijñāna* have transformed their views and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), I and all Buddhas designate this as *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, when it is said specifically that the cessation of the consciousness that cognizes the objects of discrimination is called *nirvāṇa*, although there are differences between these general and specific designations, they both intend for the seeds, latent tendencies, and active manifestations of all consciousnesses to be extinguished together.
(This can be seen in the subsequent question and answer. Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, do you not establish the eight consciousnesses?

The Buddha said: "I do establish them, Mahāmati. Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "If you do establish them, why is it that one is liberated from the *manovijñāna* and not from the [other] seven consciousnesses?"
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Because of that cause and that object of perception (*ālambana*), the seven consciousnesses arise.

(That cause and that object of perception both derive from the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); that is to say, this consciousness is able to give rise to delusions and create karma. Paramārtha says: "Mahāmati, if they are established [as existing], why do you say only that the mental consciousness ceases and not the seven consciousnesses? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Because it serves as their cause and their object of perception, the seven consciousnesses are able to arise.

Paramārtha’s intention means: because that mental consciousness serves as the cause and the perceived object, the seven consciousnesses are able to arise. The meaning of this sutra is: if the mental consciousness does not act as the cause and does not perceive objects, [the seven consciousnesses do not arise].

Then the seven consciousnesses will naturally not arise. As for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it arises from the conditions of conceptualization and attachment to segmented objects; its habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) grow and nourish the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Together with the *manas*, it gives rise to a non-disintegrating semblance of a body through the conceptualization and attachment to "I" and "mine. (Paramārtha says:

When the mental consciousness discriminates objects and gives rise to attachment, various habitual tendencies are produced which nourish the storehouse consciousness. From this, the *manas*—together with the grasping at "I" and "mine"—functions as a continuous思量 (*manana*) without a distinct physical form. The storehouse consciousness, in turn, takes these as its objects of perception.

The collection of minds arises through mutual causality by clinging to the objective realm manifested by one’s own mind. Because the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) undergoes transformation due to causes such as objective conditions, it gives rise to the sense organs, the body, seeds, and the receptacle world;

furthermore, because one clings to the objective realm manifested by one’s own mind, it is called "the arising of the collection of minds through clinging. The eight consciousnesses are the cause for the manifestation of the seven consciousnesses; the seven consciousnesses are the cause for the defiled habituation of the six consciousnesses;

the six consciousnesses are the cause for the discrimination of the five consciousnesses; the five consciousnesses are the cause for the grasping of objects by the six consciousnesses. Without the six consciousnesses, the five consciousnesses could not grasp objects; without the seven consciousnesses, the six consciousnesses could not discriminate; without the eighth consciousness, the seventh consciousness could not undergo defiled habituation; and without the seventh consciousness, the eighth consciousness could not manifest.

Therefore it is said that they arise through mutual dependence. For example, just as waves on the ocean arise or cease when blown by the wind of objective realms manifested from one’s own mind, so it is with this:

when the *manovijñāna* (consciousness) ceases, the seven consciousnesses also cease. (The ocean is a metaphor for the *ālayavijñāna*; the waves are a metaphor for the seven consciousnesses; and the wind of objective realms is a metaphor for the *manovijñāna*.

If these waves of the seven consciousnesses are not blown upon by the wind of objective realms—namely, form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects—they will no longer arise or cease. Hence it is said that when the *manovijñāna* ceases, the seven consciousnesses also cease. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this, said:
He spoke this verse in accordance with the meaning:

"I do not [take] the nature of nirvāṇa" (Paramārtha says: "I do not grasp at nirvāṇa"); "that which is produced and its marks" (Śikṣānanda says: "I do not [grasp at] self-nature, nor that which is produced, nor at marks").

"Through the extinction of these delusive thoughts and the *vijñapti*-flame, I am in nirvāṇa. (This means that the Tathāgata does not grasp at the nature of nirvāṇa, nor at that which is produced, nor at marks.)

The non-Buddhists perceive that the cessation of consciousness, which is merely known through delusive appearances, constitutes their *ātman* and *nirvāṇa*. That [consciousness] arises from its causes and its objects of perception; it forms the body of the mental faculty (*manas*)—[the note says:
"it arises from the six consciousnesses to form the body of the seventh consciousness"]—and acts as the cause for those [other] consciousnesses.

This mind is the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which serves as the support for all the [evolving] consciousnesses. Just as when the great flow of water is exhausted, waves no longer arise, so too is it with the mental consciousness.

The extinction of various consciousnesses so that they do not arise (just as when a current is exhausted there are no waves, this serves as a metaphor for how, when the seeds of the mental consciousness within the ālayavijñāna are extinguished forever in their continuity, the remaining seven consciousnesses also cease accordingly).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the general characteristics of the discrimination of the self-nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

If you and the other Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas skillfully distinguish these general characteristics of the discrimination of the self-nature of conceptualization, you will transcend conceptualization, attain the noble realization of self-awareness (*pratyātma-ārya-adhigama*),

and, being well-versed in the common paths of the non-Buddhists, you will thoroughly perceive and sever the conceptualizations of grasped and grasper, as well as the various marks of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

One no longer engages in the activity of the imagined nature through deluded conceptualization. (Iśvara says: "I shall now explain the distinct characteristics of the imagined nature so that you and all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas may thoroughly understand this meaning, transcend all deluded conceptualizations, realize the realm of noble wisdom, and know the teachings of the non-Buddhists.
One remains far removed from the discrimination of grasper and grasped, and among the various aspects of the dependent nature, one no longer clings to the imagined characteristics.

[The preceding section] stated that the cessation of deluded conceptualizing consciousness is called *nirvāṇa*; here, it precisely clarifies the cessation of the common characteristics of the discrimination of deluded conceptualizing consciousness. That is to say, there are twelve kinds of distinctions within the discrimination of the imagined nature, all of which ultimately converge upon the characteristic of deluded conceptualization.)

If you and other bodhisattvas are well able to discern the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the conceptual differentiation of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), then you will depart from all delusions and reach the state of noble self-realization (*pratyātma-ārya-gati*). Therein, seeing the dharmas of the common paths of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and so forth, you awaken to and depart from the delusion of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).

This "departing" is synonymous with "severing. As for the "nature of activity," it refers to the characteristic of the essence of phenomena (*dharma-tattva-lakṣaṇa*). Mahāmati, what is meant by the general characteristics of the conceptual differentiation of the imagined nature?

It refers to: (1) the delusion of verbal expression; (2) the delusion of the objects expressed; (3) the delusion of characteristics; (4) the delusion of utility; and (5) the delusion of the nature of things.
Because of conceptualization, there is the perception of conceptualization; conceptualization is formed, conceptualization arises, and conceptualization does not cease.
Conceptualization continues in succession, and conceptualization binds or does not bind. This is called the general characteristic of the discrimination of the self-nature of conceptualization.
Mahāmati, what is meant by the conceptualization of verbal expression? It refers to the attachment to various wonderful sounds, songs, and melodies; this is called verbal expression.
Mahāmati, what is the conceptualization of the object of discourse (*abhilāpya-vastu-vikalpa*)?
It refers to the conceptualization of speech that arises based on the intrinsic nature of the object of discourse—which is known by noble wisdom—and which one clings to as having real existence.

This is called the conceptualization of the object of discourse. (Mañjuśrī says: "It means clinging to the existence of an object of discourse as being the sphere realized by noble wisdom, and giving rise to speech based upon this. [This conceptualization involves the five dharmas and the three natures]. Mahāmati.)
What is the discrimination of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vikalpa*)? It refers to the attachment to the various things previously described, such as the mirage of a thirsty deer;

it is the attachment to the characteristics of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion in all natures. This is called the discrimination of characteristics (this refers to the conceptualization that the four great elements exist).
Mahāmati, what is the discrimination of benefit (*lābha-vikalpa*)? It refers to the delight in various kinds of gold, silver, and precious jewels; this is called benefit.

"Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—this refers to the firm grasping and attachment to the existence of wealth and profit. Mahāmati asked: "What is meant by conceptual construction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*)? It means that one maintains an intrinsic nature as being thus and not otherwise;

such a conceptual construction based on wrong views is called conceptual construction of intrinsic nature. (Paramārtha says: "It means that through wrong views one discriminates in this way: 'This intrinsic nature is determined and not otherwise. ... For example, as when one calculates that the four great elements each have a distinct intrinsic nature:

the earth element is solid, the water element is moist, the fire element is hot, and the wind element is mobile, and so forth, up to the point where both the ultimate and conventional truths each have their own distinct intrinsic natures. Mahāmati.

What is causal conceptualization (*hetu-vikalpa*)? It refers to the arising of the characteristic of causality through the conceptual differentiation of existence and non-existence regarding causes and conditions;

this is called causal conceptualization (meaning that one differentiates existence and non-existence within causes and conditions, and because of these causal characteristics, [the notion] is produced). Mahāmati, what is objective conceptualization (*dṛṣṭi-vikalpa*)?

It refers to the conceptualization and attachment to the false views of externalists—such as existence, non-existence, identity, difference, both, or neither; this is called objective conceptualization.
(This refers to the arising of the fourfold views based on existence and non-existence. Mahāmati, what is the *pariniṣpanna-vikalpa*?

It is the formation of a definitive doctrine through the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self"; this is called *pariniṣpanna-vikalpa*. (This means calculating "self" and "what belongs to self" within the five aggregates and speaking of false dharmas. Mahāmati, what is the *utpatti-vikalpa*?

It is the arising of attachment by taking existence and non-existence as its object; this is called *utpatti-vikalpa*. (This means giving rise to a mind of clinging toward the existence or non-existence of things based upon various conditions. Mahāmati...
Mahāmati, what is the delusion of non-arising? It refers to the view that all natures are fundamentally unarisen and lack seeds or causal conditions;

that they arise without causes and are without a body. This is called the delusion of non-arising. (Śikṣānanda says: it means reckoning that all dharmas are originally unarisen; that before the various conditions existed, there was already an essence that did not arise from causes;

[and] reckoning that all dharmas are fundamentally unarisen and lack an essential nature, such that those arising from causes and conditions do not depend on them, being without cause and without effect. Mahāmati, what is the delusion of continuity?

That is to say, the mutual continuity [of these two] is like gold and thread; this is called the "discrimination of continuity" (saṃtati-vikalpa). [Paramārtha says: "This and that are mutually connected, like gold and thread.

Regarding the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), one discriminates that cause and effect exist together and are mutually connected, just as when gold is made into thread, it is both in the thread and in the gold. Mahāmati, what is the "discrimination of bondage and non-bondage"?
It refers to the attachment to the causes and conditions of bondage, such as the skillful means of a person, whether in terms of being bound or being liberated.

This is called the false discrimination of bondage and non-bondage (Iśvara says: it refers to grasping at causes as being able to bind and there being something bound; for example, a person uses the skillful means of a rope to bind someone and then later releases them).

It is like calculating that there are afflictions (*kleśa*) that can bind sentient beings, and that later, through the cultivation of the path, one can release them—just as a person first binds someone with a rope and later releases them; it is exactly like this.

Regarding this false discrimination of self-nature, the general characteristics of differentiation, all foolish commoners (*bāla*) cling to existence and non-existence. Mahāmati, they cling to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Those who are attached to conceptualization cling to various imagined natures (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) that manifest like illusions in various forms.

Ordinary people, through their deluded thoughts, perceive various diverse illusions. (Realśa says: "Just as one perceives various objects based on an illusion, the ignorant, through discrimination, perceive them as different from the illusion.

... Within the dependent origination (*paratantra*), various imagined natures arise; just as one sees various illusory things based on incantations, the foolish, through their deluded thoughts, perceive them as different from the illusion and imagine them to be various real entities. O Mahāmati, as for illusion and...
The various manifestations are neither different nor non-different [from illusion]. If they were different, illusion would not be the cause of the various manifestations;
if they were non-different, there would be no distinction between illusion and the various manifestations, yet a distinction is perceived. Therefore, they are neither different nor non-different.

For this reason, Mahāmati, you and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should understand that the nature of the imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) arising from conditions like an illusion is neither different nor non-different.
"Do not be attached to existence or non-existence. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The mind is bound by objects; conceptualization and cognition follow along with them. (The new commentary states: 'The deluded mind of ordinary beings is bound by the objects of birth and death;

conceptual cognition follows along with those objects. Here, 'awakening' refers to deluded awakening. When there is nothing at all, the supreme, equalizing wisdom arises. (The "nothingness" is the most excellent state, where there is no self...)

Because it is the equality of other-natures (*parabhāva*) and because the true nature (*tathatā*) is perfectly luminous, wisdom arises. Regarding the self-nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it exists [in the sense of being imputed], yet it does not exist within dependent origination (*paratantra*).
Alternatively, one may grasp dependent origination as being non-conceptual. Mañjuśrī said: "It exists within false imagination (*parikalpa*), but it does not exist within dependent origination;

false imagination is delusion that grasps at dependent origination, which is free from discrimination. The new commentary states: "It is like relying on a vine and imagining it to be a snake; the deluded mind says it exists, but the substance of the vine in dependent origination is actually not the nature of a snake. This cites dependent origination to refute false imagination. [The text continues with] various constituent parts.
If birth is like an illusion, then those characteristics are not established; because there are various deluded thoughts, they are not established.

(This means that although the various members of dependent origination arise, they are all like illusions and thus the members are not established. Although the characteristics of dependent origination exist in their variety, they belong to deluded thought and thus those characteristics are not established.

This cites deluded thought to refute dependent origination. Those characteristics are errors, all arising from the bonds of the mind; one has no true knowledge regarding dependent origination and is deluded.

One perceives the various unreal faults of the characteristics of dependent origination as arising from the mind’s bondage to objects; because one does not understand that these are merely false imaginings and lacks true knowledge, one discriminates and calculates within dependent origination that things either exist or do not exist.

This verse shows that dependent origination arises from false imagination. These various natures of false imagination are themselves that dependent origination of false imagination, which possesses various aspects.

Regarding "these various natures of false imagination are themselves that dependent origination": it means that false imagination has no inherent nature, yet it exists because of that dependent origination; since it exists due to dependent origination...

Because there are various natures, one further conceives of a truly existent nature of delusive discrimination (*vikalpa*) within dependent origination; this verse [explains] that delusive discrimination arises from dependent origination. Regarding the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and the third, birth without cause:
the new commentary states that the three realms of birth and death, existence and non-existence, and all phenomena arise from the false conceptualization of conditions;

this is the conventional truth. If one realizes that conditions have no inherent nature and delusive discrimination ceases, this is the sphere of activity of the sages, which is the ultimate truth. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "That which is known by those who have left the world is called the ultimate truth; that which is known by worldly people is called the conventional truth. Non-Buddhists establish two [truths].

The Fifteen Truths Clarifying that the Effect Exists within the Cause: First, from the primordial darkness (*avyakta*) arises intellect (*buddhi*); second, from intellect arises the ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*); third, from the ego-consciousness arise form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and so forth.
Because they falsely conceptualize and discriminate without knowing the root of dependent origination, the Buddha refutes them as being produced without a cause.

When the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) spoken of through false conceptualization is severed, it is the realm of the noble ones' self-realized wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*). For example, just as in the practice of cultivation, various things appear within a single [object]. At that point...

The various characteristics of delusive conceptualization are thus. (This analogy refutes the pervasive nature of delusive conceptualization. For example, when followers of the Two Vehicles practice various contemplative exercises, if they form the perception of blue, heaven, earth, and all things without exception appear blue.

Because there is no place that is not blue, yet they perceive blue, it is due to the transformations of the mind; thus, within a single objective field of color, various appearances such as yellow, red, and white manifest.

Yet, in its true substantial nature, there were originally none of those various characteristics; what manifests is merely delusive conceptualization. Therefore it is said: "The characteristics of delusive conceptualization are thus. It is like various cataracts and delusive conceptualizations.
