Various forms appear as if obscured by cataracts; though there is no color and no non-color, one fails to realize their dependent origination. (This analogy refutes the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) based on causes and conditions:

just as when the eyes have various cataracts, due to the discrimination of false imagination, colors such as blue, yellow, red, and white appear; yet the cataracts themselves are fundamentally neither color nor non-color, and their dependent origination is likewise—because of attachment to these appearances, it is called "non-awakening.
For example, when refined gold is free from all impurities, and space is free from clouds and cataracts, false imagination is purified.

It is likewise so (this analogy serves to sever the delusions, falsehoods, and faults of dependent origination; thus, the nature of perfect completion is like pure gold free from dross, or like space devoid of clouds and impurities).

There is no nature of delusion, yet there is the establishment of dependent origination and its refutation—all arise from the destruction caused by delusion (meaning that the natures of delusion and dependent origination are fundamentally non-existent;

to conceive of what is not as existing, or to conceive of what is not as non-existing, constitutes both establishment and refutation, all of which are self-destroyed by delusion through the vision of reality as it is).

If false conceptualization (*parikalpita*) has no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), yet possesses the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), then that which is without nature possesses nature, and that which possesses nature arises from what is without nature.

Because it depends upon false conceptualization as its cause, one attains the characteristics of that dependent origination; these names and forms arise in constant succession, giving rise to various false conceptualizations.

When these conceptualizations are ultimately not established, one transcends all false conceptualizations. (That false conceptualization is without nature while dependent origination possesses nature is precisely because it is without nature.)

The existence of intrinsic nature arises from the absence of intrinsic nature; this is because, due to deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), there is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Thus, characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and names (*nāman*) arise like a shadow following a form, giving rise to all manner of false constructs.

If one can know that these falsely constructed phenomena are ultimately unreal, then one transcends all deluded characteristics and names—these being precisely what is meant by "characteristics and names. Thereafter, wisdom becomes pure; this is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Regarding deluded conceptualization, there are twelve links of dependent origination and six types of self-awakening. Know that these are without distinction. (Having thus transcended all deluded conceptualizations, one achieves...)

Pure wisdom thoroughly understands that the twelve kinds of false conceptualization and the six types of dependent origination exist merely as names and lack any substantial reality. Furthermore, within the realm of the noble self-awakened realization, one understands that the *jñeyāvaraṇa* (obstruction to knowledge) and those false conceptualizations and dependent originations are all empty, signless, and without distinction;

therefore, the subsequent text establishes the five dharmas and so forth as the true reality. As for the six types of dependent origination, they are precisely the six kinds of causes mentioned previously among the conditions and causes.
The five dharmas constitute the true nature (*svabhāva*), which has three aspects; when one practices by discerning these, they do not transcend suchness (*tathatā*). (From the *Zongjing*).

It is said that when one is deluded regarding suchness (*tathatā*), one gives rise to the conceptualization of names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa-vikalpa*). When one awakens to the root of names and characteristics as being like an illusion, it is then termed wisdom (*jñāna*); thus, there is no longer the conceptualization of names and characteristics, and there is only suchness-wisdom (*tathatā-jñāna*). Wisdom is established because of suchness, yet the essence of wisdom is also empty;

since suchness and wisdom are both manifest as originally and eternally quiescent, they are both empty. Now, regarding those who practice: although they may be able to distinguish between the true and the false within the five dharmas and the three natures, they have not yet been able to empty the essence of their wisdom;

therefore, it is said that they do not transcend suchness-as-such (*tathatā-tathatā*). Regarding the various marks and dependent origination: those names give rise to conceptualization, and those various marks of conceptualization arise from those conditions.

[The verse on] arising and birth (the mutual production of the dependent origination of deluded conceptualization): When wisdom observes well that there are no conditions and no deluded conceptualizations, once [reality] is established, it has no nature.

How can there be a realization of deluded conceptualization? (With the wisdom of awakening, one observes that there is no dependent origination nor any deluded conceptualizations; thus, the perfected nature is established. Once the perfected nature is established, there is no nature of existence or non-existence.
Since there is no nature of existence or non-existence, how could there further be a realization of deluded conceptualization? That self-nature of deluded conceptualization establishes two [natures].

The various manifestations of the imagined nature of self-existence (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) are the pure realm of the noble ones. That imagined nature of self-existence refers to the attachment to internal and external dharmas, establishing two kinds of self-nature:

the nature of names (*nāma*) and the nature of things (*vastu*). Although these various manifestations of imagination appear, they are not real; they are naturally pure and constitute the realm of noble wisdom. (Regarding the "nature of names and things," see the first fascicle, under the passage on the two kinds of imagined nature.
Imagination is like the colors in a painting; although it discriminates the various forms and images arising through conditions, it is devoid of [intrinsic reality].

The clinging of sentient beings to substantial entities and the arising of their deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*) regarding dependent origination is likewise so. If these were different from deluded thought, they would rely on the treatises of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). [The New Commentary states:

This clarifies that in the Buddha-dharma, one knows that the dharmas of the dependent origination of birth and death arise from the mind of one’s own deluded thought. If one reckons that the existence or non-existence of all dharmas of birth and death arises from atoms (*paramāṇu*), the principle of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), or a sovereign lord (*īśvara*), this is the doctrine of the non-Buddhists.
Deluded thought speaks of what is imagined; it arises from the conjunction of views. [Real-śa says: Because of various deluded views, one falsely calculates within the false.]

As for the separation from these two types of conceptual construction (*parikalpita*), it is thus established as the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). That is to say, when one speaks of conceptual construction regarding conceptualized objects, these two types of conceptual construction arise because of the perception of the conjunction of the sense faculties, objects, and consciousness;
by being separated from these two types of conceptual construction, it constitutes the perfected nature.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization and the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna).

If I and other Bodhisattvas thoroughly understand the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization and the Single Vehicle, we shall not rely on others to penetrate the Buddha-dharma [that is, the attainment of the body of wisdom as in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra]."
[Attaining awakening] through others. The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon this; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "That which was known by previous sages has been transmitted from one to another;

yet, regarding the absence of intrinsic nature in conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, dwelling alone in a secluded place, observe it through their own self-awakening (*pratyātma-adhigama*), not depending on others."

There are two kinds of afflictions: (1) the afflictions of views, called *vikalpa-kleśa*, which are partially severed within the minds of those in the first stage; and (2) the afflictions of cultivation, called *sahaja-kleśa*, which can only be completely severed when one reaches the fulfillment of the ten stages.

Even when these two afflictions are exhausted, there remains the residual habit of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*); only by severing this residual habit does one realize the awakening of a Buddha. Therefore, the commentary identifies these two afflictions as the four abodes of affliction (*catur-vāsa-kleśa*) and the affliction of ignorance.

[The New Commentary states: "Among all obstacles, afflictions are the most severe. Furthermore, their specific characteristics are shown here so that students may thoroughly treat them. This is called the awakening of a Buddha, whereas for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—

One who realizes this Dharma is also called a Buddha; for these reasons, I speak of the One Vehicle (because both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are also able to realize the two aforementioned dharmas of selflessness, I speak of the One Vehicle). At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

Thoroughly knowing the two kinds of selflessness, severing the afflictions of the two obstacles (as *Iśvara* says, removing the two obstacles and the two afflictions), and being forever free from the two types of death—
this is called the Buddha’s awakening.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, for what reason did the World-Honored One proclaim these words in the midst of the great assembly:
'I was all the Buddhas of the past, as well as [various beings] in diverse births;
at such times I was the Cakravartin King Māndhātṛ (Liu-chi and Shi-cha both render this as King Śīrṣa-jāta), the six-tusked great elephant, and the parrot Śakra?'"

The *Sūtra on the Hundred Thousand Births of Śikhin and the Seer Sunetra* and others state [this]. (Bodhiruci says: "Such as these hundred thousand sūtras all speak of the Jātaka; Paramārtha says: 'They speak of the matters of the hundred thousand Jātakas.

[Regarding the term "Śikhin,"] because the Buddha previously taught the dharmas such as the awakening to the two kinds of selflessness, he was named "Buddha. Mahāmati thought: "Past Buddhas were so named because they awakened to these dharmas; now the World-Honored One has also awakened to these dharmas and is thus called a Buddha.

Although the awakening to the Path is one, the past and present are different. How can you say, 'I am all the Buddhas of the past'? Furthermore, the *Jātaka Sūtras* state that the Tathāgata, in the past, performed various [deeds]."

Because he has taken birth in hundreds of thousands of lives—such as when he acted as a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), Śakra, the elephant Bhadramukha, or the parrot—it is asked about this matter by citing instances that appear contradictory (as seen in the *Jātaka* and other sūtras).

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "By virtue of four kinds of equality" (according to the secret intention of the fourfold equality in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*), the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims these words in the midst of the great assembly: "At that time, I was Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa."
The Buddha said: "What are the four equalities? They are the equality of letters, the equality of speech, the equality of dharmas, and the equality of the body;
these are called the four equalities. Because of these four kinds of equality, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims these words among the great assembly:
'What is the equality of letters? If a letter designates me as a Buddha, that same letter also designates all Buddhas; that letter is itself...'"

The absence of distinction in nature is what is meant by "equality of names" (Iśvara says: "That my name is 'Buddha' and that all Tathāgatas are also named 'Buddha,' and that there is no difference in the name 'Buddha,' is called equality of names").

What is meant by "equality of speech"? It means that just as my sixty-four kinds of Brahma-voice and linguistic characteristics arise, so too do those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas likewise give rise to sixty-four kinds of Brahma-voice and linguistic characteristics. There is no difference.

The nature of the *kalaviṅka* Brahma-voice is without increase, without decrease, and without distinction. (Realśa says: "I produce sixty-four kinds of Brahma-voice speech; all Tathāgatas likewise produce this speech.

The nature of the *kalaviṅka* Brahma-voice is without increase, without decrease, and without distinction. This is called the equality of speech. [The New Commentary] states: The *Guhyakapūrvayoga-sūtra* explains that the Buddha’s voice possesses eight inflections (*vibhakti*):

namely, the nominative, accusative, instrumental, ablative, dative, genitive, locative, and vocative. These eight inflected sounds each possess eight virtues, namely: a harmonious sound, a soft sound, a clear and distinct sound, an easily understood sound, a sound free from error, a sound free from difficulty, [a sound that is pervasive, a sound that is profound, a sound that is majestic, and a sound that is unimpeded].)

The low voice, the great voice, and the deep and far-reaching voice—these eight times eight constitute sixty-four kinds. It is not only Śākyamuni Buddha who possesses these; all Buddhas are likewise so. *Piṅgala* (here translated as "wonderful-voiced bird"):

the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states that the *kalaviṅka* utters a wondrous sound such that neither gods, humans, nor *kiṃnaras* can equal it, except for the voice of the Tathāgata. Therefore, when various sūtras describe the Buddha’s voice, they invariably cite this as a metaphor. What is meant by "the body and so forth"?

It means that there is no difference between my own dharmakāya and the dharmakāya and rūpakāya with its marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of all Buddhas, except for... [the sake of]... for the purpose of... [teaching].

Because he manifests various distinct physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) in order to subdue sentient beings within the various different realms of existence (*gati*), this is called the "equality of body" (*kāyasamatā*).

(The note states: This answers the question regarding the Buddha’s various modes of birth; it means that, apart from the expedient manifestations of various bodies for the purpose of transforming sentient beings of different realms, if it were not so, there would be no distinction. What is the "equality of dharma" (*dharmasamatā*)?
It refers to both myself and those Buddhas having attained the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*). (The new commentary states: *Bodhi* is...)

The "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*) have the meaning of "cause. These thirty-seven factors serve as the causes for awakening in all vehicles and also constitute the limbs of the path (*mārgāṅga*). As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* states: "The limbs of the path are the site of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*); they are the cause of the Dharma-body. These thirty-seven factors comprise seven general categories: 1.

The path that counteracts perversions, namely the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). 2. The path that abandons all laziness, namely the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). 3. The path that brings forth the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), namely the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*). 4. The path of skillful means for clear realization (*abhisamaya*), namely the five faculties (*indriya*). 5. The path of approaching clear realization, namely the five powers (*bala*). 6.

The path that constitutes the essence of clear realization, namely the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). 7. The path that arises subsequent to clear realization, namely the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). The meanings of these are explained elsewhere. Regarding the sequence of these seven categories: having heard the Dharma, one should first...

Following mindfulness and retention, one diligently practices; through diligence, the mind is gathered and becomes supple; through suppleness, the faculties such as faith become established as roots; as these roots increase, they become powers. The seven factors of enlightenment are distinguished, and the eightfold noble path is correctly practiced. To illustrate this Dharma-nature through metaphors: the foundations of mindfulness are like seeds; right effort is like planting them;

the bases of psychic power are like the emerging sprouts; the five faculties are like the taking root of the plant; the five powers are like the growth of the stem and leaves; the seven factors of enlightenment are like the blossoming flowers; and the eightfold noble path is like the ripening of the fruit. That which is realized by all Buddhas is no different; this is called the equality of dharmas (*dharmasamatā*).
Briefly stated, the unobstructed wisdom of the Buddha-dharmas is called the fourfold equality. Therefore, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and so forth...
The Perfectly Awakened One proclaimed these words amidst the great assembly. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, and Kanakamuni—these four, including myself, are equal; I consider them all to be my sons.”
[The Buddha] spoke thus. Mahāmati addressed the Buddha again, saying: "As the World-Honored One has said:
'From the night I attained supreme perfect enlightenment until the night I enter parinirvāṇa, in the interval between them, I have not uttered even a single word, nor have I [taught anything].'"
"It is said that what should be spoken and what is not spoken is the Buddha’s teaching" (Paramārtha says: "The Buddha’s words are non-words").

"World-Honored One, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for what reason do you say that what is not spoken is the Buddha’s teaching? (Paramārtha says: "World-Honored One, based on what meaning do you speak these words:

'Buddha’s words are non-words'? [Mahāmati asks this because the Buddha previously stated: "By means of these four kinds of equality, I have taught my sons, the Bodhisattvas"; therefore, he cites the absence of verbal characteristics to question it]. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is because of two dharmas."
He spoke thus: "What are the two dharmas? They are the dharma realized through one's own attainment and the dharma that has existed from the beginning.
These are called the two dharmas. It is because of these two dharmas that I speak in this way. What is the dharma realized through one's own attainment?
Whatever was attained by those Tathāgatas, I too have attained; it neither increases nor decreases. This is the dharma realized through one's own attainment."
The ultimate realm of the Dharma transcends both verbal conceptualization and the two paths of letters. (This is the ultimate realm of the Dharma realized by each Buddha;

it is the dharma attained spontaneously regarding worldly and trans-worldly matters, without the slightest increase or decrease—this ultimate realm of the Dharma transcends the two modes of speech and writing. What is the "primordially abiding Dharma"?

It refers to the ancient path of the sages, which is like the nature of gold, silver, and so forth, eternally abiding within the *dharmadhātu*. (The ancient path of the sages and the eternally abiding *dharmadhātu* are like the nature of gold and silver: they do not increase while in the ore, nor do they decrease when extracted from the ore.)
Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the *dharmadhātu* remains eternally constant, just like the road leading to that city.

[Bodhiruci says: "It is like the original road to a city. Since the *dharmadhātu* is not something that only becomes eternally constant because a Tathāgata appears in the world, it is like the road leading to that city.

For example, it is like a man traveling through a vast wilderness who sees the level, direct road leading toward an old city; he then follows it into the city and experiences bliss according to his wishes. [Śikṣānanda says: "He stops his wandering."]
[The Buddha] asked, "Mahāmati, what do you think? Did that person create this path and the various pleasures within the city?

[Bodhiruci says: "Did that person first create this path and then enter the city? Did he first create the various adornments? He replied, "No. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "It is likewise with me and all past Buddhas;
the Dharma-realm is eternally abiding. Therefore, it is said: 'I have come from such-and-such...'"
From the night he attained supreme perfect enlightenment until the night he entered parinirvāṇa, in the interval between them, he did not speak a single word, nor has he spoken, nor will he speak.
(This ancient city road was originally level and smooth; it did not come into existence only when that man entered it. The ancient path of the sages is likewise:

it does not exist only because the Tathāgata appeared in the world to preach the Dharma and benefit sentient beings. This means that it is apart from the characteristics of words and speech, existing only in direct realization. Therefore, it is said that "not a single word was spoken. At that time, the World-Honored One...
The World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
From the night I attained enlightenment until the night of my parinirvāṇa, during this interval, I have not uttered a single word.

This is because the Dharma realized by myself abides [of itself]. (Note: "Realized by myself" refers back to the verse's "Dharma realized by oneself," meaning it is not spoken through words. "The Dharma abides" refers back to the verse's "the Dharma-realm abides eternally.")
Furthermore, it is not by means of verbal expression that this non-speaking is clarified;
therefore, I say that there is no distinction whatsoever between those Buddhas and myself (meaning that I and all Buddhas have equally realized this Dharma of non-verbal expression).

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again requested of the World-Honored One: "I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of existence and non-existence regarding all dharmas, so that I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas may depart from the characteristics of existence and non-existence and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall explain it for you."
You have said that Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: “Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati:

“This world relies upon two kinds [of views], namely reliance upon existence and non-existence. (Paramārtha says: ‘The sentient beings of the world mostly fall into two views, namely the view of existence and the view of non-existence.

They fall into the views of nature and non-nature; their views of desire do not depart from the characteristic of departure. (Bodhiruci says: ‘Because they see the existence of all dharmas and see the non-existence of all dharmas. [Note: ‘Not departing’ refers to existence; ‘the characteristic of departure’ refers to non-existence.]”)”

"Those who rely on existence reckon that all dharmas exist; those who rely on non-existence reckon that all dharmas do not exist. Those who fall into the view of being and non-being reckon that all dharmas have 'being' as their nature, and they refute existence by calling it non-being, and name non-being 'non-nature.

Worldly beings who fall into the views of being and non-being merely desire to see the existence of dharmas and the non-existence of dharmas; therefore it is said that their desire to see does not depart from the characteristic of separation.

Mahāmati asked: "What is meant by worldly reliance on existence? It means that the world arises through causes and conditions and is not non-existent. From existence there is arising, not from non-existence. [Paramārtha’s version says: 'It means that causes and conditions truly exist...']"

"Furthermore, Mahāmati, those who say that all dharmas arise [from nothing]—that they do not exist as real entities, yet that real dharmas arise from causes and conditions, rather than arising from non-existent things—are, Mahāmati, speaking of a world that is without cause.

(Note: The non-Buddhists calculate that the world arises from the four great elements, atoms, Īśvara, and so forth; they also say that the four great elements and the like do not arise from causes, which is to say they exist without cause; therefore it is said they speak of a world that is without cause.
Mahāmati, how does the world rely on what is non-existent? It is by first experiencing the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion, and only thereafter falsely [constructing them]."

To conceptually cling to the nature or non-nature of greed, anger, and delusion—[meaning that because one first perceives the nature of greed, anger, and delusion, and subsequently gives rise to false conceptual clinging to this nature as being "non-nature," one relies on non-existence]—is not the case, Mahāmati.

If one does not grasp at the existence of a nature, then the characteristics of that nature are quiescent. (The note states: "If one does not falsely grasp at greed and delusion as having an existent nature, then the nature and characteristics of greed and delusion are originally quiescent;
thus, there is no need to negate existence in order to rely on non-existence. This means that the Tathāgatas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas do not grasp at greed, anger, and delusion.

"Is nature existent or non-existent? (The note says: This clarifies that those of the Three Vehicles know the essence of greed and delusion is free from existence and non-existence; therefore, they do not grasp it as existent, and thus there is no need to eliminate it as if it were existent or non-existent.

"Mahāmati, what herein is meant by 'one who destroys'? (Paramārtha says: "Who herein is the destroyer? [The term "destroying" has the sense of "falling into," meaning: who herein falls into the view of emptiness? Mahāmati said to the Buddha:

"World-Honored One, if one does not subsequently grasp the nature of greed, anger, and delusion after having previously grasped them... (This means: those foolish people, because they grasp greed, anger...)

"It is because one takes the nature of delusion (*moha*) to exist and does not take it to be non-existent; this is how one establishes the meaning of 'non-existence' by means of destroying 'existence.

The Buddha said to Mahāmati, 'Excellent, excellent! You understand me thus' (Paramārtha says: 'You understand my question'). Mahāmati, it is not only the nature and non-nature of greed, anger, and delusion that are destroyed;

the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and even the Buddhas are also destroyed [by this]. This person does not merely refrain from grasping greed, anger, and delusion; rather, those of the three vehicles likewise, by virtue of not grasping greed, anger, and delusion, [are destroyed]."

As for those who have attained the fruit of holiness: why is this? It is because both the internal and external are unobtainable, and because the nature of afflictions is neither different nor non-different.
[The Buddha] says, "Why is this? because the internal body and external objects are unobtainable, and the nature of afflictions is neither one nor many.
Mahāmati, greed, anger, and delusion—whether internal or external—are unobtainable; the nature of greed, anger, and delusion has no substantial body.

Therefore, because there is nothing to grasp (according to the *Ṛṣya*, because there is no substantial nature, and because there is nothing that can be grasped), neither the Buddha, nor the Śrāvakas, nor the Pratyekabuddhas are destroyers.

This is because the self-nature of the Buddha, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas is liberation; bondage and the causes of bondage have no inherent nature. Since the nature of greed, anger, and delusion—both internally and externally—is unattainable, there is no body and no grasping.

Being primordially empty and quiescent, neither existent nor non-existent, the Buddha, Śrāvakas, and so forth are not destroyers. This is because the self-nature of the Buddha, Śrāvakas, and others is liberation, [and thus] existence, non-existence, and the capacity for bondage [are absent].

Because the cause of bondage does not possess the nature of existence. (The commentary states: "Bondage" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*). "The cause of bondage" refers to sentient beings. "Lacking nature" means they have no reality. This means that because the Buddha knows that both afflictions and sentient beings lack reality, there has never been anyone who severed afflictions to attain liberation.
Mahāmati, if there were one who was bound, there would have to be a cause of bondage, for it is the cause of that bondage. (The commentary states: "The one who is bound" refers to sentient beings.

This means that if there were sentient beings who were the cause of bondage, there would have to be afflictions as the binder. Now, observing that sentient beings are empty, there is neither a cause of bondage nor afflictions as a binder. This is a further explanation of liberation by intrinsic nature.)
Mahāmati, one who speaks in such a way as to destroy [existence]—as the Ṛṣi says, "one who speaks thus is called a destroyer"—is said to possess the mark of non-existence.

(If one speaks as above, taking greed, hatred, and delusion to be what is destroyed and then asserting them to be non-existent, this is called not establishing the mark of existence; one then falls into the view of emptiness.

Mahāmati, for this reason I say it would be better to hold the view of a person as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to the view of emptiness born of the overweening pride of non-existence. (The Ṛṣi says: do not give rise to the view of emptiness harboring...)

Regarding "arrogance of non-existence" (*abhāva-adhimāna*): Mahāmati, one who possesses the arrogance of non-existence is said to be one who destroys and falls into the views and expectations regarding self-characteristics and common characteristics.

(One who gives rise to the view of emptiness of non-existence as an arrogance is called one who does not grasp greed, hatred, or delusion; such a destroyer then falls into the views and expectations regarding self-characteristics and common characteristics, and into the false conceptualizations of continuity.

Not knowing that what appears is merely the measure of one's own mind, they perceive external natures as impermanent, subject to momentary and successive destruction, and as the continuous flow of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.

The commentary states: To destroy and abandon the conceptualization of the characteristics of words—that is, to fail to understand that what appears as one's own mind is merely a manifestation (*svacittadṛśyamātra*), and to perceive external phenomena as impermanent, undergoing transformation and destruction from moment to moment;

to see that the continuity of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) flows on and eventually perishes into nothingness; and to claim that one has already abandoned the conceptualization of the characteristics of words—yet still falls into the nihilistic view of non-existence (*abhāvāśūnyatādṛṣṭi*)—this is called "one who destroys the characteristics of all dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Existence and non-existence are two extremes; even the sphere of the mind is to be purified. When that sphere is purified, the mind of equanimity is naturally quiescent. (Note:

Purifying the spheres of existence, non-existence, and the deluded mind, the mind of equanimity is spontaneously stilled. Without grasping at the nature of objects, cessation is not a state of nothingness;
all things are thusness, the very realm of the noble ones. (Note: Knowing that the nature of the sphere of craving is false and devoid of anything graspable is itself the essence.)

The nature of quiescence is not a mere nothingness; it is the primordial quiescence that transcends all else. To contemplate all phenomena as entirely equal and non-dual is the realm of the noble ones (*ārya*). "Without seed, yet there is birth; once born, it perishes again.
Conditioned by causes and conditions, it is neither existent nor non-existent, and does not abide. [I-ching’s note: "He does not abide in my Dharma. (Commentary:

The world exists through causes and conditions, and subsequently receives the name "non-existence" upon cessation. Those who interpret this existence and non-existence according to the views of non-Buddhists do not abide in the Tathāgata’s teaching of the true mark. This is not the way of non-Buddhists.
It is not produced by the Buddha, nor by a self, nor by any other causes and conditions. How then can it be said to exist? (Vimalakīrti says:

"Nor by others"—meaning it is not produced by any other collection of causes and conditions. It is able to manifest existence through conditions. (Note: This means that the dharma of arising is not made by non-Buddhists, nor by the Buddha, nor by a divine self (*puruṣa*), nor by anything else such as atoms or the four great elements;

it arises solely from false conceptualization. Since it only comes into being through the gathering of causes and conditions, it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). To lack intrinsic nature is to clarify that this dharma of arising does not exist. The dharma of arising is fundamentally non-existent.
Why need one further deny it? Who assembles causes and conditions to exist, yet then speaks of non-existence? This is the discourse of false views.

Regarding the arising of phenomena, through deluded conceptualization, one calculates them as either existing or non-existing. (The new commentary says: within the four great elements and five aggregates, each lacks a master; who then assembles them? Yet one still speaks of existence through causes and conditions. Since existence itself does not exist, how can one further speak of destroying existence to establish non-existence?

This is because external paths and false views speak of the arising of phenomena, and due to deluded conceptualization, calculate them as existing or non-existing. If one knows that there is nothing produced, then there is likewise nothing to be grasped.

"Extinction is the contemplation that all this is empty and quiescent, transcending both existence and non-existence. (Bodhiruci and Śikṣānanda both take "contemplating this" to mean contemplating the world.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me and for the other bodhisattvas the characteristics of the penetration of the ultimate principle (*siddhānta*).
If the characteristics of the penetration of the ultimate principle are skillfully distinguished, I and the other bodhisattvas shall thoroughly comprehend them."
Having thoroughly mastered these characteristics, one swiftly attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, without following discursive thoughts or the various demons and non-Buddhists (Bodhiruci says:
"without following any false conceptualizations, discursive thoughts, or demonic activities"). The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Listen attentively, listen attentively;
reflect upon it well, and I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha said:

Mahāmati, all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas have two kinds of general characteristics: the penetration of the ultimate principle (zongtong) and the penetration of verbal teaching (shetong). [The *Zongjing lu* states:

"Internally realizing the primary truth within one's own mind, abiding in the stage of self-awakening, and entering the gateway of noble wisdom—corresponding to this is called the characteristic of the penetration of the ultimate principle. This pertains to the time of practice, not the time of understanding; because understanding gives rise to practice, and when practice is perfected, understanding ceases.

Thus, words and paths of speech are cut off, and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished. It is further said: "The penetration of the ultimate principle is for bodhisattvas; the penetration of verbal teaching is for the ignorant. Mahāmati, as for the penetration of the ultimate principle, it refers to that which takes itself as its object...

Attaining the marks of superior progress, one remains far removed from the conceptualization of words and letters, proceeds toward the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), and realizes the specific characteristics of the stage of self-awakening (*svapratyātma-bhūmi*).

Being far removed from all false and deluded perceptions, one subdues all externalists and hordes of Māras, and as the light of the path of self-awakening shines forth, this is called the characteristic of the penetration of the ultimate principle (*zongtong-xiang*).
(Because one has personally attained superior progress, one is able to leave behind words and letters, proceed toward the untainted realm, and enter the stage of self-awakening.)

To realize the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), to be able to distance oneself from false conceptualizations (*vikalpa*), and to subdue all Māras and non-Buddhists—this is what is realized through the light of wisdom (*jñānāloka*) that pertains to the path of self-awakening (*pratyātma-gati*). What is meant by the "characteristic of the penetration of teaching" (*deśanā-praveśa-lakṣaṇa*)?

It refers to the teaching of the various doctrines of the ninefold canon (*navāṅga-śāsana*), which is free from such characteristics as difference and non-difference, existence and non-existence, and so forth.

By means of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), it accords with sentient beings and teaches the Dharma according to their needs so that they may attain liberation; this is called the characteristic of the penetration of teaching. (Yang says: "It is like an echo responding to a call.")

"O Mahāmati, you and the other Bodhisattvas should practice and study this. (The New Commentary states: 'This sūtra encompasses both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna and consists of twelve divisions; the present mention of nine divisions is as stated in the third fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:

"Those who protect the Mahāyāna uphold the ninefold dharma," and in the first fascicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "These ninefold dharmas of mine are taught in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings. Furthermore, treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi* state that the Śrāvaka-piṭaka lacks the Vaipulya division.

However, these various sūtras and śāstras make such statements merely by way of a single aspect. In truth, both vehicles possess all [twelve divisions]. As stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, Bodhisattvas cultivate śamatha based on the twelvefold teaching,' and in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 21, it says: 'The Buddha...'"

For the sake of the śrāvakas, [the Buddha] expounded each of the twelve divisions of the teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-dharma-pravacana*) in detail; yet, regarding the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is said that there are only nine [divisions] of the Great [Vehicle]. This is because they rely on the minor characteristics of the three categories:

in the *nidāna* (causes and conditions), they take up the causes and matters for establishing the precepts; in the *avadāna* (parables), they rely on them as means of inducement; and in the *upadeśa* (treatises/discourses), they rely on them concerning non-definitive teachings. In the *Lotus Sūtra*, the nine divisions of the Small [Vehicle] are "Great" by virtue of three characteristics: in the *vyākaraṇa* (prophecies), they take up the prophecy of attaining Buddhahood; within the *svayambhū-vyākaraṇa* (self-proclamations), they rely on the uninvited friend;

and within the *vaipulya* (extensive teachings), they rely on their vast benefit and joy for the True Dharma, extensively setting forth both the Great and the Small. Now, since this text states that all those of the two vehicles and the various bodhisattvas possess two kinds of "common characteristics," it reconciles the provisional toward the ultimate and encompasses both the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Because it is the meaning [of the teaching], it is called the "characteristic of the commonality of the teaching" (*deśanā-sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), which explains that the various teachings of the nine divisions are free from the four views of identity and difference, existence and non-existence, and so forth; this is named the characteristic of the commonality of the teaching, and it serves as an exhortation for Bodhisattvas to diligently practice and study it.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

The tenets (*siddhānta*) and the commonality of verbal teaching (*deśanā-sāmānya*), [or as Paramārtha says: the goal of the tenets (*siddhānta-artha*) and verbal expression (*abhilāpa*), as well as self-realization (*pratyātma-vedya*) and the teachings (*deśanā*), are well-seen and well-discriminated;

one does not follow various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). (This briefly cites the two meanings of tenets and teaching: if one discriminates them well, one does not follow the deluded cognitions of ordinary people.

There is no such thing as a real nature (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) as imagined by foolish people. (Bodhiruci says: "In reality, there are no external dharmas, yet they are discriminated by ordinary people. How, then, do these delusions arise?

To conceive that non-existence is liberation (the New Explanation says: if one knows that all phenomena lack a real nature and nothing can be apprehended, this is liberation; such is the ultimate intent of the Tathāgata).

To observe the characteristics of the continuity and increase of conditioned phenomena—such as arising and ceasing—within the two views and perversions, and to have no true knowledge (the New Explanation says:

to falsely conceptualize within arising and ceasing that there is a real existence, thereby increasing the two views of existence and non-existence, is the perversion of fools who lack correct knowledge and vision). This one [point] constitutes the True Truth.

To be without transgression is *nirvāṇa*. (The note states: "Equanimity and suchness constitute the ultimate truth. The *Xingfa jing* says: "The ocean of all karmic obstructions arises entirely from deluded thoughts. Thus, the commentary states: "Transgression is deluded thought; to be without deluded thought is *nirvāṇa*").
One observes that worldly delusions are like illusions, dreams, and plantain trees. (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "This body is like a plantain tree, having no solidity within;

this body is like an illusion, arising from inversion; this body is like a dream, being a false perception. [The *Xin shuo* says: "The above clarifies the fundamental tenets of the Tathāgata. It is said that the Tathāgata possesses..."])* (Note: The bracketed section represents a reconstruction of the intended meaning based on the provided fragments, as the source text appears to be a composite of various citations and commentaries.)

Because one’s own school [of thought] is realized, one knows that worldly phenomena are false and entirely like illusions and dreams; though greed, anger, and delusion exist, in reality there is no person [Yang says:

because they all arise from oneself]. From craving arise the aggregates (*skandhas*); all existence is like an illusion or a dream. (The "New Explanation" states: This verse refers to the aforementioned characteristic of verbal expression. The Buddha said: although greed, anger, and delusion exist, they are what is seen through falsehood;

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of unreal conceptualization (note:

a question regarding the characteristics of conceptualization). How does unreal conceptualization arise? (a question regarding how conceptualization arises) What kind of phenomena are designated as unreal conceptualization?

(a question regarding the essence of conceptualization) Within what kind of phenomena does unreal conceptualization occur? (a question regarding the locus from which conceptualization arises) The Buddha told Mahāmati:

The various unreal conceptualizations regarding meanings (the commentary notes: "various meanings such as forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, humans, devas, and all dharmas" refers to the characteristics of conceptualization; this answers the question regarding the characteristics of conceptualization); through attachment to these conceptualizations (the commentary notes:

(Note: It is said that not knowing that what is taken as "self" is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, one gives rise to false conceptual attachments and falls into the views of existence and non-existence, thereby increasing the four extremes of the non-Buddhists; this explains the nature of delusion in response to the preceding question. Through the mind and its mental factors (*caitta*), there arises the deluded attachment to "self" and "what belongs to self. (The upper character *xin* [mind] refers to the sovereign mind-king of the eight consciousnesses;

The mental factors (*caitta*), also called "mental concomitants" (*cittasamprayukta-saṃskāra*), these fifty-one kinds, are all dharmas belonging to the mind; they pertain to the subject that perceives and clings to form and other objects. "Mahāmati, the attachment to the habitual tendencies of conceptualization regarding various external objects gives rise to the false imaginings of the mind and mental factors, which cling to 'self' and 'what belongs to self.

(Mahāmati repeats the preceding statement to raise an objection: "World-Honored One, if it is as you say—that these various external objective characteristics fall into the marks of existence and non-existence, yet are free from both nature and non-nature, and free from the marks of views—[then] this means that if it were so, the various external objects perceived in conventional truth would fall into the marks of existence and non-existence; they would be the very nature [of things], yet free from existence and non-existence, transcending the four logical positions."

When one realizes that external appearances—whether as entities or non-entities—are merely the manifestation of one's own mind, false discrimination does not arise. (Note: To realize that existence and non-existence are the manifestation of one's own mind means that external appearances...)
Because their nature is without reality, they do not give rise to delusive thoughts by clinging to the sphere of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Mahāmati, I say that for other ignorant people, due to the various marks of delusive thoughts within their own minds, they give rise to clinging to the various natures and characteristics of objects and activities as being present before them. (The note says:

What is meant by "ignorant people"?
One attains liberation from the views of clinging to "self" and "what belongs to self," and is freed from the faults of cause, effect, and causal conditions (the note states:

One awakens to the measure of one's own deluded mind, undergoes the transformation of body and mind, and ultimately attains clear understanding of all stages and the realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization, becoming free from the views regarding the five dharmas, the three natures, and the categories of phenomena.

[The Master] said: "Regarding these delusive imaginings (*vikalpa*)—[Yang says: reaching this point, he again brushes away the traces of the five dharmas and the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)]—it is for this reason that I say delusive imaginings arise from attachment to various unreal objects.
By knowing the reality as it is (*yathābhūta-artha*), one attains liberation from the various delusive imaginings of one's own mind.

(For this reason, I say that fools cling to various unrealities and thereby give rise to delusive imaginings; if they can know the reality as it is, they will immediately attain liberation and extinguish all delusive imaginings. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

"The various causes and conditions from which this world arises are but false imaginings; Attached to the four positions [of existence, non-existence, both, and neither], they do not know my penetration. (Note:

(Note: These are the four propositions of existence and non-existence; the world does not arise from these four. How can the ignorant falsely imagine through delusion regarding causes and conditions that there is arising within them?

"That which arises from conditions has no intrinsic substance; thus one knows that all dharmas are unarisen. Yang says: "All that is produced depends on the mind. A thing does not arise from itself, for there would be the fault of two things.

Establishing reality by refuting distinctions, and establishing suchness by eliminating divergent characteristics—all these are names derived from opposition.
They are taught to break attachments and refute grasping.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught that a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should be skilled in words and meaning (*śabdārtha*), what is meant by a Bodhisattva being skilled in words and meaning? [The Meaning: The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "What is speech?

It refers to the false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of words and letters, which, depending on the throat, lips, tongue, teeth, palate, cheeks, and jaws, arises from the false discourse of 'self' and 'other'."

The arising of attachment through the habitual tendencies of conceptualization is called "speech" (*vāc*). (This clarifies that speech, letters, and so forth depend upon a basis for their conjunction;

subsequently, based on those, one becomes attached to and discriminates all phenomena through speech and the like, producing various sounds—this is called speech. Mahāmati, what is meant by "meaning" (*artha*)?
It refers to being free from all marks of false imagination and marks of verbal expression; this is called meaning. Mahāmati, regarding such meaning, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva alone...

In a solitary place, having transformed the body of habitual tendencies through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation that take self-awakening as their object, one contemplates the characteristics of the superior progress between each stage within the realm of self-awakening while heading toward the city of Nirvāṇa; this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s skill in meaning.

(Bodhiruci says: "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, relying on the power of the noble wisdom of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, sits alone in a secluded place and contemplates: 'What is Nirvāṇa? What is the path to Nirvāṇa? and observes the internal body.")

The stages of the realm of practice are characterized by the progressive excellence of cultivation at each level. Mahāmati, this is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful understanding of the characteristics of meaning (*artha*). (The wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation are called the three wisdoms.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva skilled in words and meaning contemplates that words and meaning are neither different nor not different;
the contemplation of meaning and words is likewise. If words were different from meaning, then meaning could not be discerned through words.
Entering the meaning through words is like a lamp illuminating forms (Śikṣānanda says: "It is as if a person holding a lamp to look at an object knows that this object is thus and in such a place").

[The commentary states: Because one sees form by means of the lamp, form is not the lamp; yet because one sees form by means of the lamp, one cannot say they are different, and because form is not the lamp, one cannot say they are one. This is used as an analogy for entering the meaning through words: one cannot say they are different, yet the meaning is not the words, so one cannot say they are one.

Therefore, it is said to be free from both difference and non-difference. Furthermore, Mahāmati, [the teachings on] non-arising and non-ceasing, intrinsic nirvāṇa, the three vehicles, and the one vehicle...
The self-nature of the mind is like the attachment to the meanings of conventional expressions;
one falls into views of superimposition and denial, constructing various false imaginings as if they were distinct from reality—like various illusions manifested through diverse conceptualizations.

Just as ordinary, foolish beings produce such false imaginings, they are not noble sages. (As Śikṣānanda states: "O Mahāmati, if there are those who [cling] to non-arising and non-ceasing, to self-nature, nirvāṇa, the three vehicles, the one vehicle, the five dharmas, or the various minds...")

If one grasps the meaning according to the words regarding the self-nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth, one falls into the views of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*), because one gives rise to conceptual discrimination by treating these as something other than they are—just as a fool perceives a magical illusion and reckons it to be real; this is the vision of the foolish, not that of the noble ones.

The *New Commentary* states: This clarifies that if there are those who grasp the meaning according to the words among the various phenomena of defilement and purity, such as the unborn and the unceasing, and reckon that the verbal expression and the meaning are identical, this is called superimposition; if they reckon that the verbal expression and the meaning are different, this is called denial.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Those who establish all phenomena based on the conceptualization of speech—because of such establishment, they fall into hell after death (the new commentary says:

'All foolish people grasp at the meaning according to the words and establish all phenomena; by reckoning that phenomena exist, they cannot escape the evil realms; slander is likewise). Within the aggregates, there is nothing [ultimately real]."

The aggregates (*skandhas*) are not themselves the self, yet they are not without a self, just as those false conceptualizations are. (That is to say: within the five aggregates, there is initially no self; nor is it that the five aggregates are the self.
Furthermore, it is not as those deluded worldlings falsely conceptualize—that there is truly no self at all. All things possess an intrinsic nature;

if it were as the deluded worldlings falsely conceptualize, then if it were as they perceive, everyone would see the Truth (*satya*). (If it were as the deluded worldlings perceive, then all phenomena would be seen as [merely]...)

yet as they are perceived, they are also not nothingness. (Since the nature of all phenomena is already non-existent, how could there be defilement or purity?

Nevertheless, the Sage’s perception of all phenomena is no different from that of the foolish commoner; he simply knows them to be unreal, yet not nothingness. This clarifies that it is not a nature of non-existence.)

Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the characteristics of knowledge (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*). (Note: As the Tathāgata, based on the preceding [discussion], intended for the Bodhisattvas to skillfully understand the characteristics of speech and meaning—desiring them to clearly know that "speech" refers to consciousness and "meaning" refers to knowledge—he next explains the characteristics of knowledge and consciousness.

If you and the other Bodhisattvas can skillfully discern the characteristics of knowledge and consciousness, you will then be able to penetrate the characteristics of knowledge and consciousness and swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Mahāmati, regarding that...
Wisdom is of three kinds: mundane, supramundane, and supremely supramundane. What is mundane wisdom?
It refers to the attachment to existence and non-existence held by all heterodox teachers and ordinary worldlings. What is supramundane wisdom?

It refers to the attachment to the hopes for self-characteristics and common characteristics held by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. What is supremely supramundane wisdom? [It is that which transcends these.]

This refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who, observing the dharma of non-existence, perceive that which is neither born nor extinguished and is free from the categories of existence and non-existence—the stage of the Tathāgata, characterized by the self-realization of the selflessness of persons and phenomena (meaning this wisdom arises from the noble realm of self-attainment). Supreme wisdom arises from this. (The note states: "Those bound by the objects of affliction are the deluded mind; that which perceives the objects of affliction as arising from delusion is the wisdom of non-existence, which is the eighth stage and the stage of Buddhahood.
This means that the wisdom of the eighth stage and the Buddha-stage arises from the realization of the wisdom that transcends delusion.

Mind, thought, and consciousness (the meaning is found in the note at the beginning of the first fascicle under "Detachment from Mind, Thought, and Consciousness")—having distanced oneself from conceptualization and attainment, one reaches the state of non-conceptual dharmas. O Son of the Buddha, it is not [otherwise].

The Śrāvaka (the wisdom arising from the eighth stage and the Buddha-stage realizes that the mind, thought, and all consciousnesses are illusory; by distancing oneself from conceptualization and deluded thoughts, one attains the state of non-conceptualization and the illusory dharmas;

ascending to the Bodhisattva stages, one becomes a true son of the Buddha and is no longer comparable to a Śrāvaka—hence it is said "not a Śrāvaka"). Through the supreme progress of tranquil patience (*śānti-kṣānti*), the pure wisdom of the Tathāgata arises;

within the excellent ultimate truth, all objects of practice are completely transcended. (In the *Renwang jing*, it is taught that there are five kinds of patience: *adhimukti-kṣānti*, *anuloma-kṣānti*, *anutpāda-kṣānti*, and *nirvāṇa-kṣānti*, each having lower, middle, and upper grades; these correspond to the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi.)

However, having attained the three grades of the Patience of Subjugation (*kṣānti*) across the nine stages, they are respectively assigned to the next three patiences; at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and Buddhahood, one attains the Patience of Cessation (*nirvāṇa-kṣānti*). Therefore, it is said that the "Patience of Tranquil Superior Progress" is the pure wisdom of the Tathāgata.

This clarifies that the pure wisdom of the Buddha’s patience arises from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and that all objective spheres traversed by the deluded mind and consciousness are entirely abandoned.

"I possess three kinds of wisdom that open and reveal the reality. (The commentary states: Because the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma according to the capacities of beings, there are these three kinds of wisdom. It is said that these three kinds of wisdom are intended precisely to awaken sentient beings, enabling them to attain the reality that transcends verbal expression. Regarding those [three kinds of wisdom]:
Conceptualization and reflection fully encompass all natures; the wisdom of the two vehicles is not in accord with this.
Free from all attachments to existence, one transcends the self-nature arising from the Śrāvakas and crosses over all mental measures (*cittamātra*). Thus, the Tathāgata’s wisdom is pure.

(Regarding those who give rise to conceptualization and reflection toward deluded thoughts and thereby grasp at the nature of arising and ceasing—this is worldly wisdom. The wisdom of the two vehicles can indeed leave behind all such things and does not correspond to arising and ceasing; however, they still cling to self-characteristics and common characteristics.)

"Nature" refers to that which arises from the Śrāvakas; this is supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*). To transcend the various mental measures (*citta-mātra*)—both mundane and supramundane—of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, and to attain the pure wisdom of the Tathāgata, is supramundane, supreme wisdom (*lokottara-uttama-jñāna*).
(This is a general verse summarizing the two aforementioned types of threefold wisdom.)
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are nine kinds of transformation theories among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), from which the views of transformation arise. Namely:

transformation of form and location, transformation of characteristics, transformation of causes, transformation of becoming, transformation of views, transformation of nature, transformation of the manifestation of conditions, transformation of the manifestation of actions, and transformation of things. Mahāmati, these are called the nine kinds of transformation.

The manifestations perceived by all non-Buddhists arise from this [ignorance] as theories of existence, non-existence, birth, and transformation. (The note states: the differing forms of the six realms of humans and devas are called "transformation of form and place";

the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of the five aggregates, which do not abide for even a single thought-moment, is called "transformation of characteristics"; the arising of the effect from the cessation of the cause is called "transformation of cause"; the destruction of the phenomena produced by causes is called "transformation of completion";

seeing a single phenomenon as correct at first and then seeing it as incorrect is called "transformation of view"; the shifting nature of the essence of all things is called "transformation of nature"; the incessant arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination is called "transformation of the clarity of conditions"; and the destruction of the effects produced by conditions is called "transformation of the object").

The cessation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) through manifest transformation is called the "transformation of things. Based on these nine kinds of transformations, non-Buddhists give rise to views of existence and non-existence and produce the "Theory of Transformation" (*pariṇāmavāda*).
What is meant by "transformation of shape and location" (*saṃsthāna-sthāna-pariṇāma*)? It refers to the perception of differences in shape and location;

for example, when gold is transformed into various vessels, diverse shapes and locations appear, yet the nature of the gold itself does not change. The transformation of all natures is likewise so. (The New Commentary says: To clarify this transformation of shape, it is like using gold...)

When various vessels and garments are fashioned, they possess diverse shapes and forms; one speaks of their transformation, yet it is not that the nature of the gold itself changes. The transformation of all phenomena is likewise so: the wondrously luminous true essence is eternally abiding and immutable, yet ordinary people and non-Buddhists have no knowledge of it.
There may be non-Buddhists who produce such false imaginings, even extending to the false imagining of the transformation of things;

this is because they falsely imagine them to be neither identical nor different. (Vasubandhu says: "The various attachments of other non-Buddhists are neither like this nor are they distinct; they are merely conceptual constructions. Thus it is.
One should understand that the transformation of all natures is like the ripening of milk, curd, wine, fruit, and so forth.

The transformations imagined by the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) do not actually exist; whether they are said to exist or not, external natures and non-natures are merely manifestations of one's own mind. (The new commentary states:

The non-Buddhists falsely calculate that all natures undergo transformation as neither identical nor different, citing examples such as the ripening of milk into curd, wine, or fruit. Because curd is obtained from milk, one cannot say they are different; yet because their qualities and essences differ, one cannot say they are identical. In reality, there is no such thing as a phenomenon that can undergo transformation.)

It is also said that the existence or non-existence of phenomena is a false manifestation of one’s own mind, for external natures have no reality. (That they are "not one" means they are not suchness. Mahāmati, it is thus that ordinary, ignorant beings produce [the notion of phenomena] through their own habitual practice of false imagination.
Mahāmati, there is no phenomenon whatsoever that arises or ceases, just as one perceives the appearance of forms in a magical illusion or a dream.

(Paramārtha says: "All these arise from the habit-energies of the discrimination of ignorant, deluded ordinary beings; in reality, not a single dharma arises or ceases. It is like the various forms seen in a magical illusion or a dream, or like speaking of birth and death for the son of a barren woman.")
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"Form, location, and temporal transformation; the four great elements; the sense faculties; and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arise in succession through false imagination, not from clear wisdom.

(In the original text, *antarābhava* was rendered as 'intermediate existence. The new commentary states: 'The non-Buddhists claim that form, location, time, and the four great elements act as the seeds, and the sense faculties undergo transformation. The followers of the Two Vehicles reckon that there is an intermediate existence through which birth continues in succession. "

The aggregates (*skandhas*) are entirely false imaginings. The intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which is what is meant by "intermediate existence" (*chū-yung*), is described in the *Abhidharmakośa* as the five aggregates existing between death and rebirth.

The most excellent [truth] regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is not like those false imaginings; rather, worldly dependent origination is like a city of the Gandharvas (as the new commentary states:

the Buddha knows that phenomena arising from causes and conditions are unborn, and unlike those false imaginings, he does not conceptualize that there is a transformation of various worldly dharmas within causes and conditions). However, that which arises dependently in the world is like a city of the Gandharvas, for it is fundamentally unreal.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for us the meaning of the continuity of all dharmas and the meaning of liberation.

If you skillfully distinguish the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all dharmas—[this inquiry into the meaning of the continuity and non-continuity of all dharmas, where 'liberation' refers precisely to the meaning of non-continuity]—I and the other bodhisattvas shall gain a thorough understanding."
Skillful in the means of continuity for all things, they do not fall into the attachment to the characteristics of the meanings as they have been taught;
they are well-versed in the characteristics of continuity and non-continuity regarding all dharmas,

and through the power of the seal of the *dhāraṇī* of mastery over the infinite assemblies in all Buddha-fields, they travel by means of the various transformations of the awakening that transcends the deluded conceptualizations of words, letters, and speech.
The transformative radiance illuminates and awakens wisdom, skillfully entering the ten inexhaustible phrases.

Their unconditioned practice is like that of the sun, moon, mani-jewels, and the four great elements (the illumination of the sun and moon, the color-changing of the mani, and the pervasiveness of earth, water, fire, and wind are all without effort; the Bodhisattva’s unconditioned practice is like this).

In all stages (*bhūmi*), they are free from the marks of their own deluded conceptualizations (Paramārtha says: "Abiding in the various stages, one cuts off discriminative views"). Thus they perceive all phenomena.
Like illusions, dreams, and so forth, entering the body of the Buddha-ground, he teaches the Dharma to all realms of sentient beings according to what is appropriate for them and guides them,
causing them all to dwell securely in the realization that all phenomena are like illusions, dreams, and so forth— free from the categories of existence and non-existence,

as well as the deluded conceptualizations of arising and ceasing— and his body becomes increasingly sublime (Vasubandhu says: "He severs the attachment to arising and ceasing and does not cling to words").

[The section on] "Explaining the Transformation of the Basis" (the commentary states: "The Dharmakāya becomes increasingly supreme"). The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it;
I shall speak for you. Mahāmati replied to the Buddha: "Yes, I shall receive your teaching. The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"There is an uninterrupted succession of attachment to the characteristics of all immeasurable phenomena according to the literal meaning of what is spoken" (Paramārtha translates this as: "clinging to all phenomena by grasping at their meaning according to the words").

They are deeply attached and their number is immeasurable; namely: the continuous attachment to characteristics (conceiving the characteristics of the five aggregates); the continuous attachment to conditions (conceiving the twelve links of dependent origination);

the continuous attachment to existence and non-existence (conceiving what exists and what does not exist); the continuous attachment to the false imagination of arising and non-arising; the continuous attachment to the false imagination of cessation and non-cessation;
the continuous attachment to vehicles and non-vehicles; and the continuous attachment to the conditioned and the unconditioned.

The continuity of false conceptualization and attachment regarding the specific characteristics of each stage (wherein one imagines the arising of self within each stage as if establishing rungs on a ladder where there are no rungs);

the continuity of false conceptualization and attachment regarding the uninterrupted succession of one's own false conceptualizations (imagining the uninterrupted succession of one's own false conceptualizations);

the continuity of false conceptualization and attachment based on the dualistic categories of existence and non-existence held by non-Buddhists (where non-Buddhists take the categories of existence and non-existence as their tenets); and the uninterrupted [distinction between] the three vehicles and the one vehicle.

The continuity of conceptual attachment (wherein one calculates the three vehicles and the one vehicle as being uninterrupted). Furthermore, Mahāmati, this and other ordinary, ignorant beings have a continuity of their own conceptual constructions (*sva-vikalpa*).
[Note: This refers to non-Buddhists; it means that because non-Buddhists and ordinary, ignorant beings have their own conceptual constructions, they speak of continuity.

Because of this continuity, the conceptual constructions of ordinary, ignorant beings are like a silkworm making a cocoon, binding themselves with the threads of their own conceptual constructions, and binding others in terms of existence and non-existence.
There is attachment to the characteristic of continuity (the note says: calculating that there is no arising of the characteristic of continuity).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, therein there is also neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity, because all dharmas are quiescent and false conceptualization does not arise. For this reason, Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva perceives all dharmas as quiescent.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, one awakens to the fact that external natures are without intrinsic nature, being merely manifestations of one's own mind.

Characteristics are non-existent. (Yang says: The Bodhisattva should realize that external natures are not inherently existent, being merely manifestations of one’s own mind, and are likewise fundamentally non-existent.

By conforming to and observing that all natures are the mere measure of what is manifested by one’s own mind, and because the continuity of seeing characteristics is stilled, there is neither continuity nor non-continuity regarding the characteristic of all phenomena.

(Yang says: Because one perceives the discrimination of existence and non-existence, it is called "continuity"; because one perceives the stillness of all dharmas, it is called "non-continuity. Regarding this, the Bodhisattva...)

Furthermore, Mahāmati, within that [reality] there is neither bondage nor liberation. Others, however, who fall into the state of not awakening to things as they truly are, perceive bondage and liberation.

(The note states: "This clarifies that in the ultimate principle there is neither bondage nor liberation; other deluded beings, falling into unreal conceptualization and cognition, therefore perceive bondage and liberation.
Why is this so? Because among all phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—no sentient being can be apprehended. (Real-śa says: "All dharmas, whether... )
It is as if having something yet being without it, for its essential nature cannot be found. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three continuities for fools:

namely, greed, hatred, and delusion, together with craving for future existence accompanied by delight. (The note states: "Because fools possess the three poisons in the present together with craving for future existence and delight, there is continuity.

Due to this continuity, there is the continuity of the realms of existence (*gati*). As for that continuity, it continues [beings] through the five realms of existence (the *tattvārtha* explains: "it causes all sentient beings to continue their births within the five realms"). Mahāmati...
When the continuity of wisdom is severed, there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, when one clings to the conditions of the threefold conjunction as a means, the characteristics of consciousness arise in uninterrupted succession. (Note: Non-Buddhists falsely reckon that the three conditions give rise to consciousness and produce various karmas;

therefore, the aggregates of birth and death continue without cessation. Through clinging to such means, there is continuity. When the consciousness of the threefold conjunctional conditions is severed, one perceives the three [realities].

"Liberation means that all continuities do not arise" (the note says: if one clings to the expedient means of the three conditions, there is continuity; if the consciousness of the three conditions is severed and all continuities do not arise, then one sees the three gates of liberation).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Unreal conceptualization is said to be the characteristic of continuity; if one knows that true characteristic of continuity, then the web of continuity is severed. (The note says:

Because it is unreal conceptualization, it is said that there is the characteristic of continuity; if one realizes the truth, even liberation has no web of continuity, so how could there be [continuity]?

Regarding all natures, through ignorance one clings to them according to verbal expressions, just as a silkworm spins a web and entangles itself. (*Iśvarakṛṣṇa* says: It is like a silkworm dwelling in its cocoon.)

Bound by their own deluded imaginings, the foolish are fettered by the continuity of such imaginings and fail to discern them. (The note states: "The foolish do not know that all natures are without reality;
following conventional verbal expressions, they grasp at and cling to them, failing to discern that this continuity is false and merely entangled by deluded imagination.")

Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught—that by means of various delusive imaginings one imagines various natures, yet those natures do not exist, for they are merely the nature of delusive imagination (the 'True Meaning' states: 'As the World-Honored One has taught, because of the various minds one discriminates all dharmas;

the dharmas have no self-nature, it is only false conceptualization. [This means that] by discriminating all dharmas through various delusive imaginings, one knows that the various natures imagined therein do not exist as real natures, but are merely the self-nature falsely conceived through delusive imagination)—World-Honored One..."

If the self-nature of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) were merely a relative designation of existence and non-existence, would this not contradict the Blessed One’s teaching that afflictions and purification are without intrinsic nature? Because all phenomena are the imagined nature and lack intrinsic nature. [Bodhiruci says:

"O Blessed One, if it is only the discrimination of one's own mind and not the characteristic of those phenomena, then as the Blessed One has taught, all phenomena should be neither defiled nor pure. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has said that all phenomena are seen through false discrimination and have no substantial reality."

Therefore, Mahāmati, if it were merely the nature of false imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and not in opposition to the nature of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), then there would be no nature to all phenomena.
