Would this not be a fault, contradicting what the Blessed One has taught—that the afflictions of sentient beings, the purity of the Tathāgata, and *nirvāṇa* are all without nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)—because all phenomena, being of the nature of false imagination, lack an inherent nature? This would establish the aforementioned fault that the Tathāgata’s teaching of "no-nature" is erroneous. The Buddha said to Mahāmati:
"So it is, so it is, Mahāmati, just as you have said. However, Mahāmati, it is not like the false imagination of the foolish regarding the nature of things (*bhāva-svabhāva*)."
In truth, because foolish commoners conceptualize the nature of self-nature (*svabhāva*) through false imagination and take it to be real, it is said that [self-nature] is not suchness.

This imagined self-nature does not exist as a characteristic of self-nature; rather, Mahāmati, the self-nature that exists for noble wisdom is known by noble knowledge, noble vision, and the noble eye of wisdom—such is the knowledge of self-nature.
(The above answers Mahāmati’s question regarding the fault of the non-existence of afflictions and purity, employing noble wisdom and...)

"Knowing the noble, seeing the noble, with the clear eye of noble wisdom, one knows the nature of reality (*tathatā*) and self-nature (*svabhāva*) as it truly is; this self-nature is not the same as the imagined self-nature of the ignorant and foolish. Mahāmati said to the Buddha:

"If it is as the noble ones do—by means of noble knowledge, noble vision, and the noble eye of wisdom, rather than the fleshly eye or the divine eye—to know the nature of reality and self-nature in this way, it is not like the deluded imaginings of the foolish.

[Bodhiruci says: "As for all the noble ones, relying on noble wisdom, relying on noble vision, and relying on the noble eye of wisdom—not the fleshly eye or the divine eye—they awaken to and know all things..."]

The essence of dharmas is without such characteristics; it is not as ordinary people falsely discriminate. [△] From here down to the passage "and explains the nature and activity of noble wisdom," five objections are raised according to the new exposition: (1) The objection that ordinary beings and sages are distinct. [Question:
"World-Honored One, how is it that fools, though free from these false imaginings, do not realize the reality of the nature of noble wisdom? [Answer:

"How is it that fools, having departed from the objects of false discrimination, ultimately cannot perceive the reality of the noble nature of wisdom? (2) The objection regarding neither inversion nor non-inversion. [Question: "World-Honored One, are they neither inverted nor non-inverted? [Answer: "They are neither inverted nor non-inverted."

Why is this so? It is because they do not awaken to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the reality of the noble ones (*ārya*), and because they do not perceive that which is free from the marks of existence and non-existence.

(That is to say: those who are not inverted do not awaken to the intrinsic nature of the reality of the noble ones; those who are not non-inverted do not perceive that which is free from the marks of existence and non-existence. [This clarifies the difficulty of the noble ones being identical to the inversions of ordinary people.

World-Honored One, the noble ones do not see in such a way as these deluded imaginings (*vikalpa*); they do not take the objective realm of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their objective realm.

(The Noble Ones do not produce views of inversion or non-inversion regarding phenomena, unlike the ignorant who cling to the conceptualized marks of existence and non-existence. If the Noble Ones were to regard conceptualization as conceptualization and take the realm of self-realized characteristics as an objective realm, they would fall into attachment;
therefore, it is said that they do not [do so]. World-Honored One, those [Noble Ones] also manifest the nature of self-nature through the nature of conceptualization;

this is because they do not speak of causes or the absence of causes, but rather because they fall into the view of the characteristics of self-nature. (Liuzhi says: Those Noble Ones perceive the substance of dharmas and differentiate their characteristics...)

The World-Honored One does not say there is a cause, nor does he say there is no cause. Why? Because [to say so] would fall into the characteristic of existing dharmas (*bhāva-lakṣaṇa*). (The Commentary states: "Even for sages, there is the characteristic of the true nature and self-nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), which appears as the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of ordinary deluded beings.

(The New Commentary states: "This is the formal establishment of the refutation. Regarding the different realms (*viṣaya-antara*), it is not like those [ordinary beings]; otherwise, there would be the fault of infinite regress.

This is because the World-Honored One has not awakened to the characteristic of the nature and self-nature. (The New Commentary states: "This is the repeated explanation for establishing the proof. "Different realms" means, in full, the realms of the various destinies of ordinary beings within the triple world (*tridhātu*). If it were the case that the different realms belong to ordinary beings...

It is not as those noble ones [are], for an ordinary person is contrary to a noble one; nor is it that if a noble one were not like those others, then an ordinary person in a different realm would be a noble one, which would contradict the nature of an ordinary person.

If this were so, there would be the fault of infinite regress, because one would be unable to realize the self-nature and characteristics of things. 4. Clarifying the Difficulty that the Realm of Ordinary People is Not False: "World-Honored One, it is also not the case that the self-nature of false imagination is the cause of the self-nature and characteristics of things.

How can you say that it is false imagination? It is not false imagination. To know false imagination as it truly is—Mañjuśrī said: 'The self-nature and characteristics of all dharmas do not arise from discrimination. Why then do you say...'"

Because of discrimination, all phenomena exist. This imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not exist by way of the characteristics of a causal nature (*hetu-svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*). How is it that those noble ones (*ārya*) do not regard this imagination as non-imagined? It is because they know imagination to be unreal. "World-Honored One, imagination is distinct.

[Bodhiruci and Śikṣānanda both have the character *lakṣaṇa* [characteristic] following "distinct"]. "The characteristics of the imagined nature are distinct, World-Honored One; they are not similar to their causes.
How is it that each of these is not imagined, yet fools do not understand them as such?"

[The Buddha] truly knows that because the causes for the two characteristics of the self-nature of all phenomena—which are like illusions, dreams, and false imaginings—are distinct, they are said to be "dissimilar. Because these causes are dissimilar, how could those noble ones falsely imagine the characteristics of the self-nature of false imagination?
It is because they know false imagination as it truly is; whereas foolish commoners do not know it as it truly is, and thus do not transcend false imagination.

Nevertheless, in order to cause sentient beings to transcend false imagination, [the Buddha] teaches that the characteristics of false imagination are not real as they appear. (The note states: "This is to cause foolish commoners to abandon unreal false imagination, and thus teach that all phenomena have characteristics like illusions, dreams, and false imaginings.")

[The Obstacle of Falling into the View of Existence Regarding the Five Sciences as Truly Existing] World-Honored One, for what reason do you prevent sentient beings from falling into the view of existence by causing them to abandon their attachment to the intrinsic nature of things and their attachment to the sphere of activity of noble wisdom? [The World-Honored One says:

"For what reason do I cause those ordinary people to leave behind the views of existence and non-existence, as well as their attachment to the intrinsic nature of things, so that they do not themselves become attached to the sphere of activity of noble wisdom and thereby fall into the view of existence? It is precisely because I speak of existence that the Tathāgata speaks. He teaches the dharma of emptiness and the absence of intrinsic nature, yet he speaks.

Regarding the "Reality of the Nature of Noble Wisdom" (*āryajñānasvabhāvavastu*): [Vasubandhu] asks, "Why does [the Buddha] not speak of the phenomena of quiescent emptiness and non-existence, but instead speak of the reality of the nature of noble wisdom? [The Commentary states: To say that all phenomena are empty and without reality is what the Tathāgata calls "speaking of non-existence.

To say that there is a true reality of the nature of noble wisdom known by [that] wisdom is what the Tathāgata calls "speaking of existence. Since the Tathāgata himself speaks of existence, speaks of non-existence, and speaks of things, why would he prohibit sentient beings from speaking of existence, non-existence, or things?

[The New Commentary states: The Buddha further said above that the conceptualized nature of phenomena is not as it appears; otherwise, one falls into the view of non-existence. This objection implies that even sages fall into the views of existence and non-existence. The Buddha told Mahāmati:

Wisdom is not what I call the teaching of emptiness as a lack of intrinsic nature, nor does it fall into the view of existence; rather, I speak of the reality of the self-nature of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).

However, this is for the purpose of causing sentient beings to abandon phrases that provoke terror. (From here until the end of the section on abandoning the views and marks of existence and non-existence, this collectively answers the previous five difficulties.

[Note: Sentient beings cling to existence and non-existence; if they hear it said that all phenomena are like illusions, they give rise to the terror of annihilationism. Therefore, the Tathāgata employs skillful means to teach that there is the reality of the self-nature of noble wisdom. Sentient beings have no beginning...
"Since beginningless time, sentient beings have clung to the marks of self-nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*).

Because they cling to the marks of views regarding the reality of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna-vastu-svabhāva*), which is free from existence and non-existence, I teach the emptiness of all phenomena for their sake. This is to eliminate their attachments so that they do not fall into the fault of nihilism.

Mahāmati, I do not speak of the marks of self-nature; [this concludes the preceding teaching on the emptiness of noble wisdom, which was taught solely for the sake of sentient beings, and thus I do not personally assert the existence of self-nature]."
[This is] the characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*). Mahāmati, it is only that I abide in the dharma of emptiness as realized by oneself, which is in accordance with reality;
I am free from the characteristics of delusive confusion and from the views of existence and non-existence regarding what is manifested by one's own mind.

Having attained the seal of the three liberations as they truly are, I abide in the observation of self-realized wisdom regarding the intrinsic nature of things, free from the views of the characteristics of existence and non-existence. (That is to say, I do not speak of the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of things, but rather abide in the dharma of emptiness as realized by oneself in accordance with reality.)

Because one is free from the views of delusive appearances and of the existence or non-existence of what is manifested by one's own mind, one attains the wisdom of the three emptinesses and acquires the seal of reality (*yathābhūta-mudrā*), through the self-awakened observation of the nature of things themselves, which is free from the views of existence and non-existence regarding entities and their characteristics.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, regarding the statement that "all dharmas are non-arising," a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should not establish this as a thesis (*pakṣa*).

Why is this? Because the thesis [itself] consists of the nature of all things being neither existent nor non-existent, and because it involves the characteristics of arising from causes. (Yang says: This means that if dharmas do not arise...)

Regarding the view that all natures exist or do not exist, because there is the arising of an opposing position, one establishes the thesis of non-arising. (2. Refuting through dependence on the phenomena of arising: The thesis that all phenomena are unarisen is undermined by that very thesis.
That thesis—that all phenomena are unarisen—is undermined because the thesis itself arises dependently.

(The Note states: "If one establishes the thesis of non-arising, the meaning of non-arising is itself undermined. Furthermore, the reason it undermines its own meaning of non-arising is that the established thesis of non-arising must depend upon phenomena that arise; thus, the thesis of non-arising is not [ultimately] established.')"

If arising were to arise from another, it would mean that the very nature of the phenomenon is self-contradictory and thus non-arising; as the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "If a phenomenon is established in dependence, that phenomenon is itself dependent.

(3. Refutation by showing the thesis is identical to all phenomena. Furthermore, because their position of "non-arising" is included within the category of all phenomena—(the note states: "Furthermore, this thesis of non-arising is included within the enumeration of all phenomena; 'all phenomena' refers to phenomena such as arising and non-arising, permanence and impermanence, etc.

Since establishing the thesis of non-arising places it within this enumeration of all phenomena, one cannot establish a thesis of non-arising)—and because a non-arising phenomenon does not destroy its own characteristics, they establish [it] as a single [entity].
Regarding the thesis that "all phenomena are non-arising," that [thesis] is undermined. [Yang says: "The true nature is not undermined; it is inherently non-arising from the beginning.

Now, if one establishes this thesis and enters into all phenomena, why would that establishment not be undermined? (4. The refutation of falling into existence or non-existence by means of the fivefold division of the provisional).

Mahāmati, as for the thesis that "existence and non-existence are non-arising," since that thesis is composed of various parts, and because in that thesis the characteristics of existence and non-existence regarding all natures cannot be apprehended. (Śikṣānanda says: "Furthermore, because that thesis is formed by various parts, and furthermore, because in that thesis all phenomena of existence and non-existence are non-arising. This thesis—

One immediately enters into all dharmas because both existence and non-existence are signless and do not arise. If one establishes the thesis of non-arising based upon existence and non-existence, then one enters into the nature of all existence and non-existence; since the characteristics of the nature of existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended, from where could one establish a thesis of the non-arising of existence and non-existence?

(5. Refuting the many faults in establishing a thesis. Mahāmati, if that thesis were established such that all natures are non-arising and thus the thesis itself is non-arising, then that thesis would be destroyed, because the characteristics of the nature of existence and non-existence are themselves non-arising. Therefore, one should not establish such a thesis.

If one were to establish the thesis that "all natures are non-arising" by asserting that the opponent's position does not arise, then that very thesis would be undermined; for since the characteristics of existence and non-existence are fundamentally non-arising from the outset, one should not further establish "non-arising" as a thesis.

Furthermore, the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava*) contains many faults (as noted in the preceding commentary regarding the three faults of the thesis, reason, and example: first, nine faults of the thesis; second, fourteen faults of the reason; third, five faults of the similar instance and five faults of the dissimilar instance, totaling thirty-three faults). Regarding the nine faults of the thesis (*pakṣa*), they are:

contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa-viruddha*), contradiction with authoritative scripture (*āgama-viruddha*), contradiction with worldly consensus (*loka-viruddha*), contradiction with inference (*anumāna-viruddha*), contradiction with one’s own words (*svavacana-viruddha*), contradiction with what is already established (*prasiddha-viruddha*), [the fault of] the qualifier being unestablished (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*), [the fault of] the qualificand being unestablished (*viśeṣyāsiddha*), and [the fault of] the relation between them being unestablished (*sambandhāsiddha*).

Regarding the fourteen types of fallacies concerning the unestablished nature of the reason (*asiddha-hetu*)—namely, when the specific property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is unestablished, or when both are unestablished—the first characteristic, "the property being present in the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*), has four types of non-establishment: (1) unestablished for one party (*anyatarāsiddha*), (2) unestablished regarding the locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), (3) unestablished for both parties (*ubhayāsiddha*), and (4) unestablished due to doubt (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*). The latter two characteristics [of the reason] share ten faults; among these, six are indeterminate (*anaikāntika*):

(1) the "similar class" (*sapakṣa*) is entirely indeterminate, (2) the "dissimilar class" (*vipakṣa*) is entirely indeterminate, (3) the reason occurs in one part of both classes (*ubhayapakṣaikadeśavṛtti*), (4) the common indeterminate (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*), (5) the uncommon indeterminate (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*), and (6) the indeterminate due to uncertainty.

There are four types of contradiction (*viruddha*): (1) contradiction with the specific character of the property (*dharmasvarūpaviruddha*), (2) contradiction with the specific character of the distinction (*dharmaviśeṣaviruddha*), (3) contradiction with the specific character of the subject (*dharmin-svarūpaviruddha*), and (4) contradiction with the specific character of the subject's distinction (*dharmini-viśeṣaviruddha*). The three types of similarity in the example (*dṛṣṭāntasama*) are: (1) the unestablished nature of the probandum (*sādhyāsiddha*).

The five [fallacies]—the unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*), the unestablished for both parties (*ubhayāsiddha*), the lack of application (*aprayoga*), the inverted application (*viparīta-prayoga*), and the dissimilar example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*)—are such that the reason is not excluded, the thesis (*sādhya*) is not excluded, both are not excluded, they are not separated [from the subject], and there is an inverted separation. (Note: To establish further theses upon the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava-vākya*) is considered a great fault;

this is because of the mutual difference in the characteristics of the reasons and because they are conditioned (*kṛtaka*) phenomena. Therefore, one should not establish a thesis-component. [Regarding the statement that] "the five-membered syllogism has many faults":

it refers to the mutual differences in the characteristics of the reasons, such as contradiction (*viruddha*), unestablished (*asiddha*), inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and non-exclusion, as well as the fact that they are conditioned and produced phenomena; thus, its thesis-component should not be established. The sixth [member] is refuted by analogy with the preceding cases. This refers to the first.
All phenomena are unarisen; all phenomena are empty; all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
One should not establish a thesis (meaning that one should not establish a thesis regarding the fact that phenomena are unarisen, that phenomena are empty, or that phenomena lack intrinsic nature).

However, Mahāmati, it is because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas teach that all phenomena appear like illusions and dreams, whether they manifest or do not manifest, that [they speak thus]. (Above, the refutation of the impossibility of establishing a thesis concludes. This statement is what a Bodhisattva should say: "The nature of all phenomena is identical to that of illusions and dreams.")

Because they appear like illusions and dreams, arising does not constitute true arising; because illusions and dreams do not truly appear, non-arising does not constitute true non-arising. Furthermore, because one perceives the faults of seeing and cognition—[Bodhiruci says:

"Because the characteristics of all phenomena delude both vision and wisdom"—since wisdom is thus deluded, there are inevitably errors in seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing]—one should explain that all phenomena have the nature of illusions and dreams, except for the purpose of removing the state of terror from the foolish.
[The Bodhisattva should explain that all phenomena have the nature of illusions and dreams; he should not establish the thesis that all phenomena are non-arising, except for the sake of the foolish.]

"Having no choice but to explain that all dharmas are non-arising, Mahāmati, do not let foolish people—who fall into the views of existence and non-existence—become terrified and thereby abandon the Mahāyāna.

(Bodhiruci says: "Because ordinary people are struck with alarm and fear upon hearing that things are like illusions and dreams, they distance themselves from the Great Vehicle. This is a repeated exhortation for Bodhisattvas to guide others according to their capacities.)"
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Without intrinsic nature, without expression, without objective reality, and without continuity—those deluded commoners give rise to false imaginings, like a corpse of evil discernment.

(They claim) that 'all dharmas are from the beginning without intrinsic nature, devoid of the characteristic of verbal expression, and lack any objective reality that could serve as a continuity. Because the deluded commoners give rise to such evil discernments and views, their attachments are like a corpse. Thus it was said.

It is said that "evil thoughts are like a corpse. All phenomena are unborn; this is not the tenet of those non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), for they ultimately lack the nature of being produced through conditions.

The Buddha taught that all phenomena are fundamentally unborn; it is not that those non-Buddhists recklessly take this as their tenet. All dharmas are ultimately unproduced because all natures are accomplished through conditions.
Regarding the statement "all phenomena are unborn," the wise do not form conceptualizations, whereas the followers of those [non-Buddhist] schools perceive them because they arise from causes.

All are eliminated and extinguished. (The note says: "Wisdom" means that because one knows the essence of all dharmas is non-arising, one does not form the notion of non-arising. Since that thesis of non-arising is established based on the characteristics of arising, the awakened one eliminates it entirely.

It is like a person with cataracts who, looking at something illusory, perceives the appearance of hanging hairs; their attachment to such a nature is likewise the false conceptualization of the ignorant.

(That is to say, those who conceptually construct the existence of various dharmas are like a person with cataracts seeing floating hairs or wheel-like patterns. They establish the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) through things that are neither existent nor non-existent. Self-...
The nature of giving, the discourse on phenomena, the self-nature, and the arising of conceptualization—these are the signs of phenomena established through verbal teaching.

When the mind is distracted and violently shaken, the Son of the Buddha is able to transcend and remain far removed from all such conceptualizations. (Paramārtha translates this as: "The three realms of existence are merely provisional names; there is no real essence to dharmas.

Because of these provisional designations, one discriminates and falsely calculates, and these provisional names cause the mental consciousness to be moved and disturbed. The Son of the Buddha completely transcends these and wanders in non-discrimination. [The New Translation says: "Speaking of the existence and non-existence of birth and death in the triple world."]

All phenomena possess only provisional names and lack substantial reality. Fools do not comprehend that the skillful teachings of the Sages are merely conventional designations; because of this, they engage in conceptualization and false imagination, calculating names, words, and the characteristics of things as being truly existent, thereby deluding their own consciousness.

Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattvas are able to know that the skillful speech of the Tathāgata is beyond calculation and transcends the sphere of activity of the emotional intellect; it is free from discrimination. Just as one may perceive water where there is no water (Liuqi and Realśa both say:
"where there is no water, one perceives the appearance of water"), such perceptions arise from thirst and craving. Fools are thus deluded by what is holy.

The vision, however, is not so. (The *Xin shuo* states: "Because of craving, one falsely conceives the notion of water where there is no water; this serves as a metaphor for how the deluded person, because of ignorance and craving, falsely conceives the notions of arising and ceasing, existence and non-existence, where there is neither arising nor ceasing, nor existence nor non-existence.
The Sage perceives the purity of the three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣa-samādhi*). Being detached from arising and ceasing, he wanders in the realm of non-existence;
he practices non-existence and, moreover, the equality of being, non-being, both being and non-being, and neither being nor non-being.

From this, the fruit of the noble ones arises. (Iśvara says: "Constantly practicing the realm of signlessness, and even that practice of the realm of signlessness is itself non-existent; existence and non-existence are both equal. Therefore, the fruit of the noble ones arises. The new commentary says:

"It is said that the three gates of liberation arise from the pure knowledge and vision of the noble ones. To remain far removed from arising and ceasing and constantly practice the realm of signlessness means that there are no dharmas such as existence and non-existence, or oneness and difference.

Because one awakens to the true nature of all dharmas through the equality of existence and non-existence, one is thus able to produce the fruit of the noble ones. The sphere of nothingness is precisely the realm of signlessness. What is meant by "nature" and "non-nature"?
What is meant by "equanimity"? It refers to that mind which, being unaware of the internal and external, is extremely agitated; if one can destroy that [agitation], the mind then becomes equanimous.

(The Buddha asks himself: What is nature and what is non-nature? What is equanimity? It means that those foolish people do not penetrate the fact that all phenomena are illusory, and thus they falsely conceptualize existence and non-existence, causing them to drift and fluctuate between the internal and external.

If one can thoroughly understand this, the delusory thoughts of existence and non-existence will cease, and the signs of internal and external drifting and fluctuation will vanish; then the mind’s vision will naturally become equanimous.)

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said, 'Just as when one grasps at an object, wisdom cannot [perceive it]'—[Bodhiruci says:

'As the World-Honored One has said, the observation of wisdom cannot see the phenomena of the external realm']—this refers to the fact that the wisdom observing the external realm cannot apprehend the object of its own perception.

This is the measure of conceptual designation (*prajñapti-mātra*); it is established by conceptual designation and is comprised within what is grasped. (Note: It is said that the external realm is the measure of false discrimination (*vikalpa-mātra*), established by conceptual designation. It is not [the ultimate reality].
Because there is no grasping, neither the grasped nature nor the grasper exists; thus, cognition does not arise, being merely a conventional designation.

(Dharmaruci says: "There is no dharma that can be grasped, nor is there a grasper; therefore, cognition cannot even differentiate and grasp. [Commentary: It is said that all dharmas are merely conceptual designations and names, lacking any substantial reality].

Why, World-Honored One, is it that because one does not perceive whether the self-characteristic and common characteristic of nature are different or not different, cognition cannot attain them? (Dharmaruci says: "Cognition...")
Is it because the various natures and intrinsic characteristics of lower categories are obscured by their own specific and general characteristics that cognition cannot apprehend them?

Or is it because they are obstructed by mountains, trees, stone walls, earth, water, fire, or wind that cognition cannot apprehend them? Or is it because they are too far away or too close that cognition cannot apprehend them?
Or is it because one is old, young, blind, or lacks the full sensory faculties that cognition cannot apprehend them?
(The preceding five sections consist of Mahāmati’s words of doubt; the following all follow up on the previous discourse to question it.

"World-Honored One, if one does not perceive whether self-characteristics and common characteristics are different or non-different, and thus cognition is not attained, then this should not be called 'cognition' but should be called 'non-cognition,' because there is an object that is not apprehended. (Śikṣānanda says: "This cannot be named cognition;

it should be non-cognition, because although there is an objective realm, it is not known. Furthermore, if the various natures of self-characteristics and common characteristics have their own intrinsic nature obscured—

Regarding the statement that "wisdom does not arise because of obscuration," this too is not a lack of wisdom; it is not that wisdom does not exist. Because the World-Honored One possesses such an *ālambana* (object), wisdom arises.
It is not that there is no nature [of cognition]. Because one encounters such an *ālambana*, it is called wisdom. (Śikṣānanda says: "This is also not wisdom;

it is called wisdom because it knows its object, not because it does not know. That is to say, because there is something known, wisdom arises; it is not that there is no capacity for knowing. Because one encounters the object that is known, it is called wisdom. If there are mountains, cliffs, stone walls, or the earth...

If water, fire, wind, or things extremely distant or extremely near, as well as those who are old, young, blind, ignorant, or lacking in sensory faculties, cannot perceive them through their cognition, this too is not "wisdom" (jñāna);

it should rather be "non-wisdom" (ajñāna), because there is an object that cannot be apprehended. (Śikṣānanda says: "That too is not wisdom, because although there is an objective realm, wisdom is incomplete and thus does not know it.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not so; non-wisdom should be [regarded as] wisdom, and not non-wisdom. (The Buddha’s intention is:)

"How can it be said that failing to apprehend an external object constitutes a lack of wisdom? One should know that this is in fact wisdom, not a lack of wisdom. (This refutes Mahāmati’s doubt regarding the absence of wisdom and non-wisdom.

"I do not speak in such a way as to conceal the matter of objective conditions (*ālambana*) so that wisdom fails to apprehend them; rather, this is an establishment based on the measure of conceptual designation (*prajñapti-pramāṇa*). (The note states:

The Buddha says, "I do not speak thus because there are external objects that mutually conceal one another, whereby wisdom fails to apprehend them. If one calculates that wisdom fails to apprehend because there are external objects that mutually conceal one another, this is an establishment based on the measure of conceptual designation, which is mere delusion. Awakening.
One knows that the existence or non-existence of external objects is merely the manifestation of one's own mind;

yet, because these things cannot be apprehended, cognition does not arise toward them. Thus, the wisdom that accords with the three gates of liberation is also unapprehendable. (Realśa says: "Because one realizes that external phenomena are merely what is seen by one's own mind, whether they exist or not, wisdom ultimately finds nothing therein.

Because there is nothing to be attained, no mental activity arises, and one enters the three gates of liberation; even the essence of wisdom is forgotten. [The term] "things" refers to the objects of perception. Since wisdom does not apprehend these things, that which is known [is likewise unapprehendable].

That which is not false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is the beginningless nature of both existence and non-existence; it is produced by the habitual tendencies of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), and one who knows thus does not know that [knowledge].
Because the essence of knowledge is also forgotten, it is not false conceptualization; yet the foolish person (*bāla*) conceives such a notion and dwells in such a state of knowing.

Because that fool does not know the forgetting of the essence of knowledge, they do not sever the false conceptualization regarding the characteristics and the existence or non-existence of external objects and their locations. That fool, because they do not know the forgetting of the essence of knowledge, engages in false conceptualization and discrimination regarding the forms and marks of external realms—whether they exist or do not exist.

The continuity is uninterrupted. [Regarding] the objects of external spheres produced by causes and conditions other than the stream [of consciousness] (the *Paramārtha* translation refers to them as external dharmas): one establishes and speaks of the manifestation of one’s own mind as the measure of reality (*pramāṇa*), yet clings to and conceptualizes the marks of "self" and "what belongs to self.
Being unaware that these are merely the manifestation of one’s own mind, one gives rise to false discrimination (*vikalpa*) regarding the radiance of gnosis (*jñāna-arcis*).

Because of such false discrimination, one observes that external natures have no real existence; thus, one falls into the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). (Fools establish and cling to the manifestation of their own minds as being real.)

Attached to the non-awakening that what is grasped as "I" and "mine" is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, they give rise to false conceptualization regarding the radiance of gnosis (*jñāna-jvālā*). Because existence and non-existence cannot be found through investigation by means of such conceptualization, they then rely upon the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
There are various objects of perception (*ālambana*) which wisdom does not discern; this lack of wisdom is not true ignorance, but is called "deluded conceptualization" (*vikalpa*).

[This refers to] the statement made by fools who, because they cannot discern that the various perceived objects of perception do not exist, claim it is "lack of wisdom" rather than "wisdom," and thus speak of them as deluded conceptualizations. Regarding the nature of non-differentiation, wisdom does not discern it (as stated in the verse:

"Because one does not realize that the self-characteristic and common characteristic are neither different nor non-different," etc.). Obstructions, as well as proximity and distance (as stated in the verse above).

The passage beginning with "mountains, cliffs, stone walls, extremely far, extremely near, etc. is called false knowledge (concluding the verse above: the question of Mahāmati regarding non-knowledge and not-knowledge is identified as false knowledge).

"The faculties of the old and the young are obscured and wisdom does not arise, yet there truly exists such a radiance"—this is also said to be false knowledge (these four lines conclude the preceding passage on the "blindness of the old and the young" and generally summarize that which Mahāmati asked as being false knowledge; hence it says "is also said").
Furthermore, Mahāmati, foolish ordinary beings are turned around by the beginningless, false, evil, and perverse conceptualizations (*vikalpa*).

While being thus turned around, they do not properly understand the penetration of one's own school (*svapratyātma-gati*) or the penetration of teaching (*deśanā-gati*) (meaning that because they are turned around by evil and perverse conceptualizations, they do not properly understand the two penetrations of their own school).

Because they are attached to the external characteristics of natures manifested by their own minds, they become attached to the skillful means of teaching regarding the fourfold positions (*catuṣkoṭi*) of their own school.

Regarding the pure, pervasive characteristic of incorrect discrimination (which refers to those who cling to the literal text while neglecting the essential meaning, being unable to transcend words to grasp the intent;

they conceptualize and become attached to natures and characteristics, clinging to expedient verbal teachings regarding the self-system’s pervasive dharma that transcends the four propositions), Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "It is truly as Your Reverence has taught.

I only pray that the World-Honored One will, for my sake, distinguish and explain the pervasive [teaching] and the pervasive [principle], so that I and other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas may become proficient in these two pervasions in future ages."

Ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas cannot find any deficiency [in this teaching]. (Since the fundamental doctrine is universally practiced and its understanding is consistent with reality, there are no further errors;

thus, ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles cannot find any flaw or opening. The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for you.
Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time..."
There are two kinds of teachings: the teaching of the verbal expression (*deśanā-naya*) and the teaching of one’s own school (*sva-siddhānta-naya*).

As for the teaching of the verbal expression, it refers to the preaching of various collections of sūtras according to what is appropriate to the minds of sentient beings; this is called the teaching of the verbal expression. (The Sanskrit term *sūtra* is translated here as "sūtra" [契經];

it means "conforming to principle" and "conforming to capacity. Regarding "various collections," the *Zhàhuá* states: "Conforming to principle means to accord with the two truths; conforming to capacity means to correspond with the three faculties. As for the teaching of one’s own school, it refers to spiritual practice.

This refers to those who are free from the various delusive imaginings manifested by their own minds—meaning they do not fall into the categories of identity, difference, both, or neither—and who have transcended all mind, thought, and mental consciousness (*citta-mano-manovijñāna*).

[Paramārtha reads "at this point there is the character 'you' (*yu*")] They personally realize the realm of the noble ones (*ārya-gati*), being free from the characteristics of views established by causes (both Paramārtha and Dharmaruci state:

"free from the characteristics of views associated with all causes and conditions"). This is the domain of those who have fallen into the two extremes, such as all non-Buddhists, *śrāvakas*, and *pratyekabuddhas*.

One cannot know [this]—that is to say, falling into existence or non-existence, as well as the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, or identity and difference, and so forth; the subsequent passages are like this. Mahāmati, I call this the "Dharma of the ultimate realization of one's own school" (*svapratyātma-gati-naya*).
Mahāmati, you and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should diligently train yourselves in these characteristics of the ultimate realization of one's own school and the teaching (*deśanā*).

The two modes of the school and the teaching were already clarified in the preceding text; that they are stated again now has its reason. Previously, with reference to the Three Vehicles, the school was mentioned first and the teaching second; here, with reference to the One Vehicle, the teaching is mentioned first and the school second, because the capacities and responses of sentient beings differ.
Therefore, it is not redundant. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

"I speak of two kinds: the penetration of the principle (zong-tong) and the penetration of verbal expression (yan-shuo). The speaker [of the latter] instructs the naive (tong-meng)—the new commentary says 'the ignorant and foolish are like the naive'—while the principle [of the former] is for the practitioner (xiu-xing-zhe), that is, for those who practice according to reality."
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One once said:

'Regarding the various discursive arguments of worldly treatises, you must be careful not to study or associate with them. (In the translations by Bodhiruci and Paramārtha, "worldly treatises" refers to *lokāyata*, which is translated as "left-handed world" or "evil treatises," namely the treatises of the non-Buddhists.
If one studies or associates with them, one will embrace greed and desire, rather than embracing the Dharma. (Bodhiruci says: 'That person only embraces...')"
[They] desire to eat the food of non-restraint. Why did the World-Honored One speak thus? The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"Worldly discourse consists of various phrases and expressions, adorned by the collection of causes, conditions, and parables. It seduces and deludes foolish ordinary people, who do not enter into the true self-realization;
they fail to perceive that all dharmas are but false imaginings and inversions, and thus fall into the two extremes. Such are the ignorant and foolish."
Deluded by ignorance, they destroy themselves; their continuity through the various realms of existence prevents them from attaining liberation. (The *Arthaviniścaya* states:

The discourses and treatises of the Lokāyata merely adorn words and phrases to deceive and delude the foolish and ignorant. They follow worldly, false speech that does not accord with reality nor conform to reason. They cannot enter the realm of ultimate truth, nor can they awaken to all phenomena.

Constantly falling into the two extremes, they lose the right path for themselves and cause others to lose it as well. They transmigrate through the various realms forever without emerging. Unable to realize that [the world] is the manifestation of one’s own mind, they do not depart from external [objects].

Due to the conceptual attachment to the imagined nature of intrinsic being, the various discursive explanations and debates of worldly discourse do not escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, nor the delusions and confusions thereof.

Mahāmati, although Śakra Devendra has extensively explained many treatises and composed his own work on phonology—[Śakra Devendra is fully called Śakradevendra, abbreviated as Diśi; this is a combination of both the Chinese "Emperor" and the Sanskrit "Indra"]—that is merely a worldly treatise.
One of his disciples took an image of a dragon and went to the palace of Śakra-devānām-indra to establish the essential points of his doctrinal system.
He vowed that if he were defeated by Śakra’s thousand-spoked wheel, he would cut off each of his heads one by one as an apology for his defeat.

Having made this vow, he used the teachings of Śakra to subdue him. (Paramārtha and Śikṣānanda both state that he used the teachings of Śakra to compose the treatise. Śakra fell into the position of defeat. Immediately—

Having destroyed their chariots, they return to the human world. In this way, Mahāmati, worldly discourse is adorned with causes and similes (that is, it is an adornment consisting of the collection of causes, conditions, and parables;
the same applies to all that follows), even extending to animals (Liu Zhi says: "even manifesting in the bodies of animals").
Yet these can still delude the various devas and asuras with various phrases and expressions, causing them to cling to views of arising and ceasing; how much more so for humans?
Therefore, Mahāmati, one should avoid worldly discourse, for it brings about the cause for the arising of suffering; be careful not to cultivate or frequent it.
Mahāmati, those proponents of worldly theories speak only of the realm of bodily sensations (kāya-vijñāna-gocara). [The "New Commentary" states:

It clarifies that the speech of worldly theorists speaks only of these false realms of birth, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. Mahāmati, those proponents of worldly theories number in the hundreds of thousands. (In the Xianyu [Real-Commentary] version, there are two characters following this word.)

[The Master] said: "However, in a later time, during the final five hundred years, this collection [of the Buddha's teachings]—this Dharma of consciousness—will be destroyed when it is being annihilated in the degenerate age.

This is because false perceptions (*vitarka*) arise from the prevalence of views; thus, evil disciples receive [these teachings]. Although there are many kinds of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), they do not depart from two causes and five views.

The two causes refer to the causeless view and the false cause. The five views refer to the five sharp proclivities (*kleśa*) among the ten proclivities. Because their perceptions are inverted, they are called 'false perceptions. As it is said: 'Where there is such a teacher, there will be such disciples. Thus spoke Mahāmati.
The worldly treatises (loka-śāstra) destroy [the truth] by means of various collections of words and phrases, adorned with causes and analogies, to explain the matters of non-Buddhists (tīrthika).

They are attached to their own causal conditions and lack any internal realization (*sva-prativedha*). [As Yaśomitra says: "That which is not the dharma as it truly is (yathābhūta) involves attachment.
O Mahāmati, those non-Buddhists have no treatises of internal realization; they extensively expound immeasurable hundreds of thousands of matters in other worldly treatises.

The gate has no self-communication, nor does it know itself; it is the discourse of the ignorant regarding worldly conventions (not knowing that this is the discourse of the ignorant regarding worldly conventions).

At that time, Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if the various phrases, expressions, causes, and analogies used by non-Buddhists in their worldly discourses lack self-communication and involve attachment to their own specific objects and causes, World-Honored One, [you too]..."

Is it not the case that when you preach the worldly doctrines (*lokāyata*) to the vast assembly of gods, asuras, and humans gathered from various regions, expounding upon immeasurable varieties of words and phrases, you are merely following your own conventional understanding?
(This expresses doubt that the Dharma taught by the Buddha is identical to worldly doctrine and is not the reality-as-it-is.

Furthermore, does the Dharma taught by the Buddha also fall within the category of the intellectual discourses and conceptual proliferations of all non-Buddhist paths? (This further expresses doubt that the Dharma taught by the Buddha is also included among the deluded arguments of the clever and eloquent proponents of external paths.)
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I do not speak of worldly discourse (*lokāyata*), nor of coming and going; I speak only of neither-coming-nor-going.

Mahāmati, 'coming' refers to gathering, meeting, and arising; 'going' refers to dispersing and perishing (arising through the convergence of conditions and ceasing when conditions disperse). That which is neither-coming-nor-going is non-arising and non-ceasing;
this is the meaning I teach, which does not fall within the categories of worldly discourse or the delusions of conceptual proliferation."

What is meant by "not being attached to external existence or non-existence, which is the realm of the manifestation of one's own mind, and not being turned back by the false imaginings of the two extremes"?
When one realizes that the characteristics of objects have no inherent nature and are merely the manifestation of one's own mind, then the false imaginings of one's own mind do not arise.
The non-arising of false imaginings is the entry into the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and this is called liberation. Mahāmati, I recall one...
At that time, there was a Lokāyatika Brahmin (in full, *Brahmamaṇava*, translated as "Pure Lineage") who resided in a certain place. He claimed that his ancestors were born from the mouth of Brahmā;

because they descended from the lineage of Brahmā, he called himself a *brahmacārin*—a term found only in the various scriptures of the Five Indias and not in other countries. It is also said that those of "external intent" have their own distinct lineages of scriptures, which they have inherited as their profession, whether living as householders or as renunciants;

relying on their intellectual prowess, they are arrogant. They are also called "Pure Practitioners. He came to where I was, but did not request an opportunity for leisure. (The note states: "Taking 'no-self' (*anātman*) as 'leisure. The non-Buddhist schools take 'self' (*ātman*) as [leisure].)"
Because [the self] is divine, he did not ask the Buddha about the teaching of non-self. He then asked me, "Gautama, is everything created?
I replied to him, "Brahmin, 'everything is created' is the first worldly doctrine. He asked again, "Is everything uncreated?
I replied again, "'Everything is uncreated' is the second worldly doctrine. He asked again, "Is it one..."
"Are all things eternal? Are all things impermanent? Are all things born? Are all things unborn? To this, I replied at that time:
"These are the six worldly theories, O Mahāmati. He then questioned me further: "Are all things one? Are all things different?
Are all things both? Are all things neither? Do all things manifest through various causes and conditions? (That is to say, regarding all phenomena...)

[Question: "Is it manifested through various modes of birth? I then replied: "These are the eleven types of worldly theories (*lokāyatika*). [The new commentary states: 'The Tathāgata cited his past deeds to extensively clarify the worldly theories, stating that all phenomena are created by Brahmā and others.

Because of the first question, he answered regarding the first theory; because of the second question, he answered regarding the second theory; and by combining the latter four, they are clarified as six. Furthermore, taking the former six and the latter five together makes eleven. Mahāmati, he asked again:
"Is one [theory] indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), or are all [theories] determinate? Is there a self (*ātman*), or is there no self?"
Is there this world? Is there no this world? Is there another world? Is there no other world?
Is there liberation? Is there no liberation? Are all things momentary? Are all things non-momentary? Is there space?

Is there analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—[Vasubandhu explains that *saṃkhyā* means discernment]—is there nirvāṇa? O Gautama, is it created? Is it uncreated? Does the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) exist?
"Is there no intermediate state (antarābhava), Mahāmati? I replied at that time: "O Brahmin, those who speak thus are all proponents of worldly treatises;

this is not my teaching. This is your worldly treatise. I teach only that beginningless false imagination and the habit-energies (vāsanā) of various evils are the causes of the three realms of existence (trai-dhātuka).
Failing to realize that these are merely manifestations of one's own mind, one gives rise to false imagination."

When there is an object of perception (*ālambana*) regarding external natures, as in the systems of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), knowledge arises from the conjunction of the three: the self (*ātman*), the sense faculties (*indriya*), and their objects (*viṣaya*). (Real-śā states:

"The self, the faculties, and the objects—through the union of these three, knowledge arises. The non-Buddhists claim that knowledge arises because of the conjunction of the three factors: the faculties, the objects, and the self; "knowledge" here refers to consciousness. I do not teach in this way, O Brahmin. I do not speak of a cause, nor do I speak of no cause.

I teach only the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) established through the nature of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), which is comprised of false conceptualization (*parikalpita*).

This can be realized by you and others who have fallen into grasping at a self-continuum (*ātma-saṃtati*)—[according to Paramārtha, it cannot be fathomed by you or others who cling to a self]—where "continuum" has the meaning of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Mahāmati, nirvāṇa, space, and cessation are not of three kinds; there are only three numbers, but they lack any intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

[According to Paramārtha, space, nirvāṇa, and non-analytical cessation merely have the number three; fundamentally they have no essence, so how much less can one speak of their being produced or unproduced? Furthermore, Mahāmati, at that time...
The worldling Brahmin questioned me again, saying, "Is the existence of the three realms of being caused by the karma of deluded reception, or is it without cause?
I replied to him, "Both of these are merely worldly discourse.
He questioned me further, saying, "Do all natures enter into their own-characteristics and common-characteristics? I replied again, "This too is worldly discourse," O Brahmin, and so forth.

The mind-stream falsely conceptualizes external objects (Realśikha says: "even down to the slightest movement of consciousness that discriminates external realms"). This is the worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, at that time the worldling Brahmin again asked me: "Is there anything that is not worldly discourse?
I am the master of all non-Buddhists, who speaks with various phrases, causes, conditions, and parables as adornments.
He replied again: "Brahmin, that which 'exists but does not belong to you' is neither a non-doctrine, nor is it something unspoken;

it is not devoid of various phrases and expressions, nor is it without the adornment of causes and analogies. (The World-Honored One said: "That which exists but does not belong to you" was said because he feared that worldly discourse and non-worldly discourse might otherwise be confused and indistinguishable.

As for "neither a non-doctrine nor something unspoken," this means that although it is not a product of volitional action, nor a formal doctrine, nor a verbal expression, it nonetheless does not fall into the view of nihilism; thus it is said that it is "also not without various chapters, verses, and parables. Brahmā...

The Brahmin asked, "What is that which is not worldly discourse, yet is not a non-doctrine, nor a non-exposition? (The Brahmin questioned this by following up on what the Tathāgata had previously answered.

I then replied to him, "Brahmin, there is a discourse that is not of the world, which you followers of external paths cannot know, because you cling to false imaginings and deceptions regarding external natures. (Because they cling to unreal imaginings, they are unable to know that which is not...)

Regarding this section of the discourse, there are two meanings to the response: first, establishing right and wrong through the principle of "not-knowing"; second, revealing truth and falsehood by means of "non-discourse. Therefore, the subsequent text states:

"When deluded thoughts do not arise, one clearly realizes that existence and non-existence are merely the manifestations of one's own mind. When deluded thoughts do not arise, one does not receive external objects;
when deluded thoughts are forever stilled, this is called 'non-discourse. This is my teaching, not yours, O Brahmin"—this is a brief explanation.

That consciousness (referring to the deluded consciousness of the proponents of worldly discourse) comes or goes, dies or is born, experiences pleasure or pain, sinks, sees, touches, or clings to various marks;
it is a combination of marks, a continuous succession, craving, and attachment to causes.
O Brahmins, such things as these belong to your worldly discourse and are not mine. (The original text is abbreviated here.)

[The Buddha] said: "To speak of the lower categories, all such doctrines are merely worldly treatises (*loka-vāda*). Mahāmati, when the Brahmin of the worldly treatises asked me such questions, I answered him accordingly;

he then remained silent and withdrew without further word. [The commentary notes: The Brahmin said, "I am the one honored by all non-Buddhists. From his speech, one could know that his self-conceit was not shallow.

Since he could not prevail in the discussion, he turned red with shame; therefore, he remained silent and withdrew without further word. Reflecting on his own position, he thought to himself: "The śramaṇa son of the Śākyas has emerged..."

Regarding those outside the [Buddhist] teachings who, through their own reasoning, cling to their own interpretations as being the domain of their own realization—claiming that the Dharma spoken by the Buddha lies beyond the scope of what they have perceived—[it is said]: "One speaks of non-arising, signlessness, and causelessness;
one awakens to the fact that these are manifestations of one's own deluded thoughts, and thus deluded manifestations do not arise.

(This section of the text differs in its presentation between Ratnamati and Śikṣānanda. "O Mahāmati, this is precisely what you asked me earlier: 'For what reason do you say that one should cultivate and associate with worldly treatises? (The Brahmin describes the superior Dharma of the Buddha.)
[The Buddha] explained in detail the distinction between embracing desire and not embracing the Dharma (this concludes the previous response to the Brahmin’s meaning, fulfilling Mahāmati’s request).
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, what is the meaning of the phrases regarding ‘embracing desire’ and ‘embracing the Dharma’? The Buddha told Mahāmati: “Excellent, excellent!
You are able to contemplate and inquire about such meanings for the sake of future sentient beings. This is indeed the truth.”
"Listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "That which is called 'craving' involves grasping or rejecting, contact or relishing, and being bound by attachment to external objects.

It falls into the views of the two extremes and gives rise again to the aggregates (*skandhas*), as well as birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and distress—such are its various afflictions."
All arise from craving, which stems from associating with worldly treatises and those who propound worldly treatises (namely, the Brahmins). I and all the Buddhas declare this to be greed;
it is called "clinging to desire and not clinging to the Dharma. Mahāmati, what is meant by "clinging to the Dharma"?

It means skillfully awakening to the fact that all is a manifestation of one's own mind, and perceiving the characteristics of the non-self of persons and the non-self of dharmas as being merely conceptual constructions.

Not giving rise [to conceptualization], possessing superior knowledge of the progressively higher stages (*uttarottara-bhūmi*), being free from mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*), receiving the empowerment of the wisdom of all Buddhas, being fully endowed with and sustained by the ten inexhaustible phrases, and having mastery over the non-origination of all phenomena—this is what is called the Dharma;

namely, not falling into any views and transcending all falsehoods. (This refers to the "practice of non-origination" and "mastery of one's own mind" mentioned in the first fascicle. This is named the Dharma. It is that which does not fall into any views and transcends all falsehoods.
"Mahāmati, regarding all false imaginings of all natures and all two extremes, there are many foolish outsiders who fall into the two extremes of either permanence or annihilation.

Those who are not wise and accept the doctrine of no-cause give rise to the view of permanence; those who hold that external causes destroy causal conditions and that things lack intrinsic nature give rise to the view of annihilation.

(It is said that those who are not wise, accepting this doctrine of no-cause, calculate that the four great elements do not arise from causes and thus give rise to the view of permanence; or they calculate that [the creator]..."

If one views that external causes for the destruction of form no longer arise and the nature of causal conditions is likewise non-existent, then one gives rise to the view of nihilism. Mahāmati, because I do not perceive arising, abiding, or ceasing, I designate it as "Dharma.
Mahāmati, this is called both desire and Dharma; you and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should practice and study this.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: [Verse omitted per instructions]
In all worldly treatises and the false doctrines of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), they hold to false views regarding agent and action;

thus, they possess no school of their own (Iśvara says: "They cannot establish it through direct perception"; the New Translation says: "They falsely imagine that Brahmā and others are the agents and all phenomena are the actions; such false conceptualization of agent and object cannot establish the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body as their own true school").
Only my own school is free from agent and action, and for the sake of my disciples, I teach this state of being far removed from them.

The various worldly treatises (those which, because they involve agent and action, lack a tenet of their own; whereas this [teaching], taking the single mind as its tenet, is free from agent and action) are taught for disciples so that they may abandon worldly discourse.
The measure of the mind is invisible; it does not observe the duality of the grasper and the grasped, nor the nature of existence. It is free from both extremes of annihilation and permanence.
As long as the mind continues to flow, this is merely worldly discourse and false imagination. One who does not allow such imagination to arise sees the Self.

Because the mind (the measure of mind) lacks substantial reality, it cannot be seen externally; for this reason, the non-Buddhists are unable to discern the two minds of existence and non-existence, nor that the grasping subject and the grasped object are fundamentally without intrinsic nature and are both free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.

Even until the flow of consciousness ceases, one falsely discriminates external objects; this is called worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*). One who is not turned by such false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) will see their own original mind. What is called "coming" refers to the arising of phenomena, and what is called "going" refers to the non-appearance of phenomena.
When one clearly understands that these notions of coming and going are merely false conceptualizations, they no longer arise, nor do the notions of permanence or impermanence.

"Performing what is not to be performed, this world and the next world, and so forth—all these are common worldly doctrines. (The new commentary states: "The four preceding verses briefly summarize the prose section;
the speculative attachments of worldly doctrines are as can be understood from the text.")
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding what you have spoken of as 'nirvāṇa,' what dharma do you designate as nirvāṇa?
For the various non-Buddhists each give rise to deluded imaginings. (Previously, the Buddha had told Mahāmati: "Nirvāṇa, space, and cessation—these are not three distinct entities;

it is only because of their enumeration that there are three. Therefore, I raise the question: according to the Tathāgata, what dharma is designated as nirvāṇa? Yet the various non-Buddhists each falsely discriminate, giving rise to views of nirvāṇa. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively..."
"Listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall explain it for you. The nirvāṇa imagined by various non-Buddhists is not a nirvāṇa that accords with reality (according to *Iśvarasena*:
'The nirvāṇa conceptualized by various non-Buddhists does not accord with the characteristics of nirvāṇa'). Mahāmati said to the Buddha, 'Yes, I shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: 'There are some non-Buddhists who [assert] the cessation of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) as the objective realm.'"

Having detached from desire (the commentary notes: as the non-Buddhists say, the extinction of the body of the five aggregates and detachment from the realm of the five desires), they perceive the impermanence of dharmas (the commentary notes: practicing the contemplation of impermanence).

They do not give rise to, nor dwell upon, the objects of the past, future, or present within the categories of mind and mental factors (because they take the non-arising of mind and mental concomitants to be meditative concentration, they do not bind their mindfulness to objects across the three periods of time).
When all aggregates of sensation are exhausted—like the extinguishing of a lamp or the destruction of a seed—delusive thoughts do not arise; such persons [attain] this.

One forms the conception of *nirvāṇa*—[Paramārtha says: "Like the exhaustion of a lamp, like the decay of a seed, like the extinction of fire; when all grasping ceases and discrimination does not arise, one forms the conception of *nirvāṇa*"].

Mahāmati, it is not by seeing the destruction [of phenomena] that one calls it *nirvāṇa*. [The views of the non-Buddhists hold that the destruction and cessation of dharmas is *nirvāṇa*; the Tathāgata refutes what they conceive, and thus says "it is not so"].

Mahāmati, some take going from one direction to another as liberation (Paramārtha renders the following two types of liberation as *nirvāṇa*). It is the cessation of the perception of objective realms, just like the wind.

Cessation (*śamatha*)—Yang says that moving from one direction to another means there is no perception of distinct realms; though the perception has ceased, the nature of perception does not cease, like wind momentarily subsiding.

Or again, seeing the destruction of the perceiver and the perceived is called liberation; or seeing the non-arising of discrimination regarding the permanent and the impermanent is conceived as the thought of liberation (the heterodox may reckon that the destruction of the views of the perceiver and the perceived is called liberation, or see the non-arising of discrimination regarding the permanent and the impermanent as the thought of liberation). Or they see that various marks and perceptions bring about the arising of suffering.

Reflecting upon this, they do not correctly understand that all things are merely the manifestations of their own minds (*svacittadṛśyamātra*). As the translation by Liuzhi states: "Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who speak thus:

'The conceptualization and perception of various diverse marks can give rise to all sufferings; it is through the false discrimination of one's own mind that all marks are perceived. Fearing these marks, they perceive the markless (*animitta*) and develop a deep fondness for it, conceiving it to be *nirvāṇa*.
These non-Buddhists hold such views without knowing that marks manifest from the mind. Alternatively, there are those who discern both the internal and external.
One may conceive the notion of nirvana regarding the indestructible nature of all phenomena—whether their specific or general characteristics—in the past, future, or present (the note says:

knowing that the five aggregates have a nature existing throughout the three periods of time which is not destroyed). Or one may conceive the notion of nirvana regarding the destruction of the self, persons, sentient beings, life-span, and all phenomena (conceiving nirvana through the destruction and cessation of all phenomena characterized by the four marks).
Or, like non-Buddhists who burn their wisdom with evil views, one may perceive a primal nature (*prakṛti*) or a person (*puruṣa*).
Those two "existences" (bhāva) are separated by the Puruṣa, whose name is Svabhāva (Self-nature), comparable to the Pradhāna (Primal Matter).

They consider the Guṇas to be the transformer and the Puruṣa to be the agent who conceives of Nirvāṇa. From the first [the Pradhāna] arises the Mahat (Intellect)—this is one existence; from the objects arises the Mahat—this is another existence;

thus there are two existences. "Pradhāna" refers to the Tattva of Darkness (Tamas); it means that the evil poison of the non-Buddhists is like fire that can burn wisdom. Seeing these two existences as the cause, they produce the Puruṣa (the Divine Self) as the fruit, naming it Svabhāva. It is comparable to the Pradhāna; they falsely imagine the Guṇas to be able to rely upon various conditions.

Transforming and creating all things, one takes the agent itself to be *nirvāṇa*. In the Sāṃkhya treatises, it is explained that the effect exists within the cause, and they take "oneness" as their fundamental tenet. This "one" refers to the primordial *buddhi* (intellect); before eighty thousand kalpas had passed since its initial arising, there was a state of profound obscurity and ignorance, where nothing was perceived except for the very first emergence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

By the power of past lives, one constantly recollects and imagines this; it is termed the "Primal Obscurity" (*mūlaprakṛti*), also called "World-Nature" (*lokaprakṛti*). It is said that the sentient beings of the world exist because of this primordial obscurity; thus, it is the fundamental nature of the world. Next, from *buddhi* arises the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃkāra*).

This is the "I" of self-conceit (*māna*), not the "I" of the spiritual self (*ātman*). In the Sāṃkhya system, this is called "calculation" (*saṃkhyā*). [Note: The original commentary identifies the primordial obscurity as the "Self-nature" (*svabhāva*). Some also refer to it as merit or non-merit.

Some say that when all [karmic] outflows are exhausted—[Paramārtha says: "The non-Buddhists (tīrthika) teach that because such offenses are exhausted, merit is also exhausted, which is called nirvāṇa"]—or they say that all afflictions (*kleśa*) are exhausted;

or they say that wisdom is [the cause]—[Paramārtha says: "They say that the exhaustion of afflictions depends upon wisdom"; Paramārtha further says: "Or they calculate that the exhaustion of afflictions does not depend on wisdom"];

or they perceive Īśvara as the true creator of birth and death, conceiving this to be nirvāṇa—[Paramārtha says: "Seeing that the god Īśvara creates sentient beings through false discrimination is called nirvāṇa"; they calculate that...].
They hold that the gods are the true agents who govern birth and death in human life, and thus they conceive of this as *nirvāṇa*.

Or they claim that birth and death arise through a continuous succession of mutual production, with no other cause [beyond this]—[Bodhiruci and Śikṣānanda read the word "sentient beings" (*sattva*) above the word "succession"]. Such views are attachments to causes;

because they are deluded, they cannot perceive the truth, and failing to understand it, they form the conception of *nirvāṇa*. [The new commentary states: They calculate that at the beginning of the eon, one man and one woman were born; their union led to successive mutual production.]

To know that ignorance, craving, and karma are the root—whereby all things, upon their cessation, return to that [source] and constitute *nirvāṇa*—is one view. Or there are non-Buddhists who say that attaining the path of the True Principle (*tattva*) constitutes the notion of *nirvāṇa*.
(Iśvara says: "Or they reckon the realization of the Path of Truth; through false discrimination, they take this to be *nirvāṇa*. [Note: They take the *pradhāna-tattva* as the True Principle].

Or, seeing the qualities (*guṇa*) and that which arises from those qualities as being in a state of unity, difference, both, or neither, they form the notion of *nirvāṇa*. (Note: This refers to the five [elements] arising from the qualities.)
They perceive the union of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the self-spirit (*ātman*), giving rise to fourfold views and conceiving them as *nirvāṇa*.

Or they perceive the nature of the various patterns on a peacock’s feathers, diverse precious gems, sharp thorns, and so forth; having seen these natures, they conceive them as *nirvāṇa*. (Iśvara says:

"Or they reckon that all things arise spontaneously—such as the patterns on a peacock’s feathers, the sharpness of thorns, or the various gems produced from gem-bearing mines—and they ask, 'Who could have made such things? Thus they cling to spontaneity (*svabhāva*) as *nirvāṇa*. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "This person sees that the end has no cause. Why is this?")

This person, having seen the roots of birth, knows that humans give birth to humans and realizes that birds give birth to birds; that crows have been black from the start and cranes have been white from the start; that humans and devas are fundamentally upright and animals are fundamentally horizontal; that whiteness is not created by washing and blackness is not produced by dyeing;

and that from eighty thousand kalpas onward there has been no further alteration or shift—now, at the end of this present form, it is likewise so. Yet I originally did not see bodhi; how could there be any further matter of attaining bodhi? You should know that all phenomena today are fundamentally without cause; this is of that same category.
Mahāmati, some may realize the twenty-five truths, or as kings they may protect the nation and receive the six virtues.

The treatise states that one may form the notion of *nirvāṇa* [in the following ways]: (1) Some claim that by being able to understand the twenty-five principles (*tattva*), one attains *nirvāṇa*; others say that by being able to receive the sixfold division [of duties] and protect sentient beings, one attains *nirvāṇa*.

(2) Or, seeing time as the agent, they perceive time, seasons, and the world in this way, and thus form the notion of *nirvāṇa*—the commentary notes that those who hold that time is the cause capable of producing worldly phenomena form the notion of *nirvāṇa* based on this.
(3) Or they claim it is nature (*prakṛti*), or they claim it is not nature, or they claim it is consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Regarding "non-nature" (the note states: some take existence as *nirvāṇa*, some take non-existence as *nirvāṇa*, and some take both existence and non-existence as *nirvāṇa*),

or seeing a distinction between consciousness (*vijñāna*) and *nirvāṇa* while conceiving it to be *nirvāṇa*— that is, observing that consciousness arises from the primordial darkness (*ādi-tamas*) and thus perceiving that consciousness entirely returns to quiescent extinction,

thereby conversely calculating that consciousness constitutes *nirvāṇa*— there are various such delusive imaginings (this concludes the section on how outsiders calculate that there are various such delusive imaginings).
[This is] an inference regarding *nirvāṇa*. What is taught by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) does not constitute the realization to be attained; it is rejected by the wise. (The note says:

"The *nirvāṇa* taught by the non-Buddhists does not constitute the true realization of *nirvāṇa* [to be attained]. All of the above are *nirvāṇas* of deluded thought (*vikalpa*), and because they are not dharmas as they truly are, they are rejected by the wise.
Mahāmati, all such things fall into the two extremes and are conceived as *nirvāṇa*. Such deluded conceptions of *nirvāṇa* held by the non-Buddhists are entirely absent therein [in true *nirvāṇa*].
Whether arising or ceasing—within that conceptualization of nirvāṇa, there is fundamentally no characteristic of arising or ceasing; it is merely that conceptualization itself arises and ceases.

Mahāmati, as for those various nirvāṇas of the individual non-Buddhist teachers, according to their own treatises (the note says: each of those nirvāṇas is discussed according to their own conceptualizations), when examined with wisdom, nothing at all is established.
Just like that conceptualization, the mind and intellect come and go, drifting, racing, and flowing; in none of these is nirvāṇa to be found.
"Parinirvāṇa," Mahāmati, as I have taught it, refers to the thorough realization that what appears is merely the manifestation of one's own mind.

(The preceding text stated, "The cessation of the deluded consciousness of discrimination is called nirvāṇa"; here it says, "What I call nirvāṇa is the thorough realization that what appears is merely the manifestation of one's own mind. Because of this thorough realization that what appears is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, the deluded consciousness of discrimination ceases.

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "'Nir' means non-arising; 'vāṇa' means non-ceasing. Non-arising and non-ceasing is called Great Nirvāṇa. Thus we know that the intent of these two sūtras is the same, though their phrasing differs. It is not clinging to external natures, but is free from them.
