Regarding the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), one sees them as they truly are and does not fall into the false imaginings of one's own mental manifestations—the duality of the grasper and the grasped—which cannot be apprehended.
One does not perceive any established conclusion through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Being ignorant of reality, one should not grasp at it;
having abandoned that, one attains the noble Dharma of self-realization and, knowing the two kinds of selflessness, becomes free from [dualistic attachment].
The two afflictions are purified, the two obstacles are forever abandoned, and the two types of death (the fourfold meanings of "two" have been seen in previous notes) are transcended.

In the higher and highest stages, including the stage of the Tathāgata, through various profound samādhis such as those of shadows and illusions, one is detached from mind, thought, and consciousness; this is called Nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati, you and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should practice and study this, and should swiftly distance yourselves from all external paths.
Regarding these various views on nirvana, at that time the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The views on nirvana held by the non-Buddhists each give rise to false imaginings; these arise from mental conceptions and lack the skillful means for liberation.

Those who are ignorant regarding the bonds and the banded, and who are far removed from wholesome skillful means, harbor the notion of liberation among the non-Buddhists, yet they never attain liberation."
The various wisdoms that do not arise, the different paths, and the views of the non-Buddhists—all these are entirely devoid of liberation because they are rooted in deluded conceptualization.

(The non-Buddhists give rise to various views of nirvana regarding existence and non-existence; this is being bound by nirvana itself. Furthermore, they each give rise to deluded conceptualizations and discriminations regarding nirvana;

this is being bound by conceptualization. Not knowing that these bonds arise from the mind’s perceptions, they lack the means for liberation. Thus, worldly fools rely on the non-Buddhists to give rise to various false reckonings; they become attached to them and do not relinquish them, thereby losing the means [to liberation] and giving rise to false notions.)

They conceive the notion of liberation, yet in reality there is no liberation; because these outsiders cling to this false wisdom, they claim within their own distinct realms that what they perceive is thorough penetration, unaware that they have truly fallen into ignorant delusion where no liberation exists.
All such foolish outsiders, through their false views, engage in debates concerning the categories of agent and action, existence and non-existence; none of them possess liberation.
The ignorant delight in delusive imaginings and do not hear the true wisdom; words are the root of the three kinds of suffering, while true reality is the cause for extinguishing suffering.

The *Dharmadhātu-krama* states: "Suffering is of three kinds: the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). If one takes 'affliction' as the meaning, then false conceptual speech is the root of these three sufferings. By departing from false conceptual speech and realizing true wisdom, one extinguishes the causes of suffering.
For example, although an image appears in a mirror, it does not exist [as a substantial entity]. Within the mirror of the deluded mind of false conceptualization, the foolish perceive duality.

Because the objects appearing within the mirror of the deluded mind of false conceptualization lack reality, they cannot be said to be dual. It is because the foolish do not understand this that they give rise to the view of duality regarding the reflected image. No.

When one recognizes the mind and its objects, two kinds of false discrimination arise; when one understands that both the mind and its spheres are false discriminations, such discrimination no longer arises.

(If one does not recognize the false mind and the objects it perceives, the two kinds of false discrimination regarding names and characteristics arise; if one realizes that there is only mind, the false discriminations of grasper and grasped do not arise.

The mind is that which is variously free from the characteristics of the signifier and the signified; though things appear, they do not truly exist, just as the three realms of existence are merely the false discriminations of the ignorant.
External objects do not exist at all apart from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*); yet various things appear through false conceptualization, which the ignorant and foolish cannot comprehend.

(Paramārtha and Śikṣānanda both take "external objects" to mean external realms. It is said that various objective spheres arise from the deluded mind; since they arise from the mind of false conceptualization, there is no such thing as a characteristic or a characterized object. Although things appear, they do not truly appear, just like the false discriminations seen by the ignorant.

The three realms of existence are likewise thus; the ignorant cannot comprehend this. In every sutra it is taught that false conceptualization never transcends names. If one is separated from words, [false conceptualization ceases].

Even in speaking, there is nothing that is spoken. (The note says: "Conceptualization does not emerge from names and language. [Note: "If it perishes," meaning that when one realizes the ultimate principle, both the speaking and the spoken—the conceptualizations—are entirely unobtainable.)
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Three. Man-da (upper:
mó guān), jiá (jí xié), diào (tú diào), fú (fú), cì (qī sì). (End of the scriptural text.)
Unravel (chōu, also yīn chōu). Ore (kǒng, gǔ měng). Tread (niè, yīn niè). Crevice (xì, qǐ yì). Pick up (zhì, yīn zhī). Blush (nǎn, nǎi bǎn). Sharp (xiān, sī lián). Crane (hù, hú wò).
(End of the phonetic glosses for the preceding commentary).
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Fascicle Four: Chapter Four, "The Essence of the Words of All Buddhas."

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain the Samyaksaṃbuddha (also called Samyaksambodhi, which means 'Perfectly All-Knowing'—note:
because Mahāmati had previously clarified true nirvāṇa and the supreme stages, he now raises the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya, which realizes nirvāṇa, as the subject of his inquiry).
May I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas become skilled in the self-nature of the Tathāgata, awakening ourselves and awakening others [to the Tathāgata’s self-nature Dharmakāya]."
[This is] the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Ask whatever you desire; I shall explain to you according to your questions.
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha an agent?
Is he a non-agent? Is he an object? Is he a cause? Is he a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)? Is he that which is characterized (*lakṣya*)? Is he speech? Is he that which is spoken?"
"Are these terms such as 'the awakener' and 'that which is awakened' different or not different? (Bodhiruci and Śikṣānanda [state]: Is the thing itself the fruit? The new [translation] says:
Are these terms different from the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, or are these terms the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Regarding such terms as these, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is neither the thing nor the cause. Why is that?"

Because both positions entail faults. (If one says that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is either a product or not a product, or a result or a cause, both entail errors; therefore, the Buddha negates those errors by stating in general that it is "not so.
Mahāmati, if the Tathāgata were a functional entity (*vastu*), he would be either a product or impermanent.

Because he would be impermanent, all functional entities would be the Tathāgata. This is something neither I nor the Buddhas desire. (The commentary states: "If one says that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is a resultant entity, it is identical to the fault of being a produced phenomenon and thus impermanent. If [it were] identical to... )

If "permanent" meant that all worldly fruits and activities were entirely the Tathāgata, this would be unacceptable [as Paramārtha states]. If it were not something produced by action, there would be nothing to be attained;

thus, skillful means (*upāya*) would be empty, like a rabbit's horn or the son of a barren woman, because they do not exist [as Yaśomitra states]. If it were not a product of action, it would lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);

the skillful means practiced would all be empty and useless, like a rabbit's horn or the son of a barren woman, because they are not established through the causes of action. Mahāmati, if there were no phenomenon and no cause...
That which is neither existent nor non-existent transcends the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). What constitutes the four propositions is worldly discourse;

that which transcends the four propositions does not fall within them. Because it does not fall within the four propositions, the meaning of the words of all Tathāgatas as apprehended by the wise is likewise so.
The wise should know this—that is to say, the meaning of the words regarding the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata.
As I have taught that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without self (*anātman*), you should understand the meaning of this: the nature of selflessness (*anātmatā*) is what is meant by "without self.

All phenomena possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and do not possess the nature of others, just as [the nature of] an ox or a horse. (Realśa says: "O Mahāmati, when I say that all phenomena are without self, it is because within all phenomena there is no 'self-nature' (*ātmatā*);

thus I speak of them as being without self. It is not that the intrinsic nature of phenomena does not exist. You should know that the meaning of the Tathāgata’s words is likewise so. [The New Commentary says: This cites former provisional teachings to clarify the present reality. I have constantly used skillful means (*upāya*) to speak of the One.]

Because all phenomena lack a self-nature (*ātmatva*), they are said to be "selfless" (*anātman*); it is not that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) does not exist. Just as one might compare the *dharmakāya* with the aggregates, elements, and bases, [one finds] that while the aggregates, elements, and bases lack the intrinsic nature of birth and death, the *dharmakāya* does not lack its own nature of eternal abiding.

Therefore, it should be understood that the meaning of the term "Tathāgata" is likewise so. Mahāmati, for example, it is not the nature of a cow that is the nature of a horse, nor is it the nature of a horse that is the nature of a cow;
yet in reality, these are neither existent nor non-existent. They do not lack their own nature. In the same way, Mahāmati, all phenomena are neither...
The absence of self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the presence of self-characteristic are not something that can be known by foolish people due to their deluded imaginings (*parikalpita*).

Thus, one should know that all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty, unarisen, and without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). (Real-śā states: For example, a cow lacks the nature of a horse, and a horse lacks the nature of a cow;

yet it is not that they lack their own intrinsic nature. All phenomena are likewise: there is no self-characteristic that does not exist, yet it is not that which exists. This is not something that foolish people can know. Why do they not know? Because of their conceptual discrimination. All...

The emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), the non-arising of all phenomena, and the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena are all likewise thus. The new commentary states: "One cannot say that the nature of an ox exists or does not exist upon the body of a horse; yet, it is not that the intrinsic nature of the horse's body itself is non-existent.

This serves as an analogy for the *dharmakāya* and its correspondence with the various phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*). One cannot say that the nature of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases exists or does not exist upon the *dharmakāya*; yet, it is not that the intrinsic nature of the *dharmakāya* itself is non-existent," and so forth.

It is said that there is a self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), clarifying that the *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding and possesses the self-characteristic of non-self (*anātman*). This means that what the śrāvakas, foolish worldlings, and non-Buddhists take to be the true reality of the *dharmakāya*'s self-characteristic cannot be known by śrāvakas or non-Buddhists, because they possess false conceptualization and discrimination. Only the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata possesses [this true reality].

One should know that all phenomena are empty, all phenomena are unarisen, and all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. The Tathāgata is neither different from nor non-different from the aggregates (*skandhas*).

(The Suyang and other two editions read "the Tathāgata is thus" as "thus the Tathāgata"; the commentary states: this refers to the Dharma-body being neither identical to nor separate from the aggregates.

If he were not different from the aggregates, he would be impermanent; if he were different, skillful means would be empty. If there were these two [distinctions], there would have to be a difference, like the characteristics of a cow's horns.
Because they appear similar, they are not different; yet because there are distinctions such as long and short, they are different. All dharmas are likewise so. (The note says:

"If one says that the Dharma-body and the aggregates are one, it should be impermanent. If one says that the Dharma-body and the aggregates are different, then it is like empty space and provides no beneficial substance through skillful means. If one says that the Dharma-body and the aggregates are both [different and identical], there should be distinct characteristics, like the two horns of an ox.

One cannot say they are different, for the two horns differ in length and in color—black and white. One cannot say they are not different. Therefore, Liu Qi said: 'In this way, all dharmas should have no distinct characteristics, yet they possess distinct characteristics. Part One.
Wisdom is like the right horn of an ox, which is distinct from the left horn, and the left horn is distinct from the right horn;

likewise, length, shortness, and various colors are each distinct from one another. Mahāmati, the Tathāgata is neither different nor not different from the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas). [Bodhiruci says:

"The characteristics of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body cannot be said to be identical to or different from the five aggregates. In this same way, the liberation of the Tathāgata is neither different nor not different [from it]. [Bodhiruci says: "In regard to..."]

Within liberation, it cannot be said that they are one, nor can it be said that they are different. (The New Commentary states: "The preceding explained that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is neither separate nor identical to the bound phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases;

this further clarifies that it is neither separate nor identical to the supramundane dharma of liberation. Thus, the Tathāgata is designated by the name "liberation. (Bodhiruci says: "Thus, based on liberation, he is called by the name of the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
If the Tathāgata were different from liberation, he would be constituted by material form (*rūpa*); because he would be constituted by material form, he would be impermanent. If...
If they were not different, the practitioner would attain non-conceptual correspondence; yet because the practitioner perceives differentiation, they are neither different nor not different.
Thus, wisdom (*jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*) are neither different nor not different. (Dharmaruci says:

"Mahāmati, if the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body were different from liberation, it would be identical to material form and would therefore be impermanent. If the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body were not different from liberation, there would be no distinction between the subject that realizes and the object realized. Mahāmati, yet the practitioner perceives [them as distinct].")
The means of realization and that which is realized are therefore not one; thus, O Mahāmati, this wisdom regarding the objects of knowledge is neither identical nor different.

(From here below, the true *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata is explained: "wisdom" refers to the *dharmakāya*, and "objects of knowledge" refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*).

It is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither created nor a creation, neither conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), neither the subject of awakening nor the object of awakening, and neither a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) nor...

That which is characterized is neither the aggregates nor different from the aggregates; it is neither the speaker nor that which is spoken; it is neither identical nor different, neither both nor neither, neither one nor different, neither both nor neither.
Because it is thus, it is entirely free from all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—[the commentary notes that seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing are called "means of valid cognition"].
Being free from all means of valid cognition, there is no verbal expression; being without verbal expression, there is no arising; and being without arising, there is no cessation.
Non-extinction is quiescent extinction; quiescent extinction is the nirvana of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-nirvāṇa*).
The nirvana of intrinsic nature is without objective referent and without cause. Being without objective referent and without cause, there is no object of clinging.
Being without an object of clinging, one transcends all falsehood. To transcend all falsehood is the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is the Samyaksaṃbuddha, Mahāmati.
This is called Samyaksambuddha Buddha. (Regarding *Samyaksambuddha*, see the note above. Regarding *Buddha*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the Qin language, it means 'the knower.

Because he knows all dharmas—whether sentient or non-sentient, permanent or impermanent, and so forth—of the past, future, and present, he is named Buddha. The *Hou Han Ji Saoshi Zhi* states: "In the Han language, it means 'awakened' (*jue*). The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:

'Because he possesses all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), is free from the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and is able to awaken himself to all dharmas in all their aspects, and is also able to awaken all sentient beings, he is therefore named Buddha. The present text says: 'This is called Samyaksambuddha.'")

Regarding *tathāgata*: the two characters "buddha" (awakened) manifest the meaning of being able to awaken; they possess the awakening of right universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Mahāmati, *tathāgata* and *samyak-saṃbuddha* are free from all sense organs and measures (*pramāṇa*).

(This reiterates the previous point to conclude the response to the question, clarifying that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body and right universal knowledge are forever detached from the spheres of all sense organs and cannot be measured by the false conceptualizations of consciousness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

Completely detached from all faculties, without objects and without causes; having already abandoned the perceiver and the perceived, and being detached from characteristics and the characterized—(from these seven verses, the Dharmakāya is praised as being free from thought and transcending the two views;
this verse generally clarifies "complete detachment"). The aggregates, conditions, and so forth, and Perfect Enlightenment—neither identity nor difference can be seen.
If there is no one who sees, how could there be discrimination? (If the five aggregates, the various conditions, and Perfect Enlightenment cannot be seen as either identical or different...)

How could there be further deluded conceptualization? It is neither created nor uncreated; it is not an effect, nor a cause; it is not the aggregates (*skandha*), nor does it reside within the aggregates, nor is there any other miscellaneous dharma.

One should know that the *dharmakāya* is free from such faults as these. It is not possessed of various natures as they are seen through deluded conceptualization, yet it is also not the case that this dharma does not exist.
The dharma is likewise: existence exists because of non-existence, and non-existence [exists] because of existence.

Therefore, one should neither accept existence as non-existence, nor should one conceptualize existence as existence. (Real-śā states: "Since non-existence cannot be grasped, existence also should not be spoken of.

Since existence and non-existence arise in mutual dependence, once existence and non-existence are transcended, they are empty of acceptance and conceptualization. Or else, by lingering in and becoming immersed in the verbal measures of "self" and "non-self," one destroys oneself and destroys the world through these two extremes.
(This means that fools do not know that the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata is free from existence and non-existence, and thus they cling to "self" and "non-self.")
If we are submerged by the faults of all dualistic extremes through the measure of our own discursive speech, we shall destroy ourselves and others, wandering in saṃsāra;

yet, when one correctly observes that I am liberated from all faults, this is called right observation, which does not disparage the Great Teacher. Being free from the faults of both existence and non-existence, one is able to see the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata;
thus, one’s own realization does not disparage the essential teachings spoken by the Teacher.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught that the sūtras uphold the non-arising and non-ceasing, and as the World-Honored One has further stated that 'non-arising and non-ceasing' is another name for the Tathāgata—how is it, World-Honored One, that you speak of non-arising and non-ceasing because of the absence of intrinsic nature, or is it indeed another name for the Tathāgata? (Mahāmati, based on the preceding statement...)

The Dharma-body that comes forth is without arising or ceasing, just as the Buddha previously explained in the Sūtras by distinguishing and grasping the teaching of non-arising and non-ceasing, stating that this is simply another name for the Tathāgata. However, since this non-arising and non-ceasing is itself without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), how can it be called another name for the Tathāgata?

Therefore, Mahāmati raised these two contradictory teachings to request that the Tathāgata reconcile them: "Is this [non-arising and non-ceasing] without intrinsic nature, or is it another name for the Tathāgata? The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"I teach that all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing, so that the categories of existence and non-existence do not appear. If all dharmas were to arise, they would fall into the category of existence; if they were to cease, they would fall into the category of non-existence."
Because arising is non-extinction, one transcends the categories of existence and non-existence; therefore, it is said that [dharmas] do not appear. Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, if all dharmas are non-arising, then the apprehension of dharmas cannot be obtained, because all dharmas are non-arising.

If there were any dharma within names, I pray that you would explain it for me. (At this point, Mahāmati gives rise to doubt regarding existence and non-existence, saying: "If all dharmas are non-arising and the apprehension of dharmas cannot be obtained, then all dharmas are non-arising...")
"Therefore, if there is a dharma of non-arising within that which is nameless and unarisen, we hope that the Buddha will explain it for us. The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent!
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall analyze and explain it for you. Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "I teach that the Tathāgata is not of no-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), nor is he subsumed under the categories of non-arising and non-ceasing."

All dharmas likewise do not arise nor cease because they do not depend upon conditions, yet they are not devoid of meaning. (The Tathāgata is not "without nature" means that he is neither without nature, nor is he merely non-arising and non-ceasing;

thus he encompasses all arising and ceasing dharmas, which likewise do not depend on the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing, and so are non-arising and non-ceasing, yet they are not without meaning.
Mahāmati, what I call the "mind-born dharma-body" is a name for the Tathāgata. That which is "non-arising" [is distinct from] all outsiders, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
"Mahāmati, awakening is not the domain of Bodhisattvas at the seventh stage.

That which is non-arising, Mahāmati, is another name for the Tathāgata (the Buddha taught that 'non-arising and non-ceasing' is simply a different designation for the Tathāgata’s mind-made Dharma-body). It is not the domain of the ignorant, the heterodox, the dull-witted, the two vehicles, or Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage whose mental measures have not yet been extinguished;
they are all simply unable to comprehend it. Mahāmati, it is like Indra, Śakra, and Brahmā (some say Śakradevendra, others say Purandara)."
Nanda and Kauśika are both alternative names for Śakra. In this manner, each of these various things has many names;

yet, while there are many names, it is not the case that there are multiple natures, nor is it the case that they lack intrinsic nature. As Yaśomitra says: "For example, Śakra, the earth, space, and even hands and feet—each individual thing has many names.

It is not because there are many names that there are multiple entities, nor is it that they have no entity at all. Although the Tathāgata has many names, he has no distinct entities. Thus, although Śakra has many names, his essence is one; yet it is not [the case that the names themselves are identical]."
It is not because there are many bodies that there are many natures; how much less could it be that they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)!
Thus, Mahāmati, in this Sahā world, I have three *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of names. (Sahā was formerly called Saha, also Soka; this means "Enduring. *Asaṃkhyeya* means "innumerable.
Fools hear them all and each speaks of my name, yet they do not understand that these are merely different names for me, the Tathāgata. (Realśa says: "All...")
Generally, although fools hear this and speak of it, they do not know that these are alternative names for the Tathāgata. Mahāmati, there are some sentient beings who know me as the Tathāgata;
some know me as the Omniscient One; some know me as the Buddha; some know me as the Savior of the World; some know me as the Self-Awakened One;
some know me as the Guide; some know me as the Broad Guide; some know me as the Guide of All; and some know me as the Rishi.
There are those who know him as Brahmā; those who know him as Viṣṇu; those who know him as Īśvara; those who know him as Jina;
those who know him as Kapila; those who know him as Bhūtakoṭi; those who know him as Candra; those who know him as Sūrya; those who know him as Īśa;
those who know him as Anutpāda; those who know him as Anirodha; those who know him as Śūnya; and those who know him as Tathatā.
Some know the Truths; some know the Reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*); some know the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*); some know Nirvāṇa; some know the Permanent;
some know Equality; some know Non-duality; some know the Signless; some know Liberation; some know the Path;
and some know the Mind-born (*manomaya*). Mahāmati, such as these are the three... [asamkhyeya kalpas].
Hundreds of thousands of *saṃgha* names—neither increasing nor decreasing—are known by me throughout this world and all other worlds, like the moon in water, neither emerging nor entering.

[As briefly cited above, there may be those who know thirty-three kinds of names to illustrate the vast multitude; "Viṣṇu" here means "Great Power," and "Kapilavastu" is named after the Buddha’s birth in that city, thus it is called the City of the Sage Kapila.

Such hundreds of thousands of names, filling three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, differ in their designations, yet their essence is one and the same, without increase or decrease, in this realm and in all other realms.

There are those of sharp faculties who are able to know that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body manifests according to the minds of sentient beings, appearing as reality without coming or going—just as the bright moon reflects in all waters;
how could there be any entering or exiting? Those foolish people cannot know this because they fall into the two extremes;

yet they all reverently make offerings to me, for they do not skillfully understand the meaning of words and phrases, do not discern names, do not comprehend self-realization, and are attached to various verbal expressions and chapters.

Regarding the phrases concerning non-arising and non-ceasing, they conceive of them as being without intrinsic nature; thus they do not know the distinctions among the names and titles of the Tathāgata.

(It is said that those foolish people do not know that the Tathāgata’s true Dharmakāya has no coming or going and falls into the views of the two extremes. Although they may respectfully revere and make offerings, they do not understand the meaning of names and phrases; they cannot discern the hundreds of thousands of names and titles as being nothing other than the single Dharmakāya.

They do not understand that the Dharmakāya is self-evident, but instead cling only to the verbal teachings, claiming that non-arising and non-ceasing means a lack of substantiality. They do not realize that these are the various names manifested by the Buddha according to the minds of sentient beings. It is like Indra...
The Rākṣasas, Śākyas, and Pūraṇas do not understand how to penetrate and return to the ultimate;

they cling to all phenomena according to their verbal expressions (because they do not skillfully penetrate the ultimate meaning, they cling to all dharmas following mere words). Mahāmati, those deluded people speak thus:
"Meaning is like the expression; meaning and expression are no different. Why is this? Because meaning has no body.

Apart from verbal expression, there is no further meaning; it merely stops at verbal expression. Those who are deluded claim that meaning is like verbal expression—that verbal expression itself is the meaning—and thus they do not understand its essential nature.
Furthermore, they do not understand that while meaning merely stops at verbal expression, it is beyond arising and ceasing, whereas verbal expression is subject to arising and ceasing.
Mahāmati, all verbal expressions fall into the realm of letters, but their true meaning does not.

Because it falls away from both existence and non-existence, there is neither rebirth nor a body. (Paramārtha says: "Because it is free from existence and free from non-existence, there is no birth and no substance.

The New Translation says: "It clarifies that all speech falls into names, whereas the true meaning does not fall into names; because it is free from existence and non-existence, there is no rebirth and no bodily characteristics; therefore, it does not fall [into such categories].
Mahāmati, the Tathāgata does not speak of dharmas that fall into words, for the existence or non-existence of words cannot be apprehended, except for those that do not fall into words. (Paramārtha))

It is said: "Except for those who do not fall into words. The New Commentary states: Although the various dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata according to the capacities of beings fill the dragon palaces and pervade the Dharma-realm, they in fact do not fall into words or speech, for the intrinsic nature of words and speech is free from them.

Except for those who, through skillful means, correctly manifest the true meaning and do not fall into names and teachings—this is to penetrate the subtle purport of the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma.
Mahāmati, if anyone should say that the Tathāgata speaks dharmas that fall into words, this is a false teaching, for the Dharma is apart from words. Therefore, Mahāmati...
We Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not speak a single word nor answer with a single word.

Why is this? Because the Dharma is free from words and letters. It is not that there is no meaning that benefits; rather, the speech that is uttered is for the purpose of destroying the false imaginings of sentient beings.

(Although the Dharma is free from the characteristics of words and letters, it is not that there is no meaning that provides benefit; yet the speech that is spoken is intended to shatter the deluded conceptualizations of sentient beings. Mahāmati, if one does not speak of all dharmas...
If the teachings were thus destroyed, and the teachings were destroyed, then there would be no Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Śrāvakas.

If these did not exist, who would speak and for whom? (To say there are no Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas—who would be the speaker of the Dharma, and for whom would they speak it?
Therefore, Mahāmati, O Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, do not cling to mere words; rather, preach the sūtras extensively through skillful means according to the needs of sentient beings.

Because afflictions are not uniform, I and the Buddhas teach various dharmas to sentient beings who hold diverse interpretations, so that they may abandon mind, thought, and consciousness; it is not for the sake of attaining the state of self-realized noble wisdom.

(Although we now speak of all dharmas, one must not cling to verbal expressions, for dharmas are beyond the characteristics of speech. It is only because sentient beings greedily seek after afflictions in diverse ways that we teach the Dharma according to their needs, clarifying that these skillful means and verbal instructions are the [teachings] of all Tathāgatas.)

The minds and desires of sentient beings differ, so [the Buddha] expounds the teaching for them to lead them away from the arising and ceasing of deluded consciousness; this is not spoken for those who have attained the state of self-realized noble wisdom.

Mahāmati, regarding all phenomena as non-existent and awakening to them as the manifestation of one’s own mind, and being free from the two kinds of false discrimination—bodhisattva-mahāsattvas rely on the meaning and not on the words.
If good sons or good daughters rely on the words, they will destroy their own supreme [attainment].

Furthermore, such a person is unable to awaken others; they fall into a continuity of wrong views and preach to the assembly without skillfully understanding all dharmas, all stages (*bhūmi*), and all characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), nor do they understand the words and phrases [of the scriptures]. (This shows that a bodhisattva should rely on the true meaning and not follow mere verbal expression;

for if one relies on the literal text, it will ruin both oneself and others, and one will fail to attain clear awakening. If, however, one is skilled in all dharmas, all stages, and all characteristics, and thoroughly penetrates the words and phrases...

Regarding the meaning of the perfection of phrases: one is thus able to delight oneself with the true joy of signlessness (*animitta-sukha*), establishing sentient beings in the equal Mahāyāna (Paramārtha says:
"one is also able to cause others to abide securely in the Mahāyāna"). One who thoroughly understands the meaning of the reality of the *dharmatā* as described above possesses such benefits.
Mahāmati, those who embrace the Mahāyāna embrace all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas; they embrace all Buddhas.
Bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas embrace all sentient beings; those who embrace all sentient beings embrace the true Dharma;
those who embrace the true Dharma ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed;

and those who ensure the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed are able to realize and attain the supreme locus of entry (which is the locus realized by the noble wisdom of self-awakening). Having known and attained this supreme locus of entry...
Dwelling as Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, they always attain transformation-birth and establish the ten powers of mastery (*daśavaśitā*) of the Mahāyāna.
They manifest various forms and images, penetrating the physical types, aspirations, and afflictions of sentient beings to teach the Dharma according to reality (*yathābhūtam*).

That which is "according to reality" is not different from reality (Real-śikṣā says: it is without difference or distinction). That which is "according to reality" is characterized by neither coming nor going, wherein all falsity and deception have ceased.

This is called "according with reality. Sons and daughters of good family with great wisdom should not grasp at or adhere to what is merely expressed in words, for those who realize the truth are free from letters and syllables.

(This clarifies that once Bodhisattvas have attained the superior points of entry, they desire to establish sentient beings in the Mahāyāna; by means of the ten powers of mastery, they manifest various forms and colors, proclaiming the Dharma according to reality.

As for the Dharma according to reality, it is without difference or distinction, neither coming nor going, wherein all conceptual proliferation and falsehood are completely extinguished; they thus exhort others not to cling to the literal meaning.)

Because the true Dharma is free from words and letters. [The ten powers of mastery are: first, the power of what is possible and what is impossible; second, the power of karma; third, the power of meditative concentration; fourth, the power of the faculties; fifth, the power of resolve; sixth, the power of disposition; seventh, the power of the path leading to all destinations; eighth, the power of recollecting past lives; ninth, the power of the divine eye;
tenth, the power of the exhaustion of outflows. Mahāmati, it is like using a finger to point at an object for a fool: the fool looks only at the finger and does not perceive the actual object.
In this way, fools follow the finger of verbal expression, grasping and clinging to it, never letting go until the very end.
One cannot attain the ultimate departure from the finger of verbal expression to reach the primary ultimate reality. (Fools are attached to verbal expressions and never abandon them;

it is like a person who points at an object with a finger to show someone else, yet that person looks only at the finger and not at the object. The Tathāgata is also like this: using the finger of verbal skillful means to point toward the primary true reality for the sake of fools, those fools look only at the finger of verbal expression and do not perceive the true reality.

Therefore it is said: "In the end, one cannot attain the ultimate departure from the finger of verbal expression to reach the primary ultimate reality. Below, the analogy is correctly cited to clarify this: Mahāmati, it is like an infant.
One should eat cooked food and not raw food; if one eats raw food, it will cause madness because one does not know the sequential methods for cooking it.
Mahāmati, in the same way, that which is neither born nor extinguished, if not cultivated through skillful means, is not wholesome.

(Real-śa says: For example, an infant should eat cooked food; if someone does not understand the method of maturation and eats raw food, they will become mad and disordered. Neither arising nor ceasing is likewise so; if not cultivated through skillful means, it is not wholesome.)
Therefore, you should skillfully cultivate expedient means (*upāya*) and not follow mere verbal expressions, just as one does not look at the tip of a finger.

For this reason, Mahāmati, regarding the true meaning (*tattvārtha*), you should apply yourself to cultivating expedient means. The true meaning is subtle, wondrous, and tranquil; it is the cause of *nirvāṇa*.
Verbal expression is conjoined with false conceptualization (*vikalpa*); false conceptualization is the accumulation of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Mahāmati, the true meaning arises from...
The one who is learned attains great wisdom. To be "learned" means to be skilled in the meaning, not merely skilled in words.
One who is skilled in the meaning does not follow any of the scriptures or treatises of the non-Buddhists; neither does he follow them himself, nor does he cause others to follow them.
This is what is called being a virtuous person of great learning. Therefore, those who seek the meaning should draw near to the learned—namely, those who are skilled in the meaning.

One should distance oneself from attachment to verbal expressions that contradict this. (The new commentary states: This clarifies that by awakening to the true meaning (*tattvārtha*), one attains *nirvāṇa* through the abandonment of all deluded thoughts and distractions.

"True meaning" refers to that which is obtained from those who have heard much (*bahuśruta*). Those who have heard much are those who have properly reflected upon and cultivated practice in accordance with the meaning, rather than merely being skilled in verbal expression. That which does not cause oneself or others to fall into the evil views of non-Buddhists is called "having heard much.
Therefore, those who seek the true meaning should draw near to those whose teachings accord with the meaning, and must carefully avoid those whose teachings contradict it.)
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva, further empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, there is nothing extraordinary about your demonstration of non-arising and non-ceasing. Why is this? World-Honored One, all externalists also maintain that their causes are neither born nor extinguished.
World-Honored One, you also speak of space, cessation not through conditions, and the realm of nirvāṇa as being neither born nor extinguished."

Regarding the meaning of "extinction" (nirodha)—which the Buddha taught as being neither arising nor ceasing—Mahāmati stated that since non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) also speak of various causes as being neither arising nor ceasing, there is nothing extraordinary about this; it would be no different from the World-Honored One’s teaching on the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) as being neither arising nor ceasing.

The World-Honored One [replied]: Non-Buddhists say that causes give rise to all worlds, and I too say that ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), karma, and false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) act as conditions to give rise to all worlds.
These are merely differences in the names of those causes and conditions; as for external objects, they are caused by... [the text ends here].

The conditions (*pratyaya*) are likewise thus; there is no difference between the World-Honored One’s discourse and that of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). [From the passage where Mahāmati speaks to the Buddha himself: Mahāmati’s intention is as follows:

all non-Buddhists teach that various causes are neither born nor extinguished, and the World-Honored One also teaches that the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are neither born nor extinguished. Furthermore, while the non-Buddhists teach that the various worlds arise based upon various causes, the World-Honored One also teaches that the various worlds arise with ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth as their conditions.

Moreover, the non-Buddhists teach that all phenomena arise based on external material causes and conditions, and the World-Honored One is likewise. Therefore, he doubts that what the World-Honored One has taught is no different from the discourse of the non-Buddhists. Subtle.
The nine entities—namely, atoms (*paramāṇu*), supreme matter (*paramāṇu-viśeṣa*), Īśvara, the Lord of Beings (*puruṣa-pradhāna*), and so forth—are neither produced nor extinguished.

The World-Honored One has also taught that all natures are neither produced nor extinguished, and that existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended. (The "New Commentary" states: this sets forth the meaning of non-production and non-extinction according to the non-Buddhists;

it refers to the essence of these nine entities: 1. time, 2. direction, 3. space, 4. atoms, 5. the four great elements, 6. Mahābrahmā, 7. Viśeṣadeva, 8. Maheśvara, and 9. the Lord of Beings. It means that the various non-Buddhists reckon these nine entities to be unproduced.)

That which is non-extinguishing can serve as the cause for all phenomena of birth and death; it is generally termed the "agent. According to the Buddha’s Mahāyāna teaching, all natures are fundamentally neither arising nor extinguishing; whether they are existent or non-existent, they are entirely unobtainable, and there is no difference [between them].

(The "Externalist" refers to Maheśvara, the Great Lord, and the "Lord of Beings" refers to the Lord of the World. The heterodox teachers also claim that the four great elements do not perish and their self-nature is neither born nor extinguished;

these four great elements remain eternally as the four great elements, even as they circulate through the various realms of existence without abandoning their self-nature. This is what the World-Honored One has taught.

It is also thus; therefore I say there is nothing extraordinary about it. I only wish that the World-Honored One would explain the distinctions that make it extraordinary and superior to all non-Buddhists.
If there were no such distinctions, then all non-Buddhists would also be Buddhas, because [all things] are neither born nor extinguished.
Thus, the World-Honored One has said that many Buddhas appear in a single world-system.
"It is impossible, as you have just stated, that there should be many Buddhas in a single world-system without distinction. (Mahāmati’s intention was this:

since the Dharma taught by the Blessed One is no different from what is taught by the non-Buddhists, he was implying that even the non-Buddhists are all Buddhas; furthermore, he argued that the Blessed One would surely say that many Buddhas do not appear in a single world-system.

If the Dharma just described were indeed no different from that of the non-Buddhists, then many Buddhas should appear in a single world-system without distinction. The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "I have taught..."
Non-arising and non-ceasing are not the same as the non-arising and non-ceasing of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Why is this?

Those non-Buddhists [assert] that there is a self-nature (*svabhāva*) and an intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) which possess the characteristics of non-arising and immutability—meaning they calculate that the nature of all phenomena truly exists with an intrinsic nature that attains the state of non-arising and non-ceasing, whereas mutability is precisely cessation.

I do not do so; I do not fall into the categories of existence and non-existence. Mahāmati, my [teaching] is free from the categories of existence and non-existence, and free from arising and ceasing. It is not...
Nature is not non-nature, because it appears as various illusions and dreams; therefore, it is not non-nature. Why is it non-nature?

It is because form (*rūpa*) lacks the characteristic of self-nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), appearing or not appearing according to whether it is grasped or not grasped. (Yang says: Form originally has no self-nature;

it is only through human grasping or non-grasping, and its appearance or non-appearance, that there arise views of existence or non-existence. For this reason, all natures are neither nature nor non-nature. However...

When one realizes that all things are the manifestations of one’s own mind and that false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) does not arise, there is peace, security, and happiness, and worldly affairs are forever stilled.

The activities performed through the false conceptualizations of ignorant, ordinary people are not those of the noble ones. (To calculate existence and non-existence, or arising and ceasing, is the activity performed through the false conceptualizations of fools.

Unreal false conceptualization is like a city of the *gandharvas* or a conjured person. (The above provides analogies to clarify unreal false conceptualization; the following explains the metaphors in relation to the doctrine. Mahāmati, it is like this:
The city of the Gandharvas and illusory persons—these various sentient beings, merchants coming and going—are the false imaginings of the foolish;
they think there is real coming and going, yet in reality there is no one who comes or goes, for it is merely their own false imagination.
In this same way, Mahāmati, ignorant ordinary people give rise to the delusion of birth and non-extinction; yet for them, as with that [city], there is neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned.
The birth of an illusory person is in fact non-existent; there is neither birth nor cessation, because its nature is neither existent nor non-existent, and it is devoid of anything whatsoever.

All phenomena are likewise thus, free from birth and cessation. Foolish ordinary beings fall into the false view of giving rise to the delusion of birth and cessation; they are not like the noble sages.

(That is to say, foolish ordinary beings do not understand the reality of non-arising and non-ceasing, and thus falsely give rise to the confusion of birth, cessation, and non-birth/non-cessation. One should know that this pertains to the conditioned and the unconditioned.)

Whether arising or ceasing, because existence and non-existence are both non-existent, all dharmas are free from arising and ceasing. It is only through the deluded thoughts of ordinary people that various divergent views arise; they are not those of the noble sages. That which is "not as it truly is" is not so;

it is not different from the imagined nature of self-nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*). If it were different from imagined thought, one would be attached to all natures and self-natures and would not perceive tranquility.
One who does not perceive tranquility will never be free from imagined thought. That which is "not as it truly is" is not so.

This means that ordinary beings fall into what is unreal and not as it truly is; yet there is nothing they fall into that differs from the self-nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-svabhāva*), which possesses a real nature and characteristics. This is no different from birth-and-death, deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and falsehood, all of which are unreal.

If one were to hold that the self-nature of all phenomena, possessing a real nature and characteristics, is distinct from birth-and-death, deluded conceptualization, and falsehood, one would instead be clinging to the self-nature of all phenomena as having a real nature and characteristics. Because of this, one fails to see the meaning of primordial quiescence (*ādi-śānta*).

Failing to see the meaning of primordial quiescence results in the persistence of signs (*nimitta*), and one will never be free from deluded conceptualization and discrimination. As stated in the subsequent passage: "Therefore, Mahāmati, the vision of signlessness (*animitta-darśana*) is superior, not the vision of signs. The vision of signs... [as follows].
Because it is the cause for taking birth, it is not supreme (to reckon that there is a nature and characteristics which are neither born nor extinguished is the cause for taking birth).
Mahāmati, that which is signless—wherein false discrimination does not arise, does not originate, and is not extinguished—I call Nirvāṇa.

Mahāmati, Nirvāṇa is the vision of reality as it truly is, free from the preceding false discriminations of mind and mental factors (this meaning is explained in the third fascicle), and the attainment of the Tathāgata’s own-enlightened noble wisdom. I...
While this Nirvana was being taught, at that time the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"To eliminate those theories of birth (the true meaning being: to remove the attachment to existence), I establish the principle of non-arising;

thus I preach this Dharma. Fools cannot understand it: all dharmas are unarisen, without self-nature, and non-existent. (These verses repeat the preceding points regarding nature, lack of nature, and non-existence.)
Therefore, if the Gandharvas, illusions, and dreams possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they would not arise without a cause;

yet they lack intrinsic nature. For what reason are they empty? It should be explained thus: although the nature of all phenomena exists, they do not arise because they lack intrinsic nature. For what reason do they lack intrinsic nature? Because all phenomena are empty; it should be explained in this way.
Since the nature of cognition does not manifest apart from the combination [of conditions], they are empty and unarisen. I teach that there is no intrinsic nature.

The nature [of awakening and cognition] manifests in accordance with the conjunction of the causes and conditions of all phenomena; if separated from these conjunctive conditions, this nature of awakening and cognition does not manifest spontaneously. Therefore, because phenomena are empty and do not arise, they are said to lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
This means that while each conjunctive nature manifests, it does not exist [independently]; when analyzed, there is no conjunction.

It is not like the views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) regarding dreams, floating hairs, mirages, or the *gandharva*-city, nor like the various worldly things which they claim to arise without cause.

The manifestation of signs (the phenomena of dependent origination): because they exist through the convergence of various conditions, they lack intrinsic nature; though they manifest, they are not real. Since there is no convergence, there is no arising—unlike the heterodox schools which calculate that there is arising from convergence.

Analogies such as dreams, illusions, and floating hairs illustrate how worldly affairs falsely manifest their signs while having no cause at all; "wild horses" refers to mirages and drifting vapors. To refute theories of causality and to expound the meaning of non-arising:
to expound non-arising means that the flow of the Dharma is never interrupted, blazing forth without end.

In discussing the intimidation of the various non-Buddhists (since their false doctrines have been refuted and the True Dharma is flourishing, these causeless worldly and world-transcending theories blaze like a great mass of fire, whereupon the ranks of the non-Buddhists tremble at the mere sound of it;
the Tathāgata often employs the metaphor of a mass of fire when teaching the Dharma).
At that time, Mahāmati asked in verse: "How [is it]? By what cause? (Note: The Buddha asks the non-Buddhists, 'How do you conceive the arising of dharmas?
Does it arise from a cause, or does it arise without a cause? They reply, 'It arises from a cause. Since it arises from a cause, he then asks, 'By what cause?
They reply, 'It arises from causes such as atoms, primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the four great elements, and so forth. For what reason does it arise? (Note: He asks again.)

"For what reason do those four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth arise? He replied, "The four great elements and so forth arise without cause. [Mahāmati asked: "In what place do they combine to establish this doctrine of causelessness? (The note states:

The Buddha said, "If the four great elements and so forth were without cause, then being without cause, there would be no phenomena (*dharma*). If there are no phenomena, there would be no location. If there is no location, there would be no combination. If there is no combination, there would be no arising.

How, then, can you establish the worldly doctrine that the four great elements and so forth arise without cause? Mahāmati cites the dialogue between the World-Honored One and the non-Buddhists in verse form as a counter-question.)
At that time, the World-Honored One again answered in verse:
"Observe that conditioned phenomena do not arise without cause; they have causes. The views of those who debate arising and ceasing are thereby extinguished.

(The Buddha said: "One should observe that all conditioned phenomena do not arise without cause, nor do they arise from a [permanent] cause. Therefore, by speaking of non-arising, the theories of arising and ceasing held by the outsiders are herefrom destroyed.")
The above [constitutes] the refutation of the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) tenet that [things] arise from causes.
At that time, Mahāmati spoke a verse, asking:
"What is meant by 'non-arising'? Is it the absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva), or is it that a phenomenon is called 'non-existent' because one observes its dependence upon conditions?"
The name "non-arising" (anutpāda) should not be without meaning; it must be explained through analysis. (Mahāmati asks: Is the term "non-arising" used because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature?

Or is it used because they depend upon various conditions? Or is it used because phenomena possess an intrinsic nature? Since there is the name "non-arising," this meaning of non-arising cannot be non-existent. I pray that the Tathāgata will analyze and explain this.)
At that time, the World-Honored One again answered in verse:
"It is not that there is no nature, nor is it non-arising; it is not that it depends on conditions, nor is it that there is a nature. It is called 'name,' yet it is not without meaning.
This is not the domain of any outsiders, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or those at the seventh stage. This is called 'non-existence' (nirvana)."

Regarding the characteristic of arising: (The Tathāgata answered Mahāmati’s question that it is not because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature that they are called "unborn," nor is it because there is a separate nature of arising that depends upon conditions that they are called "unborn. It is not because phenomena possess an intrinsic nature that they are called "unborn.

Since the name "unborn" exists, it does not mean that the meaning of "unborn" is non-existent; this is the name for the *manomayakāya* (mind-made body), designated as "unborn. This is not the domain of externalists, followers of the two vehicles, or Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage. It is far removed from all causes and conditions and detached from all objective entities;
there is only the subtle mind abiding, where both the perceiving subject and the perceived object are simultaneously abandoned.
I say that its body, which undergoes transformation, is non-arising. (It is only the subtle mind abiding; it is said to be "only" because it is free from existence and non-existence.

This subtle, quiescent mind remains profoundly still and eternally constant, transcending both thought and the object of thought. Thus, the mind-made body manifests according to conditions without obstruction; therefore, I say it is non-arising. There is no external nature, no lack of nature, and no grasping by the mind.
Having severed all views, I say this is non-arising. Such is the emptiness of self-nature.
These should be distinguished as follows: it is called "empty" because it is not empty [in the sense of non-existence], and it is called "empty" because it is unarisen.

(Thus, one should distinguish between emptiness that is unarisen and lacks intrinsic nature and phenomena such as causes and conditions; yet, it is called "empty" because it is not like the empty void or the emptiness of annihilation—meaning the Dharma-body is called "empty" because it is unarisen. *Note:

The above explains that the Tathāgata’s mind-made Dharma-body is considered unarisen.*) When the various factors of causes and conditions combine, there is arising and ceasing; apart from these various factors of causes and conditions, there is nothing else.

There is arising and ceasing (the note states: because there is only the transformation of the sequence of the twelve links of dependent origination, it is called "arising and ceasing"; apart from this sequence, there is no further dharma that arises). Apart from the sequence of dependent origination, there is no other distinct nature.
If one speaks of identity or difference, these are the deluded imaginings of the non-Buddhists.

The nature of existence and non-existence does not arise; it is neither existent nor non-existent. Apart from the transformation of that sequence, all such things are unobtainable. (If one is apart from...)

Apart from the twelvefold enumeration of transformations, there is no other nature of arising (*utpatti-dharmatā*) within false conditions; thus, the four propositions regarding the existence or non-existence of the nature of arising are entirely unattainable.
There are only conventional designations (*saṃvṛti-saṃkhyā*) that function as a continuous chain of links; apart from this chain of causes and conditions, the meaning of "arising" cannot be found.

(The "conventional designations" refer to the twelve links of dependent origination. [The New Commentary states: "Ordinary beings cannot comprehend these false conditions; therefore, for long kalpas they are bound by a hook and a lock, their linked rings never severed. Thus, dependent origination is designated as a 'hook and lock. Apart from false conditions, there is no separate dharma of arising. Arising...
Because there is no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), there is no arising, thereby avoiding the errors of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

I speak only of dependent origination as a chain of links; the foolish cannot comprehend this. (Since that which arises lacks intrinsic nature, it arises yet does not arise; "arising" here has the sense of "not-arising. I speak only of causes and conditions as a chain of links, yet the deluded cannot understand that there is no arising within conditions. If there were a nature of arising apart from the chain of links of conditions, then...

Question: How does one cultivate the path? Answer: One investigates the root of the twelve links of dependent origination, which is ignorance. Because of ignorance, afflictions and karma arise; because of karma, retribution arises, resulting in all manner of suffering. All of this has ignorance as its fundamental cause. It is like a person cutting down a tree: they must first sever its roots.

Question: What is this ignorance? Answer: It is the lack of awakening within the mind. Because of this lack of awakening, one falsely gives rise to a discriminating mind; externally perceiving phenomena, one asserts that they exist and... (asserts that they do not exist).

To say "it is" is called affirmation; to say "it is not" is called negation. To speak of gain or loss and to undergo the various retributions of physical and mental suffering—all these arise from ignorance (*avidyā*). I now wish to sever this ignorance; first, one must awaken to the source of the mind. One must know that whatever delusive thoughts arise according to the mind, they all stem from the non-awakened mind.

One must further understand that the nature of one's own mind is fundamentally without birth or extinction, and without coming or going. How is this known? All delusive thoughts arise suddenly; once awakened, they do not arise. What is meant by "awakening"?

When greed, anger, or delusion arise, one should again observe and investigate with one's own mind: what shape do these greed, anger, and delusion have? Are they blue or yellow, red or white? Are they of the future, the past, or the present? Do they exist within...?

When one searches internally, externally, and in between for greed, anger, and delusion, they have no form whatsoever. If they had existed from the beginning, they should also be visible at the time of present awakening; since they are not perceived upon awakening, we know that they suddenly arise through non-awakening and do not exist when there is awakening.

Thus, awakening is the antidote to ignorance (*avidyā*). This present ignorance cannot be apprehended; because ignorance is absent, all deluded thoughts and afflictions (*kleśa*) do not arise. Because afflictions do not arise, karma does not arise. Because karma does not arise, the two causes of the past do not exist.

Because these two causes are absent, the five fruits of the present do not arise. Because the five fruits do not arise, the three causes of the future—craving, grasping, and becoming—do not arise. Since these three causes of the present are absent, the two [causes] of the future...

Based on this observation and practice of the twelve links of dependent origination, there are generally three classes of practitioners: those with superior wisdom who observe it attain the *bodhi* of a Buddha; those with middling wisdom who observe it attain the *bodhi* of a *pratyekabuddha*; and those with inferior wisdom who observe it attain the *bodhi* of a *śrāvaka*. [The New Commentary states: Because of their prior ignorance, ordinary people fall into untruthfulness and give rise to [the notion of] arising and ceasing.]

"Conceptual construction is not held by the noble ones; it is said that because non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings cannot perceive reality as it is, they give rise to false views of impermanence, arising, and cessation. To say that what has been produced is subsequently abandoned is called impermanence (the "New Explanation" states: there are non-Buddhists who claim that the nature of the four great elements is beginningless, yet they produce various phenomena such as form and then abandon them;

they thus reckon that these produced phenomena are themselves impermanent). Some say that the destruction of shape and location is called impermanence (the Commentary states: this refers to the transformation and decay of the forms of the six realms of existence as being impermanent, while the four great elements are permanent).

Some say that form itself is impermanent (the Commentary states: they reckon that because form decays, it is impermanent). Some say that it is during the process of the transformation of form [that impermanence occurs].

This is called impermanence as immediate self-disintegration, like the transformation of milk into curd; it is invisible in the interval [between states], yet impermanence destroys all natures and causes them to transform. Some say that there is an impermanent dharma between the two states (the cause and effect) which transforms all natures, such that their continuity remains uninterrupted while being altered, naturally returning to extinction, just as with milk and curd. Others say that there is an impermanent dharma between the two states that is invisible, and this impermanence is able to transform all natures. (Iśvarakṛṣṇa) says: "Natures are impermanent. (Vasubandhu) says: "No. It is not so. Why? Because it would contradict the sūtras. The sūtras state: "Form is impermanent," and so forth. If one were to claim that there is a separate impermanent dharma apart from form itself, this would contradict the sūtras. Furthermore, it would contradict reason. If there were a separate impermanent dharma, what function would it have? If it were to destroy the nature, then that very nature would be impermanent. If it were to destroy something other than the nature, then that other thing would be impermanent. Since neither of these is logical, the assertion of a separate impermanent dharma is untenable. Moreover, if there were a separate impermanent dharma, it would lead to an infinite regress. If one were to posit another impermanent dharma to destroy this first impermanent dharma, and yet another to destroy that one, there would be no end to it. Therefore, it is established that the nature itself is impermanent and does not require a separate impermanent dharma to destroy it. This is because the nature itself undergoes change and destruction, just as milk transforms into curd without requiring an external agent of change. Thus, the nature itself is impermanent. (Vasubandhu) says: "If it is said that the nature itself is impermanent, then what is the meaning of 'impermanence'? It means that the nature itself disintegrates moment by moment. Just as firewood is burned by fire, so too do all conditioned phenomena disintegrate through their own power. There is no need for a separate impermanent dharma to act upon them. Therefore, it is concluded that the nature itself is impermanent. (Vasubandhu) says: "If it is said that the nature itself is impermanent, then how can one perceive its disintegration? Just as one perceives heat by feeling the warmth of water, so too does one perceive impermanence by observing the arising and ceasing of phenomena. Therefore, although impermanence is subtle and difficult to see, it is nonetheless established through reasoning and scriptural authority. (Vasubandhu) says: "If it is said that the nature itself is impermanent, then why do some claim that there is a permanent substance underlying change? This is a misconception. If there were a permanent substance, it could never undergo transformation. Since we observe that all things change and eventually perish, we know that there is no permanent substance. Therefore, the doctrine of a permanent substance is refuted by both direct perception and inference. (Vasubandhu) says: "If it is said that the nature itself is impermanent, then how can one explain the continuity of karma and its results? This is explained through the principle of dependent origination. Although phenomena disintegrate moment by moment, they leave behind a causal potential (saṃskāra) that projects a future result. Just as a seed dies when it sprouts, yet produces a fruit, so too does karma perish when it arises, yet project a future rebirth. Therefore, the continuity of karma and its results is maintained through the power of dependent origination, without requiring a permanent substance. Thus, it is established that the nature itself is impermanent. (Vasubandhu) says: "If it is said that the nature itself is impermanent, then how can one explain the stability of the world? This is explained through the distinction between primary and secondary causes. Primary causes produce effects directly, while secondary causes support and sustain them. Just as the earth supports seeds and water nourishes them, so too do various conditions support the continuity of phenomena. Therefore, while the nature of phenomena is impermanent, their continuity appears stable due to the convergence of multiple conditions. Thus, the apparent stability of the world does not contradict the doctrine of impermanence. (Vasubandhu) says: "If it is said that the nature itself is impermanent, then how can one explain the efficacy of spiritual practice? This is explained through the principle of transformation. Through the cultivation of wisdom and ethical discipline, one gradually transforms the habitual tendencies of the mind until they are replaced by pure qualities. Just as gold is refined through smelting, so too is the mind transformed through practice. Therefore, the efficacy of spiritual practice is established through the process of transformation, even though the nature of the mind is impermanent. Thus, the doctrine of impermanence is consistent with all aspects of experience and practice. (Vasubandhu) says: "If it is said that the nature itself is impermanent, then what is the ultimate goal of liberation? Liberation is the cessation of all suffering and the realization of nirvāṇa. Since suffering arises from ignorance and craving, the cessation of these afflictions constitutes liberation. Just as darkness disappears when light appears, so too does suffering cease when the truth is realized. Therefore, liberation is not a separate entity, but the natural state of the mind when it is free from defilements. Thus, the doctrine of impermanence leads to the attainment of liberation. (Vasubandhu) says: "If it is said that the nature itself is impermanent, then how can one explain the existence of a creator god? This is refuted by the evidence of causality. If a creator god existed, he would either be subject to change or not. If he were subject to change, he would be impermanent. If he were not subject to change, he could not create anything. Since neither case is possible, the existence of a creator god is untenable. Therefore, the diversity of the world is explained solely through the laws of dependent origination, without recourse to a divine creator. Thus, the doctrine of impermanence is the most rational and coherent explanation of reality. (Vasubandhu) says: "If it is said that the nature itself is impermanent, then how can one explain the persistence of memory and recognition? This is explained through the continuity of mental consciousness. Although each moment of consciousness perishes, it leaves behind a latent impression (vāsanā) that serves as the basis for subsequent moments. Just as a lamp flame persists through a series of flickering moments, so too does the stream of consciousness maintain continuity through the force of past impressions. Therefore, memory and recognition are possible despite the impermanence of the mind. Thus, the doctrine of impermanence is fully compatible with our cognitive experiences. (Vasubandhu) says: "If it is said that the nature itself is impermanent, then how can one explain the existence of a self? This is refuted by the analysis of the aggregates. A so-called "self" is merely a designation applied to the collection of the five aggregates. Since the aggregates themselves are impermanent and subject to change, there is no permanent self to be found. Just as a chariot is a name for a collection of parts, so too is the "self" a conventional label for the aggregates. Therefore, the notion of a self is a conceptual construction and not an ontological reality. Thus, the doctrine of impermanence negates the existence of a permanent self. (Vasubandhu) says: "If it is said that the nature itself is impermanent, then how can one explain the efficacy of ritual sacrifices? This is explained through the principle of karmic maturation. Rituals performed with a pure intention produce merit, which ripens as favorable results in the future. Just as planting seeds in spring yields a harvest in autumn, so too do virtuous actions lead to happiness. Therefore, the efficacy of ritual sacrifices is established through the law of cause and effect, without requiring a supernatural deity to mediate the process. Thus, the doctrine of impermanence is consistent with the principles of ethics and morality. (Vasubandhu) says: "If it is said that the nature itself is impermanent, then how can one explain the existence of a universal monarch? This is explained through the convergence of auspicious conditions. A universal monarch arises when the karma of past lives meets with favorable external circumstances. Just as a great tree grows from a small seed when provided with soil, water, and sunlight, so too does a universal monarch emerge from the accumulation of merit and the right timing. Therefore, the appearance of a universal monarch is a result of specific causes and conditions, not the manifestation of a divine power. Thus, the doctrine of impermanence is consistent with the social and political order of the world. [He replied: "Because the four great elements are unproduced and their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) is indestructible. [Bodhiruci says:

"Non-Buddhists claim that the various great elements are neither produced nor destroyed, because their own essential nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) is eternally indestructible. [The above concludes the refutation of the nature of impermanence. Regarding the impermanence of the initial creation:

it is not that there are things other than the four great elements; rather, each of the four great elements has its own distinct characteristics and self-nature (*svalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, no differentiation can be found therein.
When these [elements] are without differentiation and do not further construct through the three conditions, one should know that this is impermanence.

(This refutes the first [position]: having constructed, it is then abandoned as impermanent. The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) reckon that what is not the four great elements is impermanent; furthermore, they claim there is something distinct from the four great elements that can initiate construction, and its abandonment is called "impermanence. Their reckoning does not go beyond the three—mutuality, self-nature, and commonality—as the agents of construction.

The Tathāgata, therefore, refutes their reckoned distinctions among the great elements by means of their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa), general characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), and mutual characteristics (anyonyalakṣaṇa). Regarding specific characteristics: if they are without differentiation, no differentiation can be obtained; because there is no differentiation, they cannot independently create form on their own. Regarding mutual characteristics: they are mutually dependent.

Because they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), they cannot mutually create matter; their common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) are fundamentally separate from the beginning and cannot be brought together through skillful means (*upāya*) to co-create matter. Therefore it is said: "These do not further create, nor do the two skillful means produce.

Since the refutation of their doctrine—that what is called "initial creation" is itself impermanence—is established, where could its characteristic possibly reside? Thus, he concludes the refutation by saying: "One should know that this is impermanence. Regarding the impermanence of the destruction of shape and location (*saṃsthāna-deśa-vināśa-anityatā*), this refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*).
They do not perish, remaining ultimately unperished. O Mahāmati, "ultimately" (*anta*) means [only when] analyzed.
When one analyzes down to the subtlest atom, one observes that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) are destroyed;

yet, apart from the perception of distinct shapes and dimensions, neither length nor shortness can be found.
