It is not that the four great elements themselves are destroyed, but rather that the manifestation of shape and dimension is destroyed. This falls into the Samkhya school [of thought]. (This refutes the second [view]: the impermanence of the destruction of shape and dimension.

The non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) reckon that the primary and derivative matter (*bhūta-bhautika*) is ultimately indestructible. They claim that while one may analyze matter down to the subtlest atom, it is only the perceptions of shapes, such as length and shortness, that are extinguished, and not the essential substance of the primary and derivative matter. Thus, they hold that the four great elements do not perish, even though the four great elements [as perceived through] shape and dimension are destroyed.

In reality, there is no destruction; rather, it is only the transformation of form and location that appears as such. This view correctly falls within the Sāṃkhya treatises. As for the claim that "form is impermanent," this means that form itself is impermanent;
it is not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that are impermanent. If the four great elements were impermanent, it would contradict conventional linguistic expression.

Since conventional linguistic expression is not an inherent nature (*svabhāva*), one would then fall into the Lokāyata (Worldly) view, which holds that all natures exist merely as verbal designations.

"Seeing the arising of self-characteristics" (this refutes the third [view]: that form itself is impermanent). Non-Buddhists (tīrthika) reckon that created form (*nirmita-rūpa*) is itself impermanent. The Tathāgata says that what they reckon is, as previously stated, the impermanence of shape and location (*saṃsthāna*), not the impermanence of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

If the four great elements were impermanent, they would not be accessible through conventional linguistic expression; yet, according to worldly discourse, created form lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Thus, it falls into the worldly doctrine (*lokāyata*). This worldly doctrine arises from their false view that the nature of all phenomena exists merely as linguistic expression, and that they do not perceive the arising of self-characteristics.
"Impermanence of transformation" means that the distinct nature of form appears, but it is not the four great elements themselves—just as gold is fashioned [into various ornaments].
Just as when an ornament undergoes transformation, it is not the nature of the gold that is destroyed, but rather the configuration of the ornament that is destroyed;

so too it is with the transformation of other natures and so forth. (Śikṣānanda says: "Transformation-impermanence" means that the substance of form changes, but the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) do not. For example, when gold is fashioned into an ornament, the ornament changes while the gold remains unaltered;

this case is likewise. [This refutes the fourth type of impermanence: the transformation of matter. The new commentary states: "To reckon the alteration of the material substance of form as 'impermanence,' rather than the essence of the primary elements themselves, is what is meant by impermanence."

Therefore, the analogy of gold being fashioned into ornaments is used: while the ornaments undergo transformation and change in name and form, the gold itself remains unaltered; it is not that the gold is impermanent.

Such are the various deluded views of impermanence held by non-Buddhists (the note states this summarizes the seven types of non-Buddhist views on impermanence). When fire burns the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), their intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are not burned;

yet if each of their respective characteristics were to perish, then the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) produced from the four great elements would have to be annihilated. (The new commentary states: the non-Buddhists claim that when fire burns the four great elements, it cannot burn their various [intrinsic characteristics]).

[The opponent] says: "If the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are capable of burning, then the primary and derivative elements should eventually be annihilated; however, since they are seen not to be annihilated, one must conclude that the nature of the great elements is eternal.

Mahāmati, the arising of my dharmas is neither eternal nor non-eternal. Why is this? It is because external natures are indeterminate. [The Buddha said: "I teach that the arising of all dharmas occurs because external natures are false and their existence or non-existence is indeterminate;

therefore, they are neither eternal nor non-eternal. I speak only of the subtle mind within the three realms of existence (*traidhātuka*). [Realśikṣa says: "Therefore, the three realms are mind-only. Within or without the three realms, there is not a single thing that exists independently.

The Dharma does not arise from a subtle and true mind; it does not speak of the arising and ceasing of various marks, nor of the combination of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), nor of the distinctions between the four great elements and their derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
Through the two kinds of false discrimination, one understands the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*);

through these two kinds of false discrimination, one is freed from the two views of external existence and non-existence. (Vasubandhu says: because it does not speak of various marks, the various distinctions of the nature and location of the great elements do not arise or cease; therefore, there is neither the creator nor the created.)
Therefore, because the essential natures of both the grasper and the grasped all arise from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), one knows the nature of these two graspings as they truly are.

One who awakens to the fact that what appears to the mind is merely a measure of one's own mental projections and is a false imagination—arising from the activity of thought and volition, and not being something produced without such activity—realizes that apart from the nature of the mind, there is no nature to false imagination.

All phenomena—mundane, supramundane, and the supreme among the supramundane—are neither eternal nor impermanent. "Awakening to what appears to the mind as a measure" means that false imagination arises from...

Thoughts arise from mental formations, not from the absence of mental formations. Once one knows the place where delusive imaginings (*vikalpa*) arise, and having abandoned the mind’s conceptualization of existence and non-existence, one skillfully understands all worldly, world-transcending, and world-transcending-supreme dharmas as being neither eternal nor impermanent.

Failing to realize that these are the manifestations of one's own mind, one falls into the continuity of evil views regarding the two extremes. All non-Buddhists fail to realize their own delusive imaginings;
such ordinary people lack a fundamental basis for what they call the worldly, the world-transcending, and the world-transcending-supreme.

Furthermore, these [three] arise from the conceptualization of false discrimination (*vikalpa*) and are not realized by the foolish and ignorant. Because they do not realize that what appears is the manifestation of their own minds (*svacittadṛśyamātra*), they fall into a continuous succession of evil views regarding the two extremes.

Relying on their own false discriminations, they calculate and cling to verbal expressions. These ordinary people and non-Buddhists lack fundamental wisdom; they merely grasp at the conceptualizations of words and do not know that the worldly and world-transcending dharmas taught by the Tathāgata arise from those very conceptualizations of words.
Therefore, these three dharmas cannot be realized by the foolish and ignorant. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: [The verses follow.]
They are far removed from the deluded conceptualizations of externalists regarding the impermanence of the initial creation, the alteration of shape and location, and the impermanence of color;

(the new commentary states that these seven kinds of impermanence are the false discriminations of various externalists). All natures are without destruction, for the Great Self-nature abides eternally.

Externalists are submerged in the notion of impermanence due to their immersion in various views. (Because this Dharma abides in its own position and the characteristics of the world are eternally constant, the nature of all dharmas is non-arising.)

There is no destruction; the Great Elements (mahābhūta) are eternally abiding. Because the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) do not understand this, they reckon that the primary elements (mahābhūta) are eternal while derived matter (upādāyarūpa) is impermanent; thus it is said that the non-Buddhists, possessing the notion of impermanence, are submerged in various views.

For those non-Buddhists, there is neither arising nor ceasing, as the nature of the Great Elements is itself eternal. What, then, is meant by the "notion of impermanence"? All is merely the measure of mind (cittamātra);
the two kinds of mental flow—the subject that grasps and the object that is grasped—are devoid of self and what belongs to a self (ātman and ātmīya).

[The Buddha addressed] the non-Buddhist calculation that the four great elements are eternal and that derived matter is impermanent and subject to destruction. The Buddha said: "There is no such thing as a phenomenon that arises or perishes. Since it is said that the nature of the four great elements is eternal and indestructible, why do you conceive of derived matter as being impermanent?

Therefore, know that all things are merely the measure of the mind; they are the two kinds of phenomena—delusive thought and the flow of the mind’s perceptions—and even the two natures of grasper and grasped have neither a self nor anything belonging to a self.
"Brahmā is the root of the tree, and its branches and twigs extend everywhere; thus I have taught: it is solely the measure of that mind."

(The non-Buddhist said, "Brahmā created sentient beings and distributed them throughout the six realms. The Buddha said, "What I have taught is that such attachments held by non-Buddhists are all merely the mental constructs of their own deluded minds.")
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the sequential continuity of the cessation-samādhi (nirodha-samāpatti) of all bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.

If one is skillful in the characteristics of this sequential continuity of the cessation-samādhi, I and the other bodhisattvas shall never recklessly abandon the gate of the bliss of cessation-samādhi, nor fall into [the state of] a single [vehicle]."
All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and those of external paths are deluded. [Bodhiruci translates "cessation-samādhi" as "entering the meditative absorption of extinction. The new commentary states:

Because the preceding passage mentioned the mundane, the supramundane, and the supreme supramundane dharmas, there are bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas who sever mundane birth and death and enter the supramundane meditative absorption of extinction, as well as the characteristics of the successive continuity of the various stages.

Thus, Mahāmati raises the gate of the bliss of cessation-samādhi and the characteristics of the successive continuity of the stages to question the Tathāgata, desiring to reveal the superiority and inferiority of the noble ones and ordinary beings of the three vehicles, so that they may cultivate noble practices, realize the ocean of the Buddha-fruit, and not fall into the provisional vehicles or various false views.]

The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall speak for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, I only pray that you will explain this for me.
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the sixth stage, as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

[Note: This refers to Bodhisattvas from the first to the sixth stages, as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who equally sever the afflictions of the triple world and bring an end to mental toil and anxiety."*]

"Permanently extinguishing the mind, one enters meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). In the seventh stage, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters meditative absorption moment by moment, remaining detached from all characteristics of the self-nature of phenomena.

This absorption is not that of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; it is the absorption of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who have fallen away from the realization of the cessation of the signs of the grasped and the grasper.

[Bodhiruci says: 'Mahāmati, all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) moment by moment in the seventh stage, for all Bodhisattvas are fully capable of distancing themselves [from these signs].'"

Because they are free from the marks of existence and non-existence regarding all phenomena, Mahāmati, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are unable to enter the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) moment by moment. This is because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas enter the meditative absorption of cessation by relying on conditioned activities (*saṃskṛta-caryā*), thereby remaining within the sphere of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).

[Commentary]: It is said that in the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), one is free from the deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*) of the three realms of birth and death; thus, the nature and characteristics of the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) differ from those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), who enter meditative attainment by severing the birth and death of the three realms.

Therefore, in the seventh stage, there is no meditative attainment of moment-to-moment thought. [Bodhiruci] says: "Therefore, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot enter the meditative absorption of cessation moment by moment within the seventh stage. [They] attain all phenomena.

Because they have not yet attained the non-differentiated nature of all phenomena, it is said that they have not reached this stage (Yang says: because they have not yet realized the non-differentiation of all dharmas, it is called "not reaching the stage"; because they perceive the various distinct characteristics of all phenomena).
They realize the nature and characteristics of all phenomena as being wholesome or unwholesome, and thus enter meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).

For this reason, in the seventh stage, there is no meditative absorption of wholesome thought. (Liuzhi says: Because they realize the various distinct characteristics of all phenomena—whether phenomena exist or do not exist, and whether phenomena are wholesome or unwholesome—and because they enter the *nirodha-samāpatti* by means of these common and distinct characteristics, the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas [do not... )
Because they lack the wisdom of skillful means, they are able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) in every thought-moment within the seventh stage.

Mahāmati, in the eighth stage, the Bodhisattvas, as well as the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, extinguish the characteristics of the conceptualizations of mind, intellect, and consciousness. (The new commentary states: "In the eighth stage, Bodhisattvas abide constantly in samādhi through the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga*), without the marks of entering or emerging;

thus they are identical to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas in extinguishing the deluded mind and consciousness of nirvāṇa. From the first stage up to the seventh stage, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas contemplate the mind of the triple world.

The manas, the mental consciousness, and the faculty of cognition are free from "I" and "mine. When one fails to properly cultivate [the realization that] they are merely one's own false imaginings, one falls into the various marks of external natures. (Yang says:

The Bodhisattva of the seventh stage observes that the mind, the will, and the mental consciousness of the triple world are fundamentally free from "I" and "mine"; it is only through the improper cultivation of one's own mental false imaginings that one falls into the various marks of external natures. This refers to those who, from the seventh stage onward, fall onto the deviant paths of externalists.
Fools, through two kinds of their own minds—the grasping subject and the grasped object—turn toward ignorance; they do not perceive the faults of beginningless time, which are empty.

"Perfumed by false habitual tendencies—[referring to] the two kinds of self-mind; that is to say, the outsiders who, regarding the two extremes of existence and non-existence, cling to the grasped and the grasper, being entirely ignorant and failing to realize the faults and falsehoods of beginningless habitual tendencies, which perfume them like rust forming within iron, thereby causing them to destroy themselves.

"Mahāmati, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas at the eighth stage, as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, possess a nirvāṇa sustained by the realization of samādhi. Therefore, due to the bliss of samādhi, they do not enter parinirvāṇa. If not...

If one who maintains [the lineage] were to find the stage of a Tathāgata unsatisfactory and abandon all conditioned activities for the sake of sentient beings, the lineage of the Buddhas would surely be severed.

(Although there is a commonality in entering [nirvāṇa], there is a difference: because Bodhisattvas are sustained by the power of self-awakening through the samādhi of non-arising, they do not enter parinirvāṇa out of delight in the gateways of samādhi.

If they were not sustained by the power of awakening through the samādhi of non-arising, they would enter parinirvāṇa like those of the two vehicles; they would be unable to fulfill the stage of a Tathāgata and would abandon the task of delivering all sentient beings, and the lineage of the Tathāgatas would likewise be cut off.)—The Buddhas.

The World-Honored One, in order to reveal the inconceivable and immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata, [observes that] Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are led by the pleasure obtained through their gates of samādhi and thus conceive the notion of *nirvāṇa*. (Real-śakya says: "Therefore, the Buddhas preach the inconceivable great merits of the Tathāgata to them, so that they ultimately do not enter *nirvāṇa*;

Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are attached to the bliss of samādhi, and for this reason they give rise to the notion of *nirvāṇa* within it. The New Commentary says: "This refers to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who were formerly Bodhisattvas that had regressed from their vow for *bodhi*.")

"Even those of the two vehicles who have fixed their natures and incline toward tranquility cannot know the Dharma of the first stage (*bhūmi*), much less be able to share in the attainment of the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) of a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage?

O Mahāmati, I have divided [the stages] into seven stages for those who skillfully cultivate the characteristics of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*); who skillfully cultivate the grasping of self and what belongs to the self, as well as the selflessness of persons and phenomena;

who skillfully cultivate the characteristics of arising and ceasing, as well as specific and general characteristics; and who, through the power of certainty in the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), enter the successive stages of the gateways of samādhi."

The Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment (*Mārga-pakṣya-dharma*): [The Tathāgata] establishes the sequential divisions of the practices of the seven stages (*bhūmi*) in order to cause sentient beings to skillfully cultivate the mind, thought, and consciousness; to be liberated from the grasping of "self" and "mine"; to thoroughly understand the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and phenomena—as well as the characteristics of non-arising and non-ceasing, and the specific and general characteristics;

and to master the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the power of determination, and the gates of samādhi, thereby gradually ascending through the stages and entering the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*). Regarding the four unhindered analytical knowledges, they are: the dharma, meaning, expression, and eloquence.

This is established so that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not fail to perceive the specific and general characteristics, nor fall into the evil paths of externalists due to a lack of skill regarding the seventh stage.

Regarding the stages of the grounds (the reason for which is that the Tathāgata fears that bodhisattvas might not realize that the self- and common-characteristics of the five aggregates are false and unreal, and thus fail to understand the characteristics of the practice of the seventh ground, falling instead into the external paths of heterodox teachers based on their own prior deluded imaginings—it is for this reason that the gradations of the stages are established):
Mahāmati, in reality there is neither arising nor ceasing, apart from what is the manifestation of one’s own mind.

(Yang says: "The successive order of the grounds is all a manifestation of one's own mind; in reality there is neither arising nor ceasing. Here the Tathāgata merely points to 'mind-only,' and through this, all arising and ceasing are suddenly understood. The... [text ends]... place.
This refers to the sequential continuity of the stages (*bhūmi*) and the various modes of activity within the three realms, which foolish persons do not perceive.
That which foolish persons do not perceive is what I and all the Buddhas speak of as the sequential continuity of the stages and the various modes of activity within the three realms.

(Yang says: "The World-Honored One and all the Buddhas, for the sake of counteracting the illnesses of sentient beings, speak of the sequence of the various stages and the characteristics of the various modes of activity within the three realms; yet foolish persons do not perceive them and instead harbor attachments, failing to realize that these are taught by the Buddha.")
The teaching of the Dharma has never been taught [in its ultimate sense].
Furthermore, Mahāmati, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and those in the eighth stage of the Bodhisattvas are intoxicated by the bliss of the cessation-samādhi (nirodha-samādhi);

they are obstructed by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) regarding the self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of what is merely a manifestation of their own minds, and thus they fall into [the view of] the non-existence of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*).

Grasping at the view of false discrimination regarding the notion of nirvāṇa is not the awakening of the wisdom of ultimate cessation. (This refers to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who, within the eighth stage, become attached to the samādhi of entry into cessation;

intoxicated by it, they fail to realize that self-characteristics and common characteristics are manifestations of their own minds. Because they are obscured by habitual tendencies and fall into grasping at the view of the two kinds of selflessness, they give rise to the notion of nirvāṇa through false discrimination;

this is not the awakening of the wisdom of ultimate cessation. As for the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, he perceives the bliss of the gate of the samādhi of cessation, yet due to his original vows, his compassion, and his great pity...
Having accomplished the knowledge that discriminates the ten inexhaustible phrases, they do not falsely imagine a nirvana;

because such false imagination no longer arises, they are liberated from the false imagination of grasped and grasper. They realize that all phenomena are merely the manifestation of their own mind, and thus false imagination does not arise.
They do not fall into the false imagination of adhering to the signs of external natures and self-natures within the mind, intellect, and consciousness.
The Dharma of the Buddhas arises not from causes, but is born following wisdom, whereby one attains the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization.

(Although Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage perceive the bliss of the samādhi of cessation, they do so out of their fundamental vow, compassion, and great pity to fulfill the ten great vows and liberate sentient beings; they do not give rise to the deluded notion of nirvāṇa. Because such delusions regarding nirvāṇa have ceased for them, they are free from the delusions of grasping and the grasped, and are thus able to realize that all things are merely the manifestations of their own minds.

Since these are not the true cause of the Buddha-dharma, which does not arise from causes but arises only following wisdom—just as a fruit [arises from a seed]—they are thereby able to enter the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization. It is like a person in a dream.
In the midst of employing skillful means to cross over water, one awakens before having crossed; having awakened, one reflects: "Is this right or wrong? Neither right nor wrong.

Other than this, there are various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) arising from beginningless seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing, as well as various forms and locations, which manifest in dreams according to the presence or absence of conceptual thought within the mind, intellect, and consciousness.

(Bodhiruci says: It is like a person in a dream who employs great skillful means to cross a vast ocean; while desiring to carry himself across, he suddenly [awakens] midway before having finished crossing.)

Then, upon waking, he reflects: "Is this real, or is it false? He further contemplates that such signs are neither real nor false; they arise solely from the causes of my own beginningless, false discrimination and the熏習 (*vāsanā*, habitual perfuming) of unreal objects. Thus, due to the inverted perception of various forms and appearances caused by the perfuming of consciousness—which does not transcend existence and non-existence—he sees [the water, boat, and raft] within his dream.

[The commentary states: "Upon awakening, there is no longer any water, boat, or raft. It is not that seeing the water, boat, and raft during the dream itself was incorrect; rather, it is used as an analogy for attaining the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), where one realizes that birth and death were originally non-existent, and thus the merits of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) are not 'correct' [in the sense of being newly acquired].

Conversely, at the seventh stage and below, because one has not yet realized this, the false perception of birth and death persists, and thus the merits of the factors of enlightenment are not 'incorrect' [in the sense of being fundamentally unreal]. These are merely the results of the causes of beginningless perfuming through seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing."

Therefore, Mahāmati, the mind, intellect, and consciousness manifest as false imaginings like a dream. Thus, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reaches the eighth Bodhisattva stage, they see that false imaginings arise;

having progressed from the first stage up to the seventh stage, they perceive all phenomena as being like illusions through skillful means, and having brought to an end the mental activity of false imaginings regarding the grasped and the grasper, they employ the skillful means of the Buddha-dharma to cause those who have not yet attained it to attain it.

(This refers to the Bodhisattva of the eighth stage who, seeing all phenomena as like illusions through skillful means, transcends the mental constructions of subject and object; having abandoned all effort, they act without effort through skillful means in the Buddha-dharma, causing those who have not yet attained it to also attain this illusion-like samādhi.

Mahāmati, this is the skillful means of the Bodhisattva’s nirvāṇa, which is indestructible and free from mind, thought, and consciousness, and by which one attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.

(Having seen that phenomena are like illusions and so forth, one immediately realizes effortless practice; this is called the characteristic of the indestructible skillful means of the nirvāṇa attained by the Bodhisattva. Therefore, [it is able to... )

"Having departed from mind, thought, and consciousness, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Mahāmati, regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no sequential continuity;

it is taught as the dharma of the cessation of all false conceptualization (*parikalpa*) and non-existence. (The new commentary states: Within the ultimate truth, the paths of speech and thought are cut off; it is realized only through the correspondence of self-aware wisdom (*pratyātma-jñāna*).

One cannot speak of the sequential continuity of the stages of counteraction (*pratipakṣa*) across the ten bhūmis; this is merely designated by the name 'the dharma of cessation'). At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:"

The Mind-Measure (cittamātra) is non-existent; this is the stage of abiding (vihāra) and the stage of Buddhahood. Regarding the past, future, and present Buddhas of the three periods of time, they teach that the seventh stage is the stage of the Mind-Measure, the eighth stage is Non-existence (nirābhāsa), and the two stages [the eighth and ninth] are called "Abiding," while the stage of Buddhahood is called "Most Supreme" (*parama*).

(The new commentary states: "Abiding" is also a "stage. It means that from the seventh stage downward, it is collectively termed the "Mind-Measure"; from the eighth stage upward, it is termed "Non-existence"; and only from the tenth stage onward is one called a Buddha.)
Self-realized wisdom and its purification—this is my stage of sovereign mastery, the most excellent place of pure and wondrous adornment.
It shines like a blazing fire, its radiance pervading everywhere with unextinguishable flames that do not harm the eyes (the note says:

whereas the light emitted by a venomous dragon harms the human eye, the Tathāgata’s radiance does not harm the human eye). Its circular transformation manifests throughout the three realms of existence; it transforms the present three realms, or there may be [others].

Previously, in that transformation (wherein the provisional and real teachings of the Buddha differ in their sequence of transformation), he expounded the vehicles (Dharmaruci says: "There he taught the various vehicles," as the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"For the sake of the various classes of sentient beings, I have distinguished and taught the three vehicles"). These are all the stages of the Tathāgata: the tenth stage is the first;
the first is the eighth; the ninth is the seventh; the seventh is likewise the eighth; and the second becomes the third and the fourth.

What is the fifth? What is the third? What is the sixth? There is nothing; what sequence could there be? (The New Commentary states: "The Tathāgata’s skillful means teach the Dharma according to the dispositions of beings, and thus there are various vehicles.

However, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), how could there be any sequence? Therefore, the *Saṃcayagāthā Sūtra* says: "One who has attained the true nature of all dharmas does not go from one stage to another stage. Thus we know that when reality reflects upon expedient means, the characteristics of these skillful means are exhausted, and all are non-existent.)
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, are the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas permanent or impermanent?
(Because it was previously stated that the Buddhas of the three periods—past, future, and present—preach the Dharma, and if a Tathāgata were to fall within the three periods, he would be impermanent;

therefore, he asks whether the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha is permanent or impermanent. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are neither permanent nor impermanent. He said:
Both positions entail faults. If [the Tathāgata] were eternal, there would be the fault of being an agent;

for all non-Buddhists assert that an eternal being is a creator who performs no action. Therefore, the Tathāgata is neither eternal nor non-eternal. Since there is a fault in an eternal being who acts, [Yang says:

the eternity of the Tathāgata is not an eternity without cause, nor is it an eternity as a master-creator; both an eternal being who acts and an eternity as a creator inevitably involve faults]. If the Tathāgata were impermanent, there would be the fault of impermanence in the act of creation.

The characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) and that which is characterized by them lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). If the aggregates were to perish, the Tathāgata would necessarily be subject to annihilation; yet the Tathāgata is not annihilated.

(To say he is impermanent would entail the same faults as the world’s conditioned and constructed phenomena, such as impermanence and so forth. Since the five aggregates—both the characteristics and the characterized—are without intrinsic nature, if the aggregates were truly destroyed, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the Tathāgata would likewise be annihilated. Because he is not annihilated, he is not like something produced that is impermanent.
Mahāmati, all that is produced is impermanent, like jars, garments, and the like; thus, there is the fault that everything would be impermanent.
If wisdom, the various requisites, and skillful means were devoid of meaning because they are produced, then all that is produced would be the undifferentiated causal nature of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata is neither eternal nor impermanent. (The New Commentary states:

"If one says the Tathāgata is impermanent, it would entail the error of being identical to jars, garments, and other conditioned phenomena which are impermanent; the causes cultivated—merit, wisdom, and adornments—would all be empty and useless. Yet the merit of the Buddha-Tathāgata flows through ten thousand ages and remains eternally present.")

It remains firm throughout billions of kalpas; furthermore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in all worlds must be the Tathāgata, because they are produced from the same causal conditions. To say that the Tathāgata is either permanent or impermanent would entail the faults mentioned above. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata is not permanent in the manner of space.
If he were permanent like space, there would be the fault of rendering the various requisites for the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) purposeless.

(Bodhiruci says: Why is it that the Tathāgata is not permanent? Because the nature of space lacks the cultivation of all meritorious virtues. This means that the cultivated virtues would all be empty and without purpose.)
[The Path of Cessation] Mahāmati, it is like space: neither eternal nor non-eternal.
Because it is free from the faults of eternity and non-eternity, as well as [the categories of] oneness, difference, both, or neither, it cannot be described. Therefore, the Tathāgata is not eternal.

(The previous statement that he is "not like the eternity of space" meant that he possesses noble wisdom; this present statement that he is "like space" means that his nature is like the nature of space—unchanging, neither eternal nor non-eternal, free from eternity and non-eternity, and not falling into any of the faults such as oneness, difference, both, or neither.)

Therefore, it cannot be said that [the Tathāgata] is either eternal or non-eternal. Furthermore, Mahāmati, if the Tathāgata were an unarisen eternity, he would be like the horns of a rabbit or a horse;
because they are eternally unarisen, such a conventional designation would be meaningless. Because of the fault of being an eternally unarisen entity, the Tathāgata is not eternal.

(If one were to say that the Tathāgata is an eternally unarisen entity, then he would be like the horns of a rabbit or a horse, which are fundamentally unarisen. If he were declared eternal in the same way as the horns of a rabbit or a horse, there would be no purpose for his skillful means in bringing vast benefit to sentient beings. This is because there is a fault in the notion of an eternally unarisen existence.)
Therefore, the Tathāgata is not the same as the permanence of non-arising. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there is another reason for knowing that the Tathāgata is permanent.

Why is this? It is because the wisdom attained without interval is permanent; therefore, the Tathāgata is permanent. (The note says: "It refers to the permanent principle realized by uninterrupted wisdom as the permanence of the Tathāgata. [Yang] says:
"This describes the Tathāgata’s truly existing, eternally abiding Dharma, which is not what the world calls 'permanent' or 'impermanent. Mahāmati, whether the Tathāgata appears in the world or not...
The supramundane dharmas abide definitively in the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Tathāgatas;

they abide without interval, neither dwelling in empty space nor being perceived by ordinary fools. (Realśikṣa says: "The dharma-nature, the abiding of dharma, and the station of dharma realized by the Tathāgatas—whether the Tathāgatas appear in the world or do not appear in the world—this station is eternally unchanging.

It exists within the dharmas attained by all those of the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists; it is not a mere emptiness or nothingness, yet it cannot be known by the ignorant and foolish. 'Abiding without interval' refers to the wisdom attained by those of the two vehicles and the Tathāgatas.")

All are entirely without interval. Mahāmati, the wisdom attained by the Tathāgata is perfumed by *prajñā*, not by mind, intellect, or consciousness, nor is it perfumed by those aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or sense-bases (*āyatana*).
Mahāmati, all that exists within the three realms of existence is produced from unreal conceptualization;
the Tathāgata does not arise from unreal, false conceptualization. Mahāmati, because of these two dharmas, there is both permanence and impermanence.
"Permanent" is neither dual nor non-dual, because all phenomena are quiescent and lack the characteristic of dualistic arising (for one falsely grasps at birth and death;

when birth and death are quiescent, that is the self-nature of nirvāṇa, and thus it is neither permanent nor impermanent). Therefore, O Mahāmati, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is neither permanent nor impermanent.
As long as verbal conceptualization arises, there will be the fault of permanence and impermanence. Conceptualization...
When awakening ceases, one is free from the unpeaceful views of permanence and nihilism held by the foolish (the conceptualization of awakening and the perception of awakening).

When the perception of awakening ceases, one is forever free from the perfuming of permanence, nihilism, and neither-permanence-nor-nihilism (meaning one is free from the views of permanence and nihilism, as well as the views of neither-permanence-nor-nihilism that can perfume and transform [the mind];
thus, it is originally quiescent). At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

If one lacks the skillful means of the requisites for benefiting beings, the faults of permanence and impermanence will arise; yet, if one is free from discriminative cognition, one is eternally detached from permanence and impermanence.

(If one lacks the purpose of the requisites for benefiting beings through skillful means, then the various faults of permanence and impermanence will arise; if one extinguishes conceptualization, one is eternally detached from the views of permanence and impermanence.

According to the tenets they establish, there are various manifold meanings; however, when observing the measure of one's own mind, verbal expressions cannot be found. (The non-Buddhists establish permanence...)

If impermanence is taken as the thesis, there are four propositions and other such various, incorrect meanings; thus, both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, whether permanent or impermanent, are all unreal. The mind is placed in a state where all mere verbal expressions are ultimately unattainable.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that the World-Honored One will further explain for us the arising and ceasing of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*).
Therein there is no self; who is it that arises and who is it that ceases? Fools rely upon arising and ceasing, failing to realize the exhaustion of suffering and not knowing *nirvāṇa*.

(Because, as previously stated, the Tathāgata is not conditioned by the mind, thought, or consciousness, nor by the perfuming of those aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. Furthermore, the Buddha has constantly taught that all phenomena..."*

Because there is no self, he asked: "I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*). Since there is no self within these aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, who arises and who ceases? Yet all ordinary, ignorant people rely upon arising and ceasing; they do not realize the exhaustion of suffering and do not realize *nirvāṇa*.

If there is no dharma of arising and ceasing, and if there is no self, who would know the exhaustion of suffering and who would realize *nirvāṇa*? The Buddha said, "Excellent! Listen attentively, and I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your teaching. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The Tathāgata-garbha is virtuous and..."
Wholesome causes are able to universally produce all realms of existence, just as an actor manifests various roles while remaining free from the notions of "self" and "mine.

(The new commentary states: the *tathāgatagarbha* is the name for the intrinsically pure mind when it is within the bonds of affliction. The Buddha said: Although there is no self within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), there exists the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is capable of receiving wholesome and unwholesome causes;

therefore, it is able to universally produce the phenomena of birth and death within the six destinies. Just as an actor, by relying on incantations and arts, conjures up the forms and appearances of the six destinies—wherein the phenomena are devoid of self and mine—so too do ordinary beings, relying upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, give rise to the birth and death of the six destinies, yet these are devoid of self or mine.
The object [of perception] is also like this. Because they do not realize it, through the expedient means of the conjunction of the three conditions, externalists give rise to [false views].

Not realizing [the truth], they cling to a creator; being perfumed by beginningless false and evil habits, this is called the *ālayavijñāna*. It gives rise to the ground where ignorance dwells and coexists with the seven consciousnesses.

(This refers to the fact that the followers of the Two Vehicles do not realize the selflessness of the *tathāgatagarbha*, and thus reckon the conjunction of the three conditions—sense organs, objects, and consciousness—as the cause of birth. Externalists likewise do not realize the selflessness of the *tathāgatagarbha*...)

Therefore, when one reckons the self and so forth as the agent, being perfumed by beginningless evil habits, it is called the Tathāgatagarbha and the Ālayavijñāna; from this, ignorance arises falsely and abides together with the seven consciousnesses.

Like the body of ocean waves, it is constantly arising without interruption, free from the fault of impermanence, and free from the doctrine of a self; its intrinsic nature is stainless and ultimately pure.

Just as that great ocean, due to the wind, gives rise to waves where the characteristics of water and the characteristics of waves continue without interruption, so too is the ocean of the Tathāgatagarbha: due to the wind of ignorance, the waves of the seven consciousnesses arise, and the succession of birth and death continues without interruption. Furthermore, like...

The ālayavijñāna is, from the beginning, free from the fault of impermanence and free from the doctrine of a self-soul; its intrinsic nature is stainless and ultimately pure. As for the other consciousnesses—such as the manas and the manovijñāna—they arise and perish moment by moment.
These seven [consciousnesses] are based on unreal conceptualization and grasp at various objects, their diverse forms and locations, calculating and clinging to names and characteristics.

Failing to realize that these perceived forms and appearances are manifestations of one's own mind, and being unaware of suffering and pleasure, they do not attain liberation. This is called [the state of bondage].

Regarding the characteristics of the various entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), craving arises as craving; whether as cause or as object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), the remaining seven consciousnesses—the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and so forth—arise and perish moment by moment.

Because they grasp at various objects and their diverse forms and locations through false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), they cling to names and marks (*nāma-rūpa*). Failing to realize that form and all other phenomena are manifestations of one's own mind, and failing to realize that suffering and pleasure are not the causes of Nirvana, they do not attain liberation.

Bound by names and marks, since they arise from craving, they further give rise to craving, whether as cause or condition, as the flow of conceptualization continues. Thus far, it has been clarified that the Tathāgatagarbha acts as the cause for the tainted (*sāsrava*) wholesome and unwholesome states within the three realms. As for those various faculties of sensation (*vedanendriya*):

When the stages of cessation occur and other mental constructions of one's own mind do not arise, yet one remains unaware of suffering or pleasure, entering the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and the fourth *dhyāna*, practitioners who have attained liberation through the realization of the True Truth conceive the notion that they have achieved liberation. Although those various faculties of sensation have ceased and consciousness does not arise in succession, there still remain the mental constructions of one's own mind;

however, having forgotten suffering and pleasure, they enter the state of the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. Having attained the fourth *dhyāna* and liberation through the Four Truths, these practitioners, upon reaching this state, mostly conceive the notion of ultimate liberation. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Only when birth is exhausted..."

Death is called liberation, yet in reality, one has not yet attained all-encompassing liberation. This clarifies that the Tathāgatagarbha serves as the cause for the supramundane, untainted wholesome dharmas of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. It is called the Tathāgatagarbha and the Ālayavijñāna because it neither departs nor transforms;
the seven consciousnesses flow and transform without ceasing. Why is this so? Because those [seven] consciousnesses arise by taking it as their object-condition (*ālambana*).
It is not within the sphere of practice for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, who do not realize the absence of self in either the individual (*sva*) or the collective (*sāmānya*).

The mutual inclusion of the arising of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*): [Realśa says,] "In reality, the name 'store-consciousness' (*ālayavijñāna*) within the Tathāgatagarbha has not yet been abandoned nor transformed. If there were no store-consciousness, the seven consciousnesses would cease. Why? Because they arise dependent upon it and their respective objects.

However, this is not a realm known by any non-Buddhists, followers of the Two Vehicles, or practitioners, for they only realize the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), grasping at the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) within the aggregates, elements, and bases.

Because the store-consciousness is the support for the [seven] consciousnesses, it is called 'non-awakening to selflessness. This non-awakening to the Tathāgatagarbha as being without self [is the cause]. Seeing the Tathāgatagarbha, the five dharmas [arise] naturally...

When one realizes the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*), the stages (*bhūmi*) are extinguished in their sequential continuity, and one advances further; the views of other non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cannot shake or move such a person. (The note states:

"If one perceives the Tathāgatagarbha through the remedial gateways of the five dharmas, the three natures, and the selflessness of persons and phenomena, then [the lower stages] are extinguished. Because one perceives the Tathāgatagarbha, one further attains entry into the stages and advances until reaching the eighth stage, where the evil views of non-Buddhists cannot shake or move one.
This is called abiding in the Bodhisattva’s Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*) and attaining the joy of the thirteen gates of samādhi. III.

Sustained by the clarity of awakening, one contemplates the inconceivable Buddha-dharma and, through one's own vow, does not accept the bliss of the gates of samādhi or the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

(Yang says: Because one contemplates the Buddha-dharma through one's own vow, one is able to regard and pity sentient beings and does not stagnate in empty quiescence; therefore, one accepts neither the bliss of the gates of samādhi nor the limit of reality.
One thus advances toward the noble path of self-awakening, attaining that which is not shared with any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or followers of external paths.

The ten noble lineages, the path, the body, wisdom, and the mind-born [body], as well as the practice of samādhis free from effort—therefore, Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who desires to seek superior progress should purify the Tathāgatagarbha and that which is named the Ālayavijñāna. By turning toward the noble realization of self-awareness, one does not share this with other vehicles;

rather, one realizes the path of the noble ones of the ten stages, wherein both body and wisdom are born according to one's will and are free from the activity of effort. Therefore, a Bodhisattva who desires to seek supreme and wondrous advancement should purify these.

The false habit-energies are designated by the name "storehouse" (ālaya); it is not as with the two vehicles, which, having merely severed the death and rebirth of the limited body (pariccheda-jarāmaraṇa), claim this to be true liberation.
Mahāmati, if there were no storehouse consciousness named Tathāgatagarbha, there would be no arising and ceasing. Mahāmati, yet all ordinary beings and sages alike possess arising and ceasing;

practitioners, through their own realization of the noble state, abide in the bliss of the present dharma and do not abandon skillful means. (If there were no name for the storehouse consciousness of false habit-energies, what arising and ceasing could there be in the pure Tathāgatagarbha?)

However, the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing in all the Noble Ones is not the same as the lack of nature in wood or stone. Therefore, although practitioners attain the dharma-joy of the noble wisdom of self-realization manifest before them, they do not abandon skillful means, but rather advance toward the stage of Buddhahood;
thus, there is still arising and ceasing. Mahāmati, this Tathāgata-garbha, the storehouse-consciousness, is what is perceived by the mental conceptions of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Although its intrinsic nature is pure, because it is covered by adventitious defilements, it is seen as impure; yet this is not the case for the Tathāgatas, Mahāmati.
The Tathāgata’s manifest realm is like looking at an *āmala* fruit in the palm of one's hand.

(Because the deluded awakening of the non-Buddhists and the partial awakening of the Two Vehicles result in what they see being impure, and although the partial awakening of the Bodhisattvas is superior, it is not yet ultimate; only the Tathāgata’s manifest realm views the Tathāgatagarbha as clearly and brightly as observing a fruit in the palm of the hand.
O Mahāmati, by means of my supernormal power (*ṛddhibala*), I shall establish this meaning for Queen Śrīmālā and those Bodhisattvas who possess perfected sharp intelligence.
The Tathāgata and others proclaim and expound upon the names of the *tathāgatagarbha* and the *ālayavijñāna*, which arise simultaneously with the seven consciousnesses.

Śrāvakas adhere to the views of the non-self of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-nairātmya* and *dharma-nairātmya*). [Bodhiruci says: "For the sake of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others, he demonstrates the non-self of phenomena. Paramārtha says: "He causes the śrāvakas to see the non-self of phenomena.

This sutra states that because the followers of the two vehicles cling to and do not relinquish the state of the non-self of persons, they are caused to leave behind such clinging and attain the non-self of phenomena. Thus, Lady Śrīmālā, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power...
The Divine One said: "The realm of the Tathāgata is not the realm of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or followers of external paths.
The Tathāgatagarbha and Ālayavijñāna are the realm of wisdom accessible only to Buddhas and other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who rely upon the meaning through their sharp faculties.
Therefore, you and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently cultivate and study the Tathāgatagarbha and Ālayavijñāna; do not merely stop at hearing and understanding them."

The Conception of Contentment (The new commentary states: "It is said that the Tathāgatagarbha and Ālayavijñāna are the realm of the Buddhas, not a place traversed by the two vehicles or non-Buddhists; one should diligently observe and fully cultivate the three types of wisdom, rather than becoming complacent merely by retaining what has been heard.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The profound *tathāgatagarbha* arises together with the seven consciousnesses through two kinds of grasping (*parigraha*).

The wise one who understands this is far removed from them—namely, that the seven consciousnesses arise through these two kinds of grasping, whether as causes or as objects of perception (*ālambana*). Just as reflections appear in a mirror, the mind is perfumed by beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

One who observes this according to reality sees that all phenomena are in fact no-phenomena (the true meaning being that objective appearances do not exist at all). [Note: This is like a mirror which exists because of external objects.]

The manifestation of images is like the mirror of the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind: because it is perfumed by the beginningless false habits of the seven evolving consciousnesses, the false phenomena of the triple world—both the environment and its inhabitants—appear. To one who observes according to reality, none of these exist at all. As it is said:

"Like a fool looking at the finger pointing to the moon, he gazes at the finger but not at the moon; those who are attached to names and words do not see my true reality. (The New Commentary says: "The wise man, seeing the finger, necessarily knows there is a moon;
the fool is the opposite. Therefore, by merely observing the finger of the text, one does not attain the true Dharma. The mind acts as a skilled artisan, while the intellect...

Just as a performer has five types of consciousness as his companions when he views the audience with conceptual construction (the new commentary states that the *tathāgatagarbha*—the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)—is perfumed and maintains the seeds, manifesting as the sense organs, the body, and the vessel-world, like a performing artisan; the defiled *manas* clings to a self and dharmas, thus it is like the assistant performers;
and the sixth consciousness, which discriminates falsely, is analogous to the spectators).

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the ultimate characteristics of the five dharmas, the self-natures, consciousness, and the two kinds of selflessness.
May I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, through sequential and continuous discernment of these dharmas in all stages, enter into all Buddha-dharmas. "To enter into all Buddha-dharmas" means—
"Even unto the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization" (Paramārtha says: "even unto being able to enter the stage of the Tathāgata’s own internally realized wisdom. [Note:

Because the preceding teaching on the Tathāgata-garbha—the five dharmas, the three natures, and the non-selfhood of persons and phenomena—serves as an antidote that eliminates [dualistic grasping], he now raises the five dharmas, the three natures, consciousness, and the two kinds of non-self to pose his inquiry]).

The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well. Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "The five dharmas..."

Regarding the characteristics of the two kinds of selflessness within the consciousness of intrinsic nature and the categories of discrimination: this refers to names, signs, and conceptual constructions, as well as correct knowledge and suchness.
When a practitioner practices and enters the noble realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization, they become detached from views of annihilationism, eternalism, existence, non-existence, and so forth;

the blissful meditative absorption (*sukha-samādhi*) of the present life manifests before them. (Yang states: "This means that if a practitioner contemplates these dharmas, they enter the sphere of the Tathāgata’s self-realization.")

In this realm, one attains the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of happiness in the present life, which is constantly manifest and never obscured—just as if one were looking at an *āmalaka* fruit held in the palm of one's hand.
Mahāmati, ordinary people do not realize that those five dharmas, the self-natures, the consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness are merely the manifestations of their own minds;

they falsely imagine external natures, whereas this is not the case for the noble ones. (Paramārtha translates: "Mahāmati, ordinary fools do not understand the five dharmas, the self-natures, the various consciousnesses, and selflessness; regarding what is manifested within the mind, they see external objects and give rise to discrimination, but this is not so for the noble ones. Mahāmati said:
The Buddha said, "World-Honored One, how is it that deluded ordinary people give rise to false imaginings, while the noble sages do not? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Ordinary people are attached to conventional numbers, names, and signs; they follow after them as their minds disperse.

Once dispersed, they fall into various appearances and forms, falling into views of 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' and harboring hopes and attachments for exquisite colors. Having become attached, because they are shrouded by ignorance, defilement arises."
Having become attached and stained, they accumulate karma born of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Having accumulated it, they entangle themselves with false imaginings like a silkworm making a cocoon, falling into the ocean of birth and death and the wilderness of the various realms of existence.

Like a well-drawing wheel, because of their ignorance, they cannot understand that things are like illusions, mirages, or the moon reflected in water, and that their self-nature is free from "I" and "mine. (Translated by Bodhiruci: The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "All ordinary beings cling...")

Famous characteristics arise in accordance with the phenomena that arise in accordance with them; having seen various characteristics, one falls into a mind of false views regarding "I" and "mine. Having become attached to the characteristics of all phenomena, one enters the place of obstruction within the darkness of ignorance.

Having entered this place of obstruction, one gives rise to a mind of craving. Once the mind of craving has arisen, one is able to perform actions of greed, hatred, and delusion. Having performed these formations (*saṃskāra*), one cannot stop oneself, like a silkworm making a cocoon that entangles its own body with a discriminating mind.

One falls into the perilous ocean of the six realms of existence, revolving like a waterwheel, unaware and unknowing due to a lack of wisdom. Because of this lack of wisdom, one does not know that all phenomena are like illusions, nor does one know the absence of "I" and "mine. Thus, [the cycle] begins.
All unreal conceptualizations—characteristics and the characterized, as well as arising, abiding, and ceasing—are born from the conceptualizations of one’s own mind;
they do not arise from Īśvara, time, atoms, or primordial matter (*pradhāna*). Foolish ordinary people follow along with names and characteristics.

(Since conceptualizations are like illusions and so forth, being unreal, how could there be a characteristic or a characterized, or arising, abiding, and ceasing? Thus, one knows that all dharmas, in terms of name and characteristic, arise from conceptualization and do not arise from Īśvara or other such causes. Fools do not realize that names and characteristics are manifestations of their own minds.)

Therefore, the deluded mind takes external objects as its conditions and flows along with the sensory dust (*rajas*). Mahāmati, regarding those "characteristics" (*nimitta*): that which is illuminated by visual consciousness is called "form" (*rūpa*);

that which is illuminated by auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousnesses is called "sound, odor, flavor, touch, and phenomena" (*śabda-gandha-rasa-spraṣṭavya-dharma*). These are what are called "characteristics. (The *Xin shuo* [New Explanation] states: "The five faculties and six objects are collectively termed 'characteristics.

Furthermore, that which is seen by visual consciousness is called 'visible and resistant form' (*sanidarśana-sapratigha-rūpa*); that which is apprehended by auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses is called 'invisible and resistant form' (*anidarśana-sapratigha-rūpa*); and that which is apprehended by mental consciousness is called 'invisible and non-resistant form' (*anidarśana-apratigha-rūpa*). )

Regarding form, these three types of color-and-shape (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) are collectively termed "name-and-characteristic" (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*). Mahāmati, that which is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) establishes various names and manifests various characteristics;

it is not otherwise than this. (The *Ṭīkā* says: "This matter is thus determined and not otherwise. Names such as elephant, horse, chariot, infantry, man, and woman—these are called conceptual construction. (The *New Commentary* says:

"To establish numerous names and manifest various distinct characteristics means that when names such as 'elephant,' 'horse,' 'chariot,' and 'infantry' arise, there immediately arise the corresponding characteristics of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. It is like this.")

"Those" indicates their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); "not different" indicates their common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). To conceive of such names and characteristics is therefore called false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Mahāmati, as for true wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*), those names and characteristics cannot be apprehended; they are like passing guests.
The various consciousnesses do not arise, are neither interrupted nor eternal, and do not fall into the stages of any externalists, *śrāvakas*, or *pratyekabuddhas*.

True wisdom contemplates those names and characteristics as unreal, like passing guests; because a guest has the sense of not remaining, they cannot be apprehended, and since they cannot be apprehended, [they are thus understood].

Therefore, the reason the various consciousnesses do not arise is that wisdom is the host and names and marks are the guests. Since this wisdom is neither interrupted nor permanent, one no longer falls into the stages of ordinary beings or śrāvakas.
Furthermore, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, by means of this right wisdom, does not establish names and marks, yet it is not that he does not establish them;

he abandons the two views of affirmation and denial (establishment and repudiation). [Bodhiruci says: "Relying on right wisdom, one does not take names and marks as existent phenomena, nor does one take the non-perception of marks as non-existent. Why? Because...

Therefore, because one is free from the false views of existence and non-existence, one knows that names and marks do not arise (knowing that the essence of names and marks does not arise). This is called *tathatā* (suchness). [Bodhiruci says:

"Based on correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), one does not take names and marks as existing, nor does one take the absence of names and marks as non-existent. Why? Because one is free from the false views of existence and non-existence. Since not seeing names and marks is the meaning of correct wisdom, I therefore call this True Suchness.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, abiding in suchness, attains the realm of non-existence; thus he attains it.
When a Bodhisattva attains the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they forever leave behind all heterodox paths and evil destinies, and correctly abide in the supramundane path of dharmas.
They mature their discernment regarding all phenomena—such as illusions—and realize the nature of the path of self-awakened dharmas.

Thus, they depart from all false conceptualizations and the perception of differences in the nature of things (realizing the illusory nature of the realm and attaining the path of self-awakened dharmas, they are finally able to leave behind false conceptualizations and the perception of differences in the nature of things).

The sequence of entering the successive stages (*bhūmi*): proceeding through the stages up to the *Dharmameghā-bhūmi*, within which the power of samādhi, mastery, and supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) blossom forth.

As translated by Paramārtha: "Having entered the *Dharmameghā-bhūmi*, one subsequently uses the power of samādhi, mastery, and supernormal knowledges to adorn the stage of the Tathāgata with various flowers.

Having attained the stage of the Tathāgata, one manifests various transformations and perfect illuminations to bring sentient beings to maturity, like the moon reflected in water, having thoroughly investigated [the nature of reality].
Having fully perfected the ten inexhaustible phrases for the sake of sentient beings with their various inclinations and understandings, one discriminates and teaches the Dharma;

the Dharma-body is free from the activities of the mind—this is called the Bodhisattva’s entry into that which is attained through Suchness (*tathatā*). (Yang says: "The Dharma-body is unconditioned and entirely free from the activities of the mind;
it is here that one enters Suchness. At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, why does the World-Honored One [speak of] the three kinds..."
Regarding how the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) enter into the five dharmas as each having its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the Buddha told Mahāmati:

"The three intrinsic natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness are all included within the five dharmas. Mahāmati, those names and characteristics are the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

[The New Commentary states: "Previously, Mahāmati raised four points to question the Tathāgata, yet the Tathāgata answered by means of only one gate, that of the five dharmas; therefore, he asks again regarding the inclusion of the three intrinsic natures within the five dharmas."]

"Is there another school that maintains its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)? The Buddha replied: "The other three dharma-gates are all subsumed within the five dharmas; for by practicing a single gate, all gates are fully encompassed. The same applies to the other three. That is to say, among them, names and marks give rise to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

This imagined nature is included within the five dharmas as 'name' and 'mark. Mahāmati, if one relies on that imagined nature, the mind and mental factors arise simultaneously, just as the sun and its rays arise together.
They possess various distinct characteristics and each performs its own function; this is called the dependent origination nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)."

If the mind and mental factors arise based on those deluded imaginings, then names and characteristics are stirred up and arise simultaneously. This is like the analogy of the sun and its light: light is simultaneous with the sun, and names are simultaneous with characteristics; light is simultaneous with the sun, and names are simultaneous with characteristics.

Although the mind is fundamentally without anything to be maintained, the discrimination of various names is what maintains the characteristics, and the discrimination of various characteristics is what maintains the names. Therefore, it is said that each separately discriminates and maintains these two dharmas, and through their mutual maintenance as causes and conditions, they arise;

this is called the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature). This *paratantra-svabhāva* is included within the five dharmas as *vikalpa* (deluded imagination). Mahāmati, correct wisdom and suchness are indestructible; therefore, they are called the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).

The nature (*svabhāva*)—namely, correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*)—is not a conditioned phenomenon and therefore cannot be destroyed; this is called the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). This perfected nature is included within the five dharmas as correct wisdom and suchness. (The above clarifies how the three natures are included within the five dharmas.)

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are eight kinds of discrimination regarding the false imagination of what is manifested by one's own mind; these are the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the manas, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the five groups of sensory consciousnesses.
Because their characteristics are unreal and are merely false imagination, the grasping at "self" and "mine" ceases, and the two kinds of selflessness arise.
Therefore, Mahāmati, these five dharmas are that which śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas realize through their own direct awakening.
The characteristics of the stages of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) are continuous and sequential; all Buddha-dharmas are entirely contained within them. (The New Commentary states:

"When attachment arises toward phenomena falsely manifested by one's own mind, there occur eight kinds of discrimination consisting of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). These distinct characteristics—the eight names and marks—are subsumed within the five dharmas. The names and marks are false conceptualization (*parikalpita*);

realizing that these names and marks are all unreal and are merely the nature of false appearance, one enters into the five dharmas as correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*). Thus it is clarified that the eight consciousnesses enter into the five dharmas. Since they are all unreal and are merely the nature of false conceptualization, if one reckons them as real, the two kinds of self—namely, the name of the self and the characteristics of the self—then enter [into the five dharmas]. )

Among the five dharmas, if one can awaken to the fact that name, mark, and conceptualization are unreal—specifically regarding those two types of self—one attains the wisdom of the two-fold non-self (of persons and phenomena).
Thus, one enters the correct wisdom within the five dharmas. By clearly understanding these two kinds of non-self, one enters the five dharmas.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the five dharmas consist of mark, name, conceptualization, suchness, and correct wisdom. Mahāmati, as for "mark," it refers to location, shape, and color.

The manifestation of such forms and so forth is called "characteristic" (*nimitta*). [Śikṣānanda says: Here, "characteristic" refers to the distinct shapes of the perceived colors and so forth; this is called the characteristic. If those possess such characteristics, they are termed "vases" and so forth;

that which is precisely this and not otherwise is called "name" (*nāman*). [Śikṣānanda says: Based on those various characteristics, names such as "vase" are established; that it is thus and not otherwise is called the name.
The mental states and mental factors that designate these various names and manifest these various characteristics—such as vases and so forth—are [the consciousnesses].

"Conceptualization of names" (refers to the arising of mind and mental factors that take names and marks such as "vase" as objects; this is conceptualization of names). Those names and those marks are ultimately unobtainable; from beginning to end there is no awakening [to them].
When one is free from the mutual succession regarding all phenomena and is detached from unreal conceptualization, this is called *tathatā* (suchness).

(The note says: Because one realizes that names and marks have no reality, there is no conceptualization. Because one awakens to the realization that all phenomena have no reality, there is no mutual succession of arising and ceasing, and so forth, until one is entirely detached from unreal conceptualization; this is then called *tathatā*. This is the definitive truth.)
The ultimate nature of meditative concentration is unattainable; it is the mark of suchness (*tathatā*).
I and all Buddhas enter into it in accordance with reality, and for the sake of all sentient beings, we expound, designate, and reveal it as it truly is.

By entering into that, one realizes perfect enlightenment, free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, where false conceptualization does not arise. This accords with the noble path of self-realized sages, which is not shared by any outsiders, *śrāvakas*, or *pratyekabuddhas*.

That which is non-apprehensible in its characteristics is called right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). (Furthermore, Mahāmati, regarding the "five dharmas" below, this is a re-explanation of the meaning of the five dharmas.

Mahāmati, these are called the five dharmas, the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭa-vijñāna*), and the two kinds of selflessness (*dvi-vidha-nairātmya*); all Buddha-dharmas are entirely contained within them.
Therefore, Mahāmati, you should personally study them through skillful means and also teach others; do not follow after others. (Śikṣānanda says: regarding these dharmas...)

"In this regard, you should personally realize it through skillful wisdom and also exhort others to realize it; having realized this, your mind will become certain and will no longer follow after others.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The five dharmas, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness encompass the entirety of the Mahāyāna.

(This verse summarizes that the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two selflessnesses universally encompass all the meanings of the phenomena of the Mahāyāna. Name, appearance, and false discrimination are the two aspects of the nature of false imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

(This verse summarizes that the two natures of false imagination and dependent origination are subsumed within the three dharmas of name, appearance, and false discrimination. Correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*) are [the nature of perfect realization].
This constitutes the "characteristic of accomplishment" (the verse above refers to the two dharmas of the inclusion of self-nature within right knowledge and suchness).

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding the phrases spoken by the World-Honored One—that the Buddhas of the past were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and likewise those of the future and the present—how is it, World-Honored One, that they are 'such'?"
"If what has been said is accepted as having further meaning, I pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately explain it.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Do not accept it according to the literal words. The measure of the Buddhas of the three periods of time is not like the sands of the Ganges. Why is this?

Because it transcends worldly expectations and cannot be illustrated by any worldly analogy. (The measure of the Buddhas of the three periods of time cannot be calculated by number; therefore, it is not like the sands of the Ganges. It is subtle and supreme, surpassing all worlds, and without peer.)"

Because [the Buddhas] transcend the world, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "All phenomena within the three realms, whether existent or non-existent, cannot serve as metaphors for the Buddha. This is because ordinary, deluded people and non-Buddhists nourish evil views through their false imaginings, resulting in an endless cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
To cause them to weary of and become detached from this wheel of existence, and to encourage them toward diligent and superior progress, it is said for their sake:
"The Buddhas are easy to see; they are not like the Udumbara flower, which is difficult to encounter."

Therefore, as a skillful means to pacify [them], and in order to entice and advance the ignorant and those of external paths so that they may grow weary of birth and death, he says: "Transformation Buddhas are easy to see—like the sands of the Ganges—they have all already attained the Way;

you should not now undergo this cycle of birth and death. If he were to say that the Buddhas are as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower, these people would instead give rise to despondency and retreat, no longer advancing in their quest. (Note: *Udumbara* is also called *udumbhara*; it is translated here as "Auspicious Response.
