At other times, observing those who are to be transformed, he speaks thus: "The Buddha is difficult to encounter, like the udumbara flower."

The *udumbara* flower (the note says: seeing that his disciples receiving transformation were not diligent in their spiritual exertion, he spoke these words: "A Buddha is difficult to encounter, like the *udumbara* flower; now that you have encountered one, why do you not exert yourself to advance toward the supreme and leave birth-and-death behind?").
The *udumbara* flower has never been seen before, nor is it being seen now, nor will it be seen in the future by those who see the Tathāgata;

yet the world sees him everywhere because he does not establish himself through self-attainment. Therefore, it is said that the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is like the *udumbara* flower. Mahāmati, [it is thus].

To establish one's own realization (*svapratyātma-adhigama*) transcends worldly expectations. (The *udumbara* flower is not seen by anyone throughout the three periods of time; yet now the Tathāgata is seen by all in the world. How can it be said that the Buddha is like the *udumbara* flower?

The Tathāgata does not establish the Dharma-body through his own realization as if he were the *udumbara*. Rather, for the sake of inducing sentient beings, he speaks of an emanation-buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) that is difficult to see and easy to see. One who is able to establish their own realization within their own domain transcends worldly expectations.

That which is the realm of self-awakened noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna-gocara*) cannot be believed in by those ordinary fools, for there is nothing [in their experience] with which to compare it.

Just as the true Tathāgata transcends the characteristics perceived by mind, thought, and consciousness, such that no analogy can be made—since ordinary fools do not believe in the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization, how could they know that the true Tathāgata transcends the characteristics perceived by mind, thought, and consciousness, and cannot be illustrated by analogy?—O Mahāmati, when I say that the Buddha is like the sands of the Ganges, there is no fault in this.
(The Dharmakāya is without marks and cannot be reached by speech or analogy; saying now that the Buddha is like the sands of the Ganges is without error.)
This is because the faults [of the world] are intended to demonstrate seven kinds of profound meanings. Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges:

all fish, turtles, *śuśumāra* (or as some say *śiṣumara*, translated as "fish that kills its own offspring"), lions, elephants, horses, humans, and beasts may trample upon them, yet the sand does not think, "They are disturbing me," nor does it give rise to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Its self-nature is pure and free from all defilements; such is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

The great power of the Ganges-like river of the Tathāgata’s own realized noble wisdom, his supernatural powers, and his mastery are such that all externalists, humans, animals, and others who cause disturbance do not provoke the Tathāgata to give rise to conceptual thought. The Tathāgata remains tranquil and free from discursive ideation.
Because the Tathāgata’s original vow is to establish sentient beings in the bliss of samādhi, he is not disturbed by them, just as [the ocean is not disturbed by the waves].

It is equal to the sands of the Ganges and without difference; furthermore, because greed and anger have been severed (Vasubandhu says: there is no love or hatred), the Tathāgata’s self-realized noble wisdom is like the power of the Ganges, and his supernatural faculties and mastery are like the sands within the Ganges River.

When various non-Buddhists come to harass and disturb him, the Tathāgata never gives rise to even a single thought of anger toward them, nor does he produce the discrimination of love or hatred. For example, the sands of the Ganges are the very nature of earth;
when the kalpa ends and all is consumed by fire, although all the earth is burned, that element of earth does not abandon its own nature.

Because it arises simultaneously with the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*), other deluded worldlings conceive the notion that the earth is burning; yet the earth does not burn, because it has fire as its cause.

In this same way, Mahāmati, the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata is indestructible like the sands of the Ganges. (The earth is formed by the combination of fire and water, and since fire can produce soil, it is said that the earth does not burn.
Because sand is indestructible, it is compared to the *dharmakāya*. Mahāmati, for example, the sands of the Ganges are without limit; so too is the Tathāgata.)

The radiance is likewise thus, being without limit; for the sake of maturing sentient beings, it shines universally upon all the great assemblies of Buddhas (to say it shines upon all the great assemblies of Buddhas is like the sands of the Ganges, being without limit and comparable to the Tathāgata).
Mahāmati, just as one cannot ever find sand different from that of the Ganges even by seeking it elsewhere, so too, Mahāmati, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas have no [difference].

Because the causes and conditions for birth, death, arising, and ceasing have been severed (the new commentary states: it is purely golden sand with no shards or stones, used as an analogy for the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body which has no birth, death, arising, or ceasing;

"shards and stones" refers to the three types of causes for birth in the Tathāgata being entirely severed). Mahāmati, just as the increase or decrease of the sands of the Ganges cannot be perceived, so too, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata’s wisdom matures sentient beings without increasing or decreasing, because it is not a physical phenomenon (*kāyadharma*); whereas physical phenomena [are subject to change].
There is that which destroys the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, yet this is not a physical body (the note states: because it is not a *rūpakāya*, there is neither increase nor decrease).
Just as one cannot obtain oil by pressing the sands of the Ganges, so too do all these beings of extreme suffering oppress the Tathāgata;

yet until all beings have attained *nirvāṇa*, he does not abandon the *dharmadhātu*, for through his own vows and the joy of *samādhi*, he acts out of great compassion (Śikṣānanda says: "It is like the Ganges...").

Just as when sand is pressed and treated with great effort, one can never obtain ghee or oil from it, so it is with the Tathāgata. Although he is oppressed by the manifold sufferings of sentient beings—even down to the most minute insects—and though they have not yet reached nirvāṇa, if he desires to cause them to abandon [suffering], he cannot find within the *dharmadhātu* a deep-seated aspiration for it.

Why is this? Because he is fully endowed with and has perfected the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Sentient beings are in the midst of extreme suffering and have no means of escape; the Tathāgata, out of pity for them, employs hundreds of thousands of skillful means (*upāya*) to bring about their liberation.

This is like being oppressed by sentient beings; the rest of the meaning may be understood accordingly. Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges which flow along with the water; it is not that there is no water.
In this way, Mahāmati, all dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata flow toward nirvāṇa; therefore it is said that they are like the sands of the Ganges.
The Tathāgatas do not flow along with the currents of the various destinies (*gati*), for "flowing" implies the sense of destruction. [Bodhiruci says:

"Mahāmati, just as the sands of the Ganges flow with the water and never flow upstream, so too, Mahāmati, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings in the same way—conforming to nirvāṇa and not flowing upstream. Therefore, Mahāmati, I say they conform to the Buddha."]

"Mahāmati, as for the sands of the Ganges, the Tathāgata says that the sands of the Ganges flowing with the current do not possess the meaning of 'going. If the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possessed the meaning of 'going,' then the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, would be subject to impermanence and cessation.

Mahāmati, the sands are a metaphor for all dharmas, and the water is a metaphor for Nirvāṇa. Although the sands flow following the water, they do not depart from the water; likewise, although the dharmas flow following Nirvāṇa, they do not depart from Nirvāṇa.

Therefore, it is said that it is not as if there were no water. Mahāmati, the fundamental limit of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) cannot be known. Since it cannot be known, how can one speak of 'going'? Mahāmati, 'going' has the meaning of 'severance.'"
Fools do not know [this]. (Paramārtha translates: "The original limit of birth and death cannot even be known; since it is unknowable, how could I rely upon it to explain the meaning of 'going'?

Therefore, for the Tathāgata, there is no such thing as the meaning of 'going. Mahāmati, the meaning of 'going' is the meaning of 'severance. Foolish ordinary beings do not perceive or understand this. Mahāmati said to the Buddha:

"World-Honored One, if the original limit of sentient beings' birth and death cannot be known, how can liberation be known? (The Note states: "If the beginning—the original limit—of sentient beings' birth and death cannot be known...")

"How can it be known that liberation will be attained at the end of time? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Because the causes—the beginningless habit-energies of false imagination and the faults of delusion—are extinguished, one realizes that external objects are merely manifestations of one's own mind;
thus, the transformation of the body of false imagination constitutes liberation. It is not that [liberation] is non-extinguished;

therefore, it is 'boundless' (*ananta*), yet it is not that nothing exists at all. For that false imagination, terms such as 'boundless' and others are used as synonyms. Since 'boundless' is a synonym for false imagination, it is not real."

Furthermore, it is said that one should not say there is no limit, nor that there is absolutely nothing at all; rather, it means that by merely transforming the basis of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one attains liberation—it does not mean that false conceptualization is destroyed and becomes non-existent, for such would imply having limits.

To say there are limits is to say there are no limits; both "having limits" and "having no limits" are merely different names for false conceptualization. When observing the internal and external, one is free from false conceptualization. There is no difference between the wisdom of sentient beings and *jñeyāvaraṇa* (the veil of the knowable); all phenomena are entirely quiescent.
Because one fails to recognize that what appears before the mind is a manifestation of one's own mind, false conceptualization arises.

"If one recognizes [them], then they cease" (Śikṣānanda says: "Free from discrimination... there are no separate sentient beings; through the observation of wisdom that all internal and external phenomena, both the subject and the object of knowledge, are entirely quiescent.

O Mahāmati, all phenomena are merely what is seen through the discrimination of one's own mind; because this is not understood, the discriminating mind arises, and when the mind is known, it ceases. Not recognizing that false conceptualization manifests from one's own mind, false conceptualization arises;
if one recognizes it, it ceases"). At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
To contemplate all Teachers as being like the sands of the Ganges—neither destroyed, nor departing, nor yet ultimately [extinguished] (the note states:
this means the Dharma-body is also not ultimately empty or annihilated)—this is the impartial contemplation of all Tathāgatas.
Like the sands of the Ganges, they are entirely free from all faults; though following the flow, their nature is eternal. This is the Perfect Enlightenment of the Buddha. (New Explanation)
It is said that this verse praises the seven types of metaphors [resembling] the sands of the Ganges mentioned above, as can be understood from the text.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the characteristic of the momentary destruction of all dharmas.
World-Honored One, how is it that all dharmas are momentary? (Bodhiruci translates this as: "Explain for me the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of all dharmas.")

"How is it that the Tathāgata says all dharmas do not abide for even a single thought-moment? [This is because the Buddha previously stated that "bodily dharmas" involve decay; this refers to the teaching that the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are impermanent. Thus, he asks by citing the characteristic of the momentary destruction of all phenomena.]
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, “Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall speak for you. The Buddha said to Mahāmati, “All phenomena (sarvadharma) refer to:
wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; conditioned and unconditioned; mundane and supramundane; faulty and faultless; with outflows and without outflows;
and those to be experienced and those not to be experienced. (Śikṣānanda says: "All phenomena" refers to wholesome dharmas, unwholesome dharmas, conditioned dharmas, and unconditioned dharmas.)

This is because there are those in this world and other worlds who practice as Bodhisattvas yet take pleasure in the *nirvāṇa* of the Śrāvaka vehicle; [I speak thus] so that they may abandon the Śrāvaka vehicle."
Advancing toward the Mahāyāna, it is the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha (the transformation Buddha) who bestows the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) upon the *śrāvaka*, not the *dharmakāya* Buddha.

(The new commentary states: Because the *śrāvaka* realizes *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and considers himself a Buddha, the Buddha employs skillful means to grant him a prediction, saying: "O *śrāvaka* dwelling in the bliss of samādhi, you shall attain the most supreme body of a Tathāgata. This causes him to realize for himself that he is not [yet] a Buddha.

As he advances toward the Mahāyāna, even a bodhisattva at the initial stage who delights in the *śrāvaka* teachings is made to abandon such a mind and advance in the great practice. Furthermore, it is the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha who grants predictions to *nirmāṇakāya* *śrāvakas*; in the *dharmatā-tathāgata*, such a thing does not exist. [This answers the first question.]
For this reason, Mahāmati, it is prophesied that the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas are not different. (Note: This is because the transformation-buddhas bestow predictions upon the śrāvakas.

Mahāmati, "not different" means that for the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all Buddha-Tathāgatas, there is a single flavor (*ekarasa*) in the liberation resulting from the severance of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), but not in the severance of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

(Note: The two vehicles and the Buddhas are identical in severing the four abiding afflictions; they do not differ in the state of the single flavor of liberation. [Yang] says: The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas sever the afflictive hindrances...)

[The Tathāgata’s] identical wisdom is uninterrupted [from that of others], yet it differs from that of the Tathāgata. Mahāmati, as for the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is the superior purity of seeing the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*);

as for the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*), it is that which was previously practiced through the view of the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*) and is abandoned [thereby]. (Note: It is said that the abandonment of the cognitive obscuration means attaining the stage of a Tathāgata by seeing the selflessness of phenomena, not that of a Śrāvaka.

Yang says: This means that what was previously practiced—the view of the selflessness of persons—is abandoned at this point; subsequently, when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is relinquished, this is the abandonment of the afflictive obscuration. This answers the second question. The seven consciousnesses cease their activities.

The ultimate purity resulting from the cessation of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the *ālayavijñāna* and the liberation from the obstructions of the [seven] evolving consciousnesses—[the new commentary states:

it clarifies that the seven evolving consciousnesses, the various dharmas, the obstructions, the *ālayavijñāna*, and its habitual tendencies are the delusive substance of all sentient beings, being false, provisional, and impermanent, and thus not the cause of *nirvāṇa* nor leading to the Buddha-way; if the seven consciousnesses cease, one attains liberation from the obstructions among all dharmas, the habitual tendencies of the *ālayavijñāna* are extinguished, and there is ultimate purity;

this is called the extinction of delusive thought, termed *nirvāṇa*, and termed reaching the Buddha-way]—is due to the "Dharma abiding from the beginning" (*pūrvasthita-dharma*), and therefore has no nature of before or after. [The Buddha said: "I have realized the Dharma abiding from the beginning..."]

Abiding in the Dharma, the ancient path of the sages is like the nature of gold, silver, and so forth; the *dharmadhātu* is eternally abiding. Therefore, I say that not a single word has been spoken, nor is there anything to which an answer is given. Although within the four kinds of equality there is the equality of speech, all verbal expressions—whether at the beginning, the end, or in the middle—are devoid of intrinsic nature.
(This answers the fourth question. Because of his inexhaustible original vows, the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma without deliberation or investigation.

Since he is transformed by right wisdom and his mindfulness is never false, he is without deliberation or investigation. (The Tathāgata, by the power of his original vows, does not depend upon thought...)

Because he contemplates and observes while expounding the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, and because his mindfulness—transformed by right wisdom—is not deluded, there is neither vitarka (discursive thought) nor vicāra (sustained reflection). [This answers the fifth question.

Because the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the four stages of abiding and the stage of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) have been severed, the two types of affliction are eliminated; one is detached from the two kinds of death, realizes the selflessness of persons and phenomena, and severs the two obstacles. [The New Commentary states:

The Buddha said that because the afflictions of the four stages of abiding and the habit-energies of ignorance have been severed, one is called a True Buddha. A Transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) manifests forms through skillful means to transform sentient beings; it is not a True Buddha.]

[This answers the sixth question. Mahāmati, the seven moments—the mind (*citta*), the intellect (*manas*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*)—have their cause in habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Because they belong to the category of the wholesome and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), they do not revolve [in saṃsāra] again. Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, as well as of suffering and pleasure;

it cannot be realized by those of deluded minds, those of confused wisdom, or foolish ordinary people. (It is said that the seven kinds of consciousness have the habit-energy of false discrimination as their cause, and are momentary.)

The eternal nature is detached from the wholesome and the untainted; it is not a dharma of transmigration and cannot wander through the six realms. The *tathāgatagarbha* can sustain the flow of birth and death and serves as the cause for both nirvāṇa and suffering and pleasure. To point to emptiness in confusion is the intent of the śrāvakas; to point to sound is the intent of the non-Buddhists.

Because the śrāvakas and non-Buddhists are attached to emptiness and existence and cannot achieve awakening—due to their lack of distinction in their biased attachments—they are collectively called "foolish ordinary beings. (This answers the seventh question.
"O Mahāmati, those who are followed and protected by the Vajrapāṇi are merely transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇabuddha*), not the true Tathāgata. O Mahāmati, the true Tathāgata..."
This is because one has transcended all faculties and measures, and having extinguished all the faculties and measures of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists,

one attains the dwelling in happiness in the present life through the patience regarding the knowledge of the uninterrupted dharma; it is not protected by the Vajrapāṇi-guards, nor does it belong to any transformation-buddha,
for those transformation-buddhas who do not arise from karma are neither Buddhas nor separate from Buddhas, being like a potter’s wheel and such.

The Dharma is taught according to the characteristics of the actions performed by sentient beings; it is not taught from the standpoint of one’s own realization, but rather from the realm of self-awakened realization.

(Transformation Buddhas manifest through skillful means in accordance with the characteristics of sentient beings, appearing similar to human phenomena; therefore, they rely on protection. The true Tathāgata is beyond all sensory measures (*indriya-pramāṇa*), which is the characteristic of being invisible and thus does not require protection. This means that all transformation Buddhas arise according to the roots of goodness of people and do not arise from substantial karma;

they are not the "true" Buddha. Nevertheless, although transformations arise based on the True [Buddha], they do not depart from the True Buddha. Just as a potter’s wheel produces hundreds of thousands of vessels, all of which are due to the characteristics of the actions performed by sentient beings, so too does the teaching return to the explanation of both specific and general characteristics.)

"In teaching the Dharma, the Buddha personally penetrates his own sphere and awakens to his own realm of realization. (This answers the eighth question. Furthermore, Mahāmati, foolish commoners give rise to the view of annihilation based on the cessation of the seven consciousnesses;
because they do not realize the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), they give rise to the view of permanence due to their own false imaginings.

Because they do not know the fundamental limit and because the wisdom of their own false imaginings has been extinguished, they attain liberation. (It is said that ordinary people see only the cessation of this body and do not see future births, and thus they give rise to the view of annihilation; because they do not realize that the storehouse consciousness flows and pours forth from moment to moment, they give rise to the view of permanence.)

Because the false discrimination of what is manifested from one’s own mind is called birth and death, there is no beginning; because the wisdom of false discrimination has been extinguished, it is called liberation. (This answers the ninth question.
Because the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the four stages of dwelling and the stage of ignorance have been severed, all faults are severed. (The New Commentary says:

Transformation Buddhas manifest various faults and evils through skillful means according to what is appropriate for sentient beings, but the true Tathāgata has completely severed the afflictions of the four stages of dwelling as well as the habit-energies of ignorance, and thus possesses no such faults. This answers the tenth question. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this, [spoke the following verse].
He spoke this verse in accordance with the meaning:

"The three vehicles are also not vehicles (for the purpose of establishing the One Vehicle); the Tathāgata does not perish, and all Buddhas bestow their predictions (the true meaning being that there is no nirvāṇa for Buddhas, as they all receive the prediction of becoming Tathāgatas);

he speaks of being free from all faults and evils" (the note says: the Buddha predicts that those of the two vehicles will become Buddhas, causing them to leave behind the faults and evils of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
In order to encourage those of inferior capacity toward various uninterrupted wisdoms and nirvana without remainder, [the Buddha] speaks with intentional concealment.

(That is to say, desiring that they achieve ultimate omniscience, sever the cognitive obstructions, and realize the Buddha’s great parinirvāṇa without remainder, he thus provides such concealed and secret teachings.
The wisdom arising from all Buddhas is precisely the analytical exposition of the various vehicles; these vehicles are not [truly] vehicles, for they are not nirvana.

Although the Tathāgata, arising from his compassion and wisdom, expounds these various paths for the sake of sentient beings, they are in reality contained within the One Vehicle; thus it is said that "the various vehicles are not truly vehicles.

Yet those Śrāvakas, calculating their own attainment of *nirvāṇa*, claim it to be Buddhahood, which is not true *nirvāṇa*. Desire, form, existence, and views—these are called the four abodes (*catasraḥ pṛthivīsthānāni*). [The note says:

the four abodes are the abode of all views, the abode of desire-attachment, the abode of form-attachment, and the abode of existence-attachment. They are what arises from the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the dwelling place of the mind (*manas*), and the house of consciousness. (New Explanation)

It is said that the birth-and-death of the triple world, as well as the afflictions of view, thought, and ignorance, are all the mind, mentation, and consciousness of sentient beings, which mutually serve as causes for one another, manifesting through habitual perfuming. The eight consciousnesses constitute the abode of the seventh mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
[Some] speak of the cessation and extinction of the mental faculty and the visual consciousness, etc., as impermanence, or they hold the view of *nirvāṇa* and speak of it as permanence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati asked in verse:
"Regarding those bodhisattvas who are resolutely seeking the Buddha-way, how should they regard alcohol, meat, and onions as food?
We pray that the Unsurpassed Honored One will, out of compassion, explain this for us—how these things are foul and impure, yet objects of craving for the foolish."
It is said that tigers and wolves delight in such things; how then can they be eaten? To eat them gives rise to various faults, while not eating them is a source of merit and goodness.

I only pray that you will explain for me the transgressions and blessings of eating and not eating. (Note: When the Tathāgata was preaching the Dharma within the palace of the King of Ghosts, the yakṣas and others thought that mealtime was approaching and that they could not eat unless there was meat.
Mahāmati, wishing to cause these ghosts to give rise to a compassionate heart, therefore requested the Tathāgata to speak on the merits and evils of eating meat and abstaining from eating meat.)
Having spoken these verses, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I pray that the World-Honored One will explain for us the merits and faults of eating and not eating meat. For myself and all other bodhisattvas, as well as for those sentient beings in the present and future who have various cravings for meat, may you distinguish and expound the Dharma so that those beings may turn toward one another with hearts of loving-kindness."

Having attained the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*), each dwells in their respective stage (*bhūmi*—Śikṣānanda says "the stage of a bodhisattva"), pure and clear, swiftly attaining ultimate, unsurpassed *bodhi*.
Having brought rest to their own stages as śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas (Śikṣānanda says "or temporarily resting in the stages of the two vehicles"), they also quickly achieve unsurpassed *bodhi*.

[The New Commentary states: "Worldly sentient beings revolve in the wheel of birth and death, bound by a continuous chain of enmity; falling into the various evil destinies and undergoing great suffering and affliction, all is due to eating."

Meat leads to mutual slaughter and the increase of afflictions, preventing one from attaining liberation. Those who can renounce the flavor of meat to seek the flavor of the Dharma, who face one another with a compassionate heart, and who practice with purity, clarity, and according to reality, shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Even among the various non-Buddhists who follow evil and heterodox doctrines—those with false views who cling to the perversions of eternalism and nihilism—there are prohibitions that do not permit the eating of meat;
how much more so for the Tathāgata, the protector of the world, who has perfected the True Dharma, yet would eat meat? This is impossible.
[Yaśomitra says: "Lokāyata" refers to various non-Buddhists such as the Lokāyatas who give rise to views of existence and non-existence and cling to the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism;

since they still have prohibitions that do not permit the eating of meat, how much less would the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—the Great Compassionate One who nurtures all beings and is the refuge of the world—permit himself or others to eat meat? The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "Excellent, excellent!
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall speak for your sake. Mahāmati replied to the Buddha: "Yes, I shall receive [your teaching]."
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There are immeasurable causes and conditions for which one should not eat meat; however, I shall now briefly explain them for you.
That is to say, all sentient beings have, from the very beginning, been related to one another through a succession of causes and conditions as parents, children, brothers, and so forth.

Because they have always been our kin, one should not eat their flesh. (Śikṣānanda says: All sentient beings, since time immemorial, have revolved incessantly within the cycle of birth and death, such that there has never been one who has not been one's father, mother, or brother...")"

One’s younger brothers, sons, daughters, kinsmen, and even friends, loved ones, and servants are easily reborn as the bodies of birds, beasts, and so forth; how could one take them from among these to eat?
Because the meat of donkeys, mules, camels, foxes, dogs, oxen, horses, humans, and other animals is sold mixed together by butchers, one should not eat meat.
Because it grows from impure elements and odors, one should not eat meat. When sentient beings smell its odor, they all become terrified, just like the outcaste *caṇḍālas*.

Furthermore, because dogs such as the *caṇḍāla* (also called *caṇḍāla*, translated here as "butcher") and the *taṃba* (translated here as "dog-eater," who are also hunters) see [meat] with loathing and fear and bark at it in packs, one should not eat meat. Moreover, because it prevents the arising of a compassionate mind in practitioners, one should not eat meat.
Finally, because it is what the ignorant and foolish crave, being foul-smelling, impure, and lacking a good reputation, one should not eat meat.

One should not eat meat because it prevents the success of various mantras and incantations; one should not eat meat because those who kill living beings perceive the form and give rise to consciousness, becoming deeply attached to its flavor;
one should not eat meat because those who eat it are abandoned by the devas;
one should not eat meat because it causes foul breath from the mouth; one should not eat meat because it results in many evil dreams; [and] because of solitude...
Because tigers and wolves in the forests will smell the scent [of meat], one should not eat meat. Because it causes one’s eating and drinking to lack moderation, one should not eat meat.
Because it prevents practitioners from developing a sense of revulsion [toward worldly things], one should not eat meat.

I have often said that whatever food or drink one consumes, one should regard it as the flesh of one's own child or as taking medicine; therefore, one should not eat meat. Those who permit the eating of meat [are at fault].
"It is impossible [that meat-eating leads to liberation]. Furthermore, Mahāmati, in the past there was a king named Siṃhasaudāsa who ate various kinds of meat until he eventually ate human beings.
His ministers and subjects could no longer endure this and plotted rebellion; they cut off his stipends because such are the faults of one who eats meat.
Therefore, Mahāmati, one should not eat meat. Furthermore, Mahāmati, all those who kill [beings] act for..."
For the sake of profit, they slaughter, butcher, and trade; those deluded beings who eat meat use money as a net to capture various meats (meaning that "profit" is equivalent to a "net";

Dharmaruci said: "Therefore, the buyer is no different from the killer"). Those who take life—whether by means of wealth or by hooks and nets—kill and slaughter various beings of the air, water, and land for the purpose of butchering, trading, and seeking profit.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) likewise does not exist without teaching, seeking, or imagining; yet there are fish and meat. For this reason, one should not eat meat.
(Regarding the meat of the world, there is none that can be obtained without killing. Even if one obtains it without teaching, seeking, or imagining, it must have originated from killing;
therefore, one should not eat it. Mahāmati, at times I have spoken of prohibiting five kinds of meat, or restricted ten kinds; now, in this sutra, in every respect and in all ways, [I prohibit them].

At all times, one must exclude and sever all expedient means; [for while] various sūtras permit five kinds or ten kinds [of meat] because they cannot suddenly cause sentient beings to cease eating flesh—there still being permitted exceptions as expedient means—this present sūtra severs all of them entirely, serving as the final, pure, and clear instruction.

As for the "ten kinds," these refer to human, snake, elephant, horse, dragon, fox, pig, dog, lion, and macaque. As for the "five kinds," these refer to that which is not seen, not heard, not suspected, that which is left by birds, and that which dies of itself.
O Mahāmati, even a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has nothing to eat, much less would he eat [meat].

Regarding fish and meat, the Tathāgata did not even instruct others to eat them; since he takes only the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna as his sustenance, he consumes nothing at all—how much less would he instruct others to eat meat, whether pure or impure?
Because he is preceded by great compassion, he regards all sentient beings as if they were his only son;

therefore, he does not permit the eating of a son's flesh. Among the five precepts, the abstention from killing is primary; among the five constant virtues, benevolence (*ren*) is foremost. To stay far from the kitchen, to fish without using nets, to hunt without shooting at nesting birds, and not to kill embryos or cause premature death—all these are the beginnings of benevolence.

To fail to refrain from eating meat—our Buddha, the World-Honored One, regards the consumption of sentient beings as the foremost precept, viewing even the smallest insects and crawling creatures no differently than his own infant children—to claim that one can remain without this restraint and yet still possess the seeds of compassion and wisdom is to be far removed from the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Having formerly been all one's own kinsmen, they are base, filthy, impure, and produced amidst various impurities;

the mere scent of them inspires total terror (this verse summarizes the preceding passage on the foul odors of the parts of the body). One who practices the path should always remain far removed from all meats, scallions, leeks, garlic, and various intoxicating liquors that lead to heedlessness;
likewise, one should always avoid sesame oil and beds with perforated slats, for those [things]...

Within it, tiny insects are utterly terrified. (The new commentary states that from this point onward, the various verses mostly demonstrate its faults so as to cause one to distance oneself from it; there are few verses and mostly prose. Regarding the phrase "leaving off sesame oil":

according to foreign customs, they pound sesame until worms are produced and then press them to extract the juice, believing it increases fatness. How can such things be eaten? Furthermore, beds with cracks and crevices often harbor swarms of insects;

one must never sit or lie upon them, for the insects become terrified during the act of sitting or lying down. Food gives rise to negligence (*pramāda*); negligence gives rise to discursive thoughts (*vitarka*)—the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* reads "perverse thoughts" (*mithyā-vitarka*). From these thoughts...
Because the arising of desire occurs through eating, one should not eat. From eating arises desire; desire causes the mind to become deluded and intoxicated.
This intoxication increases craving, and one is not liberated from birth and death. (The New Commentary says: Drinking alcohol, craving meat, and so forth cause the mind to be largely negligent;

all various evil thoughts and observations follow and grow. Therefore, one revolves in the wheel of birth and death and cannot escape it. To kill sentient beings for profit and to ensnare meat with wealth—both of these are evil.
One who dies through such karma will fall into the Raurava Hell. If there is no instruction, perception, or request [for the meat], then those three types of "pure meat" do not exist;

since they do not exist without a cause, one should not eat them. (The New Commentary states: "Since there is no instruction, perception, or request, the three types of pure meat do not exist. As for all meats, they are obtained by killing living beings; how could they be eaten?
Because of this, all those practitioners should completely distance themselves from it. All the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, [prohibit it].

They all rebuke one another and, after devouring each other until death, fall into the class of tigers, wolves, and the like—beings born into foul, filthy, and loathsome conditions who are perpetually ignorant.
They are mostly born among the *caṇḍālas*, hunters, *tāmba* castes, or as *ḍākinīs* (Liu Zhi says "rākṣasī women";
Xuanzang says "rākṣasa women"), as well as among various flesh-eating rākṣasas, cats, wildcats, and so forth; they are found everywhere in such states.

Those born in the intermediate state (referring to those who, though by nature free from the stench of raw meat, mostly fall into this category), Baddhasimha, Mahāmegha, Aṅgulimāla (Baddhasimha was translated as Xiàngyè [Elephant-Axilla] by Liu Zhì, while Paramārtha translated it as Xiàngxiè [Elephant-Ribs];

Aṅgulimāla was translated as Yǎngjué móluó by Paramārtha, while the actual meaning is Yǎngjué mó [Finger-Garlander], both being names of sūtras), and this Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra—I have all prohibited the eating of meat.
It is censured by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas; to eat it and yet feel no shame is a transgression.

How shameful that one is constantly born into delusion and darkness! Although I have previously declared that all conceptualizations regarding meat—whether seen, heard, or suspected—are severed, because they do not realize this, they are born into places where meat is consumed. (The Buddha has previously taught that meat which is killed for one’s sake through seeing, hearing, or suspecting should not be eaten;

yet those foolish people do not understand the Tathāgata’s regulations on pure and impure meat, and having already been told to cease [eating it], they give rise to various conceptualizations regarding the provisional means of permission and prohibition, claiming that pure meat is permitted to be eaten. This is like the obstacle caused by the fault of greed.
The Noble Ones’ liberation is such that wine, meat, onions, leeks, and garlic all constitute obstacles to the Path of the Noble Ones.

Sentient beings of future generations will be deluded regarding meat and will say, "This is pure and without fault; the Buddha permitted us to eat it. One should eat with the thought that it is like taking medicine (Śīla says:
even pure food is like medicine), and as if eating the flesh of one's own child. Being content and giving rise to revulsion, one should practice the alms-round for food.

(Regarding the instruction to "regard food as if taking medicine" and "regard food as the flesh of one's own son," this is because those foolish people falsely claim that there is no fault in eating the five kinds of pure meat; thus, the preceding text is cited to refute them. The Tathāgata’s intention is this:

if one should maintain thoughts such as taking medicine even when receiving pure food and drink, how much more so when it comes to hearing that one may eat the five kinds of pure meat? This is to admonish all bhikṣus to practice begging for food with contentment and weary detachment, in order to sever greedy attachment.

For those who abide in a mind of loving-kindness, I say they should always feel weary detachment toward tigers, wolves, and other evil beasts, and may constantly dwell and move together with them. If [they] eat various...
All sentient beings who possess flesh and blood are terrified by this; therefore, the practitioner should cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and not eat meat.

Eating meat lacks compassion and wisdom, and it forever turns one away from true liberation and violates the outward signs of the noble ones. For these reasons, one should not eat it. (The new commentary states:

"Turning away from true liberation" means that due to the absence of compassion and wisdom, one fails to benefit oneself or others and violates the noble ones' ceremonial standards for protecting living beings. One may thus be born into the lineage of the Brahmins and all those who practice...

One who practices this path will be reborn into a wealthy and noble family; this is due to abstaining from meat. (The previous conclusion stated that those who eat meat receive retribution in defiled places—namely, among the Caṇḍālas, Taṃbas, cats, and wildcats.

This conclusion states that those who abstain from meat receive retribution in the families of sages and saints—namely, the pure lineages of the Three Vehicles and the Tathāgatas. "Wealthy" means that the wealth of Dharma is inexhaustible; "noble" means that their status as a sage is unsurpassed. This is how the Tathāgata takes the Dharma-realm as his home.

It is precisely because of abstaining from meat that one can purify the karma of body, speech, and mind, providing the support for the awakening of the noble wisdom of self-realization, gradually ascending through the stages until reaching the fruit of Buddhahood. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: [...]*Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: [text omitted]* *Note: The bracketed section indicates the omission of the specific citation from the Śūraṅgama Sūtra as per the instruction to provide only the translation.*

"You all should know that even if these meat-eaters attain a mental opening that resembles samādhi, they are all great rākṣasas; when their retribution ends, they will inevitably sink into the bitter sea of birth and death. Those with knowledge should not fail to take this as a painful warning and establish it as a precept."
